item.title: Analysts fear rush to impeach Trump henchmen is a trap
item.description:
The impeachment push against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is not itself the trap. The trap is allowing a likely doomed removal vote to substitute for the harder work of exposing what the Trump administration has done, who benefited and which institutions enabled it. As Democrats prepared to take control of Congress in January, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries declared himself a “hard yes” on impeaching Hegseth. But removal would still require 11 Republican senators to join the Democrats’ reported 56-seat Senate majority—an outcome The New Yorker’s Ruth Marcus warned was unlikely.

That arithmetic matters because impeachment can establish responsibility, but it can also become political theater when lawmakers know the Senate will acquit and have no broader strategy for accountability. Hegseth and President Donald Trump have already demonstrated how they would stage such a defeat: as vindication, not merely survival.

Acquittal is not exoneration

On the morning of the impeachment vote described by Marcus, Hegseth held his first news conference in six months and recast an effort to remove him as an attack on Trump and the military. “This is not patriotism—this is sabotage,” he said. After the vote, a spokesman claimed “total victory,” while Trump proclaimed the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”

That language performs a familiar bait-and-switch. A failed removal effort would establish only that the necessary Senate supermajority did not exist. It would not resolve the underlying allegations, defend Hegseth’s record or transform partisan protection into factual exoneration. Yet the administration’s message deliberately collapsed those distinctions, wrapping one official’s political survival in the prestige of the armed forces.

The troops did not cast the congressional votes. Hegseth held office through presidential appointment and Senate confirmation, and senators would determine whether he remained there. Casting scrutiny of the defense secretary as sabotage against service members redirects attention from the officials exercising power toward the institution they invoke as a shield.

Marcus also noted that Trump’s emphatic public loyalty can expire quickly, particularly for an official associated with an unpopular war. Hegseth’s usefulness to Trump may therefore depend less on any durable presidential commitment than on whether he can remain an effective symbol of grievance.

The record extends beyond one Cabinet official

Marcus argued that the incoming Democratic majority would inherit an essential oversight task: documenting the administration’s reported cruelty, incompetence and corruption, then determining how to prevent their recurrence. The matters she identified included alleged pay-to-play pardons, no-bid contracts and the use of government service to accumulate personal wealth, as well as the administration’s treatment of immigrant detainees and its dealings with Nvidia.

Those subjects call for records, testimony and sustained investigation. An impeachment proceeding could serve that work if it were built around establishing facts and assigning responsibility. It could also consume congressional attention while giving Trump a single, emotionally useful spectacle: another prosecution he can portray as persecution.

That is the strategic distinction Marcus’s warning exposes. Accountability asks what happened, under whose authority and with what consequences. Political payback begins and ends with punishing an antagonist. Trump benefits when Democrats allow him to erase the former by accusing them of the latter.

Voters’ financial concerns do not excuse misconduct, and Congress is capable of legislating while conducting oversight. But Democrats would still have to show that their use of institutional power materially serves the public. A procession of failed impeachment votes—especially another attempt against Trump—could let the administration turn congressional scrutiny into a recurring victimhood pageant while the underlying conduct remains insufficiently examined.

Hegseth’s personnel purge demands scrutiny

The strongest case for sustained investigation lies in what Hegseth has reportedly done with the Pentagon, not in how unpopular he has become inside it. Michael N. Schmitt, a New York University law professor, wrote in Just Security that since January 2025 the Defense Department had removed, replaced or pushed into early retirement an extraordinary group of senior officers with extensive operational experience.

According to Schmitt, those affected included the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the chief of naval operations, the Army chief of staff and the head of U.S. Cyber Command, who also directs the National Security Agency. Gen. Christopher Donahue was subsequently forced out as commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa and as NATO’s commander of Allied Land Command. Schmitt described Donahue as among the most decorated and combat-experienced officers of his generation.

Public explanations, Schmitt wrote, were sparse and generally vague when offered at all. That does not by itself establish an unlawful motive. It does make congressional examination necessary. Removing that concentration of military leadership affects continuity, expertise and command at the Pentagon, in cyber operations and across NATO. Congress should establish who ordered each change, what reasons were documented, whether established procedures were followed and what operational costs resulted.

An impeachment vote cannot answer those questions merely by occurring. Nor would an acquittal make them disappear. If Democrats reduce Hegseth’s record to a removal effort they cannot complete, they risk handing him a propaganda victory while leaving his exercise of power inadequately exposed.

The choice is not between accountability and attention to voters’ material lives. It is between accountability built to produce facts and consequences, and a symbolic confrontation whose most predictable result is another false declaration of “total victory.”

item.title: It’s 2026 —and Trump’s FBI is still interrogating Georgia over 2020
item.description:
Six years after Donald Trump lost Georgia, his administration is still using federal law enforcement to pursue the fraud narrative that failed to survive the state’s audits, recounts, court proceedings and Republican-led investigations. On Friday, two FBI agents and two federal prosecutors questioned former Fulton County elections director Richard Barron for more than two hours in Atlanta, according to The New York Times. No criminal charges have emerged from the investigation.

This is not merely Trump refusing to move on. The federal government has placed personnel, investigative authority and public money behind another attempt to validate his grievance. One of the officials questioning Barron was Dan Bishop, a former Republican congressman who voted against certifying Trump’s 2020 defeat and whom the Justice Department appointed its top election-fraud prosecutor in April.

An election official questioned over rejected theories

Barron oversaw Fulton County’s vote count in 2020 and left the job in 2022. He told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution that agents approached him last week and that he agreed to be interviewed at his lawyer’s office without a subpoena. Prosecutors have indicated that they want another meeting.

Their questions returned to allegations promoted by conservative activists Garland Favorito and Kevin Moncla. Barron said Bishop specifically mentioned Favorito. Moncla, cited in an affidavit supporting an FBI ballot raid, had submitted a 263-page report alleging “fictitious ballots” and fabricated tabulator poll tapes in Fulton County.

Asked by the AJC whether the activists’ theories were reasonable, Barron rejected them. He said investigators concentrated on the 2020 machine recount and minor administrative matters unrelated to the result. Barron maintained that neither he nor his staff committed crimes.

That distinction matters. Administrative irregularities are not proof of fraudulent votes, much less evidence that an election result was stolen. Treating routine details as possible fragments of a vast crime allows investigators to keep the premise alive even when the conclusion has repeatedly failed.

Trump’s grievance now has federal staffing

The inquiry extends well beyond one voluntary interview. Federal authorities have contacted other current and former Fulton County election workers, The New York Times reported. In January, agents raided a county election warehouse for ballots in an operation attended by Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard. FBI special agent Hugh Raymond Evans, who signed the affidavit supporting that raid, also participated in Barron’s questioning.

FBI Director Kash Patel separately assigned hundreds of intelligence analysts to examine records from the 2020 election, according to an internal bureau directive described in the reporting. The scale reveals the power imbalance at the center of the story: former local election employees must retain lawyers and answer federal investigators, while the president’s disproven account of his own defeat receives the resources of the Justice Department, the FBI and the intelligence apparatus.

Bishop’s role makes the institutional choice especially stark. He did not approach the matter as a detached figure with no recorded position on the election. As a member of Congress, he voted to reject certification of the defeat that his office is now helping investigate. That history does not establish misconduct in the present inquiry, but it does make claims of neutral fact-finding difficult to separate from the political project that preceded his appointment.

Georgia already counted the votes three times

Georgia’s result was confirmed through three tallies, including a hand audit of the paper ballots. State and federal courts addressed challenges, while investigations led by Republican state officials found no basis to overturn the outcome, according to the Georgia secretary of state’s office.

The renewed federal effort therefore does not begin with an unresolved count. It begins after the count was checked repeatedly and after the proposed alternatives failed. The government is not filling an obvious evidentiary void; it is reopening the search under officials selected by the man who benefits politically from portraying his loss as theft.

Fulton County Commission Chairman Robb Pitts told the AJC that he remains confident the county conducted a secure and fair election. He said the current and former officials approached by agents would continue to reinforce that conclusion.

Perhaps they will. But the investigation already imposes a consequence even without charges: it subjects election workers to recurring federal scrutiny while laundering a defeated political claim through the prestige and coercive capacity of law enforcement. After three counts and years of failed challenges, the unanswered question is no longer whether Georgia counted its ballots. It is how long Trump’s administration intends to make public servants defend that count against the president’s refusal to accept it.

item.title: Top Republican reduced to 'begging' as party falls apart
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson, facing the end of Republican control after a crushing midterm defeat, has resorted to pleading with his own members to attend work. Absences during the lame-duck session have left the House GOP unable to pass legislation on party-line votes, according to AlterNet’s account of reporting by MS NOW columnist Zeeshan Aleem. The immediate failure is procedural; the political failure is more revealing. Republicans still hold the chamber’s governing power, but some are no longer willing to perform even the basic labor required to use it.

A speaker without a working majority

“Barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term,” Johnson wrote in a letter to his conference. He told members that they had 44 days to remain engaged and advance additional Republican priorities before the next Congress.

The request was not for bipartisan negotiation, difficult committee work or an unforeseen emergency. Johnson was asking elected lawmakers to appear at the institution they still control. Poor attendance had already deprived Republicans of the votes needed to move party-line measures.

Johnson closed with an all-caps exhortation: “LET’S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!” Aleem compared the appeal to a coach attempting to rally a team losing by 40 points with two minutes remaining. The analogy captures Johnson’s predicament, but it also risks making institutional abandonment sound like a morale problem. Republican representatives are not exhausted volunteers. They retain salaries, offices, votes and public authority until their terms expire.

Johnson holds the speakership, but his leverage depends on members who have apparently decided that an election loss relieves them of present obligations. His letter exposes the limits of leadership inside a conference whose lawmakers can disable the House simply by staying away.

The absenteeism follows a record of meager work

A lame-duck Congress is ordinarily busy precisely because power is changing hands. Outgoing majorities race to complete unfinished business, incoming leaders prepare their agenda, and lawmakers confront spending measures needed to avoid a government shutdown. Yet MS NOW’s Hayes Brown described a House with must-pass bills remaining on its calendar but otherwise little apparent purpose.

The disengagement did not begin with the midterm result. Aleem cited Washington Post reporting that the House cast 362 votes in the first session of the current two-year Congress, the fewest in any first session this century. During 2017, when Republicans also controlled the House in Donald Trump’s first year as president, the chamber held roughly twice as many votes.

Pew Research Center found that, as of October, the current Congress had enacted the second-fewest laws of any Congress in the previous four decades. Only the preceding Congress enacted fewer, and that government was divided between a Republican House and a Democratic Senate. The present Republican record therefore cannot be explained merely by an opposition party blocking a unified agenda.

Those figures do not prove that every uncast vote or unenacted bill represents work that should have been done. Legislative volume is not the same thing as legislative merit. But paired with a governing majority unable to assemble its members for party-line votes, the record undermines any attempt to describe the current paralysis as an abrupt case of post-election fatigue.

Defeat did not end Republican responsibility

Aleem attributed the collapse in morale to what he called the party’s largest electoral blowout in roughly half a century. That defeat explains why Republicans may see little political reward in their remaining weeks. It does not transfer responsibility for the House to the incoming majority ahead of schedule.

The distribution of power remains clear: Republicans control the chamber during the lame-duck session, Johnson remains speaker, and Republican absences are preventing the conference from exercising that authority. Blaming the congressional calendar, low morale or generic “senioritis” would obscure the decision at the center of the story. Lawmakers with unfinished terms are choosing not to provide the attendance their own leader says he needs.

Johnson’s begging is humiliating because it makes the arrangement plain. The speaker can demand loyalty, invoke the full two-year mandate and promise one last burst of conservative lawmaking. He cannot compel members of his own defeated majority to show up. Until power formally changes hands, however, their refusal does not leave Washington without responsible actors. It identifies them.

item.title: 'Rot at the top' surreptitiously siphoning your money into billionaire pockets
item.description:
Robert Reich’s charge is that the “rot at the top” operates through government decisions that transfer public wealth, regulatory favors and market power to politically connected billionaires. But his AlterNet column does not establish that every favor he lists was purchased. It assembles a sprawling set of reported events and allegations, then asks whether money, investments and personal interests explain official conduct. The distinction matters: the conflicts demand investigation precisely because questions of corruption cannot be settled by insinuation alone.

The institutional structure Reich describes is less ambiguous. A small group of executives commands companies that increasingly shape economic growth, retirement accounts, military procurement, communications and access to information. The Trump administration and Republican-controlled Congress, meanwhile, possess the authority to regulate those companies, award contracts, approve technology exports, grant tariff exemptions and direct public subsidies. That is the arrangement under scrutiny: billionaires seeking government decisions from officials whose political operations, personal holdings or family businesses may benefit from the same corporate class.

An AI boom built on concentrated power

Reich places artificial intelligence at the center of the story. He reports that AI-related companies account for more than one-third of the value of shares traded on the U.S. stock market and nearly half of economic growth during the previous two years. He identifies Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk as members of a tiny executive circle whose decisions now carry economy-wide consequences.

According to Reich, Huang resigned after revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese spy who helped China acquire Nvidia chips. He also alleges that Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had known for at least six months that Huang was sending advanced chips to China and failed to intervene. Reich asks whether that inaction was connected to Nvidia’s reported $25 million contribution to Trump’s ballroom, Trump’s reported ownership of $12.5 million in Nvidia shares or money being made by Lutnick’s children. Those are presented as questions, not demonstrated explanations.

The market events Reich recounts show why the underlying concentration matters even before any corrupt bargain is proved. Anthropic reportedly reached a $2 trillion valuation after a public offering, adding an estimated $20 billion to the wealth of each of its seven co-founders. Early investors sold more than $25 billion in shares when trading began. Reich characterizes that arrangement as resembling a Ponzi scheme and asks why regulators permitted such an early exit.

A day later, he reports, Anthropic’s market value fell 9 percent, wiping out $109 billion. Nvidia dropped 20 percent, the Nasdaq surrendered its 2026 gains and more than $4 trillion in market value disappeared overall. Reich does not establish that early investors possessed improper knowledge or that AI companies cannot service their debt; he raises both possibilities. But the exposure is real within his account: Americans do not need to own individual technology stocks to absorb losses when their 401(k)s track indices dominated by Big Tech.

That is the political trick embedded in financial concentration. The windfall belongs overwhelmingly to founders and early investors; the downside travels through retirement funds and the broader economy. Regulators decide the terms under which insiders may cash out, yet ordinary workers are expected to treat the resulting losses as impersonal market weather.

Public authority, private beneficiaries

Reich’s case extends beyond AI. He points to a series of federal decisions benefiting industries and billionaires with political or financial relationships to Trump and Republicans.

He asks why Elon Musk put a reported $500 million into the 2026 midterms, suggesting that Musk’s satellite position, defense contracts and the personal data Reich alleges DOGE obtained could provide motives for seeking continued influence. He similarly questions whether Jeff Bezos’s position in online retail has gone unchallenged because Bezos gave Melania Trump a multimillion-dollar gift and restrained The Washington Post from editorializing against Trump.

Reich also says Larry and David Ellison were allowed to acquire CBS and CNN after actions that benefited Trump: removing Stephen Colbert, paying $16 million to settle Trump’s lawsuit and agreeing to soften “60 Minutes.” The column presents those events as grounds for inquiry, not proof that regulators traded approval for favorable treatment.

The same pattern appears in energy policy. Reich reports that Big Oil gained expanded access to public lands and $190 billion in subsidies, tax reductions and loopholes after spending $450 million supporting Trump and Republicans in 2024 and another $182 million in the 2026 midterms. Whatever the causal explanation, elected officials made the policies; the industry receiving the benefits also spent heavily to help keep those officials in power. Describing that merely as ideological agreement would erase the material exchange surrounding the policymaking process.

Other questions concern the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s termination of an inquiry into Trump’s memecoin and what its largest buyers receive beyond White House gala dinners. Here the conflict is unusually direct: an administration agency reportedly abandoned scrutiny of a financial product associated with the president while top purchasers gained access to presidential events.

Foreign policy and the family business

Reich argues that the same entanglement reaches national-security decisions. He asks whether Trump’s posture toward Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin is connected to alleged efforts by China and Russia to influence the 2024 election for Trump and the 2026 midterms for Republicans. The column does not establish either a transactional agreement or Trump’s motive, so those remain attributed allegations and questions.

More concrete within Reich’s account are technology-transfer decisions. Trump approved sales of F-35 fighters to Saudi Arabia and Nvidia chips to the United Arab Emirates despite concerns among some U.S. officials that sensitive technology could reach China. Reich asks whether Saudi and Emirati investments in businesses belonging to Trump and his family affected those approvals. The reported overlap creates an obvious conflict requiring scrutiny, but it does not by itself prove that the investments determined policy.

Reich also contrasts Trump’s protection of Flávio Bolsonaro, who faces corruption investigations in Brazil, with the administration’s return of asylum seekers to countries where they may face danger. He asks whether Bolsonaro’s use of private money to advance a shared political agenda with Trump helps explain the difference. The contrast exposes how executive discretion can become selective: politically aligned elites may receive refuge while vulnerable migrants encounter the coercive edge of the state.

Oversight cannot stop at rhetorical questions

Reich calls on Democrats taking oversight power on January 3 to investigate the identities of Anthropic’s early sellers, Trump’s memecoin buyers, the financial institutions involved in federal purchases of stakes in Intel, critical-minerals producers and L3Harris’s missile business, and any holdings that Trump, Lutnick, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, their families or Trump’s billionaire donors may have in those companies.

He also wants scrutiny of Apple’s exemption from Trump’s China tariffs. That example captures the governing hierarchy running through the column: tariffs are sold as a national policy, but the executive can decide which powerful corporation escapes them. The public receives the doctrine; connected companies negotiate the exceptions.

Reich’s weakest move is to compress every allegation, market decline, regulatory decision and foreign-policy dispute into a single declaration that Trump’s corruption has “infected” the private economy. His column supplies a basis for aggressive oversight, not a completed corruption case covering every named actor. Treating suspicions as verdicts would make the inquiry easier to dismiss.

The stronger indictment lies in what is already visible: officials control exemptions, subsidies, contracts, export approvals and enforcement decisions while wealthy beneficiaries finance politics and, in some cases Reich identifies, maintain financial relationships with the president or his family. Democrats will have the power to subpoena records and compel testimony. If they settle for campaign language about billionaires without tracing who received which benefit, who approved it and who profited, they will preserve the very opacity Reich is challenging.

item.title: Critics bristle as Trump deploys 'secret weapon' against colleges
item.description:
The Trump administration has finalized regulations that turn college accreditation into a federal instrument for policing campus ideology. Beginning in the 2027–28 academic year, accreditors must assess whether colleges promote “intellectual diversity and the free exchange of ideas”—a vague political standard attached to institutions’ access to more than $100 billion a year in federal student loans and Pell Grants.

Donald Trump advertised the mechanism during his 2023 presidential campaign. Calling universities captive to the “radical left,” he said the accreditation system would be his “secret weapon” for reclaiming them. The new rules convert that campaign promise into administrative power: Washington can pressure the organizations that determine whether colleges remain eligible for federal aid, while presenting the intervention as a defense of free inquiry.

Federal funding becomes ideological leverage

Accreditation is not an honorary seal. It is the gateway through which colleges gain access to federal student aid, making adverse decisions potentially devastating to institutions and their students. Requiring accreditors to enforce an undefined conception of intellectual diversity therefore gives the Education Department influence far beyond its direct regulatory reach.

“This rule opens up an entirely new avenue for the federal government to exert influence over institutional policies and practices that have historically been the purview of colleges and universities themselves,” Antoinette Flores, vice president for policy and research at the Council for Higher Education Accreditation, told The Hill.

The danger lies partly in the standard’s elasticity. “Free exchange” can sound unobjectionable while leaving unanswered who decides whether a curriculum, hiring policy or campus dispute satisfies it. When the executive branch controls federal recognition of accreditors, ambiguity does not produce neutrality. It gives officials room to reward compliant interpretations and punish disfavored ones.

Education Department officials deny that they are imposing a federal speech code. They argue that accreditors have strayed from core academic standards and cite survey findings suggesting that most college students feel pressure to profess progressive views to succeed academically. But evidence of student self-censorship does not itself establish that executive oversight of accreditation is a remedy—or that the administration will apply its new criteria consistently rather than politically.

Columbia showed how the pressure campaign works

The administration has already demonstrated its willingness to use accreditation disputes against a prominent institutional target. According to CBS News, it formally told the Middle States Commission on Higher Education that Columbia University had violated federal antidiscrimination law and urged the accreditor to strip the university’s accreditation. The commission declined.

That episode matters because it reveals the chain of power behind the administration’s language about open inquiry. The White House does not need to rewrite a syllabus itself. It can accuse a university of violating federal requirements, pressure the accreditor responsible for its institutional standing and leave the school facing the possible loss of access to federal aid.

The accreditor’s refusal in Columbia’s case shows that such pressure does not guarantee obedience. The finalized regulations, however, create another basis on which federal officials can scrutinize accreditors’ judgments. An administration that openly identified accreditation as a weapon is now expanding the conditions under which that weapon can be invoked.

Measurable outcomes bundled with political discretion

The overhaul also requires accreditors to evaluate quantitative measures including graduation, retention and post-graduation earnings. Those provisions give the package a technocratic surface: colleges will ostensibly face scrutiny for what students achieve, not merely for political controversies.

But measurable outcomes and ideological supervision are different forms of regulation. Graduation rates can be counted. “Intellectual diversity” cannot be assessed without contestable judgments about which ideas deserve representation, what constitutes pressure and when institutional criticism becomes suppression. Bundling those mandates does not make the ideological test objective.

The rules also reduce barriers for new accrediting organizations seeking federal recognition. Conservatives have long sought to weaken the established accrediting associations and create alternative routes for colleges. In practice, easier recognition could foster competition; it could also cultivate accreditors more receptive to the administration’s political priorities. The reported rules establish the opening, not which new organizations will use it.

The administration’s misdirection is to cast concentrated federal leverage as liberation from concentrated academic power. Universities and traditional accreditors are powerful institutions and can enforce orthodoxies of their own. But the government is not merely another participant in a campus debate. It controls the recognition system tied to billions of dollars in student assistance.

Trump described that asymmetry accurately before his administration wrapped it in regulatory language: accreditation was the “secret weapon.” The secret was never what the administration intended to target. It was how easily coercion through federal funding could be marketed as freedom.

item.title: The clowns running the circus took a chainsaw to America —and can't fix it
item.description:
A cascade of technology failures disrupted aviation, banking, government communications, and consumer services in the same period, but no verified evidence has established either a coordinated cyberattack or a common cause. What the breakdowns did establish is more politically concrete: after Donald Trump’s administration cut federal technical capacity and installed inexperienced leadership, it could neither provide a comprehensive explanation for the failures nor present a documented plan for repairing one of the country’s most vulnerable systems.

The government’s inability to explain the cluster is not proof that its cuts caused it. It is evidence that an administration built around institutional demolition has weakened its own ability to diagnose a crisis—and then treated that weakness as somebody else’s problem.

A cascade without an established common cause

The reported failures were extensive. Microsoft platforms went down, affecting more than 80 percent of its servers. The following day, an FAA communications outage grounded flights nationwide. United Airlines subsequently reported a separate failure involving its departure-information system.

Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank also lost online access to their accounts. Two days later, the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications system reportedly went offline, followed by disruptions to Apple services.

The timing invites scrutiny, but timing is not causation. No verified evidence cited by AlterNet establishes that the incidents were coordinated, resulted from a cyberattack, or shared a technical origin. Treating an extraordinary cluster as conclusive proof of sabotage would replace investigation with suspicion.

The responsible question is not whether coincidence feels plausible. It is whether the government can identify what failed, determine whether the incidents were connected, and protect essential infrastructure from the next disruption. On that test, the Trump administration has offered little reassurance.

Trump dismantled capacity, then dismissed the consequences

Trump, Elon Musk, and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought led a campaign to shrink federal agencies and remove professional staff. Musk’s DOGE operation cut personnel across FEMA, the Transportation Department, the FAA, the Commerce Department, and NOAA. The administration also placed national cybersecurity under a leader with no technical experience, according to AlterNet; that official was replaced during the week covered by the report.

Those decisions do not, by themselves, prove what caused any particular outage. They do identify who controlled the government’s capacity to prepare for failures and respond to them. Trump and his appointees did not inherit powerlessness. They exercised institutional power to eliminate expertise, narrow staffing, and subordinate technical administration to a political project of rapid contraction.

When asked about the simultaneous failures, Trump answered: “That’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

It was not fine for grounded passengers, locked-out bank customers, airlines, or businesses dependent on Microsoft’s systems. The airline losses were estimated in the billions, while global productivity losses attributed to the Microsoft outage were estimated at $16 billion and rising. Trump’s answer converted government accountability into weather: systems fail, life happens, nobody is responsible.

That is misdirection from the person with the most authority to demand answers.

The FAA explanation did not settle the dispute

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the FAA ground stop on a private contractor and a router problem during appearances on Sunday news programs. But he did not provide a convincing account of the remedy, and the explanation was disputed by air traffic controllers interviewed by a reporter.

All 60 controllers questioned reportedly rejected the administration’s account. Among their objections was the timing: the upgrades blamed for the failure would ordinarily be performed late at night, while the system crashed during a busy Friday workday.

Their disagreement does not independently establish another cause. It does mean the administration’s account cannot reasonably be treated as settled merely because Duffy repeated it on television. The dispute concerns people working inside the system challenging the political leadership responsible for explaining its failure.

Trump officials have floated no comprehensive account covering the wider cluster. Experts have suggested several possible causes, including the administration’s rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, but those remain theories in the reporting. The NSA had not announced a date for a detailed public explanation.

A vulnerable system and a rapidly expanding price tag

The FAA network had been identified as vulnerable before the outage. Congress appropriated modernization money in July 2025, when Republicans included $12.5 billion for air traffic control upgrades in their tax and spending law. Of that amount, $4.75 billion was designated for telecommunications infrastructure and systems.

That spending choice sat inside a broader law that, according to AlterNet, cut $930 billion from Medicaid and $285 billion from SNAP while delivering $4 trillion in tax reductions benefiting wealthy donors. The contrast matters: congressional Republicans found room to shift enormous resources upward while an essential aviation network remained exposed.

After the outage, Duffy used the system’s failure to press for substantially more money. He initially described the $12.5 billion appropriation as a down payment and said the FAA required an additional $30 billion, for roughly $42.5 billion in total modernization funding. Within a week of the November 13 ground stop, he sent a letter putting the estimate at $50.1 billion—about four times the administration’s previous $12.5 billion proposal.

A larger need may be legitimate. Duffy’s presentation did not demonstrate it. When he brought the request to Congress, he had no itemized project list, prompting one lawmaker to describe the proposal as a ransom demand without a plan.

Speed without a documented cost

The warning signs preceded the outage. A September Government Accountability Office report found that the FAA was emphasizing speed over cost control and the avoidance of disruption. It also found that projects were being scheduled at the same locations without optimizing work to reduce flight interruptions. The agency lacked a documented estimate of costs across the projects’ full life cycles.

The FAA and Transportation Department had already created an online modernization dashboard called “Modern Skies.” By late August, its tracker showed that only nine of 612 planned terminal radar systems had been deployed.

That gap between announced ambition and delivered infrastructure is the central governance failure in the story. The administration is asking Congress to multiply its modernization budget while lacking an itemized public plan and while federal auditors have already identified basic deficiencies in cost estimation and project coordination.

One week after only the third nationwide flight grounding in U.S. history, the administration still had not supplied a full explanation for the FAA failure. Nor had it established whether that outage had any relationship to the Microsoft, bank, United Airlines, NSA, or Apple disruptions.

The strongest indictment is not the unproven theory that Trump’s cuts caused every crash. It is the documented sequence: his administration stripped expertise from agencies responsible for complex systems, failed to credibly explain a major breakdown, presented a sharply inflated repair bill without an itemized plan, and then had the president tell the country that such failures are simply “life.”

item.title: Lame-duck Lauren Boebert torpedoes GOP leaders on the way out the door
item.description:
Lauren Boebert’s answer was blunt: She skipped House votes because Republican leaders told her she was not needed and, in her judgment, had scheduled nothing consequential enough to justify her presence. The outgoing Colorado congresswoman made that defense in a late-Friday video after Speaker Mike Johnson criticized absentee lawmakers and warned that missing members could obstruct the remainder of President Donald Trump’s agenda, including supplemental funding for the war in Iran. Boebert did not merely reject Johnson’s complaint. She accused her own party’s leadership of manufacturing “fake outrage” to conceal an empty legislative schedule.

Johnson’s warning meets the whip operation

Johnson had pointed to 14 absences on one tally as evidence that departing lawmakers were abandoning their responsibilities during the lame-duck session. That framing placed responsibility on individual members: The agenda was supposedly in jeopardy because lawmakers had stopped showing up.

Boebert’s account, reported by The Daily Beast and summarized by AlterNet, complicates that story. She said she consulted Republican whips before missing Tuesday’s proceedings and was told her vote was unnecessary. “I didn’t miss anything of consequence,” she said.

Neither Johnson’s office nor the House GOP whip operation had publicly answered that assertion at the time of the report. If Boebert’s account is accurate, leadership’s complaint was not simply about an undisciplined rank and file. The party’s own vote-counting apparatus approved at least one of the absences that Johnson later treated as evidence of institutional neglect.

That distinction matters because House leaders control the schedule and party whips decide which absences threaten passage. Johnson invoked the authority of the speakership to shame missing members, but Boebert responded with the mechanics of that same leadership structure: Republicans knew she would be gone and allegedly told her it would not matter.

A U-Haul was more compelling than the floor

Boebert said she returned to Washington for a single noon vote Wednesday, only to find it so broadly supported that, as she put it, “my time was better spent loading a U-Haul instead.” The remark is self-serving, but it lands because it targets the gap between congressional performance and congressional power.

Casting a vote is still a basic obligation of office, even when the outcome is predetermined. Boebert’s defense turns that duty into a calculation of personal leverage: If her presence cannot change the result, she sees little reason to be there. Yet Johnson’s criticism relies on a different fiction—that every absence is equally dangerous, even after party officials have counted the votes and released members from attendance.

The fight is therefore less about legislative principle than control of the blame. Johnson wants departing Republicans held responsible if the party fails to move Trump’s remaining priorities. Boebert wants the failure assigned upward, to leaders who set the agenda, manage attendance and decide what reaches the floor. Her broadside is particularly damaging because it comes from inside the caucus and describes leadership’s outrage as something staged after the fact.

Defeat loosens party discipline

Boebert lost her bid for a fourth term earlier in November amid what The Associated Press described as a broader Democratic wave in Colorado. With no reelection campaign left to protect and no place in the next Republican House conference, she has little incentive to absorb criticism quietly for Johnson.

She denied that she had abandoned the job, saying she planned to serve through the end of her term rather than stay home like some previous lame-duck members. But her promise to remain in office sits beside her claim that attending certain votes is pointless. That is not a complete retreat from congressional work; it is a declaration that she, rather than party leadership, will decide which parts still deserve her time.

Her post-defeat explanations have been similarly selective. Boebert told the Associated Press that Trump’s veto of a clean-water pipeline project in southeastern Colorado contributed to her loss, along with continuing damage from her conduct during a 2023 performance of Beetlejuice. She also faulted Republican leaders for failing to pursue mass deportations aggressively enough.

Those explanations point in different directions. One blames Trump for blocking a local infrastructure project. Another acknowledges a scandal of Boebert’s own making. A third claims the party failed because it did not push a harsher immigration program. Together, they show a defeated politician distributing responsibility among nearly every available target while conceding only one plainly personal liability.

The majority ends in accusation

Republicans were preparing to surrender control of the House in January, while members had already chosen Trump ally Jim Jordan to succeed Johnson as their leader, according to The New York Times. That approaching transfer of power changes the function of the lame-duck session. Leadership is trying to extract the last usable votes from a weakened conference; outgoing members are deciding how much obedience they still owe; and factions are positioning themselves for the recriminations that follow defeat.

Boebert’s attack does not make her a credible reformer of congressional dysfunction. It does, however, expose the convenience of Johnson’s account. Leaders who choose the floor schedule and direct the whip operation cannot plausibly treat attendance as an entirely individual failure when their own officials allegedly approved an absence.

The unresolved factual question is narrow and important: Did Republican whips tell Boebert she could miss Tuesday’s votes because she was not needed? Until Johnson or the whip team answers, his public scolding remains undercut by the possibility that leadership authorized the conduct it later condemned. Boebert may be loading a U-Haul, but the House Republican majority is packing its failures into a blame campaign.

item.title: Above the Law, By Design: How America Turned Government Accountability Into a Legal Obstacle Course
item.description:
From sovereign immunity to qualified immunity, the American legal system has developed an extraordinary collection of protections for the very people entrusted with enforcing the law. Congress now has an opportunity to begin dismantling them.

The Government Has Immunity. How Convenient.

Imagine owning a business.

You follow the regulations. You obtain the permits. You pass the inspections. You invest your savings, hire employees, and build something that supports hundreds of families.

Then, one morning, a government official arrives and announces that your business must close.

Not because you violated the law.

Not because you failed an inspection.

But because another company caused environmental damage that the government failed to detect.

Your business is now considered dangerous, even though you have done nothing wrong.

You lose your income. Your employees lose their jobs. Your investment evaporates.

Naturally, you decide to sue the government responsible for the regulatory failure.

And then comes the magic phrase:

“Government has immunity.”

How extraordinarily convenient.

This scenario is inspired by an episode of the television series Drop Dead Diva, in which a hot-sauce factory is ordered closed after residents develop respiratory problems.

The factory has operated legally for years. Its pepper fumes are blamed for making people sick.

Eventually, investigators discover that the underlying problem is chemical contamination from another industrial facility, one that operated for approximately twenty years without the follow-up inspection required by its temporary permit.

The government failed to perform its regulatory responsibilities. Residents became sick. An otherwise compliant business faced bankruptcy.

In the fictional courtroom, an attorney raises governmental immunity as a defense.

And there, buried beneath the television drama, lies a remarkably real problem.

In America, the government can exercise enormous power over your life while enjoying legal protections that make holding it accountable exceptionally difficult.

The Sovereign Is Dead. Long Live the Sovereign.

Sovereign immunity is an inheritance from a political system Americans supposedly rejected in 1776.

Its historical roots lie in the principle that the sovereign cannot be sued without its consent.

That made a certain twisted sense in a monarchy, where the king was treated as the source of governmental authority.

But the United States was supposedly founded on a radically different proposition.

Government derives its legitimate authority from the people.

Public officials are servants of the law, not masters of it.

Nobody is supposed to be above the law.

And yet American jurisprudence preserved substantial governmental immunity, modified and expanded through constitutional interpretation, legislation, and judicial precedent.

The federal government can be sued under statutes such as the Federal Tort Claims Act, but the permission comes with restrictions and exceptions. State sovereign immunity creates additional obstacles, and officials may invoke several distinct forms of personal immunity.

These doctrines have different histories and legal justifications. They are not interchangeable.

But their combined consequences should concern anyone who believes governmental power requires meaningful accountability.

Consider the asymmetry.

When an ordinary citizen violates the law, the government can impose penalties, seize property, or initiate criminal proceedings.

When the government violates someone's rights, the victim may first have to establish that the government has consented to being sued, that an exception applies, or that the particular official lacks immunity.

One side possesses the authority to enforce the law. The other may have to overcome a collection of legal barriers merely to demand enforcement against the authorities themselves.

That is not equality before the law.

It is institutional privilege masquerading as legal sophistication.

Congress Created a Remedy. The Supreme Court Created an Escape Hatch.

In 1871, Congress enacted legislation intended to combat abuses of governmental power during Reconstruction.

Part of that legislation survives as 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

It allows individuals to bring civil actions against people acting under color of state law who deprive them of federally protected rights.

The historical context matters.

The legislation emerged during a period when violence, intimidation, and official complicity were being used to undermine the rights of newly freed Black Americans.

Congress recognized a problem: rights written on paper mean very little when the officials responsible for enforcing them are themselves participating in their violation.

The remedy was straightforward.

If someone wielding state authority violates your federal rights, you should have a legal avenue to seek redress.

But over the following century, the Supreme Court developed an additional defense.

In Pierson v. Ray (1967), it recognized a good-faith defense for police officers based on historical common-law principles.

In Harlow v. Fitzgerald (1982), the Court adopted the modern objective standard of qualified immunity.

Today, the doctrine generally protects officials from civil damages unless their conduct violates a right that was “clearly established” at the time.

Notice the critical distinction.

The question is no longer simply whether a government official violated your constitutional rights.

The victim must also overcome an additional inquiry concerning whether the law sufficiently established the unlawfulness of that conduct.

And that requirement creates some truly remarkable consequences.

The Constitution Has a Precedent Problem

Suppose a police officer violates someone's constitutional rights through a particularly unusual form of misconduct.

The victim files a lawsuit.

A court examines the facts and concludes that no sufficiently similar precedent clearly established the relevant constitutional rule.

Qualified immunity may protect the officer.

Now suppose another officer subsequently engages in similar misconduct.

Surely the first lawsuit established the necessary precedent?

Not necessarily.

In Pearson v. Callahan (2009), the Supreme Court held that judges need not decide whether a constitutional violation occurred before granting qualified immunity.

Courts can instead resolve a case by determining that the relevant right was not clearly established.

The result is a potentially self-perpetuating problem.

A court can avoid establishing that a particular act violates the Constitution because no sufficiently clear precedent exists.

Then, when similar conduct occurs again, the next plaintiff may confront the same lack of precedent.

Not every qualified-immunity case follows this pattern. Courts can recognize clearly established law without factually identical earlier cases, and they retain the discretion to decide constitutional questions.

Nevertheless, the structural problem is undeniable.

The doctrine can obstruct the development of the very precedent that victims need to overcome the doctrine.

Imagine applying this reasoning elsewhere.

A company invents a novel method of committing fraud.

Its executives argue that nobody has previously been held liable for that precise method.

The court responds that, since no sufficiently similar precedent exists, the executives receive a special immunity unavailable to ordinary defendants.

And then refuses to determine whether the conduct was unlawful, preserving the uncertainty for the next company.

We would recognize that system as absurd.

Yet a version of this problem exists in litigation involving violations of constitutional rights by government officials.

The Supreme Court has created a legal architecture in which the novelty of misconduct can become an obstacle to accountability.

Who Actually Pays When Government Officials Break the Law?

Here comes another particularly ugly detail.

One of the traditional justifications for qualified immunity is that government officials need protection from potentially ruinous personal liability.

The argument sounds reasonable at first.

Nobody wants a public employee financially destroyed for making an understandable mistake while performing a difficult job.

But empirical research complicates that justification considerably.

In a landmark 2014 study, UCLA law professor Joanna C. Schwartz investigated indemnification practices across American law enforcement agencies.

Her research found that governments paid approximately 99.98% of the money plaintiffs recovered in the studied police misconduct cases.

In other words, taxpayers were already paying almost all the damages.

Officers themselves rarely contributed.

The findings do not establish that every officer is automatically indemnified or that every jurisdiction uses identical policies. Later research also reveals important complications involving denied indemnification and negotiated settlements.

But the broad pattern is revealing.

The legal system protects individual officials from personal financial exposure while public funds already absorb most successful claims.

So who ultimately bears the cost?

Frequently, the same taxpayers whose rights the system is supposed to protect.

The official commits the violation. The government handles the litigation. The public pays the bill.

And unless the institution faces meaningful consequences beyond writing a check, the incentives for preventing future misconduct may remain weak.

This is not an argument that every public employee should personally finance every judgment.

It is an argument for distinguishing ordinary mistakes from reckless misconduct, deliberate violations, and institutional negligence—and ensuring that accountability reaches the people and organizations actually responsible.

Otherwise, compensation becomes just another operating expense.

The Permit Problem: When Government Failure Becomes Your Responsibility

Return to our fictional hot-sauce factory.

Its owner followed the rules.

Another company's contamination changed the environmental conditions around her business.

The government failed to perform an inspection that might have detected the underlying problem.

Yet the immediate consequence fell upon the compliant business.

There is an important principle here.

A government permit must create meaningful legal reliance.

When the government grants permission after completing its required review, citizens and businesses must be able to make reasonable investments based on that authorization.

That does not mean a permit entitles its holder to violate environmental standards, ignore safety regulations, or continue an activity that creates imminent danger.

Nor does it mean every risk can be discovered before construction or that government should ignore newly discovered hazards.

It means the consequences must be allocated fairly.

If an operator violates the permit, enforcement is appropriate.

If the government makes a negligent decision, the government should face responsibility for the resulting harm.

If a third party causes the damage, that third party should face liability.

And where public safety requires temporarily shutting down an innocent, compliant business, the government should provide an appropriate compensation mechanism rather than simply transferring the entire financial burden to the owner.

Protecting the public and compensating innocent parties are not mutually exclusive responsibilities.

The state should be capable of doing both.

That is what government accountability looks like when it is treated as an obligation rather than a public-relations slogan.

The American Immunity Industry

Qualified immunity is not the only doctrine that raises serious concerns.

In Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982), the Supreme Court recognized absolute presidential immunity from civil damages for official acts within the outer perimeter of presidential responsibilities.

Then, in Trump v. United States (2024), the Court recognized sweeping protections against criminal prosecution for presidential conduct classified as official.

These doctrines differ substantially from qualified immunity.

Presidential criminal immunity involves separation-of-powers questions that do not arise in ordinary police misconduct litigation.

But they illustrate a recurring tension in American constitutional law.

The more governmental authority someone exercises, the more elaborate the arguments become for protecting that person from legal consequences.

Presidents need immunity to act decisively.

Police officers need immunity to make split-second decisions.

Government agencies need immunity to perform public functions.

Every institution seems to need protection from accountability in order to function.

What about the citizens whose rights are being violated?

Who protects them from the consequences of all this supposedly indispensable governmental freedom?

The United States has developed an extraordinary collection of legal theories explaining why powerful officials must be protected from lawsuits.

It is long past time to devote comparable ingenuity to ensuring that ordinary people can obtain meaningful remedies when those officials abuse their power.

Democrats Have Won Congress. Should They Act Now?

The November 2026 midterm elections transformed the political landscape.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

The incoming Senate majority stands at 56 seats, counting the two independents who caucus with Democrats. The House majority is substantial.

But Donald Trump remains president, and the Democrats do not possess the sixty Senate votes ordinarily necessary to defeat a legislative filibuster.

They also lack the two-thirds majorities required to override a presidential veto.

This creates an uncomfortable political calculation.

Should Democrats introduce legislation abolishing qualified immunity immediately, knowing that it may be blocked?

Or should they wait until 2029, hoping to win the presidency and secure a governing trifecta?

They should act immediately.

Not because success is guaranteed.

Because congressional majorities are supposed to be used.

And qualified immunity is a particularly appropriate target because Congress has already demonstrated its authority to create civil remedies for governmental abuses.

The relevant legislation is not merely hypothetical.

In January 2026, Senator Edward Markey introduced S. 3625, the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act of 2026.

Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced companion legislation, H.R. 7046.

The House proposal would remove qualified immunity as a defense for federal, state, and local law enforcement officers in covered civil rights actions. It would also extend a statutory civil remedy to federal law enforcement officers.

These proposals provide a starting point, though a comprehensive reform should address the broader universe of government officials and institutional liability.

Democrats should not leave these bills gathering dust.

The incoming Congress should hold hearings, hear from victims and constitutional scholars, develop comprehensive legislation, and bring it to a vote.

If Republican senators oppose the bill, they should explain their objections.

If the president vetoes it, the administration should explain why it believes the existing immunity regime deserves preservation.

And if Democrats cannot enact the legislation during this Congress, they should establish a complete, publicly debated proposal ready for the next opportunity.

The absence of a guaranteed victory is not an excuse for refusing to fight a legislative battle.

But symbolic votes are not enough.

Democrats should simultaneously pursue reforms that are achievable without presidential cooperation.

States can strengthen civil-rights remedies under their own laws and restrict the availability of qualified-immunity-like defenses in state-law litigation.

Congress can conduct oversight, investigate governmental misconduct, and expose the financial and human consequences of existing immunity doctrines.

Those efforts can produce real results even while federal legislation remains blocked.

Abolish Qualified Immunity. Restore Accountability.

The objective should not be to make every government employee personally liable for every mistake.

That would be neither just nor practical.

The objective should be to eliminate special barriers that prevent people from pursuing valid legal remedies merely because the defendant holds government authority.

A serious reform should establish several principles.

First, abolish qualified immunity as a special defense to civil rights claims.

Officials should be able to defend their conduct on the merits, using ordinary legal defenses and protections appropriate to their duties.

They should not receive an additional escape hatch simply because no sufficiently similar previous case exists.

Second, establish effective remedies against government institutions.

Individual liability is insufficient when violations result from official policies, inadequate supervision, defective training, or systematic misconduct.

Victims should have meaningful avenues to seek relief from the institutions responsible.

Third, reform governmental indemnification.

Ordinary negligence and good-faith mistakes should not automatically bankrupt individual public servants.

But deliberate wrongdoing, reckless violations, and corruption should not be treated as ordinary employment expenses either.

Personal consequences should be proportionate, legally established, and supported by due process.

Fourth, strengthen compensation for wrongful governmental action.

When regulatory negligence or unlawful governmental conduct destroys an innocent person's livelihood, compensation should not depend on navigating an obstacle course of arbitrary immunities.

The government must have the legal authority to protect public safety.

It must also accept responsibility when its actions—or legally culpable failures to act—cause harm.

Finally, preserve the right to bring a claim before an independent court.

The right to sue does not mean the right to win.

A plaintiff must still prove the required elements of the case.

But government should not possess a general privilege to prevent legitimate claims from being heard simply because the defendant is the government.

The Rule of Law Cannot Have a Government Exception

Americans are taught from childhood that nobody is above the law.

It is repeated in classrooms, political speeches, judicial opinions, and presidential addresses.

It is practically a national incantation.

But a principle is only meaningful if it survives contact with reality.

When a citizen breaks the law, the machinery of government can descend upon them with extraordinary force.

When an official violates a citizen's constitutional rights, that citizen may discover that the very machinery supposedly established to protect those rights comes equipped with elaborate defenses against accountability.

Sovereign immunity.

Qualified immunity.

Absolute immunity.

Procedural barriers.

Jurisdictional limitations.

Every additional obstacle creates another opportunity for a legitimate grievance to disappear without an effective remedy.

Not every immunity doctrine serves the same purpose, and not every application is unjustified. But their cumulative effect demands far more scrutiny than the American legal system has traditionally afforded it.

Government exists to serve the public.

Public authority is a responsibility, not a personal privilege.

And the constitutional rights of ordinary people should never depend on whether a court can locate an earlier lawsuit involving sufficiently similar misconduct.

The newly elected Democratic Congress has an opportunity to begin correcting this imbalance.

It may not have the power to finish the job immediately.

But it has the power to begin.

And it has no legitimate reason to postpone that beginning.

A government powerful enough to enforce the law against its citizens must be accountable when it violates that law itself.

Anything less is not the rule of law.

It is the rule of law—with an employee exemption.

item.title: Alex Murdaugh’s 'Hail Mary' to escape murder retrial backfires big time
item.description:
Alex Murdaugh’s attempt to avoid a second murder trial failed Friday when Circuit Court Judge Debra McCaslin upheld the indictments charging him with killing his wife and son. The ruling leaves the retrial scheduled for April 5, 2027, while exposing a serious law-enforcement failure that the court found troubling—but not serious enough to invalidate a prosecution supported by substantial other evidence.

Murdaugh’s lawyers argued that Special Agent David Owen of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division gave false or misleading testimony to the grand jury that indicted Murdaugh in July 2022. McCaslin agreed that Owen had mishandled important information. She did not agree that his conduct justified dismissing two murder counts and two related weapons charges.

A compromised prosecution is not an erased case

At a nearly two-hour hearing in Lexington on Nov. 13, the defense challenged Owen’s statements about alleged blood spatter on Murdaugh’s white T-shirt and shotgun ammunition found at Moselle, the family’s Colleton County hunting estate.

According to the defense, Owen failed to tell grand jurors about a state laboratory report finding no human blood in the tested pieces of the shirt. He also incorrectly said shotguns at the property were loaded with the same combination of shells used to kill Murdaugh’s 22-year-old son, Paul.

McCaslin rebuked Owen in an 11-page order reported by the Associated Press, writing that failures of this kind “undermine public confidence in the integrity of the criminal justice system.” That is not a procedural footnote. A state agent appearing before a grand jury carries institutional authority, and grand jurors rely on that authority when deciding whether criminal charges should proceed. Failing to review an available laboratory report before describing forensic evidence is an abuse of that trust, whether it resulted from recklessness or incompetence.

But the judge found no intentional fabrication or bad-faith misconduct. More importantly for the motion before her, she ruled that the uncontested evidence still overwhelmingly established probable cause even after the disputed claims were removed.

That evidence includes cellphone and other digital records, shell casings connected to those recovered near the body of Murdaugh’s 52-year-old wife, Maggie, and a video from Paul’s phone placing Murdaugh at Moselle shortly before the killings. Probable cause is not a murder conviction; it is the threshold permitting the state to prosecute. McCaslin found that threshold easily met without Owen’s challenged testimony.

The state already lost one conviction through misconduct

Murdaugh was convicted in March 2023 of murdering Maggie and Paul on June 7, 2021, and received two consecutive life sentences. Those convictions did not survive institutional misconduct surrounding the trial.

In May 2026, the South Carolina Supreme Court overturned the verdicts after determining that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill had improperly influenced jurors. That decision did not acquit Murdaugh or dismiss the charges. It nullified convictions reached through a tainted proceeding and required the state to try the case again if prosecutors wished to pursue it.

The distinction matters. Murdaugh’s legal guilt for the killings must now be decided in a new trial, not presumed from the discarded verdicts. His consistent denial that he killed his family also remains exactly that: a denial to be tested against the evidence.

Yet the defense’s failed motion also illustrates why the state’s misconduct cannot simply be waved away as irrelevant because other evidence exists. First the clerk interfered with jurors; now a judge has condemned a lead investigator’s failure to review forensic findings before testifying to a grand jury. Neither error, according to the rulings described here, eliminates the prosecution. Together, however, they show officials repeatedly jeopardizing a case the government insists is strong.

The retrial has been moved to Sumter County, away from Colleton County, where the Murdaugh family’s influence was embedded for decades in the Lowcountry legal establishment. The change of venue may reduce the local pressures surrounding the case. It cannot retroactively repair the officials’ earlier conduct.

A fallen dynasty does not excuse official shortcuts

The killings at Moselle helped expose the collapse of a family long associated with legal power in the region. Prosecutors argued at the 2023 trial that Murdaugh murdered Maggie and Paul to gain time and divert attention as his finances approached ruin. Investigators later uncovered a years-long scheme in which he stole millions of dollars from clients and his own law firm.

Murdaugh has pleaded guilty to dozens of state and federal financial crimes. He is serving concurrent prison sentences of 27 and 40 years, so he will remain incarcerated regardless of the murder retrial’s result.

That record makes him an unusually unsympathetic defendant. It does not lower the government’s obligations. The state holds the power to investigate, indict and imprison; its agents therefore bear the burden of presenting evidence accurately, especially in secret grand-jury proceedings where the defense is not present to correct them.

Murdaugh’s motion failed because McCaslin found that Owen’s errors were not intentional and that the remaining evidence independently supported the indictments. The ruling is a major defeat for the defense, but it is no vindication of the investigation. South Carolina may take Murdaugh to trial again on April 5. This time, after one overturned conviction and a judicial reprimand of a state agent, its officials have even less room to blame anyone else if their own conduct compromises the case.

item.title: Trump’s collapse could finally save Thanksgiving with your MAGA relatives
item.description:
AlterNet’s promise that Donald Trump’s “collapse” could rescue Thanksgiving outruns the evidence it presents. The story establishes neither a measurable political collapse nor a family reconciliation already underway. What it does document is narrower and more revealing: anti-Trump pollster Sarah Longwell and Fox News co-host Jessica Tarlov believe some Trump supporters may become more willing to talk if disappointed by his performance—and they advise estranged relatives to listen without rushing to humiliate them.

That may be useful advice. It is not a political reckoning. The estrangement described in Longwell’s focus groups did not emerge from a misunderstanding at the dinner table. It grew from political choices, a Republican messaging apparatus that fused partisan loyalty with religious identity, and Trump supporters’ refusal to recognize why backing him carries moral consequences for people around them.

Estrangement without accountability

Longwell, publisher of the center-right anti-Trump outlet The Bulwark, discussed Zoom interviews with Trump voters during a Saturday podcast with Tarlov, her co-host on Raging Moderates and a panelist on Fox News’s The Five. Longwell said many Republicans regard Democrats as emotionally manipulated people who cannot see the “bigger picture.” At the same time, those voters struggle to understand why others consider Trump dangerous to themselves, their families or the country.

That disconnect runs through the focus-group remarks. One Trump supporter complained that liberal acquaintances did not want to hear even about gardening, much less politics. Another mourned the loss of friendships spanning decades and blamed “so much anger on the liberal vote” and “so much hatred against Trump.”

The grievance is carefully arranged. Trump supporters appear as people bewildered by rejection, while those reacting to their political commitments become the agents of division. The account skips over the decision at the center of the conflict: continuing to support a president whom relatives regard as racist and dangerous. Longwell said participants did not connect that support with what their relatives saw as a moral failure.

That is not merely a communication problem. Refusing to consider why a political choice changes another person’s judgment of you is itself a political posture—one that demands exemption from the social consequences of allegiance while assigning all blame to those unwilling to grant it.

When party loyalty becomes Christian obedience

The most revealing testimony concerned a participant whose grandmother began supporting Democratic Texas state Sen. James Talarico. The participant described that shift as abandonment of Christian faith, blamed her mother for having “corrupted” the grandmother and said she responded by sending Bible verses intended to pull her back toward Trump-aligned politics.

Tarlov identified the inversion: support for Talarico was treated as betrayal of Christianity, while loyalty to Trump and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was presented as the path back to religious fidelity. She called that position “fully untethered to earth.”

The participant’s account also folded vaccines into the alleged corruption of her grandmother. Political disagreement, public-health behavior and religious apostasy had become parts of the same story. That fusion did not materialize spontaneously inside one family. Tarlov pointed to a Republican messaging machine that has successfully taught voters to treat a Democratic ballot as a betrayal of Christianity.

This is where the holiday-reconciliation framing risks misdirection. The conflict is not sustained only by relatives who “dunk” on one another online. A powerful political apparatus has converted partisan identification into a test of faith, giving its audience a moral vocabulary in which dissenting family members are not simply mistaken but corrupted. The resulting family fracture is then presented as excessive liberal anger.

A possible opening is not a collapse

Longwell argued that Trump’s alleged catastrophic failure could create an opening for conversation. Her recommendation was tactical restraint: do not force an admission, let disillusioned supporters approach first, and ask how they now feel. Tarlov summarized the posture as “sharp but not cruel” and urged people to move from hectoring toward conversation.

Nothing in the supplied reporting demonstrates how many Trump voters have changed their minds, what failure has driven such a change or whether the focus-group participants themselves are abandoning him. “Collapse” is the assessment offered by the podcast’s hosts and adopted by AlterNet’s framing, not a result established by the material presented.

Longwell also warned that the politics would likely survive the politician. A younger generation raised within MAGA could preserve the movement by insisting that authentic “America First” politics was never actually attempted. That familiar escape hatch protects an ideology from the record of those who wield power in its name: failure becomes proof that the project needs another champion, not evidence against the project itself.

Listening may help families speak again. But reconciliation purchased by pretending that everyone merely became too emotional would reproduce the original evasion. Trump supporters described here want relationships insulated from judgment about their political choices, even as some of them condemn a Democratic vote as religious betrayal. A quieter Thanksgiving table cannot resolve that contradiction. It can only make space for someone to confront it.
