item.title: GOP senator’s defection imperils Trump’s last-minute nomination spree
item.description:
Donald Trump’s rush to install loyalists before Democrats take control of Congress in January hit an obstacle Thursday when Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said he would hold Michael LoSapio’s nomination to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The break came after LoSapio, a Palantir security executive, told senators he did not believe the January 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol was an attack.

A hold does not automatically kill a nomination. But with the incoming Democratic majority narrowing the time available for confirmation, Tillis’s move—joined by Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden—makes LoSapio’s installation at CISA substantially less likely. One Republican’s refusal to cooperate has exposed how little margin Trump’s final confirmation drive has left.

A basic question, then a revealing refusal

LoSapio’s nomination foundered on a question that required neither specialized cybersecurity knowledge nor a partisan judgment.

“Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021?” Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked during Thursday’s testimony.

“I, I, I don’t know,” LoSapio initially answered. After further questioning, he settled on a denial: “No, I don’t believe it was an attack, no.”

Blumenthal paused before asking whether LoSapio was really giving that answer. The nominee then tried to relocate the matter outside his claimed area of competence: “I wasn’t involved in politics.”

“You weren’t involved in politics? Were you alive on the planet?” Blumenthal replied.

That exchange was not a dispute over terminology at the margins. Trump nominated LoSapio to run the federal agency responsible for cybersecurity and election security. A prospective CISA director who declines to recognize an assault on the constitutional transfer of power is not avoiding politics; he is adopting a politically useful description of an event central to the office’s mission.

Wyden made the objection explicit: “You can’t have an insurrectionist Palantir executive in charge of our nation’s cybersecurity and election security.”

Tillis did not publicly give a specific reason for his hold. But AlterNet reports that he informed Punchbowl News of the decision shortly after LoSapio’s January 6 testimony. The timing leaves the exchange as the reported catalyst without turning an inference into a stated explanation.

Trump’s confirmation machine loses a vote

Tillis’s intervention matters because Republicans are trying to confirm as many Trump nominees as possible before control of Congress changes. The pressure is institutional, not procedural trivia: confirmation would place Trump’s choices in powerful federal posts that outlast the frantic closing days in which the Senate approved them.

Tillis, who is retiring, has become more willing to resist MAGA positions as his departure approaches. That freedom is revealing. Republican senators facing continued dependence on Trump’s political apparatus have stronger incentives to accept nominees whose testimony would ordinarily invite rejection. Tillis’s looming exit reduces that leverage over him; it does not explain why comparable independence should require retirement.

His resistance also extends beyond LoSapio. On Thursday, Tillis placed a hold on Eric Ueland’s nomination to lead the Government Accountability Office. He raised concerns that Ueland, an Office of Management and Budget official with close ties to the Trump administration, could not objectively direct an institution charged with government accountability.

The two holds point to the same governing problem from different directions. Trump sought to put a loyal administration figure in charge of auditing government performance and a nominee unwilling to call January 6 an attack in charge of protecting election infrastructure. Tillis’s decisions interrupt that effort, but they also underscore how far it had already advanced: both men reached the stage where a single senator’s late objection became decisive.

Denial meets an agency already stripped down

LoSapio’s January 6 answer was not the only concern raised by his testimony. Opponents also questioned his approach to CISA’s staffing and budget. He argued that additional money or personnel would not necessarily produce “more security.”

As an abstract proposition, that is unobjectionable; spending alone does not guarantee capacity. In the circumstances AlterNet describes, however, it functions as a convenient evasion of the agency’s actual condition. CISA insiders said the agency has struggled since former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem oversaw the departure of thousands of employees. Remaining staff have warned that the country’s lead cyber-defense agency is under-resourced while a series of technology-system outages has disrupted the nation over the previous week.

That context makes LoSapio’s posture consequential. The nominee was not being asked to manage an agency bloated with unused capacity. He was seeking control of one reportedly depleted of thousands of workers while dismissing any straightforward connection between resources and security.

The nomination therefore joined two forms of denial: refusal to describe January 6 in plain language and reluctance to acknowledge the operational implications of a gutted cybersecurity workforce. Neither demonstrates the candor required to lead an agency whose value depends on recognizing threats before political convenience makes them impossible to name.

LoSapio may not be formally finished, and a Senate hold is not a rejection. But the administration’s last-minute timetable has converted delay into a serious barrier. Trump’s nomination spree depended on Republican compliance; Tillis withheld it, and the candidate’s own testimony supplied the reason other senators needed to stop pretending this was a routine appointment.

item.title: Top Republican comes out swinging against Trump Cabinet officials
item.description:
Sen. Tom Cotton says he warned President Donald Trump’s administration that U.S. artificial-intelligence chips were reaching China through Chinese Communist Party front companies—and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick failed to respond adequately before the Nvidia controversy erupted. Cotton’s complaint is not merely that officials missed a foreseeable risk. It is that they received repeated warnings from the Republican chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and acted too late, leaving the government to assess what he called “the damage that’s been done.”

The Arkansas Republican has not demanded Lutnick’s resignation. He has instead left that judgment to Trump, who has publicly defended his commerce secretary and said he does not plan to replace him. That distinction matters: Cotton is attacking the administration’s handling of China policy while preserving the president’s authority—and responsibility—to decide whether failure carries consequences.

Warnings met with inaction

Cotton told The Wall Street Journal that he sent Lutnick multiple letters about Chinese front companies and the risk of advanced American chips being smuggled into China.

“If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about these Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously,” Cotton said.

His account places the Commerce Department at the center of the failure. The department had regulatory authority relevant to the reported chip transfers; Cotton says its leadership was repeatedly alerted to the danger. If that account is accurate, the administration cannot plausibly reduce the episode to an unforeseeable breach. The dispute is about whether officials with power to act discounted warnings until the consequences became politically impossible to ignore.

Cotton welcomed the administration’s eventual movement toward his harder line on China, singling out national-security adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as an official who shared that view. But he described the shift as badly delayed.

“I’m glad that some folks in the administration are finally coming around to a view that I have championed and that others in the administration have as well,” he said. “It’s just a bit late, regrettably, and I think we need to catalog the damage that’s been done.”

That demand is more consequential than the personnel drama. A serious accounting would identify what technology reportedly reached China, which companies or intermediaries moved it, what warnings officials received, and which decisions allowed the transfers to continue. Cotton’s remarks, as reported, do not provide that inventory. They establish his allegation that preventable harm occurred and that the administration’s response lagged behind warnings he had delivered.

Trump retains the power—and the blame

The headline spectacle is a senior Republican “swinging” at Cabinet officials. The institutional reality is less convenient for Trump: Lutnick remains in office because Trump wants him there.

Trump has defended Lutnick’s handling of the Nvidia controversy and said he has no plans to replace him. Cotton’s formulation accommodates that hierarchy. He said that if Trump has lost confidence in Lutnick, the president should request his resignation. Cotton did not claim the authority to make that decision, because he does not have it.

This is the familiar structure of loyalty-centered government. Subordinates may absorb public criticism, but the president chooses them, protects them and decides whether failures have professional consequences. Blaming the Commerce Department without confronting Trump’s continued support for its leader would misdirect responsibility downward. Cotton stops short of doing that entirely, but his conditional language allows Trump to remain the final judge of an official whose performance Trump has already endorsed.

Cotton also argued that Trump should move quickly to nominate any successor while Republicans still control the Senate. According to the report, Democrats are set to take control of the chamber in January 2027. His urgency therefore reflects more than national-security policy: it reflects the partisan advantage Trump would retain in installing a replacement before control changes hands.

A dissent contained within Trump’s authority

Cotton says Trump has known his position on China since the transition before Trump’s first term in 2016. His criticism is therefore not the conversion of a loyalist after a controversy became public. He presents it as the culmination of a decade-long argument, including specific warnings delivered to the current administration.

But the senator’s challenge remains carefully bounded. He accuses officials of taking China too lightly, says the failure was preventable and calls for an assessment of the resulting damage. He does not call on Lutnick to leave. He does not demand that Trump reverse his defense of the commerce secretary. Instead, he offers Trump a timetable for replacing Lutnick if the president independently decides trust has been broken.

That is a sharp indictment of the administration’s conduct, but not a rebellion against its governing logic. Cotton has identified an alleged national-security failure, the official he believes mishandled it and the president empowered to impose accountability. Trump, for now, has chosen loyalty to Lutnick. Whatever damage the administration eventually catalogs will belong not only to the officials who allegedly ignored the warnings, but to the president who was warned and continues to stand behind them.

item.title: Melania tells Fox she’s 'not really' into Trump’s 'tacky' obsession
item.description:
Melania Trump did not call her husband’s gold-heavy White House makeover “tacky.” What she did, during a Friday appearance on Fox & Friends, was reject host Brian Kilmeade’s joking prediction that the Christmas decorations would feature “more gold.” Raising a hand, the first lady answered: “No. Not really.” It was a small exchange, but a revealing one: even Donald Trump’s wife would not endorse extending his gilded aesthetic into the holiday display.

A joke built on presidential excess

Melania Trump appeared on Fox to promote her new series about life in the White House. Near the end of the segment, host Ainsley Earhardt praised the Christmas decorations, and the first lady invited the panel to visit. Kilmeade then supplied the gold joke.

It worked because Trump’s fixation is not subtle. According to AlterNet, he has added gold-painted molding and ceiling details, urns, coasters and a thick “Trump” paperweight to the White House during his second term. Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported in Regime Change that the president personally glued gold ornaments to the Oval Office fireplace.

AlterNet also reports that Trump proposed placing a golden winged figure atop a 250-foot triumphal arch and had a collection of Washington horse statues coated in gold. The recurring theme is less decoration than self-mythology: public space treated as a setting for the president’s preferred image of wealth and grandeur.

Melania’s “not really” should not be inflated into a political break or even a comprehensive verdict on the renovations. She was responding to a joke about this year’s Christmas decorations. But her dismissal punctured the premise that Trump’s taste automatically defines every part of the White House simply because he occupies it.

The People’s House as personal branding

Presidents inevitably alter the building where they live and work. The political question is what those alterations communicate. Trump’s additions turn the executive mansion toward the visual language of his private brand, complete with his own name rendered as décor.

That matters because the White House is not a personal resort or a monument awarded to its current tenant. Trump holds the institutional authority to reshape its presentation, and his aesthetic choices repeatedly collapse the distinction between the presidency and the president’s ego. The gold does not establish strength or prosperity. It advertises his preferred version of both.

The media framing around Melania risks misdirecting attention toward a familiar marital sideshow: Does she secretly dislike his taste? Is she rebelling? The reported exchange establishes only that she did not want “more gold” associated with the Christmas display. The consequential actor remains the president, who has used his control over the executive mansion to impose that aesthetic throughout it.

A carefully managed counter-image

Holiday decoration has traditionally fallen largely within the first lady’s domain, and AlterNet describes Melania Trump’s choices as mostly conventional. Some displays nevertheless became spectacles of their own. Her stark 2019 design was criticized as joyless; the 2018 scarlet trees prompted comparisons to The Handmaid’s Tale; and commenters likened the 2017 décor to the horror film The Babadook.

Her Fox appearance was itself part of another image-making project. The series she was promoting was produced and released by Jeff Bezos’ Amazon, which had already produced a documentary about her. AlterNet reports that the documentary held a 9 percent Rotten Tomatoes rating, while reviews of the newer series were harsh: The Guardian called it a “dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment,” and The Telegraph compared it to an “audition for a movie supervillain.”

That context makes the gold exchange more than idle banter, but less than dissent. Melania was selling a controlled account of White House life on a friendly network when an unscripted joke invoked the president’s conspicuous vanity. Her response briefly separated her presentation from his. It did not challenge the power that allowed him to turn the nation’s executive residence into another extension of the Trump name.

item.title: Trump teases a Stephen Miller 2028 presidential run
item.description:
President Donald Trump floated White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller as a possible 2028 presidential candidate on Friday, publicly elevating the architect of his deportation agenda over Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The remark may have been improvised, but the power behind it was not: Trump had just called Miller “the most powerful man in the world,” an extraordinary description of an unelected aide whose promotion gives one of the administration’s most extreme figures greater control inside the White House.

Trump stages a succession contest

The suggestion came during a White House press conference that wandered through potholes, former President Joe Biden, Republicans’ midterm losses and Trump’s relationships with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump dismissed critics of his friendliness toward the two authoritarian leaders as “stupid people” and insisted, amid the digressions, that he does not “ramble at all.”

He then abruptly introduced Miller as “the most powerful man in the world” and invited him to speak. Miller responded with lavish praise, cataloguing what he called the administration’s victories and describing Trump as an “extraordinary” leader.

When Trump reclaimed the microphone, he gestured toward Vance and Rubio, who had been standing behind them, and announced: “Breaking news — he was better than these two guys!” He then asked Miller, “Do you want to run for president?”

The performance placed three potential successors into a loyalty contest controlled entirely by Trump. Vance and Rubio hold constitutional or Cabinet offices and have both been widely presumed to harbor 2028 ambitions. Miller’s authority comes from something more useful in this White House: proximity to the president and a demonstrated willingness to advance Trump’s harshest policies.

The joke rests on real power

Treating the exchange only as campaign gossip misses the consequential part. Trump did not merely tease a Miller candidacy. He advertised Miller’s institutional clout after installing him as chief of staff.

Miller has long been one of Trump’s most trusted advisers and, as AlterNet reports, a principal architect of the administration’s brutal deportation project. His elevation places a committed proponent of Trump’s most extreme impulses in a position to shape access, information and decision-making throughout the executive branch.

Whether Miller will actually seek the presidency is not established by the exchange. Trump asked the question; Miller did not announce a campaign. But presidential teasing functions as patronage in Trump’s political operation. He can raise a subordinate’s profile, humiliate presumed heirs and remind every faction that advancement depends less on formal rank than on his personal approval.

That is why Vance and Rubio’s awkward presence mattered. Trump turned senior officials into scenery while praising the aide whose power is least accountable to voters. The spectacle was unserious in form and revealing in substance.

Loyalty is the governing credential

A Republican succession struggle is already taking shape under the burden of the administration’s unpopularity. AlterNet reports that Vance’s political standing has fallen over the past year, while Rubio has received comparatively less damaging coverage. Polling released Thursday found Republican respondents preferred Rubio to Vance for the 2028 nomination.

One poll does not settle a nomination years in advance, and Trump’s question does not create a Miller campaign. It does, however, expose the governing hierarchy. Vance may be vice president and Rubio may lead the State Department, but Trump publicly presented Miller as the more impressive performer and the more powerful man.

Miller earned that praise immediately after delivering an effusive tribute to Trump. In this administration, policy radicalism and personal flattery are not competing qualifications. They reinforce each other.

The unresolved question is therefore not whether Trump’s latest provocation predicts the 2028 ballot. It is what Miller will do with the authority he already has. For people subject to the deportation machinery he helped design, that is the contest with immediate consequences.

item.title: Critics erupt with laughter over Melania Trump's claims about Donald's diet
item.description:
Melania Trump defended President Donald Trump’s fast-food habit during a Fox Business Network interview, insisting his diet is “good” and that he eats McDonald’s only “sometimes.” The response drew ridicule because it collided with years of accounts describing McDonald’s, KFC, pizza and Diet Coke as staples of Trump’s routine. But the exchange was more than a spouse minimizing an unhealthy menu: it showed a friendly television interview converting a legitimate question about an 80-year-old president’s fitness into lifestyle banter, then offering reassurance without meaningful scrutiny.

A denial tailored for friendly television

Fox Business host Stuart Varney asked Melania whether her husband’s diet was “really as bad as people say.” She blamed the perception on press speculation.

“No, not it’s not,” she replied. “I think, the media makes those assumptions and those reports, but his diet — it’s good. He has sometimes McDonald’s, of course. When you’re traveling, it’s sometimes, it’s much easier.”

That answer did several jobs at once. It softened a reported pattern into an occasional convenience, cast contrary accounts as media invention and replaced a question about presidential health with a wife’s personal assurance. Melania said she also eats McDonald’s, though less often than her husband.

AlterNet reports that Trump’s customary order has widely been described as two Big Macs, two Filet-O-Fish sandwiches, a Quarter Pounder, fries and a chocolate malt or shake. The article does not establish how often he eats that meal. It does, however, cite a substantially older account from two former aides. In their 2017 book Let Trump Be Trump, David Bossie and Corey Lewandowski wrote that aboard Trump Force One, the “four major food groups” were McDonald’s, Kentucky Fried Chicken, pizza and Diet Coke.

Against that history, “sometimes” sounded less like clarification than image management.

Ridicule filled the vacuum left by the interview

Online critics responded with laughter rather than belief. One compared Melania’s claim that Trump only sometimes consumes McDonald’s and Diet Coke to saying he was “sometimes bald.” Another asked whether defending the diet was required by her prenuptial agreement. A third called the interview “a hostage video.”

Those comments establish mockery, not medical evidence. Their force came from the obvious mismatch between Melania’s casual description and the public mythology Trump and his own aides have helped build around his fast-food consumption.

Trump aide Natalie Harp reinforced that mythology while attempting to defend the first lady. She wrote that Melania was ensuring “a healthy balance,” then celebrated the way Trump’s preference for McDonald’s follows him abroad. Harp pointed to a recent Philippines visit during which the country’s president reportedly arranged a fried-chicken delivery for Trump’s team, exclaiming: “FAST FOOD AND WORLD DIPLOMACY!”

That is not a rebuttal to concerns about his diet. It is branding: the president’s habits become an endearing spectacle, and foreign accommodation becomes evidence of his cultural reach. The health question disappears beneath the merchandise-ready persona.

The unanswered question is presidential fitness

Trump says he is in “stellar health,” while critics contend that he is experiencing physical and mental decline. The supplied reporting offers no medical finding that resolves that dispute, and a fast-food preference alone cannot establish cognitive or physical incapacity.

That makes Varney’s framing especially weak. Asking Melania whether the diet is “as bad as people say” invites a personal defense, not an accountable answer. She is neither presented as Trump’s physician nor asked to supply medical information. Fox Business obtained precisely the reassurance its question was designed to produce, while Melania redirected skepticism toward “the media.”

The relevant power structure is straightforward. Trump holds the presidency. His family and aides help manage his public image. A sympathetic television platform gives them room to substitute familiarity for evidence. Critics on social media can laugh, but they do not control access to his health information or determine how candidly the White House addresses questions about his capacity to serve.

The result is a familiar form of political misdirection: scrutiny of an elderly president becomes a culture-war complaint about hostile coverage, and documented accounts from Trump’s own former aides are folded into a harmless fast-food joke. Melania’s “sometimes” claim became funny because it strained credibility. The institutional problem is that the interview never required it to withstand examination.

item.title: Trump ally’s urgent pardon plea exposed in newly obtained emails
item.description:
Cleta Mitchell, a key participant in Donald Trump’s effort to overturn the 2020 election, privately pressed the Justice Department in fall 2025 to accelerate presidential pardons for the people who signed false elector certificates. Her stated urgency was not about correcting a federal injustice. It was about getting Trump to intervene before defendants went to trial in state criminal cases—and, in Georgia, using federal pardons to help create political momentum for disposing of the remaining charges against Trump himself.

Emails obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request by American Oversight and provided to The Guardian, as reported by AlterNet, show Mitchell working directly with Pardon Attorney Ed Martin while he drafted a memorandum supporting clemency. “Time is of the essence,” she wrote, calling it “essential” to act before trials were scheduled and defendants incurred further costs and “mental anguish.”

“Please let me know what else I can do to help get this done,” Mitchell added.

Martin’s response was terse but receptive: “Thank you for this. Very helpful.”

Clemency as protection from accountability

At the time, criminal proceedings involving false electors remained pending in Georgia, Michigan, Arizona, Nevada and Wisconsin. Mitchell’s emails treated those prosecutions not as matters for courts to adjudicate, but as obstacles that Trump’s administration should help neutralize.

In Arizona, she urged action before a grand jury filed charges, arguing that a pardon would be “optimum to stop the persecution of these defendants.” She specifically noted that the group included two senior figures from Charlie Kirk’s Turning Point USA. Kirk had been murdered in Utah weeks earlier, and Mitchell’s invocation of his organization appears designed to make political affiliation part of the case for presidential intervention.

Her argument concerning Michigan and Wisconsin centered on the personal toll of prosecution. Some defendants, she wrote, had exhausted retirement savings, mortgaged homes to cover legal expenses and endured years of emotional hardship. “Allowing a trial to proceed is simply unacceptable,” she declared.

Legal proceedings are often financially and emotionally punishing. But Mitchell’s emails did not seek a broadly available remedy for defendants confronting those burdens. She used privileged access to the federal pardon apparatus on behalf of political allies accused of participating in an effort to negate lawful election results. The weaker actors in this story were not people denied access to power; they were the voters whose ballots the false certificates sought to displace.

A federal pardon aimed at state cases

Trump ultimately issued blanket pardons on November 10, 2025. Because presidential clemency reaches federal offenses rather than state charges, the pardons did not terminate the prosecutions Mitchell was trying to head off. American Oversight executive director Chioma Chukwu described them as federal pardons that left the ongoing state cases intact, while saying the records revealed how Mitchell and other Trump allies used their access to secure presidential action.

That jurisdictional limit did not make the effort politically meaningless. Mitchell’s Georgia email shows that she expected prompt federal pardons to influence what happened next at the state level. The case against Trump and the false electors was then before Georgia’s Prosecuting Attorneys’ Council. If Trump acted before a replacement prosecutor was chosen, she argued, the council could seek dismissal of the remaining charges, including those against Trump.

A prosecutor later dismissed the Georgia charges for reasons unrelated to the pardons. That distinction matters: the emails document Mitchell’s desired strategy, not proof that clemency produced the dismissal. But the strategy itself is revealing. She was not merely asking the president to show mercy to supporters. She was exploring how federal executive power might be deployed to weaken state accountability and benefit the president who controlled that power.

Mitchell did not respond to a request for comment.

“We stuck the landing”

The clearest description of how officials involved viewed the process came after Trump signed the pardons. Martin received a congratulatory email that day and replied: “It was a long project. But I am glad we stuck the landing.”

The phrase strips away the public language of persecution and hardship. Inside the administration, the pardons were a project to complete—one advanced through private access, coordinated advocacy and a Justice Department official’s work product. The beneficiaries were political allies facing prosecution over conduct intended to keep Trump in power after he lost the 2020 election.

The pardons could not erase the state charges. They did, however, place the presidency and the federal pardon office behind the defendants, recasting accountability for an election-subversion effort as mistreatment and rewarding those involved with the symbolic protection of the man whose defeat they had tried to overturn.

item.title: Fox News panel erupts as host claims Trump 'most pro-communist' president
item.description:
Harold Ford Jr. called Donald Trump “the most pro-communist American president” of his lifetime on Fox News’ The Five after Trump met the leaders of China and Russia in Shenzhen and publicly greeted Vladimir Putin as a friend. Ford’s charge was not about Trump adopting communist economics. It was a blunt indictment of a president offering warmth and prestige to authoritarian rivals while, Ford argued, returning from the summit without meaningful concessions.

The ensuing argument revealed more than a disagreement over foreign policy. Faced with questions about what Trump obtained from Xi Jinping or Putin, Jesse Watters reached for Joe Biden, then piled on unrelated boasts and an unsupported claim. The spectacle substituted partisan noise for the central issue: what the sitting president surrendered, secured or legitimized through the meeting.

A summit rich in symbolism, thin on returns

The Shenzhen gathering was described as the first trilateral meeting among the United States, China and Russia. According to AlterNet’s account, its “peace declaration” amounted primarily to an agreement to begin denuclearization talks—not a completed deal or a concrete breakthrough.

That gap between ceremony and substance drove Ford’s criticism. He asked whether Trump had pressed Xi to stop Chinese spying and theft, then argued that no American president had treated Russian and Chinese leaders more favorably while obtaining so little in exchange.

“I would not have sat with these guys if I hadn’t gotten some concessions,” Ford said.

That is the material question obscured by the segment’s ideological branding. “Pro-communist” was imprecise as an economic description, and Watters predictably answered by calling Trump “the most capitalist president we’ve ever had.” But Ford’s underlying point was about the use of presidential power: Trump granted access, recognition and personal warmth to Xi and Putin, while Ford saw no corresponding gain for the United States.

Trump’s “He’s my friend” greeting to Putin mattered for the same reason. Presidential friendliness is not merely personal when displayed at a summit. It is diplomatic currency, especially for a Russian leader whose government was identified during the exchange with the attack on Ukraine. If Trump chose to spend that currency, the relevant measure is what he bought with it.

Biden as an all-purpose escape hatch

Watters did not initially answer Ford’s questions about Xi, spying or concessions. Instead, he blamed Biden for Russia’s attack on Ukraine, saying it happened “under Joe Biden’s watch” and accusing the former president of doing “absolutely nothing.”

The maneuver reassigned responsibility from the officials exercising power at the Shenzhen summit to a former president who was not there. Ford responded with an intentionally jarring comparison: “I’ve gotten over slavery, I’m forgiving after slavery. Get over Biden!”

Watters refused. “I’ll get over Biden when I damn well feel like it!” he shouted.

That answer was inadvertently clarifying. Biden remained useful precisely because discussing him prevented scrutiny of Trump’s conduct in the present event. Whatever judgment one makes of the Biden administration’s Ukraine policy, it does not establish what Trump obtained from Putin or Xi in Shenzhen. Watters used an earlier administration as a shield against questions about the current president’s choices.

The evasion continued when Watters claimed Trump had defeated China in a trade war and “wiped out Maduro” and “the Ayatollah.” He then asserted, without evidence, that a new ayatollah was gay. None of those declarations answered Ford’s challenge about the summit. The unsupported remark added provocation where facts were required—a familiar television tactic for making the outrageous more memorable than the unanswered question.

Fox turns accountability into entertainment

Watters ultimately dismissed Ford as “nitpicky.” The label exposed the standard being applied: demanding identifiable concessions from a high-level meeting with powerful authoritarian leaders was treated as fussy obstruction, while sweeping claims and irrelevant taunts counted as rebuttal.

Ford also insisted his criticism was not partisan, saying he would have judged Barack Obama or Biden the same way. That defense should not have been necessary. Asking what an American president achieved in exchange for elevating rival leaders is basic scrutiny, not party disloyalty.

Yet The Five converted that scrutiny into a televised eruption. Greg Gutfeld closed by congratulating the panel on how “exciting” the confrontation had been, and Dana Perino replied that she was “thrilled.” The network got its combustible segment. Watters got to defend Trump without accounting for Trump’s reported results. And the summit’s consequential question—what the United States received for the legitimacy and warmth its president conferred—remained unanswered.

item.title: New signs Trump struggles with ‘neurological decline’ unmasked by expert
item.description:
AlterNet’s report does not establish that President Donald Trump is experiencing neurological decline. It establishes that psychologist John Paul Garrison watched footage from Trump’s final day in China and interpreted several visible behaviors—including an unsteady-looking escalator ride, an uneven gait and apparent sleep during a meeting—as possible signs of neurological dysfunction. Garrison explicitly described those conclusions as personal opinions, not a psychological evaluation. That distinction matters when the subject is an 80-year-old president exercising immense state power.

An escalator encounter becomes a medical inference

Garrison reviewed footage of Trump with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. On an escalator, Trump reached backward in a movement Garrison thought resembled an attempt to hold hands. Xi then took Trump’s arm.

Garrison inferred that Xi may have believed Trump was unsteady and intervened to prevent a fall—and the unwanted spectacle that would follow. The footage may support concern about Trump’s balance, but Xi’s reason for grabbing his arm is not established in the report. It remains Garrison’s interpretation of an ambiguous interaction.

The psychologist also said Trump appeared unable to walk in a straight line and repeatedly drifted left. He identified what he considered trouble with Trump’s right leg, frequent leg tapping and an apparently involuntary spasm in the president’s right arm. According to Garrison, similar right-arm movements have appeared repeatedly.

Those observations describe conduct visible on video. Calling them evidence of neurological decline goes further: it converts outward movement into a medical explanation without an examination, clinical history or diagnosis. Garrison himself stopped short of claiming that authority.

Apparent sleep at a consequential meeting

The report’s most politically significant episode occurred during the three leaders’ first trilateral meeting. As Xi spoke and Putin took notes, Trump appeared to have fallen asleep, according to Garrison. He also identified what he called brief “micro sleeps,” followed by moments in which Trump seemed to look around and reorient himself.

Garrison rejected age alone as an adequate explanation. “There are plenty of people around 80 years old who are capable of sitting through meetings with world leaders with bright lights on and not falling asleep,” he said. He attributed the episode partly to what he characterized as Trump’s inability to sustain attention when someone else was speaking.

That interpretation is not a diagnosis either. But the underlying conduct, if the footage is as described, warrants scrutiny for reasons that do not depend on remote medical speculation. A president apparently sleeping while the leaders of China and Russia speak is not merely an embarrassing image. Attention is part of the job, especially in a meeting where every gesture can affect diplomacy, leverage and the judgments other governments make about American leadership.

The presidency is the issue, not amateur certainty

Garrison said Trump appeared to struggle with social cues and suggested that the behavior “could be related” to forms of neurological dysfunction he had previously discussed. He also called Trump’s manner toward Putin “ridiculous, almost cartoonish” and “almost childlike.”

Those descriptions mix observable behavior, political judgment and medical conjecture. Trump’s conduct toward Putin can be assessed on its own terms; describing it as fawning is an interpretation of a public interaction. Linking it to neurological dysfunction requires evidence the report does not provide.

The headline’s promise that an expert “unmasked” neurological decline is therefore stronger than the article’s contents. Garrison is identified as a clinical and forensic psychologist and body-language expert, but his video was not an evaluation of Trump, by his own account. He offered hypotheses from footage. AlterNet reported those hypotheses; it did not report a clinical finding.

That overreach risks misdirecting attention from the institution that matters. The central question is not whether viewers can diagnose Trump from a gait, an arm movement or a closed-eye moment. It is whether a president who appeared unsteady and disengaged during high-level diplomacy can perform the office’s duties—and whether the people around him will address any genuine impairment candidly.

Medicalized speculation can obscure that question by turning public accountability into a contest over labels. No neurological diagnosis is necessary to judge a president’s visible performance. Nor should a suggestive video be promoted as proof of an illness its commentator concedes he did not evaluate. The reported footage may justify serious concern; it does not justify pretending that concern has already become a medical conclusion.

item.title: Something’s changed about the way Marco Rubio talks about his future
item.description:
Marco Rubio’s posture toward 2028 has shifted from waiting for Donald Trump to clear his path to considering whether remaining in Trump’s administration could damage it. Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Rubio and his advisers were weighing his departure after Republicans’ midterm wipeout, while CNN reported Thursday that Trump may delay endorsing a successor rather than immediately anointing one. Rubio has made no decision, and the State Department denied that he was considering resignation. But the change is unmistakable: the secretary of State is no longer being described only as a loyal aspirant seeking Trump’s blessing. He is also being described as a politician calculating the cost of staying.

From chosen heir to undeclared contestant

For much of the year, the emerging Republican succession contest revolved around two men already inside the administration: Rubio and Vice President JD Vance.

In March, The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had been privately soliciting assessments of their strengths and weaknesses from advisers, donors and friends. Trump was not merely observing a future primary. He was using his control over the MAGA coalition to pit two ambitious subordinates against one another while deciding who might inherit it.

That arrangement exposed where the operative power lay. Rubio’s prospects did not principally depend on assembling an independent constituency or offering a distinct governing program. CNN reported that many of his allies believed he would run only if Trump endorsed him and effectively removed serious competition. The prospective candidate’s first electorate was one man.

Trump encouraged that dependency. CNN’s Adam Cancryn, Kylie Atwood, Kristen Holmes and Jennifer Hansler reported that he repeatedly asked allies whether they preferred Vance or Rubio, while publicly suggesting the two should share a ticket. The exercise kept both men competing for favor without giving either certainty.

Rubio appeared to gain ground by June, when a conservative publication reported that Vance’s standing with Trump had declined after the vice president criticized the administration’s decision to declare war on Iran. In that telling, proximity to the nomination depended partly on avoiding disagreement with the president—even on a decision as consequential as war.

The midterms changed the calculation

Republicans’ Election Day losses altered the incentives. Trump had previously been preoccupied with selecting an heir; CNN now reports that, in the aftermath of the midterms, he has signaled that he may withhold an endorsement until later in the 2028 primary.

That leaves Rubio without the guarantee his allies reportedly considered essential. It also changes the value of his Cabinet service. Holding two powerful posts—secretary of State and national security adviser—gives Rubio status, access and a claim to governing experience. It also ties him directly to an administration whose political standing has just suffered a major rebuke.

Bloomberg’s Alan Wickham reported that Rubio had spoken with White House officials about stepping down and had been asked to remain. According to people familiar with the internal deliberations, Rubio and his advisers were reviewing his options, but he had neither decided to leave nor established a timetable. The State Department disputed the central claim, denying that Rubio was thinking about resigning.

The disagreement matters. A reported internal discussion is not a resignation, and it does not establish Rubio’s motive. But the political logic is plain enough: departure has become an option worth discussing precisely when association with Trump may carry greater electoral liability and Trump’s endorsement has become less certain.

Loyalty with an expiration date

Rubio’s predicament is a product of the power structure he accepted. Trump has been able to treat the next Republican nomination as a succession he controls, testing Vance and Rubio against each other while reserving the right to delay his choice. Their ambitions remain subordinate to his timetable.

Now that Republicans have suffered an electoral defeat, Rubio faces a familiar problem for politicians who build their futures around personal loyalty to a dominant leader: they must eventually decide whether to share responsibility for the leader’s failures or attempt a separation that itself looks opportunistic.

Nothing in the reporting establishes that Rubio will resign, run in 2028 or openly distance himself from Trump. What has changed is the reported nature of his calculation. Earlier accounts cast him as a contender waiting for Trump to hand him an unobstructed route to the nomination. The latest reporting casts him as an official considering the exits while Trump, after an electoral wipeout, declines to guarantee anyone the inheritance.

item.title: MAGA media in death spiral while 'Never-Trump' sites are booming
item.description:
The clearest answer is not that MAGA media is dying while anti-Trump conservatism triumphs. It is that one media business built around interpreting Donald Trump’s coalition expects $30 million in revenue this year, while major right-wing outlets built to feed that coalition have suffered steep audience losses. The difference matters: The Bulwark has turned conservative estrangement from Trump into a durable subscription product, while publishers that relied on harvesting partisan attention are discovering how little loyalty an outrage machine buys when its audience loses interest.

According to Puck reporter Dylan Byers, publisher Sarah Longwell’s operation is expanding rather than preparing for Trump’s departure. The Bulwark’s wager is that the political constituency it serves — conservatives alienated by Trump, centrists seeking Republican interpreters, and liberals who value credentialed dissent from the right — will outlast the president who brought that audience together.

The profitable business of Republican exile

Longwell launched The Bulwark in 2018 as a home for center-right opponents of Trump, including figures from the defunct Weekly Standard. Its roster includes Bill Kristol and Tim Miller, conservatives whose break with the Republican Party made them familiar presences on cable television.

That positioning gives The Bulwark a useful role in the political-media economy. Its writers can explain the Republican coalition to an audience outside it while retaining the authority of former insiders. Longwell’s polling and focus-group work with Trump voters adds reporting value beyond televised indignation: the publication is selling access to a political world its readers may fear, oppose or struggle to understand.

Longwell told Byers that she rejects the assumption that The Bulwark’s relevance ends with Trump.

“The Bulwark transcends the Trump moment. We have been built to be durable, and I’m going to continue to build it to be durable.”

The reported revenue supports her confidence. So does Puck’s observation that Longwell appears reluctant to sell despite a media market favorable to investment. The publication is not merely a protest newsletter waiting for its antagonist to leave. It is an institution whose identity, audience and commercial prospects were forged by the Republican Party’s transformation.

That does not make The Bulwark politically neutral, nor does it prove that its preferred version of conservatism is returning. Its success shows something narrower: there is a paying audience for conservatives who can describe Trumpism without flattering it. A lucrative refuge for Republican dissent is not the same thing as a revived anti-Trump Republican electorate.

The click machine loses its audience

The numbers reported for pro-Trump media are far less forgiving. Citing data from conservative-news aggregator TheRighting, the New York Sun reported in June that 90 percent of leading right-wing sites lost visits between May 2025 and May 2026. Every one of the 20 largest sites it monitored posted a double-digit decline.

The losses extended well beyond marginal MAGA blogs. Traffic fell by 47 percent at the Daily Wire, 46 percent at Blaze and 52 percent at the Federalist. Visits declined 38 percent at the Washington Free Beacon and 33 percent at the Daily Caller.

Bloomberg also reported a 28 percent decline in Fox News’s prime-time audience ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, describing it as a possible sign of reduced conservative enthusiasm about the contests. That evidence supports a serious contraction in attention. It does not, by itself, establish why each audience shrank or whether every outlet faces the same underlying problem.

AlterNet nevertheless packages those declines as a “death spiral” for MAGA media and ties them to Trump entering his political “final act.” The traffic figures are substantial; the prophecy is less secure. Falling visits over a defined year and weakening television viewership before an election can demonstrate audience erosion. They cannot establish that Trump’s movement, or the media apparatus serving it, is approaching extinction.

Attention was the asset, not allegiance

The more defensible political judgment is also the more revealing one. Publishers built around constant Trump-centered stimulation made themselves dependent on the emotional intensity surrounding a single political figure. They treated anger, grievance and spectacle as renewable resources. The reported traffic collapse exposes the weakness of that model: an audience trained to chase the next provocation can also stop clicking when the product becomes repetitive or the politics becomes demoralizing.

The Bulwark made a different bet, but it remains tied to the same political system. MAGA outlets monetize identification with Trump; The Bulwark monetizes alarm about what Trump did to the Republican Party. One sells affirmation to the movement’s participants, while the other sells interpretation to its opponents and defectors. Both businesses emerged from Trump’s dominance of American political attention.

That is why the contrast should not be mistaken for a clean transfer of power from extremist propaganda to sober conservatism. The reported figures concern media consumption and revenue, not control of the Republican Party. The Bulwark may be thriving precisely because the faction it represents lost that institutional struggle. Its contributors have influence as analysts and television guests, but Trump and his allies remade the party they once inhabited.

The declining outlets still retain platforms, wealthy proprietors and access to a political movement with substantial institutional power. The Bulwark’s growth proves that dissent from Trump can sustain a successful publication. It does not prove that the forces its writers oppose have been displaced.

The sharper story, then, is not a morality play in which responsible conservatives prosper while MAGA collapses. It is a market correction inside a political media industry that spent years converting Trump into clicks. The Bulwark appears better prepared for the day attention shifts because it built a broader product around the rupture he created. The pro-Trump sites now losing traffic built their businesses as though the rupture itself would remain endlessly exciting.

item.title: Dems coming after insurers behind Trump’s purge of 760,000 Americans
item.description:
A dozen Democratic senators are preparing to use their incoming congressional majorities to investigate how the Trump administration and 10 private insurers canceled Affordable Care Act coverage for 760,000 people in late August. The inquiry, launched before the midterm elections, now carries the prospect of subpoenas and public hearings—and could expose whether the administration’s fraud campaign removed legitimate enrollees through a process insurers helped execute.

The central question is not whether improper ACA enrollment exists. It does. The question is whether federal officials used fraud as an evidentiary finding or as a political label broad enough to justify mass cancellation without reliably distinguishing fabricated accounts from eligible people who missed a message, lacked certain data, or had not yet used their insurance.

Insurers turned nonresponse into names for cancellation

The operation began in June, when the administration directed insurers to contact more than 1 million people whose enrollments it considered suspicious. Insurers returned the names of policyholders who failed to answer emails, calls, or letters within 30 days to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. By late August, 760,000 policies had been canceled.

That process made private insurers operational partners in a federal purge. The senators want to know whether proper removal procedures were followed, how many eligible people lost coverage, and whether the administration’s targeting criteria actually identified fraud.

Those criteria reportedly included missing Social Security numbers or other information, receiving a full subsidy, not having used medical benefits, and failing to respond to outreach. None of those circumstances, standing alone, establishes that an enrollee is fictitious or knowingly obtained coverage improperly. Treating them as substitutes for proof shifts the burden onto people with less institutional power: answer correctly and quickly, or lose health insurance.

The senators sent 28 questions to Elevance Health, Cigna, Oscar Health, AmeriHealth Caritas, Centene, Florida Blue, Health Care Service Corporation, Imperial Insurance Companies, Molina Healthcare, and UnitedHealthcare. The companies had until November 6 to respond. By November 10, a spokesperson for Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden reported “varying levels of responsiveness.”

That phrase will acquire sharper meaning when Wyden is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee in January. Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders, another leader of the inquiry, is expected to take control of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. As Georgetown health-law expert Katie Keith told the outlet, insurers now face lawmakers able to subpoena records and convene hearings—not merely send letters executives can answer selectively.

CMS declared “phantom accounts” before showing its work

CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz defended the cancellations at an October 14 press conference by asserting that the government had “already determined” the affected policies were “760,000 phantom accounts.”

“That is fraud, we believe,” Oz said, blaming brokers for manufacturing accounts without Social Security numbers. He claimed officials had tried repeatedly to reach the enrollees: “We call, we write, we send carrier pigeons—like, no one answers.”

The flourish obscures the evidentiary problem. Failure to respond may support further investigation; it does not itself prove that 760,000 people do not exist, did not authorize enrollment, or were ineligible. Oz’s own phrasing—“fraud, we believe”—also sits uneasily beside his categorical claim that CMS had already determined every canceled account was phantom.

CMS told KFF Health News that fewer than 0.01% of those removed had contacted the federal marketplace seeking reinstatement. That figure does not resolve whether the cancellations were accurate. The agency had not released details establishing whether everyone affected knew coverage had ended. Silence after cancellation is no more conclusive than silence during a 30-day outreach period, particularly when the consequence at issue is the loss of a policy rather than an immediately visible government payment.

The administration’s operation is continuing. Another 419,000 ACA enrollments remain under review in a second phase. Some applicants must now complete additional online identity checks, while insurers received October guidance asking them to identify suspicious conduct by agents and brokers and consider measures including withholding commissions. Whether any insurer followed that voluntary guidance was unclear in the reporting.

Courts have blocked other pieces of the administration’s broader campaign, including heightened income verification for certain low-income enrollees and a moratorium that could have prevented as many as 19,000 new agents from assisting consumers during open enrollment. The administration nevertheless retains substantial authority to pursue cancellations through executive action.

“Fraud” is doing political work

Improper enrollment can include invented identities, incorrect data, manipulated income estimates, unauthorized sign-ups by brokers seeking commissions, or people unknowingly placed into plans. But acknowledging those problems does not validate the administration’s scale estimates or its chosen remedy.

Conservative groups argue that enhanced subsidies created incentives for abuse by making more plans available at no monthly premium. Brian Blase, president of the Paragon Health Institute, predicted Congress would find that the cancellation program contained adequate safeguards and called it “commonsense good governance.” His organization has argued that low use of insurance can indicate widespread improper enrollment.

But not using a policy is not proof that its holder is fictitious. Insurance exists precisely because people cannot predict when they will need care. Converting nonuse into suspicion allows the government to recast ordinary enrollment patterns as evidence against the insured.

The Trump administration and Republican candidates promoted fraud claims while Democrats campaigned on health-care affordability. The political utility is plain: if enrollment can be portrayed primarily as a pool of cheats, brokers’ inventions, and waste, removing people from coverage becomes enforcement rather than retrenchment. Those who lose insurance disappear behind the allegation made against the category.

Democratic senators described that strategy more bluntly, accusing Republicans of “weaponizing fraud falsehoods” to weaken the ACA marketplace and remove more people from coverage. The investigation will need to establish the narrower and more consequential facts beneath that charge: who designed the screening standards, what insurers knew about their reliability, how CMS reviewed returned names, and how many valid enrollments the dragnet captured.

Oversight can expose the machinery, not necessarily stop it

Democratic control of Congress changes the balance of investigative power but not the location of executive authority. Jonathan Oberlander, a University of North Carolina health-policy professor, said lawmakers cannot simply prevent the administration from canceling policies under its asserted anti-fraud powers. Stopping the operation legislatively would require a measure capable of surviving a presidential veto or inclusion in a larger budget agreement.

That leaves oversight as both a meaningful tool and a limited one. Hearings and subpoenas could force disclosure of the administration’s criteria, internal deliberations, error rates, reinstatement process, and communications with insurers. They could also establish whether companies merely complied with federal instructions or helped construct a system that treated missed outreach as grounds for erasing coverage.

Democrats also plan to seek restoration of the enhanced ACA subsidies that expired at the end of 2025. Marketplace enrollment for 2026 stood at about 19 million, down from nearly 22 million in 2025. Restoring the subsidies faces political obstacles, and an unsuccessful vote would not replace anyone’s insurance.

For the 760,000 people already removed—and the 419,000 still under scrutiny—the immediate issue is less abstract. The administration has presented a mass cancellation as a completed fraud finding while withholding the detail necessary to test that claim. Insurers supplied the names. Congress will soon have the authority to compel both sides to explain exactly how nonresponse became guilt.

item.title: Trump suffers 'vulnpocalypse' of competence — and Americans have had enough
item.description:
A five-day run of disruptions affecting flights, banking, email and government communications has exposed a Trump administration unable to provide either a convincing explanation or credible reassurance. AlterNet describes the episode as a “vulnpocalypse,” but the reporting establishes something narrower and more consequential: essential systems were failing, senior officials responded with indifference and speculation, and the FBI did not open an investigation until the interruptions had persisted for five consecutive days.

The outages may have damaged public confidence, but AlterNet offers no polling to establish that Americans “have had enough.” Its stronger case lies in the administration’s conduct. President Donald Trump publicly said he did not care about the interruptions, according to the outlet, while his own travel and bank access remained unaffected. That is not proof of a national revolt. It is evidence of a president treating failures that disrupt other people’s lives as somebody else’s problem.

Reassurance without an explanation

The administration reportedly offered assurances that the disruptions were not part of an organized cyberattack or coordinated effort to probe American systems. Yet the account supplies no corresponding technical explanation for what caused them.

That gap matters because the government’s cyber defenses had already been weakened by Trump administration firings, AlterNet reports. Officials were therefore asking the public to trust a conclusion from an apparatus the administration itself had diminished. Whether the outages resulted from hostile activity, copycats, routine denial-of-service attacks or unrelated technical failures remained unresolved in the reporting.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin filled that vacuum with conjecture. Based on a single conversation with what he called “a technology expert,” Mullin speculated that artificial intelligence might be outpacing conventional programming and producing backups severe enough to interrupt services. The article also cites reports of people using ChatGPT to search for ways into other computers, but it does not connect those reports to these outages.

Artificial intelligence thus became a convenient possibility before investigators had supplied a cause. Officials could gesture toward an emerging and poorly understood technology while avoiding the more immediate question: why did institutions paid to protect critical systems fail, and why did the federal response take so long to become investigative rather than rhetorical?

Officials insulated from the breakdown

Mullin’s behavior sharpened the contrast between public disruption and official privilege. During the nationwide airport scramble, AlterNet reports, he used a federal jet to attend a college football game and sat with a lobbyist who conducts business with his department.

The significance is not that one official watched football during a crisis. It is that the official responsible for Homeland Security reportedly enjoyed government transportation while ordinary travelers confronted delays and cancellations—and did so alongside someone with a financial interest in his department’s decisions. That arrangement invites scrutiny even without evidence that the lobbyist received any favor.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, meanwhile, responded by demanding $50 billion for airport work extending beyond the safety-related conversion of aging electronics to digital systems. AlterNet characterizes the demand as extortionist and reports that several Republican senators reacted poorly to it. Whatever upgrades airports need, using an unfolding disruption to press for a vastly broader spending package substitutes leverage for an accounting of failure.

Trump’s reported indifference completes the picture. The president was more engaged, AlterNet argues, in defying a court order so he could build a golf course on national parkland in Washington than in systems affecting Americans’ ability to work, pay bills or reach family events. The contrast is politically revealing because presidential attention is itself an exercise of power: it tells agencies what matters, officials what will be rewarded and the public whose inconvenience counts.

A crisis of credibility, not a proven “no confidence” vote

AlterNet ties the outages to unfavorable midterm results and continuing complaints about Trump family enrichment, health care, measles, war and diplomacy. Those issues may form part of a broader judgment about the administration, but the article moves too quickly from signs of discontent to a declaration that public trust has collapsed across the country.

There is no survey in the supplied reporting measuring confidence in the administration’s response to these interruptions. Nor does the account establish that the outages shared a cause or were too coordinated to be coincidental. Calling the episode a “vulnpocalypse,” as the Drudge Report did, captures the atmosphere of exposure; it does not diagnose the systems involved.

The more defensible indictment does not require inflated certainty. Americans watched critical services fail while the president reportedly dismissed the consequences, the homeland security secretary traveled to a football game and speculated from one expert conversation, the transportation secretary sought $50 billion, and federal investigators waited until the fifth consecutive day of interruptions to act.

Those are decisions by people with institutional authority, not an impersonal evaporation of “Trust.” The unanswered question is whether the FBI investigation will identify a common cause. The answer already supplied by the administration’s conduct is that the people in charge did not need certainty about the threat to display urgency—and chose not to.

item.title: Ron Johnson doubles down under fire after saying the quiet part out loud
item.description:
Sen. Ron Johnson did not merely insult Social Security from the sidelines. The Wisconsin Republican, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee and sits on the committees overseeing finance and aging, called the program “grotesque” and a “Ponzi scheme” in a Fox Business interview, then said, “you can’t fix it, you just shut it down and hope that you can recover some of your money.” Hours later, according to AlterNet, he used a Budget Committee hearing on Social Security’s future to repeat the “Ponzi scheme” attack.

The significance lies in Johnson’s power, not simply his language. He helps control the congressional machinery that can protect, restructure or weaken the retirement system. When an official in that position describes Social Security as inherently fraudulent and beyond repair, the remark reveals how at least one powerful Republican approaches a program tens of millions of Americans depend upon.

Denial after repetition

Johnson repeated the characterization when Alex Lawson of Social Security Works confronted him outside the hearing, the organization’s president, Nancy Altman, wrote for AlterNet. After a day of criticism online and from Senate Democrats, Johnson insisted that he had never said he wanted to eliminate Social Security.

That defense cannot erase his recorded formulation. Johnson paired “shut it down” with the claim that the system cannot be fixed. His later denial may dispute how listeners interpreted those words, but it does not make the words disappear.

Johnson then introduced legislation bearing the exquisitely evasive name “Stop Scaring Seniors Act.” The proposal would authorize the use of general federal revenue to finance Social Security. Naming the bill after the fear surrounding benefit cuts shifts attention from the officials empowered to impose those cuts to the people warning beneficiaries about them. Johnson generated the alarm by describing the system as irreparable; his bill’s title treats the resulting scrutiny as the offense.

Altman argues that moving Social Security toward general-revenue financing would weaken one of its central political defenses: the program is financed separately and does not add to the federal deficit. Once folded into ordinary budget politics, its benefits could become more exposed to deficit-cutting campaigns and recurring funding confrontations.

That concern is not detached from Johnson’s record. In 2022, he advocated moving Social Security spending into the discretionary budget, where Congress could reconsider it during annual appropriations battles. His new proposal is not identical, but it points toward the same political terrain: retirement benefits subjected more directly to lawmakers who routinely manufacture fiscal crises.

The shortfall presents a choice, not an inevitability

Social Security faces a funding shortfall around 2032 that, absent congressional action, would trigger an automatic benefit reduction of more than 20 percent, according to Altman. That outcome is not an unavoidable mechanical failure. Congress writes the financing rules and has the authority to change them.

The existing structure stops collecting Social Security contributions once a worker’s annual income exceeds $184,500. Altman points to a Democratic alternative that would require wealthy Americans to contribute on income above that threshold, including investment income. The Social Security Expansion Act, sponsored by Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, would use additional revenue not only to avert cuts but also to increase benefits by $200 a month, with further increases for some vulnerable groups.

No Republican senator has co-sponsored that legislation, although Altman notes that Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno has expressed openness to changing the contribution cap. That leaves the dispute in concrete terms: Congress can raise more revenue from affluent households, reduce benefits, expose the program to annual budget warfare, or produce another proposal. Calling Social Security a scam obscures those choices by portraying a politically constructed financing problem as proof that the institution itself is illegitimate.

Altman reports that only 2 percent of Americans support any benefit reduction. Whatever the precise electoral consequences, that opposition explains why Republican officials often deny plans to cut Social Security even as figures such as Johnson promote mechanisms that could make cuts easier. The public sales pitch is protection; the governing architecture creates vulnerability.

A powerful official protects the wrong party from scrutiny

Altman also reports that Johnson is worth about $40 million. His wealth does not by itself establish why he favors a particular policy. It does, however, sharpen the distributive question his rhetoric avoids. The Democratic proposal would collect more from people with high earnings and investment income. Johnson’s approach leaves that option untouched while changing how the program can be funded—and potentially how it can be attacked.

That is the misdirection at the center of the episode. Social Security beneficiaries did not create the statutory contribution ceiling. Seniors did not assign committee gavels or decide which revenues Congress would collect. Lawmakers did. Yet Johnson describes the program as the swindle, as though an institution built by Congress had somehow deceived the officials who control its rules.

Johnson’s fellow Republicans need not endorse the phrase “shut it down” to enable the policy direction behind it. They can establish their position through votes: support additional revenue, offer a workable alternative or block legislation and accept the resulting risk of benefit cuts. Silence and slogans preserve ambiguity, but legislative power eventually requires a choice.

Johnson briefly dispensed with that ambiguity. Then, facing the predictable consequences, he tried to relocate the scandal from what he said to the people who heard him clearly.
