item.title: MAGA is already whining about Grand Theft Auto’s female lead
item.description:
Grand Theft Auto’s first female lead has provoked a familiar grievance campaign from right-wing commentators who decided, before playing the game, that putting Lucia Caminos behind the wheel would make the franchise “woke.” Their complaints arrived as the new installment reportedly posted enormous early sales and strong reviews, making the backlash less a consumer revolt than an attempt to police who is permitted to occupy the center of a mass-market story.

The verdict came before the game

Markus Meechan, the Scottish YouTuber known as Count Dankula and a former UK Independence Party election candidate, told The Times there was “definitely” a risk that Grand Theft Auto would become too woke because of its female protagonist. He predicted that the male character would be portrayed as incompetent while Lucia repeatedly rescued him.

That was speculation presented as diagnosis. Meechan, who has more than a million YouTube subscribers and was fined in 2018 over a video showing his girlfriend’s dog performing a Nazi salute, did not identify a played scene establishing this supposed dynamic in the account reported by The Times.

Other commentators dispensed with even that thin pretense. Before the release, AndyPantsGaming called the game “girl boss slop” and claimed Rockstar Games was staffed by “a bunch of fat white women.” Sargon of Akkad complained that players would have to “deal with” a female protagonist in what he predicted would be “Grand Theft Auto for women.”

The point was not criticism of the game’s mechanics, writing or design. The objection was the woman herself. A franchise built around theft, armed robbery and indiscriminate violence apparently crossed a line when it gave a female character narrative authority.

An invented takeover meets Rockstar’s workforce

The suggestion that women have captured Rockstar is especially strained by the company’s reported employment figures. Women represented 18.4 percent of its workforce in April 2025, according to The Times, up from 15.7 percent in 2019. That is an increase of 2.7 percentage points, but it still leaves women a small minority inside the company.

This is how the grievance economy manufactures dispossession: modest representation becomes domination, and one female lead after decades of male-centered storytelling becomes proof that men are being displaced. The language of consumer preference disguises a demand for cultural control. Women may appear, but they are not supposed to drive—literally in this case, and narratively in every other sense.

Game writer Rhianna Pratchett put Rockstar’s decision in its less hysterical context. “Lara Croft has been around for 30 years so a game having a female protagonist is hardly new,” she told The Times, adding that Rockstar was “a little behind the curve” in placing women at the center of its stories.

Developer Gisela Vaquero described what distinguishes Lucia’s role: “She drives both the car and the narrative.” Lucia is not decorative representation attached to someone else’s adventure. She helps shape the story. That agency, more than her mere presence, is what the backlash treats as an intrusion.

The audience did not follow the outrage merchants

The campaign appears to have failed at its most basic commercial task. The Times reported that the game was on course to break records after going on sale at midnight following a 13-year wait. Sensor Tower estimated that 19.1 million copies had sold by Thursday morning, producing roughly $1.84 billion in revenue. The reported total was more than twice the $800 million earned by the previous installment on its opening day in 2013.

Those figures do not establish what every buyer thinks about Lucia, but they do show that the loud predictions of a market poisoned by female leadership did not translate into the collapse these commentators implied. Critics were also enthusiastic, according to the report.

AlterNet widens the story into a claim about women’s growing disillusionment with MAGA politics, citing Intelligencer reporting on young women encountering the far right’s “valorized” sexism. The connection is plausible but should not be overstated: one video-game release does not explain women’s political or religious behavior. What the episode does expose is the underlying political habit. Influencers convert the diminished cultural monopoly of men into a story of male persecution, then monetize the resentment.

Lucia Caminos did not seize an institution from men. She became the first woman to lead one installment of a nearly three-decade-old franchise. The people calling that intolerable were not uncovering a hostile takeover. They were demonstrating how little change is required before a movement organized around male entitlement begins to howl about its own imagined exclusion.

item.title: Hecklers batter MAGA city council’s mandatory prayer with squirrels
item.description:
Battle Ground’s Christian nationalist city council wanted prayer embedded in public meetings. Residents answered with a giant squirrel.

At a council meeting in the southwest Washington city, a protester wearing a squirrel mask delivered an invocation to an “omnipresent all-knowing” rodent, invoked the “harsh cold winters of theocratic silliness,” and offered a ceremonial “holy snackrament.” The performance was absurd by design. It exposed the council’s prayer policy as an exercise of government power that becomes much less comfortable for its sponsors when the same platform is available to beliefs they do not share.

The headline’s description of “mandatory prayer” overstates what AlterNet’s account establishes. The reporting does not say residents were compelled to pray. It says the council, over local opposition, made invocations an unavoidable part of its meetings. That distinction matters: the documented problem is not forced worship, but officials using a civic forum to institutionalize a religious ritual.

The squirrel was invited by the policy

AlterNet, citing Friendly Atheist, reports that a more “Trumpified” and fundamentalist council added prayer before meetings after Christian nationalist members gained dominance. Protesters have since used the invocation period to challenge the policy on its own terms; Satanists had appeared at earlier meetings, while the latest reported protest substituted a furry rodent deity.

“All hail the squirrel in her omnipresent all-knowing grandeur,” the masked speaker began. He asked the squirrel for strength against oppression, offered audience members’ souls for purification through the “ancient rite of the holy snackrament,” and encouraged council members to take that sacrament into their mouths to experience the animal’s warmth and love.

The joke worked because the council had already made the underlying argument for him. Once officials create an invocation forum that cannot be reserved exclusively for Christianity, they must confront the pluralism they tried to manage from the dais. A ritual meant to confer solemnity and religious authority on council business instead became a stage for mocking the presumption that government meetings require divine endorsement.

Friendly Atheist summarized the bargain bluntly: “They wanted invocations? They got invocations.” The publication argued that officials should expect more performances of this kind unless they eliminate a practice that serves no civic function.

Public power, private faith

The important conflict is not between conservative Christians and a man in a squirrel mask. Only one side controls the meeting agenda.

Residents can heckle, satirize and exploit whatever access the policy leaves open. Council members decide whether a religious observance occupies official time in the first place. Treating the episode primarily as culture-war spectacle risks misdirecting attention toward the flamboyant protest while letting the exercise of institutional power fade into the background.

The squirrel invocation did not intrude on a neutral chamber. It responded to elected officials who had already altered that chamber by placing prayer inside the machinery of municipal government. The protesters’ tactic turned the council’s preference into a practical dilemma: tolerate invocations its Christian nationalist members may find ridiculous or objectionable, or reveal that the policy was never really about religious expression in general.

That does not make every invocation equivalent in belief or intent. The squirrel ceremony was plainly parody. But parody is especially effective here because it tests whether officials defend a neutral rule or merely expect public institutions to ratify their own theology.

A changing district behind the spectacle

Battle Ground sits north of Portland in Washington’s 18th Legislative District, an area AlterNet describes as a longtime Republican stronghold that has recently moved toward Democrats. NPR reported that conservative Christianity remains highly visible in and around the city, where churches appear every few blocks, even as families relocate from the Portland metropolitan area in search of more affordable housing.

Democratic consultant Dean Nielsen attributed the political shift to suburbanization. The district, he said, had been Republican through most of his 30 years in politics, but newer residents include young families alienated by the national Republican social agenda and Donald Trump in particular.

AlterNet also reports that Republican state representatives John Ley, Stephanie McClintock, Kevin Waters and David Stuebe lost to Democratic challengers during the midterms. The article does not supply the election date, so those results should not be treated as a fresh development. They do, however, provide context for the local struggle: broader electoral change can remove state legislators while low-turnout municipal contests still leave ideologically committed factions with direct control over public institutions.

That is where Christian nationalism often becomes concrete—not as an abstract debate about national identity, but as an agenda item approved by officials with enough votes. Battle Ground’s protesters cannot repeal the council’s policy from the microphone. What they can do is deny its sponsors the dignified religious monopoly they appeared to expect.

The council placed prayer in the meeting. The squirrel merely demonstrated whom that invitation had to include.

item.title: Trump proves he’s 'lost touch with the real world' once and for all
item.description:
President Donald Trump responded to a week of disruptive technology failures with a shrug. Asked during a trip through Asia whether he was concerned about outages affecting Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, Chase Bank and other major institutions, Trump said: “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

The breakdowns described by AlterNet were not fine. They suspended air travel, disrupted communications and logistics, damaged economic activity and left some Americans stockpiling cash and supplies. Yet the official with the greatest political authority treated the failures as background noise—not as a governing problem requiring explanation, coordination or repair.

A crisis met with fatalism

MS NOW political columnist Zeeshan Aleem called Trump’s response evidence that the president is “staggeringly out of touch.” The more immediate problem is not simply Trump’s personal detachment. It is what his answer says about how he exercises power.

A president cannot personally repair a bank’s systems or diagnose an airline’s software. He can demand answers from federal agencies, direct officials to assess national-security risks, communicate what the government knows and mobilize resources against further disruption. Trump instead described systemic failure as an inevitable feature of life.

That fatalism is politically convenient. If severe outages merely “happen,” nobody has to answer for fragile infrastructure, weak safeguards or an inadequate government response. A failure demanding investigation becomes an inconvenience the public is expected to absorb.

The disruptions were unusual enough to provoke legitimate questions about whether they were connected, whether artificial intelligence or cyberattacks played a role and whether more failures might follow. According to the account, Friday’s FAA ground stop was only the second since the September 11 attacks. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy struggled to explain what had occurred, while the clustering of outages fueled public suspicion that coincidence might not be an adequate explanation.

Those suspicions are not proof of a common cause. They are, however, a reason for the administration to establish facts rather than wave away concern.

Wealth does not excuse failure

Trump’s claim that breakdowns are natural when an institution is “big and powerful” and has “all the money” reverses the ordinary logic of public capacity. Wealth and power provide the resources to build redundancy, employ specialists, maintain infrastructure and recover quickly. They create responsibility, not an exemption from it.

Aleem suggested that Trump’s “you” may have referred less to the affected institutions than to Trump himself: a wealthy and powerful man insulated from the consequences of failed services. That is an interpretation, but it fits the political hierarchy exposed by the remark. A grounded flight, inaccessible bank account or severed communications link can upend an ordinary person’s work, finances or safety. For someone surrounded by government transport, staff and security, the same breakdown can remain an abstraction.

Calling the outages “fine” transfers their costs downward. Executives and senior officials retain their mobility and institutional protection; travelers, workers and customers lose time, money and access. Trump’s language erased that distribution of harm while presenting elite insulation as evidence that no urgent problem existed.

The administration still owes an explanation

AlterNet’s account says determining what went wrong—and strengthening the country’s digital infrastructure against another wave of failures—will require substantial expertise and effort. That work begins with recognizing the event as a problem.

Aleem’s sharpest point was therefore less about tone than purpose: “‘Things happen’ is not what you say when you are looking for a solution.” Trump did not identify a cause, describe a federal response or tell the public when answers might come. He converted an unresolved infrastructure crisis into a fact of nature.

The outages may ultimately prove unrelated; the supplied reporting does not establish their cause. But the president’s response is already clear. At the moment when the government needed to distinguish coincidence from coordination, malfunction from attack and inconvenience from systemic vulnerability, Trump offered the governing philosophy of the insulated: the systems failed, other people suffered, and therefore everything was fine.

item.title: The real crisis isn’t the glitches —it’s the Soviet-style lies nobody believes
item.description:
A cascade of failures across the systems Americans rely on—from air travel and banking to email and classified communications—has produced no public proof of a coordinated attack. The deeper crisis, as AlterNet argues, is that the Trump administration has exhausted the credibility required to reassure anyone that these were isolated technical problems. When officials with a record of falsehood and concealment say “glitch,” even members of the president’s own party hear something else.

The reported sequence was extraordinary. The National Security Agency’s classified internal network went offline, an outage the agency attributed to scheduled maintenance. A day earlier, a software problem reportedly blocked Chase customers from accessing their money while hackers inserted malicious code into the websites of 178 major organizations. That followed an FAA stoppage of airline departures nationwide and a worldwide failure of Microsoft’s email system, amid other disruptions involving Apple, Wells Fargo and Charles Schwab.

Asked about the failures in Manila, President Donald Trump offered no explanation and little concern. “It’s life,” he said.

That shrug did nothing to resolve the obvious question: coincidence, institutional decay or hostile action? The supplied reporting establishes no answer. But the administration’s insistence that the disruptions were ordinary accidents now competes with the distrust its own conduct has cultivated.

Even Trump’s allies are rejecting the reassurance

Republican Sen. Josh Hawley called the cluster of incidents potentially “the greatest coincidence in the history of the world” and said the claim that a malfunctioning router could disable the national air-traffic system was “a little hard to believe.”

Hawley did not present evidence of sabotage. His remark matters for another reason: a Republican senator publicly signaled that explanations coming from Trump’s executive branch no longer command automatic belief.

That is the political consequence of treating official communication as an instrument of obedience rather than a public obligation. The Washington Post documented 30,573 false or misleading claims during Trump’s first administration, according to AlterNet. The article also reports that administration nominees appearing before the Senate have refused to state that Joe Biden won the 2020 election. The point is not merely that Trump lies. It is that loyalty to his lies has become a test for officials seeking power under him.

Once a government makes factual surrender a condition of advancement, truthful statements lose their institutional backing. The public is then left to guess whether an official explanation reflects evidence, political convenience or fear of contradicting the president.

A credibility deficit built by officials

AlterNet points to two more episodes that have damaged the administration’s standing. It reports that officials labeled Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old ICU nurse at a Veterans Affairs hospital, a “domestic terrorist” after he was killed by ICE; Vice President JD Vance called him an “assassin.” According to the article, those characterizations were not retracted.

The publication also cites New York Times reporting that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Pentagon officials concealed the extent of deaths and damage from Iranian strikes on U.S. forces and facilities. It further cites The Intercept’s finding that the official casualty tally fell far short of more than 900 service members reportedly killed or wounded. Those are attributed claims, not findings independently established by the supplied material. But they illustrate why routine assurances about routers, maintenance and software bugs now meet suspicion.

This does not prove that officials lied about the recent outages. Nor does the proximity of several failures establish coordination. Modern infrastructure is tightly connected, software is fragile, and attackers can exploit vulnerabilities quickly. The administration’s credibility problem is not evidence of a cyberattack; it is the reason plausible explanations fail to settle the matter.

Washington weakened the agency charged with watching the systems

Distrust becomes more consequential when paired with decisions that reduce the government’s ability to prevent and investigate cyber failures. AlterNet reports that Trump and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency pushed out roughly one-third of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s workforce. It says the administration eliminated CISA’s “Red Team,” whose specialists searched government systems for weaknesses before adversaries could exploit them, while congressional Republicans sought another $707 million cut to the agency.

Those are choices made by people with institutional power, not mysterious malfunctions. If the government dismisses cyber defenders, dismantles specialized testing capacity and reduces the remaining agency’s budget, it makes critical infrastructure harder to protect regardless of what caused this particular series of outages.

The article also notes an earlier warning from U.S. intelligence agencies that Chinese government hackers had penetrated American communications, energy, transportation and water systems to prepare for possible disruption during a crisis. AlterNet says Trump ignored that warning. Against that background, demanding a serious investigation is not paranoia. Declaring without evidence that the week’s failures were a coordinated demonstration by China or Russia would be.

AlterNet itself crosses that line only as an explicitly fictional exercise, imagining Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping using the disruptions to coerce Trump over Ukraine and Taiwan. That scenario is speculation, not reporting. It should not be smuggled into the factual case. The established political indictment is already substantial: the administration weakened defensive institutions while its history of dishonesty made its subsequent reassurances less credible.

Secrecy creates the opening for conspiracy

Hawley and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries have demanded answers, according to AlterNet. Immediate public hearings could establish what failed, which warnings existed, how agencies responded and whether personnel cuts impaired prevention or recovery. They would also force officials to defend their explanations under scrutiny rather than repeat them from behind executive authority.

The article further raises National Security Presidential Memorandum 7, saying it has been used against protesters and to organize investigations of groups, nonprofits, individuals and writers characterized as “anti-capitalist, anti-Christian, and anti-American.” Its relevance here is not proof that the outages were engineered to justify emergency powers. No such evidence is supplied. The danger lies in a government expanding coercive machinery while weakening oversight and forfeiting public trust.

A state does not become credible by demanding that people stop noticing contradictions. Nor can congressional Republicans spend years enforcing submission to Trump and then act astonished when explanations from his administration are doubted. Democrats, for their part, hold enough institutional power to demand records, convene hearings where they control the relevant bodies and make obstruction visible where they do not.

Bad routers can be replaced. Software can be patched. Cybersecurity teams can be rebuilt, if the people controlling budgets and appointments choose to rebuild them. Restoring credibility is harder because it requires officials to abandon a political system in which demonstrable falsehoods are rewarded, correction is treated as betrayal and accountability begins only after the machinery stops working.

item.title: Republicans have only one choice left before Trump sinks them all
item.description:
Republicans’ remaining choice, as AlterNet columnist D. Earl Stephens frames it, is to abandon Donald Trump before his political collapse becomes theirs: stop defending him, permit impeachment to advance and supply the Senate votes needed to remove him. That conclusion follows Stephens’ account of a historic midterm repudiation, with Democrats emerging 12 seats ahead in the Senate and 85 ahead in the House after Trump urged voters to treat the election as a referendum on him.

The reported result matters because it would transfer institutional power, not merely momentum. A Democratic House could investigate Trump and impeach him. A commanding Senate majority would leave Republicans with a stark decision over conviction: continue protecting the president or provide the additional votes required to remove him. The break Stephens anticipates is therefore not an awakening of conscience. It is political self-preservation after voters made loyalty to Trump catastrophically expensive.

Trump demanded ownership of the election

Stephens reports that Trump repeatedly placed himself at the center of the midterm campaign, effectively asking Americans to vote as though his name appeared on every ballot. On the columnist’s account, they obliged—and punished the candidates who had spent a decade subordinating themselves to him.

The scale of the reported losses was extraordinary. Stephens says Democrats won Texas by 12 points, North Carolina by 20 and Georgia by 18, while Mississippi elected a Black senator. Those results, combined with the congressional margins he cites, would amount to more than a routine midterm correction. They would show the danger of constructing a party around one man’s resentments, legal exposure and demand for personal obedience.

Trump cannot reasonably claim sole credit when Republicans win and assign responsibility everywhere else when they lose. Yet Stephens says that was precisely his response: blame others, intensify the same politics of grievance and elevate Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. The lesson was not misunderstood. It was rejected.

Republican officials enabled this predicament. They confirmed Trump’s appointees, defended his conduct and treated submission to him as a qualification for office. Whatever electoral damage now follows is not something Trump inflicted on innocent bystanders. It is the foreseeable consequence of choices made by lawmakers and party leaders who possessed the power to resist him and repeatedly declined to use it.

Government failure followed personal loyalty

The electoral collapse described by Stephens arrived amid two conspicuous failures of governance. On Tuesday, 666 days into Trump’s second term, the United States lost its measles-elimination status from the Pan American Health Organization. The country was also recovering from an aviation breakdown that grounded thousands of planes.

Stephens connects those events to a Cabinet chosen for loyalty rather than competence, naming officials including Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Pam Bondi and Tulsi Gabbard. His language is polemical, but the political point is concrete: when a president treats the executive branch as a court of personal retainers, administrative failure is not separate from the governing model. It is one of its products.

The public consequences are not abstract. Losing measles-elimination status means a preventable disease again achieved sustained transmission. An aviation failure that strands thousands exposes the cost of dysfunction in systems people must trust with their safety and movement. A government organized around flattering its leader still has to administer public health and transportation. Loyalty cannot perform those functions.

During the airport disruption, Stephens reports, Trump was neither seen nor heard from publicly for four days. That absence is relevant because the president holds responsibility for the executive branch during a national operational failure. Stephens goes much further, speculating about Trump’s health and possible medical treatment without establishing those claims. That speculation weakens the case by substituting grotesque imagery for what the reported facts already show: the president was publicly absent while his administration failed thousands of travelers.

The stronger indictment is institutional, not anatomical. Trump built the administration, selected its senior officials and demanded that government revolve around him. His physical appearance does not explain those decisions, and dwelling on it offers Republicans an easy distraction from their own participation.

Removal would require Republican permission

Stephens expects House Democrats to pursue impeachment over Trump’s alleged misuse of public money and self-dealing. He predicts that evidence of financial abuse will make the case politically overwhelming. That remains a forecast in the column, not a completed investigation or adjudicated finding.

The power structure, however, is clear. Democrats could initiate the process with their reported House majority, but conviction would still require a two-thirds Senate vote. Even after a devastating election, Republicans would retain the capacity to decide whether Trump remains protected from removal.

That is why “only one choice” overstates the moral certainty while accurately describing the strategic pressure. Republicans have another choice: continue defending him. They have made it repeatedly. What changed, in Stephens’ telling, is the price. After the midterm rout, continued loyalty would mean tying the party’s next presidential campaign to a leader voters had just rejected on an unprecedented scale.

Stephens also anticipates that Rupert Murdoch’s media apparatus will eventually transfer its attention to another Republican contender. He says there are already signs Murdoch is prepared to leave Trump behind, though the column does not detail them. If that rupture comes, it will not erase the media system’s role in manufacturing and sustaining Trump’s power. Rebranding the product after it becomes electorally toxic is not accountability.

Nor would Republicans deserve credit merely for removing a president once protecting him ceased to benefit them. They supplied the votes, platforms and institutional compliance that allowed Trump to dominate the party. A late break would confirm the governing principle that brought them here: not fidelity to law or public duty, but obedience calibrated to political survival.

The question after the losses Stephens reports is not whether Republicans can recognize that Trump has become a liability. It is whether enough of them will act before the next election—or wait until abandoning him becomes the final available method of saving themselves.

item.title: 'He's here but not here': Trump biographer spills the beans on the president
item.description:
Michael Wolff’s answer to the question hanging over Donald Trump’s latest political defeat is blunt: the president is physically present but increasingly unable to grasp what has happened around him. People close to Trump described him as “here but not here,” Wolff told AlterNet, after watching him respond to disastrous midterm returns with misplaced optimism, selective memory and a retreat into the one result he could still treat as a victory.

That account is not a medical diagnosis. It is a political warning about a president whose power remains immense even as associates reportedly question his ability to process setbacks—and whose staff, rather than confronting him with reality, reinforce the version he prefers.

Defeat, translated into victory

As the midterm results deteriorated for Republicans, Trump reportedly insisted the outcome was “not so bad” and claimed the party was doing “much better than they thought we would do.” According to Wolff, an aide identified as Harp answered, “So much better.”

That exchange captures more than Trump’s familiar appetite for flattery. The people surrounding a president control what information reaches him, how forcefully it is presented and whether obvious falsehoods are challenged. In Wolff’s telling, Trump’s aides did not correct his interpretation of the returns. They helped sustain it.

Trump then narrowed his attention to Florida, the principal Republican bright spot identified in the account, apart from Memphis-area districts the article says Republicans had gerrymandered. “It’s all about Florida,” he repeatedly said, before revisiting his 2016 victory there and declaring that he had transformed the state permanently.

The maneuver was characteristic: isolate favorable evidence, discard the broader result and convert political repudiation into personal mythology. But Wolff argues that something has changed. What once functioned as aggressive message discipline now appears, to some people around Trump, to be a failure of comprehension. Sources quoted by Wolff said Trump “really doesn’t get it,” had “left the building” and might still not understand what the midterms meant.

The courtiers still have agency

Wolff describes an 80-year-old president who is overweight, clumsy and visibly aging, citing public sleepiness, mumbling, unusual sounds during speeches and conversations with people close to him. He suggests Trump may have experienced undisclosed health problems and portrays the election loss as a psychological blow.

Those observations support scrutiny; they do not establish a clinical conclusion. Terms such as “trauma,” “PTSD” and “inner collapse,” as used in the account, remain characterizations by Wolff and his sources. The reported conduct is politically significant without converting speculation into medicine.

The sharper institutional question concerns the officials enabling the behavior. A diminished president does not exercise power alone. Aides choose whether to correct him. Cabinet officers decide whether to indulge him. Party leaders determine whether his inability—or refusal—to absorb electoral reality matters more than their access to the presidency.

Calling them lackeys may describe their posture, but it can also obscure their responsibility. They are not furniture in Trump’s decline. If Wolff’s account is accurate, they are active participants in managing information around the person who commands the executive branch.

A party built around one man

Wolff argues that the Republican setback was unusually personal because Trump himself had become the party’s “singular issue.” He compares the repudiation to the 1974 midterms after Watergate, casting Trump as a Nixon-like figure whose political damage leaves a lasting historical mark.

That comparison is Wolff’s judgment, but the power structure he describes is plain. Republicans tied their identity to Trump, organized their politics around his grievances and accepted his manufactured reality while it served them. An electoral defeat does not suddenly turn those choices into something Trump inflicted on an otherwise passive party. The GOP’s setback belongs to the politicians who made loyalty to him an organizing principle.

Now, Wolff says, allies are adjusting to perceived weakness. He describes Trump’s vice president as “feral in his opportunism,” moving quickly to exploit the opening, while foreign leaders are likely recalculating their own approach. Political systems that reward personal dominance invite this kind of succession struggle: deference lasts only until vulnerability becomes more useful than loyalty.

Power without recognition

Wolff’s central claim is that age, political failure and Trump’s own mistakes have caught up with him, but Trump may be unable to recognize the change. He predicts a “weird twilight” in which the president continues behaving as the dominant Trump of his own imagination while others increasingly see “a much-diminished Donald Trump.”

There is human cruelty in aging under relentless public scrutiny, and Wolff acknowledges concern for Trump as a person. But the presidency is not a private convalescence. If those closest to Trump genuinely believe he cannot understand an election centered on him, their obligation is not to flatter him through it and then whisper alarming descriptions to a biographer.

“He’s here but not here” resolves the headline’s tease, but it also exposes the convenient ambiguity surrounding Trump’s court. It portrays a president detached from political reality while leaving fully aware subordinates in place to interpret, indulge and wield his authority. Trump’s reported condition may explain the strange optimism. It does not excuse the people who answered it with, “So much better.”

item.title: Leaker reveals Trump unprepared as DHS insiders warn 'the big one is coming'
item.description:
A former senior Homeland Security official says the remaining cyber specialists inside the department fear a major digital crisis is approaching while the Trump administration has left the federal cyber-defense apparatus badly understaffed. Miles Taylor, who served as a DHS deputy chief of staff during Donald Trump’s first term and leaked information from that White House, said agency experts are staying in government despite lucrative private-sector prospects because they worry no one will be at their posts when a large-scale disruption hits.

The warning followed a week of outages affecting aviation, banking, the National Security Agency and other systems. Those failures disrupted air travel, damaged economic activity and raised national-security concerns, according to AlterNet. The reporting does not establish that the outages shared a cause or resulted from a cyberattack. But the government’s failure to give a clear, consistent account has left room for concerns about emerging threats, including attacks enhanced by artificial intelligence.

A warning from the staff left behind

Taylor said he had spoken with AI and cybersecurity specialists still working inside DHS. In his account, they could leave immediately for private-sector salaries of roughly $2 million a year but have chosen to remain because they believe “a major cyber upheaval is coming.”

That assessment is not a formal government forecast, and “the big one” is not identified as a particular operation, adversary or target. Its significance lies elsewhere: the people Taylor describes as closest to the government’s cyber defenses reportedly believe the institution may soon face a severe test after losing substantial capacity.

Trump, traveling abroad as the outages unsettled critical systems at home, told Americans to “relax.” Reassurance is not preparedness, particularly when the administration offering it cannot explain what happened and has reduced the workforce responsible for preventing, diagnosing and containing digital emergencies.

Election retaliation became a security liability

Taylor traces the damage at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to Trump’s grievance over the 2020 election. CISA’s previous director refused to support Trump’s false claim that the election had been rigged, and Trump fired him by tweet.

That episode matters because it shows political loyalty being imposed on an agency whose usefulness depends on technical competence and factual reporting. Trump punished an official for declining to validate his preferred election narrative. Taylor’s contention is that the retaliation did not end with one dismissal: the agency now operates with a depleted staff after years of hostility rooted in that dispute.

Under former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, thousands of CISA employees were pushed out, according to the supplied reporting. Politico has also reported significant cuts at the agency during Trump’s second administration. Whatever justification the administration attached to those staffing decisions, the consequence described here is concrete: fewer specialists are available to protect systems on which transportation, finance and national security depend.

This is how an authoritarian demand for personal affirmation can become an operational vulnerability. An agency created to assess threats cannot function safely if telling the president an unwelcome truth is treated as disloyalty.

The secretary who “wasn’t there”

Congress has begun pressing DHS for answers. At a Wednesday hearing, even Republican lawmakers sought more information about CISA’s staffing decisions. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin could not provide specific answers about rehiring.

Asked whether forcing out technical experts had been a mistake, Mullin replied that he “wasn’t there” when it happened. The response tries to convert institutional responsibility into personal absence. Mullin may not have made the earlier decisions, but he now leads the department living with their consequences. His obligation is to know what capacity was lost, what risks followed and whether the government intends to rebuild it.

The White House itself reportedly has so little confidence in Mullin’s public performance that it has put him on a “timeout” from television appearances. That is a communications judgment, not a cybersecurity plan. Keeping an ineffective messenger away from cameras does nothing to restore technical personnel or answer lawmakers’ questions.

Taylor said the situation was not “confidence inspiring.” The phrase is restrained. The administration dismantled expertise, failed to explain a series of consequential outages, and sent an unprepared secretary to Congress without firm answers. Its public message, meanwhile, amounted to an instruction not to worry.

The strongest evidence that concern is warranted may be the people who have not left. According to Taylor, highly marketable specialists are accepting government pay because they fear what could happen if their posts are abandoned. Their presence offers some protection. The fact that they believe they must personally hold together a weakened federal defense system is the warning.

item.title: Lobbyists laugh off Stephen Miller's new White House crackdown
item.description:
Stephen Miller’s order restricting lobbyists’ access to the White House complex has not restricted their access to administration officials. It has merely shifted some meetings to bars, hotels and Zoom—a result Republican lobbyists described to NBC News as convenient rather than consequential. The policy, issued after Miller became President Donald Trump’s chief of staff, projects control while leaving the influence operation largely intact.

Permission required—unless the meeting moves elsewhere

Miller’s directive requires White House officials to obtain approval from the White House counsel before meeting lobbyists inside the complex, according to NBC News reporting cited by The Daily Beast. That gives the chief of staff another mechanism to monitor activity within the building and potentially control which outside interests receive formal access.

But the order described in the reporting regulates location and procedure, not the underlying contact. It does not prevent officials from meeting lobbyists outside the White House or speaking with them by video.

For the professionals paid to secure access, this is an inconvenience easily converted into an advantage. “It is a blessing in disguise,” one longtime Republican lobbyist told NBC News, explaining that an off-site meeting eliminates the time required to travel to the White House and pass through security.

Another Republican lobbyist said the directive would not have “a major impact,” adding: “I understand what Stephen is doing. It sends a message, and that’s who he is, but we all have Zoom.”

That distinction is the substance of the story. Miller can tighten control over the visible symbols of access without curtailing the private exercise of influence. The lobbyists still get the meetings; the public gets fewer opportunities to know that those meetings occurred inside the seat of executive power.

A crackdown built for appearances

Calling the policy a crackdown gives it more force than the reported facts support. Nothing in the account indicates that the administration has barred lobbyists from contacting officials or limited the interests they may represent. The directive instead creates an approval process for meetings held at one address.

Its immediate effect may therefore be displacement. Conversations that once took place within a controlled government complex can move to less formal settings, beyond the restriction Miller imposed. That does not make the contacts improper by itself. It does, however, expose the weakness of a policy aimed at the optics of access rather than access itself.

The lobbyists’ amusement is revealing because they occupy the stronger position outside Miller’s internal chain of command. He can dictate procedures to White House personnel and scrutinize their calendars inside the complex. He cannot erase Washington’s network of private relationships, nor can he make a hotel table or video call disappear through a memo governing the building.

Miller’s order may still discipline officials by forcing them to seek legal approval before hosting lobbyists at the White House. But based on the reporting, its reach stops well short of the sweeping control its presentation implies.

Consolidating the building, not the influence industry

The directive fits Miller’s reported governing style. Miles Taylor, who served in the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s first term, described Miller as a micromanager who made late-night calls and unexpectedly entered meetings. Taylor also said that Miller’s command of the bureaucracy—and his willingness to insert himself into sessions where officials did not expect him—made him “very formidable and very effective.”

That history suggests the lobbyist memo is best understood as an instrument of internal supervision. It tells administration officials that outside meetings inside the White House are subject to review, while reinforcing Miller’s authority over who enters the formal policymaking space.

His promotion had already drawn criticism from people who saw it as Trump’s decision to concentrate more power in an aide closely identified with the administration’s most aggressive agenda. Politico legal affairs reporter Kyle Cheney noted at the time that Miller was closely associated with the policies and political demeanor that had preceded the Republicans’ reported midterm losses. Democratic strategist Adam Parkhomenko pointed specifically to Miller’s role in Trump’s mass-deportation program and argued that the appointment showed Trump responding to electoral defeat by empowering its architect.

Those objections concern what Miller may do with institutional authority. The lobbyist directive demonstrates both the reach and the limits of that authority: he can impose another layer of permission on White House staff, but the influence business can route around it before lunch.

The lobbyists are laughing because the order burdens the people Miller controls more than the people it ostensibly targets. They retain their contacts, lose the security line and move the meeting somewhere his memo does not reach.

item.title: Trump's new weakness leaves Americans 'prepping for survival'
item.description:
A series of technology outages disrupted air travel, banking, communications and other services, leaving some Americans questioning whether the systems governing daily life can be trusted. An Indiana information-technology specialist and mother of five told The Washington Post that preserving food had shifted from a hobby to something more ominous: “Now I’m prepping for survival.” No explanation from national leaders, she said, had reassured her.

AlterNet casts that fear as evidence of President Donald Trump’s weakness. The reporting supports a narrower and more concrete indictment: essential services have become dependent on opaque, concentrated technology systems, while government officials and industry leaders offer assurances that do not address the fragility people can see for themselves.

“Not a cyberattack” is not an explanation

Officials reportedly moved to reassure the public that the outages were not caused by a cyberattack. That distinction matters for identifying the immediate event, but it does little to answer the larger question raised by simultaneous failures across critical services: why are systems this consequential so vulnerable to disruption?

Jake Smith, a content creator quoted by the Associated Press, described the resulting sense of powerlessness. Seeing several outages close together, he said, had forced people to recognize how much of their lives they had surrendered to systems they do not fully understand.

The surrender is not merely a collection of individual consumer choices. Airlines, banks, communications providers, technology companies and government regulators built an economy in which participation routinely requires dependence on centralized digital infrastructure. When that infrastructure fails, ordinary people absorb the missed flights, inaccessible accounts and interrupted communications. The institutions controlling it retain the power to describe the breakdown as temporary, technical or benign.

Trump’s reported response — “It’s fine” — is revealing precisely because it substitutes dismissal for an account of what failed, who was responsible and what will change. The Indiana mother summarized the political consequence: “You’re supposed to trust the government to give you information and protect you.” Instead, she said, worried people are treated as though they are being silly.

Artificial intelligence expands the vulnerability

Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said artificial intelligence has been searching for security gaps faster than institutions can manage the consequences. He suggested there was reason to believe the disruptions were unintended effects of attempts to make systems safer.

That description presents a disturbing governing arrangement even without assuming malicious intent. Companies are deploying technology capable of finding weaknesses at enormous speed, while the public is expected to accept that damaging consequences may arrive before regulators or operators can contain them.

Cybersecurity expert Zeb Larson told the AP that AI has made launching attacks easier while remaining less effective at repairing the vulnerabilities it exposes. His criticism went beyond technical imbalance: AI companies, he said, are “empowering hackers while billing themselves as the only line of defense.” He called the business model “a protection racket.”

That is an accusation, not an established explanation for the reported outages. But it identifies the conflict officials should confront. Firms that profit from accelerating AI adoption can also profit from selling protection against the risks that adoption creates. Their incentive is expansion; the public’s need is resilience. Treating those interests as interchangeable amounts to outsourcing public safety to the companies with the strongest financial reason to minimize the costs of their own products.

AlterNet’s case outruns its evidence

The source article attributes the public’s insecurity to Trump’s corruption, deregulatory agenda and relationships with technology executives. It reports that Trump discarded AI rules and standards ordered under President Joe Biden, and that Google, Microsoft, Apple, Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and other companies contributed millions toward his ballroom project. Those claims, if established, describe a government granting powerful firms favorable treatment while accepting their money.

But the article does not establish that Trump, AI companies, China or any foreign government caused the outages. Its speculation that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang collaborated with the Chinese Communist Party, paid Trump to ignore him and helped China acquire sensitive technology is presented without evidence in the supplied reporting. So is the suggestion that someone may have been deliberately switching American systems off and on. Suspicion is not proof, and piling geopolitical conjecture onto genuine infrastructure failures obscures the accountability that can be established.

The same problem weakens the article’s use of foreign policy. Trump’s reported opposition to Taiwanese independence, his willingness to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin and a reported effort to pressure allies to end support for Ukraine are consequential actions. They do not, by themselves, explain failures in banking, aviation or communications. Calling every development “weakness” collapses distinct decisions into a slogan.

The sharper charge is not that every outage can be traced to the president. It is that Trump reportedly dismantled AI safeguards while cultivating financial relationships with companies positioned to benefit from looser oversight, then answered visible disruption with “It’s fine.” That is a specific exercise of power: weaken public constraints, privilege corporate expansion and dismiss the people left managing the risk.

The Indiana mother’s survival preparations are therefore not proof of AlterNet’s broader conspiracy narrative. They are evidence of institutional failure at ground level. She saw systems falter, heard leaders minimize the danger and concluded that her family needed a backup plan. Her fear should not be recruited to support claims the reporting cannot prove. It is damning enough on its own.

item.title: Trump health again under scrutiny after ‘exoskeleton device’
item.description:
A rigid bulge beneath President Donald Trump’s suit prompted online speculation that the 80-year-old was wearing an “exoskeleton” or another medical device while greeting Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. But the footage establishes only that something protruded near Trump’s right hip. Neither AlterNet nor the Daily Beast report identified the object, and social-media guesses do not turn an odd silhouette into a diagnosis.

That distinction matters. Trump’s health is a legitimate subject of public scrutiny because he exercises presidential power, not because strangers on the internet can identify medical equipment through a suit jacket.

A video becomes a diagnosis machine

The footage was posted Thursday by Trump communications adviser Margo Martin. According to Daily Beast reporter Erkki Forster, the protrusion appeared at the back of Trump’s suit as he approached Putin, shook his hand and leaned in to whisper something that drew a broad smile from the Russian leader.

Independent journalist Aaron Rupar called attention to Trump’s “contraption.” Other users proposed a pump, a bag or an exoskeleton worn over clothing. None of those comments, as reported, came from Trump’s physician, the White House or anyone shown to have direct knowledge of what was beneath the president’s clothes.

The “exoskeleton device,” then, is not an established explanation. It is the most sensational entry in a chain of conjecture. The reporting supplies no confirmation that the bulge was medical equipment at all.

That makes the framing weaker than the underlying public-interest question. A president’s capacity to perform the job warrants serious reporting; viral inspection of his backside does not provide it. Treating speculation as evidence lets the White House avoid the question that only officials with access to Trump’s medical information can answer.

Privacy does not settle the public-interest question

S. Jay Olshansky, a University of Illinois Chicago emeritus professor who studies mortality, told AlterNet in September that he could not assess Trump’s cognitive functioning from the president’s daily decisions because he lacked the information needed to do so. That is a useful limit, and one the online commentary ignored.

Olshansky also said he had changed his position on medical disclosure by presidents and presidential candidates. He once regarded their records as private, but now argues that the office should carry disclosure requirements comparable to the medical evaluations imposed on airline pilots. Presidential decisions, he noted, can directly or indirectly affect other people’s health.

The analogy identifies the actual power imbalance. The public is not entitled to every intimate detail about an older person’s body. But a president is not merely an older person asking to be left alone. He controls the executive branch and makes decisions with consequences far beyond himself. The institution grants extraordinary authority while largely allowing the person who holds it—and the staff whose power depends on him—to manage what the public learns about his fitness.

Olshansky drew another necessary line: ordinary age-related physical limitations are less consequential than cognitive impairment. A problem with a knee, hip or eye does not by itself establish an inability to govern. He said a reliable cognitive assessment would have to come from the individual’s physician, with the relevant information made public.

Spectacle is a substitute for disclosure

Trump’s appearance in the video cannot answer the medical question, and the Putin encounter does not change that. Their conspicuously friendly exchange may warrant political scrutiny on its own terms, but Putin’s smile offers no evidence about the object beneath Trump’s suit or Trump’s health.

The episode instead shows what fills the vacuum when presidential health information is controlled by the president and his aides: zoomed-in footage, amateur diagnoses and headlines built around the most provocative guess. That arrangement serves official power remarkably well. The public conversation becomes a fight over mockery and decorum while the people who possess the relevant facts remain outside the frame.

Trump may have been wearing a medical device, or the protrusion may have had another explanation. The supplied reporting does not resolve it. The defensible conclusion is narrower and more consequential: a mysterious bulge is not medical evidence, and speculation about an “exoskeleton” is no substitute for a credible, publicly available assessment of the president’s fitness.

item.title: Trump’s ‘vascular dementia’ warning sign caught on camera: psychologist
item.description:
The footage does not establish that President Donald Trump has vascular dementia. It shows Trump making an unexplained sound during remarks in the Philippines, after which psychologist John Paul Garrison offered several possible neurological explanations—including vascular dementia—while explicitly acknowledging that he had not conducted a psychological evaluation and was expressing an opinion.

That distinction is the story. AlterNet’s headline turns a speculative interpretation of video into a “warning sign caught on camera,” granting diagnostic weight to an episode that Garrison himself described far more cautiously. A president’s capacity to perform the job is a legitimate matter of public concern. Remote diagnosis dressed up as political reporting does not answer it.

An unexplained sound becomes a diagnosis-shaped headline

At a luncheon hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang Palace, Trump was discussing the history shared by the United States and the Philippines when he made a sound that Garrison said was not a word. Trump continued speaking without an apparent reaction.

Garrison interpreted that absence of acknowledgment as evidence that the sound was involuntary. He also said Trump subsequently appeared to construct his sentence one word at a time. From those observations, he raised “a wide variety of potential neurological explanations,” including brain scarring and different forms of dementia.

That is a hypothesis with an expansive range, not a finding. Garrison said the video was “not a psychological evaluation of any kind” and characterized his conclusions as “just my opinions.” His strongest claim was narrower: he felt confident that Trump had not made the sound intentionally.

AlterNet’s framing collapses those categories. A clinician naming vascular dementia among multiple possibilities is not the same as identifying a clinical sign of vascular dementia in a patient. The article supplies an interpretation of behavior, not a diagnosis, and its headline outruns the qualification contained in its own reporting.

More footage, more inference

Garrison, a clinical and forensic psychologist who describes himself as a body-language expert, has spent months publishing videos about what he views as Trump’s neurological decline. During Trump’s arrival in China, he identified what he called a “myoclonic jerk” in Trump’s right arm. He also attributed an apparent collision with Chinese President Xi Jinping to reduced coordination.

Garrison further interpreted Trump’s near-embrace of Xi as “social disinhibition,” arguing that difficulty reading social cues can accompany the kinds of neurological dysfunction he has discussed. He said the behavior appeared to be progressing and that Trump seemed to struggle during the Asia trip, which also brought him face to face with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

These observations may justify questions. They do not settle them. A movement can be described from video; its medical cause cannot simply be read off the screen. The same limitation applies to an awkward encounter between heads of state. Calling it evidence of neurological decline gives one interpretation the authority of clinical language without the examination needed to support a clinical conclusion.

Speculation is not accountability

The presidency concentrates extraordinary coercive, diplomatic and administrative power in one person. That makes credible evidence about a president’s health consequential, especially when the reported behavior occurs during meetings with foreign leaders. It also raises the standard for reporting, rather than lowering it.

The political temptation is obvious: translate an unsettling moment into a hidden medical explanation, then make the explanation carry the burden of criticizing the president. But Trump’s public decisions, statements and uses of executive power can be evaluated directly. Assigning them to an unestablished neurological condition risks replacing political accountability with amateur pathology.

It can also misdirect responsibility. If aides or officials have concerns about a president’s capacity, they possess access, information and institutional duties that a YouTube commentator does not. If they have no such concerns, a psychologist’s review of clips cannot substitute for evidence from people positioned to observe Trump consistently or assess him clinically. Either way, the relevant power lies with the president and the officials surrounding him—not with viewers being invited to diagnose a sound.

Garrison is entitled to describe what he believes he sees. AlterNet is responsible for representing the limits of that claim. The footage captured an unexplained vocalization and other moments Garrison considered abnormal. It did not catch vascular dementia on camera.

item.title: Ex-con Trump official begs Supreme Court for help as Dem probes loom
item.description:
Peter Navarro is asking the Supreme Court to make congressional contempt harder to prosecute just as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January 2027 and investigate Trump administration officials. The former Trump trade adviser, now serving as senior counselor for trade and manufacturing, wants the justices to overturn his 2023 conviction for refusing to cooperate with the House committee investigating Jan. 6. His lawyer is explicit about the practical benefit: winning could mean fewer contempt prosecutions when Democrats gain subpoena power.

Navarro’s petition is therefore more than an attempt to erase the legal consequences of his own defiance. It asks the Court to weaken Congress’s ability to enforce subpoenas at the moment that enforcement could constrain the administration Navarro serves.

A claim of privilege Trump never invoked

A jury convicted Navarro on two counts of contempt of Congress after he refused to provide documents and testimony to the Jan. 6 committee. He claimed executive privilege, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found a decisive defect in that defense: only the president could invoke the privilege, and Donald Trump had not extended it to Navarro.

The appeals court also rejected the argument now at the center of Navarro’s petition. Under its ruling, a person violates the federal contempt statute by deliberately refusing to comply with a congressional subpoena even if that person mistakenly believes the refusal is lawful.

Navarro wants prosecutors to face an additional hurdle: proving that the target actually knew the noncompliance was illegal. That is not a minor technical adjustment. It would allow subpoena recipients to turn their asserted legal beliefs into a potential shield, making accountability depend partly on what they claim was in their minds when they withheld evidence.

Abhishek Kambli, Navarro’s attorney, told Fox News that such a ruling would make contempt cases “much harder to prove” and result in fewer prosecutions. He presented that weakening as a way to “tone down the weaponization that could potentially occur” under Democratic control.

The misdirection is embedded in the word weaponization. Congress issues subpoenas under lawful investigative authority; refusing one is the conduct Navarro was prosecuted for. Requiring compliance is not transformed into persecution merely because the official facing scrutiny works for a president who opposes the investigation.

The coming transfer of subpoena power

The timing supplies the political context. After Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, lawmakers announced plans to investigate Trump administration officials. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, posted a blunt warning on X: “LAWYER UP.” Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January.

Navarro filed his petition a week before Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan called for an investigation into alleged administration corruption. Slotkin said cases involving people who “enabled” Trump could send a “deterrence message” to young people considering administration jobs.

Those remarks preview an aggressive use of congressional oversight and deserve scrutiny on their own terms. But they do not retroactively validate Navarro’s refusal to comply with a different Congress investigating Jan. 6. Nor do they establish that future subpoenas will be illegitimate. Navarro’s allies are using anticipated Democratic investigations to argue for a legal rule that would diminish Congress’s enforcement power before those investigations begin.

Mike Davis, founder and president of the Article III Project, which filed a brief supporting Navarro, said Democrats had used Congress to imprison Navarro for defending Trump’s privilege “in good faith.” That formulation launders the central fact identified by the appeals court: Trump never invoked the privilege for him. “Good faith” is doing political work here that the claimed legal protection could not.

A Court positioned to redraw the boundary

The petition arrives after the Supreme Court in April vacated the D.C. Circuit’s ruling against Steve Bannon, another former Trump adviser who served four months in federal prison for defying the Jan. 6 committee. The justices acted after the Justice Department moved to dismiss Bannon’s indictment.

Navarro is asking the Court to go further by changing what prosecutors must prove in contempt cases. If the justices take his case and accept that argument, the effects would extend beyond one former prisoner or one investigation. Future officials could refuse congressional demands and force prosecutors to establish not merely intentional noncompliance, but the official’s knowledge that the refusal violated the law.

Congress’s contempt authority already depends on executive-branch prosecution and judicial enforcement. Navarro’s proposed rule would add another escape route for officials protected by an aligned administration and willing to profess confidence in their own legal position.

The political inversion is stark. Navarro held executive power, withheld information from the legislative branch, served his sentence and returned to a senior White House role. Now, as control of Congress changes hands, his camp portrays the possibility that administration officials may have to answer subpoenas as the abuse—and asks a Supreme Court with the power to rewrite the rule to insulate them from the consequences of refusal.

item.title: Trump’s Cabinet caught 'spitballing' as America teeters on collapse
item.description:
A cluster of failures across airlines, banks, major technology companies and federal systems has exposed more than brittle infrastructure. According to Zeteo’s Prem Thakker, senior Trump administration officials responded to the disruption with improvised theories, conflicting explanations and an admission that essential systems were merely “being patched.” The outages may have had different causes; the governing failure was common. Officials responsible for transportation and homeland security could not tell the public what had happened, even as they speculated on television about routers, hackers and artificial intelligence.

Cabinet speculation in place of an explanation

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy appeared on Fox News after an FAA failure stranded travelers around the country. He said he had asked the FBI to determine whether the incident involved hacking, then offered a list of possibilities: “I think it was a network problem, or a router problem, or uh, uh, an installation error.”

That was not a finding. It was a Cabinet secretary guessing on air while an investigation remained unresolved. Duffy separately called an outage at United Airlines a “head-scratcher,” another confession of uncertainty packaged as public reassurance.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin supplied a different theory. On Fox, he said an unnamed but “very smart” technology figure had suggested that artificial intelligence—not hackers—was responsible for the outages. “That kinda makes sense to me,” Mullin said. According to AlterNet’s account of Thakker’s reporting, Trump officials have called the technology “SI,” for “super-intelligence.”

A private remark from an unidentified person, followed by a secretary’s impression that it sounded plausible, is not an official assessment. Nor did the administration establish that the failures at Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, the FAA and the NSA shared a cause. Treating temporal proximity as proof of a single technological culprit would merely replace uncertainty with mythology.

Duffy and Mullin were not even presenting a coherent administration line. At a joint appearance about the FAA ground stop, Duffy appeared to bump Mullin and shake his head while Mullin blamed new technology for overwhelming the system. The spectacle mattered because these officials control agencies expected to coordinate during precisely this kind of disruption. Their disagreement was not a seminar-room dispute. It unfolded while travelers and critical systems were absorbing the consequences.

The unanswered question belongs to the administration

Members of both parties criticized the response. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told Thakker that repeated outages look less coincidental as their number grows, though that observation did not establish a common cause. Mocking the administration’s performance, he said, “We’ll wait for the mastermind at DHS to tell us.” Of Mullin’s theory, Massie added that “the American people deserve a better answer than that.”

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, identified in the report as the incoming House Judiciary Committee chair, said the response “does not inspire a lot of confidence in the secretary or this administration.” He also accused Trump of spending time on “trivia and nonsense,” including his ballroom, while essential systems faltered.

The White House’s Wednesday briefing provided the report’s clearest—and most damning—description of the government’s posture. A senior administration official said the systems were “being patched.” Asked what would happen during a real cyberattack, the official replied: “That is a question the American people should be asking.”

The public is already asking it. The official empowered to answer shifted the burden back onto people who neither run the agencies nor control their budgets, personnel and contingency planning. That is institutional misdirection in its purest form: authorities retain power while outsourcing responsibility for understanding their failures.

Performance above preparedness

Thakker reported that Duffy had spent months filming a family travel reality series. Mullin, meanwhile, reportedly used a government aircraft to attend a college football game while passengers remained stranded during the FAA outage. Those details do not explain the technical failures, and they should not be mistaken for evidence about their cause. They do illuminate the administration’s priorities.

Publicity and privilege become politically relevant when the officials enjoying them cannot provide a settled account of nationwide disruption within their own jurisdictions. A television project does not prove administrative incompetence; neither does travel to a football game. But when a transportation secretary meets cascading failures with guesses and a homeland security secretary advances an anonymous acquaintance’s AI theory, the extracurricular self-promotion stops looking incidental.

The report does not establish that the United Airlines outage, the FAA failure and the problems affecting technology companies, banks and the NSA were coordinated, malicious or even technically related. It establishes something the administration itself demonstrated in public: the people with institutional authority lacked an agreed explanation and offered speculation anyway.

Systems can fail under competent governments. The political indictment here is not that every outage occurred on Trump’s watch. It is that officials charged with managing the response treated uncertainty as airtime, substituted unnamed expertise for evidence and acknowledged patchwork infrastructure without presenting a credible plan for a more dangerous event. When asked about an actual cyberattack, the White House left Americans with a question. That question was also an answer.

item.title: Trump humiliates himself with error-riddled ramble to world leaders
item.description:
Donald Trump used an appearance before world leaders in Shenzhen to make false claims about U.S. inflation, recast artificial intelligence under his preferred branding and warn other governments against regulating it. The humiliation was not merely that the president mangled facts at the APEC Summit. It was that he deployed the authority of the presidency to turn personal improvisation into an international policy message: trust his numbers, adopt his terminology and leave a powerful industry largely unconstrained.

Inflation fiction on an international stage

Speaking Thursday during a trip that also included meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump claimed inflation had remained below 2 percent for three months.

“The last three months, inflation was down to a number that was not expected,” he said. “We’ve got it less than 2 percent for the last three months.”

The figures reported by AlterNet contradict him. The most recent inflation rate was 3.7 percent in September, while the lowest rate during the preceding year was 2.4 percent in January and February. Trump was not offering a debatable interpretation of economic conditions; he was describing numbers that did not exist.

The claim echoed his effort during the midterm campaign to blame the Biden administration for persistently high prices. But Trump was speaking as president, after Republicans had lost control of both the House and Senate. That matters because incumbency changes who possesses the power to act. Continuing to invoke a predecessor may be politically convenient, but it does not transfer responsibility for present policy back to the previous administration.

A presidential rebrand becomes federal vocabulary

Trump then moved from fictitious inflation figures to artificial intelligence, which he calls “Super Intelligence,” or “SI.” He described it as “the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution,” briefly interrupting his own declaration to add that it “seems to be true.”

He also announced that “Americans invented” SI and said it was already producing extraordinary prosperity around the world. That sweeping national claim disregards the field’s international intellectual foundations. British mathematician Alan Turing, widely regarded as a foundational figure in theoretical computer science, posed the question of whether machines could think in his 1950 paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence.

More revealing than Trump’s loose history was his treatment of a branding preference as public policy. According to AlterNet, he directed federal agencies to replace “AI” with “SI.” A president has the institutional reach to impose that vocabulary throughout the executive branch, giving an invented label the appearance of technical legitimacy without making the underlying technology safer, more intelligent or more comprehensible.

His explanation supplied little substance. The technology, Trump said, was “almost completely good,” although it contained unspecified “bad elements” that required careful management. He did not identify those elements in the remarks reported by AlterNet or explain what management would entail.

The risks are real until regulation becomes inconvenient

Trump’s own conduct demonstrates some of the technology’s political hazards. He has repeatedly circulated AI-generated videos on Truth Social, including one depicting former President Barack Obama being arrested. In September, amid public anger over the possible effect of data centers on energy bills, Trump accused Democrats of perpetrating an AI “Hoax.”

Those data centers have also generated voter concern about employment. The infrastructure powering the industry consumes resources and can disrupt communities, while automation raises fears about displaced workers. These are not imaginary complications or mere resistance to innovation. They are consequences over which governments have regulatory authority.

Yet Trump’s message to other countries was categorical: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle SI, and we won’t allow that to happen, frankly.”

That formulation performs a familiar piece of misdirection. Regulation becomes “globalist” interference, while the corporations developing and profiting from the technology disappear from view. Workers worried about their jobs and households worried about electricity costs are cast as obstacles to technological progress rather than people bearing risks created by decisions made far above them.

Trump said the technology must be watched, managed and protected from its “bad elements.” He then warned governments not to control it. The contradiction leaves a clear governing priority: presidential power may rename the industry, advertise its promise and shield it from oversight, but the public is expected to absorb the consequences.
