item.title: Your Mistake, Your Problem. The Government’s Mistake? Still Your Problem.
item.description:
How America’s permitting system demands absolute obedience from citizens while allowing the government to escape responsibility for its own decisions.

There is an old legal principle that almost everyone has heard:

Ignorance of the law is no excuse.

File your taxes incorrectly, and the IRS may come knocking.

Miss a regulatory deadline, and you may face penalties.

Build something without the required permit, and the government may order you to tear it down.

Violate a zoning ordinance, and you might find yourself paying fines while lawyers argue over exactly what you're allowed to do with your own property.

The rules are the rules.

The law is the law.

And the government expects you to know both.

Fair enough.

But here's a question that apparently hasn't occurred to enough people:

What happens when the government doesn't know its own rules?

More specifically, what happens when you follow every procedure the government requires, obtain its approval, spend your own money acting on that approval, and then discover that the government made a mistake?

In far too many cases, the answer is astonishingly simple.

You pay.

Not the official who made the mistake.

Not the agency that approved your application.

You.

The citizen who did exactly what the government told you to do.

And somehow, we've accepted this as a reasonable arrangement.

First, They Make You Ask Permission

In an earlier Systemic Error article, we examined the American housing crisis and the extraordinary power zoning regulations give existing residents over development.

In cities such as San Francisco and Los Angeles, restrictive land-use rules, discretionary approvals, and neighborhood opposition can make building desperately needed housing an expensive legal obstacle course.

Want to replace a single-family house with a small apartment building?

Not so fast.

Perhaps the zoning doesn't allow it.

Perhaps you need a variance.

Perhaps the neighbors object.

Perhaps the project requires another environmental review.

Perhaps someone files an appeal.

Perhaps that appeal becomes a lawsuit.

Perhaps the project spends years in bureaucratic limbo while the cost of housing continues climbing.

The absurdity is difficult to overstate.

People complain that housing is unaffordable while supporting regulations that make constructing additional housing more difficult and expensive.

And the system frequently gives disproportionate influence to people who already own homes, at the expense of people who would like to have one.

But the problem extends far beyond housing.

The underlying principle is the same: property ownership does not necessarily convey a predictable right to use the property.

Instead, the owner must navigate a labyrinth of permissions.

And once those permissions are obtained, there's another problem.

The permission itself may not be reliable.

Then, They Change Their Minds

Consider the case of Panhandle Bike Ranch in Idaho, which we explored in our second article.

Scott and Jennifer Kalbach purchased approximately 170 acres of wooded land to develop a mountain bike park.

They didn't secretly build an illegal facility.

They hired a land-use consultant.

They submitted their plans.

They applied for the required conditional-use permit.

Bonner County approved the project in 2024, and county commissioners subsequently upheld approval after appeals.

The couple proceeded to develop the property, bringing in professional trail builders and investing approximately $2.5 million.

Then, just eleven days before the park's scheduled June 2025 opening, a judge vacated the permit.

Why?

Among other problems, the county had failed to provide adequate findings supporting its decision to classify the proposed operation as a recreational facility rather than a commercial resort.

The county had also failed to adequately establish water availability for fire suppression.

Notice what the court did not establish.

It did not find that the owners had fraudulently obtained their permit.

It did not determine that the park's trails were inherently dangerous.

It did not establish that a wildfire was imminent.

The decision identified deficiencies in the government's justification for granting permission.

Now, judicial review is important. Government agencies must follow the law, and affected parties have a legitimate right to challenge unlawful decisions.

But consider the consequences.

The applicants submitted their proposal to the authority designated to review it.

That authority approved it.

They invested millions in reliance on that approval.

Then they lost their authorization because the authority's decision was legally deficient.

The government made the mistake. The private citizens absorbed the financial consequences.

And that brings us to the central argument of this article.

A Permit Should Be a Contract, Not a Lottery Ticket

I propose a rather straightforward principle.

Once the government grants a permit, that permit is final. Period.

There should be one exception: fraud or material deception by the applicant.

If you falsify documents, conceal important information, or deliberately misrepresent your intentions to obtain approval, you have forfeited the protection that approval would otherwise provide.

You lied. The government relied on your lie. The consequences are yours.

Perfectly reasonable.

But if you submitted accurate information, followed the prescribed procedures, and obtained approval in good faith?

That's it.

The permission is granted.

The government cannot subsequently revoke it because an official overlooked a regulation, interpreted a provision incorrectly, failed to complete an inspection, or neglected to document a finding.

Government error must not invalidate an innocent citizen's legitimate reliance on government approval.

Think about what a permit actually represents.

The government requires you to submit detailed information about a proposed activity.

It claims the authority to evaluate that activity against applicable laws and regulations.

It charges fees for performing that evaluation.

And it issues an official document declaring that you are authorized to proceed.

If that document doesn't create a binding obligation on the part of the government, what exactly have you purchased with your application fees?

An opinion?

A suggestion?

A temporary expression of bureaucratic optimism?

A lottery ticket that might turn out to be worthless after you've invested your life savings?

That is not how a reliable regulatory system should function.

When a bank guarantees a financial obligation, that guarantee has consequences.

When a company signs a contract, that contract creates enforceable commitments.

When a citizen signs a declaration to the government, the citizen can be held accountable for its accuracy.

But when the government issues an authorization, its ability to escape responsibility for mistakes can be remarkably broad.

That asymmetry needs to end.

“But What If the Government Approves Something Dangerous?”

This is the predictable objection.

What if a building is approved and subsequently discovered to have a serious structural defect?

What if a permitted activity creates an imminent danger?

Surely the government must be allowed to revoke the permit?

No.

And before anyone starts screaming about public safety, allow me to explain.

The government must be allowed to correct a dangerous situation. What it should not be allowed to do is transfer the cost of its own failure to the innocent person who relied on its approval.

These are two completely different questions.

Imagine that you hire licensed engineers and architects to design a building.

You submit the plans to the building department.

The department reviews them.

The inspectors examine the technical specifications.

The government grants the construction permit.

You construct the building exactly as approved.

A year later, inspectors discover a structural defect that should have been identified during the permit review.

The building needs substantial reinforcement.

Under the system I'm proposing, the answer is not to revoke the permit and demand that you demolish or repair the building at your expense.

The answer is:

The government fixes it. The government pays for it.

If the building presents an immediate danger, the authorities can evacuate it and perform whatever emergency measures are necessary to protect human life.

But the authorization remains binding. The government must finance the corrections needed to fulfill the legitimate expectations created by its original approval, including appropriate compensation for losses caused by the intervention.

The owner submitted the plans.

The government approved the plans.

The owner built according to those plans.

The government missed the defect.

So why should the owner be financially punished for a failure in the very review process the government required?

Now, if the owner secretly substituted inferior materials, departed from the approved design, or concealed defects, that's different.

The government never approved those deviations.

But where the owner acted honestly and complied with the authorization, the government should bear responsibility for mistakes within its review.

That's not an argument against public safety.

It's an argument for making the institution responsible for certifying public safety accountable for its certification.

You Don't Fight a Forest Fire With a Garden Hose

The Idaho mountain bike park provides another illustration.

One of the issues raised in the litigation concerned inadequate documentation of water availability for fire suppression.

Let's remember what we're discussing.

Approximately 170 acres of wooded, mountainous terrain.

A forest.

Anyone familiar with wildland firefighting knows that controlling a large forest fire is fundamentally different from extinguishing a burning kitchen.

Wildfires require specialized crews, vegetation management, firebreaks, heavy equipment, and sometimes aerial support.

Certainly, a recreational facility should provide appropriate emergency access, evacuation procedures, and fire protection for buildings.

But those are matters for the permitting authority and responsible fire district to evaluate before granting permission.

The county's original approval already contemplated fire-risk assessments, mitigation planning, and emergency-services requirements.

If those provisions were inadequate, the government should have identified the deficiencies before approval.

And if it failed to do so?

Then it should correct its failure.

At its expense.

The taxpayers might reasonably be unhappy about funding corrections to an improperly approved project.

But that's precisely the point.

Government mistakes should have consequences for the government.

When the financial cost of incompetence is transferred entirely to private citizens, public authorities have weaker institutional incentives to avoid errors.

When mistakes affect public budgets, there is at least an opportunity for taxpayers, auditors, elected officials, and oversight bodies to demand explanations and reforms.

Government accountability should not consist of issuing another order to the person who trusted the government's previous order.

“But the Taxpayers Would Have to Pay!”

Yes.

They would.

And that objection deserves a serious answer.

Government agencies don't possess magical pools of money.

When they pay damages or finance corrective work, those expenses ultimately come from public resources.

But consider the alternative.

Suppose a government agency makes a costly mistake affecting a private business.

Why should the entire financial burden fall on the one business owner unlucky enough to receive the defective approval?

That person pays taxes, too.

That person followed the law.

That person paid the required fees.

That person had no authority over the internal workings of the permitting agency.

Yet somehow, they are expected to shoulder the consequences.

The public collectively establishes the government, grants it regulatory authority, funds its operations, and benefits from its services.

There is a reasonable argument that the public should collectively bear the financial risks of government errors rather than imposing them arbitrarily on whichever innocent individual happens to be affected.

And if those errors become expensive, the public has every reason to demand better administration.

That means proper training.

Clearer regulations.

Competent technical reviews.

Auditable decisions.

Independent oversight.

And consequences for officials whose negligence or misconduct causes substantial public losses, subject to appropriate due process.

In other words, actual accountability.

Not merely another layer of bureaucracy designed to insulate the bureaucracy from accountability.

Won't This Make Permits Harder to Obtain?

Possibly.

And this is where the proposal needs another essential component.

If every approval carries binding financial responsibility, agencies might respond by delaying decisions indefinitely.

They could demand endless studies, additional inspections, more documentation, and increasingly expensive technical reports.

The government, fearful of making a mistake, could simply refuse to make a decision.

We've already seen what happens when discretionary land-use approvals become an obstacle course.

So a binding-permit system must also have binding decision deadlines.

The government should receive a reasonable, clearly defined period to evaluate a complete application.

Within that period, it must approve the application or reject it with specific, documented reasons grounded in existing law.

If additional information is genuinely necessary, the agency must identify exactly what is missing.

It should not be allowed to restart the process indefinitely or manufacture new procedural requirements simply because a project is controversial.

And applicants must retain access to prompt, meaningful review when an agency rejects an application or fails to act.

The goal is not to force officials to approve unsafe projects without adequate review.

The goal is to prevent administrative caution from becoming administrative paralysis.

The government must have enough time and resources to do its job, but it must actually do the job.

This also requires adequate technical staffing and competent inspectors. Financial liability alone cannot substitute for the expertise necessary to make defensible decisions.

What About the Neighbors?

There's another objection worth addressing.

What happens when neighbors oppose a proposed development?

Shouldn't they have a say?

Of course they should.

But having a right to be heard is not the same thing as having a right to dictate what someone else does with their property.

During the approval process, neighbors should be able to raise legitimate, demonstrable concerns.

Will the development exceed the capacity of existing roads?

Will it create noise above established limits?

Will it contaminate groundwater?

Will it interfere with drainage or create measurable environmental hazards?

Will emergency vehicles have adequate access?

These are pertinent questions. They concern actual impacts that can be measured, evaluated, and addressed.

But other objections have no legitimate place in the decision.

“I don't want it here.”

Not a valid reason.

“It will change the character of our neighborhood.”

Not without identifying an actual impact that violates a legitimate standard.

“What about my property value?”

Your property is an investment, not a government-guaranteed asset. You don't acquire authority over neighboring land simply because someone else's lawful development might affect what buyers are willing to pay for your house.

And then there's the particularly revolting variation:

“I don't want those types of people living/working here.”

Whether dressed up as concerns about “neighborhood character,” “community compatibility,” or “preserving our way of life,” prejudice doesn't become a legitimate planning objection merely because someone presents it at a public hearing.

The government should not give discriminatory preferences the dignity of regulatory consideration.

Nor should it allow personal dislikes to masquerade as technical objections.

If someone claims that a proposed apartment building will cause unacceptable traffic, require evidence about traffic.

If someone claims a mountain bike park will create dangerous noise levels, require measurements or credible projections against applicable standards.

If someone claims a development will destroy property values, that alone should not be grounds for denying permission.

The burden should be on the objector to identify a genuine, legally relevant impact—not on the applicant to prove that every neighbor will be happy.

And once the government has evaluated those concerns and granted approval, the matter is settled.

The permit is final.

If the government subsequently discovers that it overlooked a legitimate danger, it must address that danger at its own expense, without imposing the financial consequences of its mistake on an innocent permit holder.

The neighbors retain their right to protection against actual harm.

The property owner retains the right to rely on the government's authorization.

And the government assumes responsibility for the decision it made.

That's how the balance should work.

Your right to enjoy your property does not include the right to control mine.

And your fear that my property might attract people you don't like is not a planning consideration.

It's your problem.

Not mine.

We Already Demand This Standard From Citizens

Now let's return to the fundamental double standard.

If you make an error on your tax return, the government generally doesn't respond:

“That's understandable. Mistakes happen. We'll absorb the consequences.”

You may owe additional tax, interest, and, depending on the circumstances, penalties.

If you fail to obtain a required permit before constructing a building, you can face enforcement action even if you genuinely misunderstood the rules.

If you miss an important filing deadline, you may lose rights or opportunities.

The government expects diligence.

It expects accuracy.

It expects compliance.

It frequently demands these things regardless of whether you intended to do anything wrong.

And there are good reasons for many of those requirements. A legal system cannot function if every citizen is free to disregard the rules whenever compliance becomes inconvenient.

But why shouldn't the same fundamental expectation apply to the government itself?

Why should an ordinary citizen be expected to understand and comply with complicated regulations while the agency responsible for administering those regulations can make mistakes without necessarily bearing the financial consequences?

Why should an entrepreneur have to hire consultants to navigate zoning rules while the government retains the ability to issue a legally deficient approval?

Why should a property owner lose millions because an agency failed to produce adequate findings?

There is a simple principle of fairness here:

If ignorance of the law is no excuse for the citizen, incompetence in administering the law should be no excuse for the government.

That doesn't mean every government employee who makes an honest mistake should be personally ruined.

It means the institution must be accountable for the decisions it makes.

The state cannot demand strict compliance with its rules while reserving the right to disclaim responsibility for its own authorizations.

This Is Not the Law Today. It Should Be a Serious Reform Proposal.

American law already recognizes concepts such as vested rights, equitable estoppel, and government liability in certain circumstances.

But their application varies across jurisdictions, and they do not provide the universal protection proposed here.

Courts frequently distinguish between permits lawfully issued and approvals granted in violation of applicable law.

Government immunity doctrines can further restrict compensation for administrative errors.

The result is that an innocent applicant may discover that even substantial reliance on an official approval provides less protection than expected.

The principle proposed here is deliberately stronger.

It would require legislative changes and, in some jurisdictions, potentially constitutional adjustments.

It would establish that good-faith reliance on a government permit creates an enforceable obligation.

It would prohibit revocation based solely on mistakes attributable to the issuing authority.

It would require the government to pay for necessary corrections to dangers arising from defects in its approval process, rather than imposing those costs on innocent permit holders.

It would preserve remedies for fraud, deception, and unauthorized deviations from approved conditions.

And it would establish clear deadlines and accountability mechanisms so agencies cannot escape responsibility simply by refusing to decide.

There would be difficult implementation questions, particularly where correcting an unsafe approval requires substantial changes to property or activity. Compensation, temporary safety interventions, disputes over causation, and the responsibilities of private engineers or contractors would all require careful legal design.

But those are reasons to develop the principle into workable legislation, not reasons to abandon the underlying question.

Why should government authorization create binding obligations for the citizen but not for the government?

The One-Way Street of Accountability

There is something deeply revealing about a society that celebrates private property and entrepreneurship while tolerating a permitting system in which official approval can prove financially unreliable.

We tell people to invest.

We tell them to create businesses.

We tell them to build housing.

We tell them to create jobs.

And then we subject them to regulations so complicated that even the agencies administering them can fail to apply them correctly.

When citizens make mistakes, we demand accountability.

When the government makes mistakes, we often demand patience from the citizens affected.

Patience while another hearing is scheduled.

Patience while another appeal proceeds.

Patience while another official reviews another document.

Patience while investments sit idle and legal bills accumulate.

And, sometimes, patience while an entire business opportunity disappears.

The Kalbachsʼ mountain bike park is one particularly visible illustration.

But the larger issue affects anyone who needs government authorization before making a substantial investment.

A homeowner building an addition.

A small business opening a restaurant.

A developer constructing affordable housing.

A farmer installing infrastructure.

An entrepreneur creating a recreational facility.

All of them are required to trust the government's decision-making process.

That trust should carry reciprocal obligations.

A permit should mean that the government has completed its review and stands behind its decision.

If the applicant lied, revoke it.

If the applicant disregarded its conditions, enforce them.

But if the government made the mistake, the government must correct it—and bear the cost.

No retroactive excuses.

No casually shifting financial losses onto innocent applicants.

No treating official permission as something that can evaporate after the citizen has already paid the price of relying on it.

We cannot build a serious culture of accountability on rules that operate in only one direction.

The government insists that citizens answer for their mistakes.

It's time to insist that the government answer for its own.

You made the rules. You reviewed the application. You granted the permission. You own the consequences.

Because accountability is not a one-way street.

And a government that demands obedience to its decisions should be required to stand behind them.

item.title: Permission to Build, Permission to Lose Everything: America’s Zoning Absurdity
item.description:
How a $2.5 million mountain bike park in Idaho became a monument to bureaucratic incompetence, NIMBY obstruction, and the American illusion of private property rights.

Americans love to talk about freedom.

Freedom to pursue happiness. Freedom to start a business. Freedom to own property. Freedom from excessive government interference.

It's practically a national religion.

But apparently, that freedom comes with a few conditions.

You can purchase 170 acres of land. You can hire consultants. You can submit your plans to the county government. You can obtain the required permits. You can invest millions of dollars in developing your property.

And then, just days before you open for business, the government can effectively tell you:

“Sorry. We didn't explain our own approval properly. You'll have to shut everything down.”

Welcome to Bonner County, Idaho, where the American Dream apparently requires the neighbors' permission—and even that might not be enough.

A $2.5 Million Lesson in American Bureaucracy

In 2023, Scott and Jennifer Kalbach purchased approximately 170 acres of rural land near Sandpoint, Idaho, with an ambitious but relatively straightforward idea.

They wanted to build a mountain bike park.

Not a chemical factory. Not a nuclear waste facility. Not an industrial slaughterhouse.

A mountain bike park.

Trails through wooded hillsides. Recreational opportunities for families. Visitors spending money at nearby businesses. Local employment. Outdoor activities for young people.

The sort of project one might expect a rural community to welcome.

And the Kalbachs didn't simply start bulldozing trails and hope nobody noticed.

They hired a land-use consultant. They approached Bonner County. They applied for a conditional-use permit, as required by local zoning regulations.

In April 2024, the county approved the project. Following appeals, county commissioners approved it again in June.

The approval came with restrictions governing operating hours, the number of riders, parking, emergency services, and other aspects of the operation.

In other words, the system worked exactly as its defenders insist it should.

The applicants followed the rules.

The government reviewed their proposal.

The government granted permission.

So the Kalbachs proceeded.

They brought in professional trail builders, including Gravity Logic, a company associated with the renowned Whistler mountain biking facilities in Canada.

They hired local workers.

They built trails.

They invested approximately $2.5 million.

Their opening was scheduled for June 13, 2025.

Then, on June 2, a judge vacated their permit.

Eleven days before opening.

Two and a half million dollars invested under a government approval that the government had failed to justify adequately.

You really couldn't invent a better advertisement for American entrepreneurship.

The Neighbors Have Entered the Chat

Of course, no American land-use controversy would be complete without the local chapter of the Not In My Backyard movement.

Some neighboring property owners opposed the bike park.

Their objections included increased traffic, dust, noise, and concerns about the character of the surrounding rural community.

Now, let's establish something important.

People have every right to raise legitimate concerns about developments near their homes.

A narrow road might genuinely struggle with increased traffic. Dust can be a nuisance. Noise can affect quality of life. Fire safety matters, especially in wooded rural areas.

These are reasonable issues for a planning authority to investigate.

But there is an enormous difference between regulating a project's measurable impacts and allowing neighboring property owners to obstruct a lawful land use indefinitely.

A traffic problem calls for traffic management.

Dust calls for dust mitigation.

Noise calls for enforceable noise standards.

Fire risk calls for proper emergency planning.

What none of those concerns automatically justifies is giving nearby residents an effective veto over what someone else does with their land.

Yet that is precisely the danger of a zoning system that makes development depend on subjective classifications, discretionary approvals, and litigation that can continue long after construction begins.

The Kalbachs' neighbors challenged the permit in court.

And they won.

But here's where the story becomes especially revealing.

The Government Made the Mistake. The Property Owners Paid for It.

The June 2025 ruling did not determine that the mountain bike park was inherently unsafe.

It did not establish that the trails were environmentally destructive.

It did not conclude that mountain biking was an unacceptable activity in rural Idaho.

Instead, the court found that Bonner County had failed to provide adequate factual reasoning for classifying the project as a permitted recreational facility.

That classification mattered.

Under the county's zoning rules, a recreational facility could receive a conditional-use permit. A commercial resort, as defined by the local code, could not be approved in the same zoning district.

The county had approved the project under one classification without sufficiently explaining why that classification was appropriate.

The judge also identified inadequate evidence supporting the county's finding about water availability for fire suppression.

These are genuine legal deficiencies. Governments must justify decisions according to the laws they administer. Neighbors are entitled to challenge approvals that fail to meet those standards.

But consider the practical result.

The property owners had applied through the official process.

The county had granted the permit.

The owners had relied on that approval to make an enormous investment.

And when the county's decision failed judicial review, it was the owners who lost the ability to operate.

The government's inadequate paperwork became the entrepreneur's multimillion-dollar problem.

There is something profoundly dysfunctional about a regulatory system in which a government agency can authorize a major investment without providing the level of legal certainty necessary to protect that investment.

Should unlawful approvals be immune from judicial review? Of course not.

But shouldn't the permitting authority be required to produce a legally defensible decision before inviting people to spend their life savings?

Apparently, that would be asking too much.

The Forest Fire Excuse: Bring a Garden Hose

One of the issues identified by the court was inadequate documentation concerning water for fire suppression.

And this is where the absurdity of the entire situation becomes particularly instructive.

Look at the property.

It is approximately 170 acres of wooded, mountainous terrain.

A forest.

You do not combat a major forest fire with a garden hose.

Wildland firefighting involves specialized crews, firebreaks, vegetation management, heavy equipment, and sometimes aircraft. It requires coordinated emergency response, not merely a convenient faucet beside a mountain bike trail.

Now, to be fair, adequate fire protection is a legitimate concern.

If the park has buildings, firefighters need to be able to protect them. If people are riding through forested terrain, evacuation routes matter. Emergency vehicle access matters. An adequate water source for applicable firefighting operations matters.

But those requirements need to be defined according to the actual risks.

Protecting a building from fire and extinguishing a wildfire across 170 acres are not the same engineering problem.

And here is the especially revealing detail.

The county's original approval already required a fire-risk assessment, a mitigation plan, and fire-suppression and emergency-services planning satisfactory to the responsible fire district.

Yet the court subsequently found that the county had not demonstrated adequate water availability. The county had relied partly on the property's location within a fire district and a requirement to dig a well, without establishing an adequate water-supply standard.

The court did not conclude that the park actually lacked adequate water. It concluded that the county had failed to establish that adequate water was available.

Again, the distinction matters.

And it raises an obvious question:

What fire-protection requirements apply to neighboring properties occupying similar wooded terrain?

Do comparable facilities face the same standards? Are those standards based on measurable risks? Is there a consistent threshold for adequate water supply?

If the answer is yes, good. Apply it consistently.

If the answer is no, then the county has some explaining to do.

Fire safety should be a matter of engineering, not a convenient procedural weapon in a zoning dispute.

When Is a Park Not a Park?

Having lost their conditional-use permit, the Kalbachs tried a different approach.

They reorganized the operation as a nonprofit and moved toward a donation-based model.

The reasoning was straightforward.

Bonner County's zoning code permits noncommercial parks in the relevant rural district.

So, if the mountain bike facility was operated as a nonprofit community park rather than a commercial enterprise, perhaps it qualified under that designation.

Not so fast.

The county disputed that interpretation.

A facility with mountain bike trails, recreational programs, and community activities apparently presented a difficult philosophical question:

What, exactly, is a park?

The distinction was legally consequential. Nonprofit status does not automatically settle whether an activity is commercial under a zoning ordinance, and the county argued that the operation still required a conditional-use permit.

But the sheer complexity of the dispute exposes the problem.

Instead of focusing primarily on the actual impacts of the activity—traffic, noise, sanitation, safety, environmental protection—the controversy became entangled in definitions of commercial recreation, donations, nonprofit operations, and permissible categories of land use.

The question is no longer simply whether the facility can operate safely.

It is whether the facility fits the correct bureaucratic box.

And if it doesn't, perhaps the answer is to spend another fortune on lawyers.

From Zoning Dispute to Surveillance

By July 2026, a court injunction had forced the bike ranch to halt public operations.

The county argued that the facility was operating without the authorization required under its zoning code, and the court found sufficient grounds to issue a preliminary injunction.

That is an important legal fact. The owners are not automatically entitled to disregard an injunction simply because they disagree with the county.

But the conflict didn't stop there.

According to the bike ranch's published account, neighboring opponents monitored activity at the property using cameras, and county officials later pursued information about people visiting the facility.

The owners say the county sought to hold them personally in contempt over gatherings they maintained were limited to friends and family, an exception they argue was allowed under the injunction.

The Kalbachs also say they resisted providing visitors' identifying information because of privacy and harassment concerns. Those allegations remain part of a contested legal proceeding, not established findings of official misconduct.

Nevertheless, consider how far this controversy has traveled.

What began as a question about whether a mountain bike facility belonged in a particular zoning category has escalated into litigation over who may visit privately owned land and under what circumstances.

A permit dispute has turned into a fight over the boundaries of personal relationships, public access, and property rights.

The county may have legitimate enforcement interests. The owners may have violated conditions imposed by the court. Those questions belong to the judicial process.

But a regulatory system that produces this degree of conflict over a recreational facility should prompt some serious examination of whether its underlying rules are fit for purpose.

The Same Disease That Makes Housing Unaffordable

This story is not fundamentally different from the zoning nightmare affecting housing development in American cities.

In San Francisco, Los Angeles, and countless other communities, restrictive land-use rules and lengthy approval procedures can prevent property owners from constructing additional housing even where demand is enormous.

Existing residents object.

Neighborhood organizations mobilize.

Developers face hearings, appeals, lawsuits, environmental reviews, design restrictions, and political pressure.

Projects become more expensive.

Some never get built.

And then everyone wonders why housing costs so much.

The Idaho bike park exposes the same structural weakness from another angle.

The problem is not merely that some neighbors dislike change.

People have disliked change since the invention of neighbors.

The problem is that American land-use systems can give those objections enormous procedural power while exposing applicants to extraordinary financial uncertainty.

A developer can spend years navigating approvals without knowing whether the project will survive a challenge.

And the longer the process takes, the more expensive it becomes.

Which brings us to another delicious irony.

The system that claims to protect ordinary communities can end up favoring the largest and wealthiest developers.

A major real estate corporation can employ specialized lawyers, consultants, planners, engineers, lobbyists, and public-relations professionals.

It can maintain several projects simultaneously, absorbing losses on one while others move forward.

A family investing its savings into a recreational facility has considerably less room for error.

The Kalbachs reportedly invested around $2.5 million.

A large corporation might treat that as a disappointing line item.

For a family, it can represent a financial catastrophe.

Who benefits from a regulatory system that requires enormous financial resources simply to establish what people are allowed to do with their property?

It certainly isn't the small entrepreneur.

Private Property, Subject to Everyone Else's Approval

America has elevated private property rights almost to the level of sacred doctrine.

Politicians invoke them.

Courts defend them.

Entire political movements build their identities around protecting individuals from government overreach.

But when someone actually tries to use private property for a project that some neighbors dislike, those principles suddenly become considerably more flexible.

Your land.

Your money.

Your investment.

Your financial risk.

But someone else's preferences may still determine whether you can proceed.

Of course, property rights have never been absolute. Nor should they be.

Nobody should be allowed to dump toxic waste into a neighbor's drinking water or create dangerous conditions simply because the offending activity takes place on private land.

The state has legitimate responsibilities to protect public health, safety, and the environment.

But those powers should be exercised through clear, objective, proportionate rules.

Not an unpredictable maze of discretionary classifications and approvals that can unravel after millions have already been spent.

The relevant question should be:

Can this proposed use operate while meeting reasonable, demonstrable standards for safety and its effects on surrounding properties?

If yes, approval should be predictable.

If no, the applicant should be told precisely why, preferably before committing substantial capital.

And if the government approves a project, it should have an obligation to make that approval legally defensible.

Anything less creates an intolerable imbalance: the government controls the permission, while the applicant carries almost all the risk.

What a Functional System Would Look Like

Reforming American land-use regulation does not require abolishing zoning or declaring open season on environmental protection.

It requires recognizing that government permission should mean something.

First, rules should focus on measurable impacts rather than subjective preferences about what belongs in a neighborhood.

Traffic capacity, noise, drainage, sanitation, environmental damage, fire access, and building safety can all be evaluated against published standards.

Second, the permitting authority should establish the facts and produce a legally adequate decision before granting approval.

If the county cannot explain why a project qualifies for a permit, it has no business issuing that permit and allowing the applicant to proceed under false confidence.

Third, appeals should be subject to clear deadlines, with potentially fatal deficiencies resolved before construction proceeds whenever practical.

Fourth, when an approval is overturned because the government failed to perform its own duties, there should be meaningful mechanisms to address the applicant's reliance losses where appropriate. That does not mean taxpayers must automatically guarantee every investment, but neither should government error be consequence-free for the agency responsible.

Finally, existing residents should have a voice without automatically possessing a veto.

Their legitimate concerns deserve examination and mitigation.

Their personal preference that nothing ever change should not, by itself, dictate the future of surrounding property.

The Cost of Saying No

As of November 2026, Panhandle Bike Ranch remains closed to the public under a court order.

Its owners are pursuing additional approvals and legal remedies, hoping to reopen for the 2027 season.

The trails are there.

The investment has been made.

The infrastructure exists.

But the public cannot use the park.

And lawyers continue to get paid.

The tragedy is not simply that a mountain bike park has been caught in a zoning dispute.

It is that an entrepreneur can follow the government's procedures, obtain its approval, invest millions in reliance on that approval, and still find the entire venture imperiled by deficiencies in the government's decision.

Meanwhile, a system ostensibly designed to protect communities can become a mechanism for freezing them in place.

Housing that isn't built.

Businesses that never open.

Jobs that never materialize.

Recreational facilities that sit unused.

All in the name of protecting the public from developments that, in many cases, could have been accommodated through reasonable standards and straightforward mitigation.

Americans are fond of declaring that government should get out of the way of entrepreneurship.

Perhaps they should start by demanding that when government grants permission, that permission actually carries some weight.

Because when the state can authorize a multimillion-dollar investment and then effectively shrug as its own inadequate approval collapses in court, something is profoundly wrong.

In America, you may own the land. You may finance the project. You may assume every dollar of risk.

But apparently, you still have to keep asking for permission to use what is yours.

And sometimes, even after they say yes, the answer is still no.

Sources

  • Bonner County Daily Bee — Panhandle Bike Ranch permit approval, April 24, 2024

  • Bonner County Daily Bee — Court vacates use permit, June 7, 2025

  • Sandpoint Reader — Court decision and fire-suppression findings, June 2025

  • Sandpoint Reader — Court injunction, July 15, 2026

  • Bonner County Daily Bee — October 2026 permit and litigation developments

  • Panhandle Bike Ranch — Owners' account and litigation timeline

item.title: If Buying Isn't Owning, Then Piracy Isn't Stealing
item.description:
From video games to heated seats and farm tractors, corporations are turning ownership into a subscription—and expecting us to thank them for the privilege.

There was a time when buying something meant you owned it.

A revolutionary concept, apparently.

You walked into a store, handed over your hard-earned money, and walked out with a product. A book, a television, a car, a video game. It was yours. You could use it, lend it, repair it, resell it, or leave it gathering dust in your attic for thirty years.

The manufacturer might not like what you did with it, but that was largely irrelevant.

They had your money. You had the product. The transaction was complete.

Somewhere along the way, corporations decided this arrangement was terribly unfair.

To them, naturally.

Why should a company make money from a customer only once when it could continue extracting payments indefinitely? Why sell a product when you can sell permission to use it? Why allow someone to repair something they purchased when you can charge them for the privilege of having you repair it?

And so began one of the most brazen corporate efforts in modern history: the systematic dismantling of consumer ownership.

A YouTube short about the increasingly bizarre world of video games recently led me to a comment that summarizes the entire problem in eleven magnificent words:

“If buying is not owning, then piracy is not stealing.”

That sentence should be printed on a billboard outside every major technology company's headquarters.

Because underneath the provocative wording lies a question corporate executives would very much prefer consumers never ask.

If I don't actually own what I paid for, what exactly did you sell me?

The Video Game Industry: You Bought It, Until We Decide You Didn't

Let's begin with video games.

Once upon a time, buying a game meant purchasing a cartridge or disc containing the software. You could play it ten years later. Twenty years later. Fifty, if the hardware survived.

You could lend it to a friend, sell it secondhand, or pass it down to your children.

Publishers didn't particularly enjoy the secondhand market, of course. From their perspective, every used game represented a transaction from which they earned precisely nothing.

But that's how ownership works.

Ford doesn't receive a commission when someone resells a used Mustang. Penguin Random House doesn't get paid every time a paperback changes hands. And Nintendo wasn't entitled to a percentage when a kid traded his copy of Super Mario Bros. for another game.

Then digital distribution arrived.

And publishers discovered something wonderful.

For them.

Suddenly, they could distribute games without manufacturing physical media, packaging products, shipping inventory, or worrying about unsold copies collecting dust on store shelves.

Those savings could have been passed on to consumers.

Instead, the industry increasingly retained traditional retail pricing while stripping away many traditional ownership rights.

You can't resell most digital games. You generally can't transfer them to another account. You often can't lend them. And depending on the platform, authentication requirements, and licensing arrangements, your continued access may depend on decisions made by a corporation years after your purchase.

And when someone complains?

They point to the terms of service.

You didn't buy the game. You purchased a license.

How convenient.

When they're advertising, it's “Buy Now.”

When you're demanding ownership rights, it's “Please refer to Section 17, Paragraph 4, Subsection B of our End User License Agreement.”

When they want your money, it's a purchase. When you want your rights, it's a license.

The Game That Disappeared

Consider Ubisoft's The Crew.

Released in 2014, the racing game depended on online infrastructure even for activities players might reasonably expect to enjoy alone.

In March 2024, Ubisoft shut down its servers.

The result was that legitimate owners could no longer play the game through its normal, authorized operation.

A product people had purchased became unusable because its publisher decided maintaining the servers was no longer worthwhile.

Now, operating servers costs money. Nobody seriously disputes that.

But there's an enormous difference between saying, “We will no longer maintain online multiplayer services,” and saying, “The product you purchased will no longer function at all.”

Publishers should not be compelled to operate online infrastructure forever.

They should, however, be expected to make reasonable provisions for preserving the functionality of products they sold—especially when those products contain substantial single-player experiences.

An offline mode. Community-hosted servers. A final patch removing unnecessary authentication dependencies.

Any of those would be preferable to turning a purchased game into a digital tombstone.

Instead, the customer gets a corporate farewell message.

Thank you for your money. Your product has expired.

And please consider purchasing our next release.

BMW: Subscribe to Your Own Heated Seats

If you thought video game publishers had cornered the market on corporate absurdity, allow me to introduce BMW.

The German luxury automaker decided that certain features already physically installed in its vehicles could be activated through subscriptions.

Among them?

Heated seats.

Yes. Seats.

The ones already installed in the automobile you purchased.

The heating elements were physically present. The wiring was physically present. The electronics were physically present.

But their functionality could be locked behind a software-controlled paywall.

In some markets, BMW offered customers the option to pay monthly to activate the heating equipment already sitting beneath their backsides.

Imagine explaining this to someone in 1985.

“Congratulations on your new luxury automobile, sir. The seats are heated.”

“Wonderful!”

“Would you like to use that feature?”

“Of course.”

“Excellent. That'll be another monthly payment.”

“Didn't I just buy the car?”

“Yes, sir. But you haven't subscribed to the warmth.”

The backlash was entirely predictable.

BMW discontinued its heated-seat subscription experiment in 2023, acknowledging the negative customer reaction.

But don't mistake this for a philosophical awakening.

BMW continued pursuing subscription-based features, including advanced parking assistance, camera-based functionality, and other electronic conveniences. Its newer offerings have included paid access to capabilities supported by hardware already installed in compatible vehicles.

To be precise, BMW's basic rearview camera isn't simply switched off until you pay a monthly fee. The continuing subscriptions concern more sophisticated parking and camera-assisted features, such as automated parking.

The distinction matters technically.

It doesn't eliminate the underlying question.

Why should the physical capabilities of something you purchased remain subject to the manufacturer's continuing permission?

BMW argues that subscriptions provide flexibility and that some connected services involve ongoing operating costs.

And for genuinely ongoing services, that's a reasonable argument.

Cloud storage costs money. Cellular connectivity costs money. Real-time information services cost money.

But heating an already-installed seat?

Activating a local hardware capability?

That's not a continuing service. That's a manufacturer discovering it can place an artificial tollbooth between you and your own equipment.

And once that business model becomes acceptable, where does it end?

A subscription to use the air conditioning?

A monthly fee to access the passenger-side electric windows?

Perhaps the premium “Rain Visibility Package,” allowing your windshield wipers to operate at full speed.

Don't laugh too hard.

A few decades ago, paying monthly to activate your own car seats would have sounded equally ridiculous.

John Deere: You Bought the Tractor. We Own the Wrench.

Then there's John Deere.

And this example moves beyond consumer inconvenience into something potentially far more damaging.

Farmers depend on their equipment.

A tractor isn't a recreational gadget. A combine harvester isn't a luxury accessory. These machines are essential tools in an industry where delays can destroy a season's income.

When a tractor breaks down during harvest, a farmer doesn't have the luxury of waiting three weeks for an authorized technician.

Historically, farmers repaired their own equipment or hired local mechanics.

Then agricultural machinery became increasingly computerized.

Computerization itself wasn't the problem. Modern electronics can improve efficiency, performance, diagnostics, and agricultural productivity.

The problem arose when manufacturers began controlling access to the software tools necessary to diagnose and repair those machines.

John Deere became the poster child for this controversy.

Farmers could physically own tractors costing hundreds of thousands of dollars while lacking access to certain diagnostic and repair capabilities necessary to maintain them independently.

A mechanical component could be replaced, yet the machine might still require proprietary software procedures before returning to normal operation.

And who controlled those tools?

John Deere and its authorized dealer network.

The message, effectively, was breathtaking:

You own the tractor.

But we control whether you can fix it.

In January 2025, the Federal Trade Commission sued Deere, alleging anticompetitive restrictions that forced farmers toward authorized repair services, increased costs, and created unnecessary delays.

Deere disputed wrongdoing.

In 2026, the company agreed to a proposed $99 million class-action settlement concerning repair restrictions. Separately, in July, the FTC and five states reached a settlement requiring Deere to provide farmers and independent repair providers access to repair resources equivalent to those available to authorized dealers, subject to the settlement's terms.

That's an extraordinary development.

Government intervention was needed to defend the principle that a farmer who purchased a tractor should be able to repair that tractor.

Think about that.

A farmer buys a machine.

A farmer owns the machine.

A farmer wants to repair the machine.

And somehow, in the twenty-first century, this becomes a matter for antitrust enforcement.

We have reached a point where companies are treating ownership as a defect in their business models.

It's Not About Technology. It's About Control.

Defenders of these practices often argue that modern products are more complicated than their predecessors.

Software needs maintenance. Security vulnerabilities must be patched. Online services cost money. Complex equipment requires specialized knowledge.

All true.

And almost entirely beside the point.

Nobody is arguing that a manufacturer must provide free technical support forever.

Nobody is arguing that online servers should operate indefinitely without funding.

Nobody is arguing that every consumer must be given unrestricted access to proprietary source code.

The argument is much simpler.

Once a company sells a product, it should not retain unreasonable power to prevent its owner from using, maintaining, repairing, or preserving that product.

A company has every right to charge for additional services.

What it should not have is an unlimited right to manufacture artificial dependencies solely to monetize capabilities the customer has already purchased.

There is a meaningful difference between a real service and a software lock.

One delivers continuing value.

The other withholds existing value until the customer pays again.

And corporations have become exceptionally skilled at blurring that distinction.

Piracy, Theft, and the Convenient Abuse of Language

Which brings us back to that wonderfully provocative comment:

“If buying is not owning, then piracy is not stealing.”

Let's get one thing clear.

Copyright infringement is not automatically legal simply because the copyright holder behaves badly.

Unauthorized distribution can cause genuine economic harm, particularly to independent developers and smaller creators whose livelihoods depend on sales.

Nor does owning a software license automatically entitle someone to redistribute unlimited copies.

But there is an important distinction between copyright infringement and theft.

If I steal your physical copy of a game, you no longer possess that copy.

If I reproduce the software without authorization, the original remains in your possession.

That doesn't mean copying is always harmless. It means the two actions are not identical, economically or legally.

And that distinction becomes particularly relevant when consumers are denied access to products they legitimately purchased.

Consider someone who pays full price for a game, only to discover years later that a discontinued authentication service has rendered it unusable.

An enthusiast releases a modification allowing the software to run offline.

The owner downloads that modification.

Depending on the circumstances and applicable law, circumventing technological protections or distributing modified software may still violate copyright law.

But is the person morally equivalent to someone stealing merchandise from a store?

I would argue emphatically not.

They aren't attempting to obtain something without paying for it.

They are attempting to recover the functionality of something they already paid for.

And if a corporation insists that the transaction never transferred ownership, then it shouldn't be surprised when consumers begin questioning why its preferred definition of property should govern everyone else's behavior.

You cannot demand absolute respect for property rights while treating your customers' property rights as optional.

The Subscription Economy Is Becoming a Protection Racket

The most disturbing aspect of this trend is how closely it resembles an artificial dependency business model.

First, sell someone a product.

Second, maintain control over an essential component of its functionality.

Third, require continuing payments or authorized intervention to use that component.

Fourth, describe the arrangement as an innovative customer experience.

A video game that depends on unnecessary online authentication.

A luxury vehicle with locally installed features locked behind digital permissions.

A tractor that cannot complete certain repairs without manufacturer-controlled software.

Different industries.

Different technologies.

The same basic principle.

We sold you the machine. Now pay us for permission to use all of it.

In extreme cases, the company doesn't even have to charge a subscription.

Simply controlling access to repair tools, replacement parts, or authentication systems can create continuing economic leverage over the customer.

That's why right-to-repair legislation matters.

That's why software preservation matters.

And that's why transparency about digital purchases matters.

California took a useful step in 2025 by requiring clearer disclosures when certain digital products advertised for purchase are actually sold as revocable licenses.

But disclosure is only the beginning.

Telling consumers that they don't own what they're buying doesn't solve the fundamental problem.

It merely makes the problem more visible.

Ownership Needs a Legal Comeback

The solution shouldn't require consumers to become hackers, reverse engineers, or amateur contract attorneys.

It requires restoring meaningful rights to ownership.

If a company markets a digital product as a purchase, the customer should receive durable rights to access the purchased functionality, subject to clearly defined limitations.

If a manufacturer sells a machine, the owner and qualified independent technicians should have reasonable access to the tools necessary to maintain and repair it.

If a product includes hardware functionality that can operate locally without ongoing manufacturer services, the company should not be free to impose arbitrary recurring fees merely to keep that functionality enabled.

If a publisher discontinues a game that has meaningful offline functionality, it should take reasonable steps to preserve that functionality rather than simply pulling the plug.

And when genuine ongoing services are involved, companies should identify and price them transparently instead of disguising hardware restrictions as service offerings.

These aren't radical demands.

They are attempts to preserve principles consumers took for granted for generations.

Manufacturers deserve compensation for the products they create.

Developers deserve payment for their work.

Inventors deserve protection for legitimate intellectual property.

But customers also deserve rights.

And a business transaction shouldn't be a one-way ratchet in which the manufacturer collects permanent money while granting temporary permission.

The Corporate Dream: You Own Nothing, But Keep Paying

There's a particularly ugly vision emerging from all this.

A future in which every object becomes a platform.

Every platform becomes a service.

Every service becomes a subscription.

And every subscription becomes another opportunity for a corporation to remind you that your possessions work only at its pleasure.

Your music is licensed.

Your movies are licensed.

Your games are licensed.

Your car's features are licensed.

Your tractor's repair capabilities are controlled.

And every month, another corporate department meets to discuss how much more revenue can be extracted from customers who already paid for the underlying product.

The executives call it recurring revenue.

Investors call it predictable cash flow.

Marketing departments call it flexibility.

Consumers have a simpler word for repeatedly paying to use something they've already bought.

Bullshit.

The original comment isn't a complete legal theory, and it shouldn't be mistaken for one.

It's something arguably more powerful.

It's a refusal to accept the corporate fiction that ownership should mean one thing when a company is collecting payment and something entirely different when the customer exercises their rights.

Because the issue was never simply piracy.

It was never merely heated seats.

And it certainly wasn't just farmers wanting to repair tractors.

It's about whether purchasing a product still means anything at all.

If corporations want customers to respect ownership, perhaps they should start by respecting it themselves.

And if buying isn't owning?

Then the problem isn't that consumers have forgotten what ownership means.

It's that corporations remember perfectly well—and have decided they would rather we didn't.

Subscriptions Aren't the Problem. Charging Twice Is.

Now, before anyone accuses me of opposing every conceivable subscription model, let me propose something.

Suppose BMW sells a fully equipped car for $60,000.

Now suppose BMW offers me that exact same vehicle for $36,000—60% of the original price—with certain convenience features disabled unless I pay a subscription.

Would I consider buying it?

Absolutely.

Because now we're talking about an actual commercial bargain.

BMW gets the opportunity to collect recurring revenue. I get a car for $24,000 less than its normal purchase price. I know exactly which features are included, which require additional payments, and what happens if I stop paying.

I can decide whether heated seats are worth another monthly expense. Perhaps I don't care about them at all.

Fine. I just saved $24,000.

And if BMW wants to offer a permanent unlock for a one-time payment, even better.

But here's the essential condition: all of this must be disclosed before the purchase, in plain language, with a genuine and substantial reduction in the vehicle's price.

No discovering additional charges after signing the paperwork. No burying critical restrictions on page 47 of a software agreement. No advertising a vehicle as fully equipped when half its capabilities are locked behind recurring payments.

And no artificial discount created by inflating the supposed original price.

There must be a real economic advantage to accepting the restrictions.

Alternatively, BMW could retain ownership of the car and charge me monthly for using it.

We already have a name for that revolutionary concept.

Renting.

We also have leasing and financing. The automobile industry has offered different arrangements for purchasing or using vehicles for generations.

BMW doesn't need to reinvent commerce.

It simply needs to decide which business it's conducting.

If I'm renting your car, charge me rent.

If I'm financing your car, charge me installments.

If I'm buying your car at a substantial discount in exchange for clearly disclosed feature restrictions, let me decide whether the bargain is worthwhile.

But if I'm paying the full purchase price?

Then stop trying to charge me rent on equipment you've already sold me.

That's not a subscription service.

That's an attempt to collect the purchase price and keep the privileges of ownership.

And the remarkable thing isn't that some executive thought this was a good idea.

It's that an entire corporate culture has become comfortable describing it as innovation.

item.title: The Sidewalk Paradox: Public Infrastructure, Private Responsibility, and the Bureaucratic Art of Passing the Buck
item.description:
How cities demand accessibility while outsourcing the responsibility for providing it to the people who happen to own the nearest building.

Look at the photograph accompanying this article.

It's a sidewalk in São Paulo, Brazil.

Or, more accurately, it's a collection of concrete slabs, improvised ramps, abrupt changes in elevation, exposed tree roots, and questionable paving decisions masquerading as a sidewalk.

Some sections are tiled. Others are bare concrete. One section looks like it has been cultivating its own ecosystem.

There are steps where there shouldn't be steps, slopes where there should be level ground, and obstacles that make walking an exercise in concentration.

Now imagine navigating this mess in a wheelchair.

Or with a walker.

Or pushing a stroller.

Or simply being elderly and having the audacity to leave your house.

Welcome to modern urban accessibility, where governments proudly proclaim everyone's right to mobility while leaving the actual implementation to whoever owns the nearest piece of real estate.

And before American readers dismiss this as another example of Brazilian infrastructure problems, there's something they should know.

The United States does much the same thing.

The Public Sidewalk That Somehow Became Your Problem

In São Paulo, Municipal Law 15,442/2011 generally requires property owners to construct, maintain, and repair the sidewalks bordering their properties.

The city establishes technical standards, accessibility requirements, and penalties for noncompliance.

But the practical responsibility for maintaining much of this public infrastructure falls on private individuals.

Think about that arrangement.

The sidewalk is public. Everyone has the right to use it. Its primary purpose is to allow people to move safely through the city.

Yet its condition depends on the financial resources, competence, willingness, and maintenance priorities of individual property owners.

One homeowner installs attractive tiles.

The neighbor pours concrete.

Another raises the sidewalk to accommodate a garage entrance.

Someone else ignores a growing crack for fifteen years.

And the municipality expects these independently maintained fragments to magically become a coherent pedestrian transportation network.

That's not urban planning. That's wishful thinking with a municipal ordinance attached.

America: Different Language, Same Absurdity

Consider New York City.

Under Section 19-152 of its Administrative Code, property owners are generally responsible for installing, repairing, and maintaining the sidewalks adjoining their properties.

The New York City Department of Transportation can inspect sidewalks and issue violations. In certain circumstances, the city can arrange repairs and bill the property owner.

There are exceptions, including special arrangements for some damage caused by city-owned trees.

But the underlying principle is familiar: public pedestrian infrastructure, private maintenance responsibility.

And New York is hardly the only American jurisdiction that uses some version of this arrangement.

The details differ from city to city, but the basic model appears across the country.

Meanwhile, American governments have accessibility obligations under the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Which produces a remarkable contradiction.

The government is responsible for ensuring accessibility, but it can leave significant portions of the physical infrastructure needed to achieve that accessibility in private hands.

The legal obligations don't simply disappear because a city delegates maintenance. But the fragmentation makes consistent implementation considerably more difficult.

It's a system practically designed to generate inconsistent results.

Imagine If We Did This to Roads

Here's a thought experiment.

Imagine your city announced that, starting tomorrow, every property owner would be responsible for maintaining the portion of the roadway directly in front of their property.

You would have to pay for the asphalt.

Your neighbor could choose concrete.

The person across the street might prefer cobblestones.

Someone with a little extra money could build a beautifully finished section.

Someone struggling financially might leave a pothole untouched for years.

And the fellow with the oversized pickup truck might decide that raising the road surface by six inches would make entering his driveway more convenient.

The municipality would establish technical standards, of course.

It would publish manuals.

It would threaten fines.

It might even launch a public awareness campaign explaining that roads should be smooth and safe.

But actually maintaining the road?

That's your problem.

The result would be a transportation network consisting of thousands of disconnected construction projects, each maintained according to the resources and priorities of a different individual.

We would immediately recognize the absurdity.

Yet when the infrastructure serves pedestrians instead of automobiles, we somehow accept the same logic.

Why is the roadway treated as a unified transportation system while the sidewalk is treated as a collection of private chores?

Accessibility Doesn't Work One Property at a Time

Accessibility has a fundamental characteristic that this model ignores.

It requires continuity.

A wheelchair-accessible sidewalk that ends at a six-inch step isn't an accessible route.

A beautifully paved stretch followed by broken concrete isn't an accessible route.

A compliant ramp leading directly into a tree trunk isn't an accessible route.

And a pedestrian network where 95% of the route is perfectly accessible but the remaining 5% is impassable may be functionally useless to someone who cannot cross those barriers.

Accessibility isn't something you achieve by counting how many individual property owners have complied with the rules.

It's something you achieve by ensuring that a person can travel from one location to another without encountering an obstacle that makes the journey impossible.

That requires coordinated planning, consistent engineering, maintenance schedules, and accountability across property boundaries.

In other words, it requires exactly the kind of centralized infrastructure management that municipalities already perform for roads.

The sidewalk is not merely decorative concrete outside someone's house.

It is part of the city's transportation network.

The Convenient Economics of Passing the Bill

Of course, there's a financial reason municipalities find this arrangement attractive.

Sidewalks cost money.

Construction costs money.

Repairs cost money.

Tree-root damage costs money.

Accessibility improvements cost money.

And shifting those costs onto adjacent property owners reduces the amount municipalities must pay directly from their own budgets.

From a narrow accounting perspective, it's convenient.

But transferring a cost doesn't eliminate it.

It merely changes who receives the bill.

Worse, it creates a system where public infrastructure quality can depend on private wealth.

A prosperous homeowner may afford proper reconstruction.

A struggling family may postpone repairs.

An absentee landlord may do the bare minimum.

And the pedestrian who needs to use the sidewalk has absolutely no control over any of these decisions.

The elderly woman with a walker doesn't care whether the adjacent property owner is financially comfortable.

The wheelchair user doesn't care whether the landlord is waiting for a contractor.

The parent pushing a stroller doesn't care whose responsibility it is to fix the broken pavement.

They need a safe, continuous route.

And the public authority responsible for managing the city's transportation system should be accountable for providing one.

But What About Property Owners Who Cause Damage?

There's an obvious objection.

What if a property owner damages the sidewalk?

What if someone illegally modifies it to accommodate a driveway, allows construction equipment to destroy the pavement, or installs an obstruction?

Should taxpayers pay for that?

Of course not.

There is a perfectly reasonable distinction between responsibility for maintaining public infrastructure and liability for damaging it.

The municipality should own the responsibility for designing, constructing, inspecting, and maintaining the pedestrian network.

If a private individual or company damages that infrastructure, the municipality should have the authority to require restoration or recover the costs.

The same principle can apply to utility companies excavating sidewalks to install pipes, cables, or other equipment.

This isn't complicated.

We already understand that someone who damages public property can be required to pay for the damage without becoming responsible for maintaining that property forever.

Why should sidewalks be different?

A Better Model: Treat Sidewalks Like Streets

The alternative doesn't require revolutionary technology or some elaborate new administrative philosophy.

It requires governments to treat pedestrian infrastructure as actual infrastructure.

Municipalities should assume responsibility for the design, construction, reconstruction, and maintenance of public sidewalks.

They should establish consistent standards for surfaces, gradients, drainage, tree placement, and accessibility.

They should inspect pedestrian routes as connected networks rather than isolated property frontages.

They should prioritize repairs based on safety, accessibility, pedestrian traffic, and the needs of vulnerable populations.

And they should fund this work through transparent public budgets, just as they fund road maintenance.

That doesn't mean every sidewalk in every city can be rebuilt overnight.

It means the government takes responsibility for a coherent, long-term program instead of expecting thousands of independent property owners to somehow produce a unified result.

Nor does it necessarily mean abolishing every form of local cost recovery. Cities can debate how infrastructure is financed.

But financing a public service and fragmenting responsibility for delivering that service are two very different things.

The municipality should be accountable for the outcome, regardless of how the work is funded.

The Real Test of a City's Accessibility

Politicians love announcing accessibility initiatives.

New ramps.

New regulations.

New public awareness campaigns.

New penalties.

New slogans about inclusive cities.

But there's a much simpler test.

Put someone in a wheelchair at one end of a residential block.

Ask them to reach the other end without entering the roadway, requiring assistance, or encountering an impassable obstacle.

Then repeat the experiment across the neighborhood.

That tells you far more about a city's actual commitment to accessibility than a hundred pages of regulations.

Because accessibility isn't a legal declaration.

It's a physical reality.

And if the infrastructure doesn't allow people to move safely, the existence of a law promising that they should be able to do so is cold comfort.

The Systemic Error

The photograph that started this discussion isn't remarkable because it shows an unusually bad sidewalk.

It's remarkable because the scene is so ordinary.

Millions of people encounter variations of this problem every day.

We've become so accustomed to broken, uneven, disconnected pedestrian infrastructure that we barely question why it exists.

We blame careless homeowners.

We blame poor workmanship.

We blame insufficient enforcement.

And sometimes those criticisms are justified.

But they miss the structural problem.

We have organized the maintenance of a continuous public transportation network as thousands of disconnected private obligations.

Then we act surprised when the resulting infrastructure is disconnected.

The problem isn't simply that people fail to follow the rules.

It's that the rules themselves create a fragmented system for delivering something that must function as a unified whole.

A sidewalk shouldn't become unusable because you've crossed an invisible property boundary.

A person's ability to move safely through a city shouldn't depend on whether the next homeowner has enough money for concrete.

And governments shouldn't be able to congratulate themselves for passing accessibility legislation while leaving the practical delivery of accessibility to a patchwork of private actors.

We would never accept that arrangement for a major roadway.

We shouldn't accept it for the people walking beside one.

Public infrastructure deserves public accountability.

And a sidewalk is public infrastructure.

It's time we started treating it that way.
