item.title: Startled Trump nominee gets torn apart by unexpected Senate ally
item.description:
President Donald Trump’s judicial nominee James P. Sullivan expected help from a Republican Senate racing to confirm Trump’s judges. Instead, at a Wednesday Judiciary Committee hearing, he ran into Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a loyal Trump ally who exposed how quickly Sullivan’s professed constitutional philosophy collapsed under a concrete question: If “originalism” makes the public meaning of the Constitution in 1791 controlling, why would punishments accepted then—such as cutting off an ear—be unconstitutional now?

Sullivan never gave Kennedy a coherent answer. He retreated to Supreme Court precedent, insisted that a district judge could not “grade” the justices’ work, and eventually suggested that the Court only “sometimes” follows originalism. Kennedy’s reply was blunt: “You’re talking in circles.”

A doctrine meets its consequences

Mediaite reported that Sullivan’s hearing had already gone badly when he struggled to recall the subject of the 22nd Amendment, which limits presidents to two elected terms. Kennedy then moved from constitutional trivia to the practical meaning of Sullivan’s judicial ideology.

Kennedy asked whether Sullivan would uphold a congressional statute authorizing the mutilation of people convicted of crimes, noting that cutting off ears and branding people were accepted punishments around the time the Eighth Amendment was adopted. Sullivan initially answered that, as a district judge, he would be bound by Supreme Court precedent.

That answer described the hierarchy of the federal courts but evaded Kennedy’s question. Sullivan had identified himself as an originalist. Kennedy wanted to know whether he would follow that doctrine to its stated conclusion when interpreting the prohibition against “cruel and unusual punishments.”

“Are you an originalist or not?” Kennedy demanded.

Sullivan said he was, while also arguing that originalism should be used to understand the judicial power established by Article III. Kennedy pressed again: If the constitutional meaning fixed in 1791 controls, what makes an ear-cutting statute unconstitutional?

Sullivan again cited Supreme Court precedent. When Kennedy asked whether that meant the Supreme Court itself had rejected originalism, Sullivan said it was not his place to “grade their homework.” He then conceded that the Court “sometimes” does not apply the approach he said he would use. Kennedy caught the contradiction immediately: “It sounds like you just did.”

The confirmation machine briefly jams

Kennedy’s questioning was notable because it came from inside Trump’s own political coalition. Republicans were moving quickly at the time to confirm as many Trump judicial nominees as possible before Democrats took control in January. Nearly one-third of active federal judges were already Trump appointees, according to the reporting.

That campaign made the hearing more than an academic exercise. A Senate majority was using its institutional power to give Trump’s legal movement durable control over federal courts. The officials receiving lifetime appointments would continue shaping constitutional rights long after the electoral coalition that installed them had lost power.

Kennedy’s motives are not established by the exchange. The AlterNet report itself allowed that the confrontation might have been substantive scrutiny or political theater. But the questioning still revealed something the usual confirmation choreography works to obscure: “originalism” is often presented as a neutral restraint on judges until its premises produce an indefensible result. Sullivan could not explain how his declared method treated historical meaning as binding while allowing modern precedent to prohibit punishments once considered acceptable.

The problem was not that a lower-court nominee recognized the authority of Supreme Court decisions. He was required to do so. The problem was that Sullivan marketed a sweeping interpretive creed, then treated precedent as an escape hatch when Kennedy forced him to account for its consequences.

Rejection by voters, rescue by appointment

Trump nominated Sullivan after Texas voters removed him from the Texas Supreme Court in the midterm elections, Mediaite reported. Losing an elected judicial seat did not end Sullivan’s path to power; a president and Senate majority could place him on the federal bench instead.

That sequence captures the institutional stakes more clearly than the hearing’s spectacle. Voters rejected Sullivan for one judgeship, but the federal appointment system offered political allies another route—this time toward a position insulated from future elections.

Kennedy momentarily interrupted that process by demanding an intelligible answer. Whether the Senate ultimately treated Sullivan’s performance as disqualifying was not established in the supplied reporting. What the hearing did establish was narrower and damning enough: when asked to reconcile originalism with the Eighth Amendment’s application to barbaric punishment, Trump’s nominee could repeat the doctrine or invoke precedent, but he could not make the two answers fit.

item.title: Rival GOP lawmakers erupt in profane shouting match on Senate floor
item.description:
John Cornyn and Ted Cruz turned the Senate floor into a venue for their political grievance Tuesday, shouting over a blocked Trump judicial nominee while exposing the machinery beneath the dispute: presidential favoritism, senatorial veto power and a Texas Republican feud sharpened by electoral collapse. Cornyn accused Cruz of lacking credibility and erupted with “Oh, that’s bulls——!” before walking across the aisle, according to Washington Sun reporting cited by AlterNet.

The confrontation was vulgar, but not mysterious. Cornyn is withholding the procedural approval needed to advance T. Elliot Gaiser, a conservative Ohio lawyer nominated to a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Texas. Cruz wants the nomination moving. Cornyn says the White House handled it so badly that he cannot support Gaiser. Behind that fight sits another: Cruz’s political operation helped the candidate whose Trump-backed primary victory ended Cornyn’s Senate career.

A blue slip becomes a pressure point

The immediate conflict concerns Cornyn’s refusal to return a blue slip for Gaiser. The Senate Judiciary Committee’s blue-slip practice gives home-state senators substantial influence over district-court nominees, and Cornyn is using that leverage to stop the nomination.

Cornyn, himself a former judge, told the Sun that the White House committed “a lot of different process fouls.” His fundamental objection, he said, is that Gaiser is not a Texas lawyer.

“I don’t know why a Texas senator would agree to a nomination of somebody from Ohio for one of the most important district benches in the state, in Dallas,” Cornyn said.

That is a concrete objection, whatever else is driving the hostility: a federal district seat in Texas would go to a lawyer from Ohio through a selection process that, by Cornyn’s account, alienated one of the senators whose cooperation the nomination requires. The White House chose the nominee; Cruz supported the choice; Cornyn retained enough institutional power to obstruct it.

Cruz’s explanation for the resulting explosion was studied detachment. Asked why Cornyn was upset, he replied, “You’d have to ask him.” That answer treats a conflict Cruz was actively arguing about as somebody else’s emotional episode.

The career Cornyn says was ended

During the exchange, Cornyn told Cruz that he was angry at someone “for ending my career!” Reporters could not determine whether he meant Cruz or Trump. The ambiguity matters because the reporting gives Cornyn reasons to blame both.

Trump endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton against Cornyn in the Republican Senate primary, effectively ending Cornyn’s career. Cruz publicly remained neutral. But Axiom Strategies, Cruz’s political operation, worked with Paxton and helped him win the nomination, according to the Sun.

Public neutrality paired with political assistance is not neutrality in any meaningful sense. It is distance maintained for public consumption while aligned operatives shape the result. Cornyn’s response was blunt: “I just knew he was never one of my supporters.”

Paxton then lost to James Talarico, helping produce a Democratic wave across Texas that Cornyn had warned would follow Paxton’s nomination. The result left Cruz as the only statewide elected Republican entering the coming term, according to the report. What Republicans lost was not merely Cornyn’s seat. Their primary electorate, encouraged by Trump and aided by Cruz’s operation, selected a nominee who then helped drag the party into a statewide defeat.

Republican damage, redirected

The Senate argument followed that electoral “shellacking,” as the Sun described it, but its participants aimed their anger inward only after their choices carried consequences. Trump used his endorsement to dislodge an incumbent Republican senator. Cruz’s political apparatus assisted Trump’s preferred candidate while Cruz avoided publicly taking a side. Paxton won the primary and lost the general election. Cornyn, still possessing a senator’s procedural leverage, is now denying the White House a judgeship.

None of this was caused by a powerless faction, an unruly protest movement or an administrative misunderstanding. The actors are a president, two senators, a statewide officeholder and the political professionals working around them. They controlled the endorsements, the campaign support, the nomination and the blue slip. Their dispute is over which powerful Republican should absorb the cost of decisions made within their own party.

That is why the shouting matters beyond its spectacle. The Senate floor offered a rare unfiltered view of how institutional power and personal retaliation can converge. Cornyn presents substantive objections to Gaiser’s selection, including the nominee’s lack of Texas legal roots and the White House’s process. But the clash also arrived after Trump helped terminate Cornyn’s career and Cruz’s operation aided the instrument of that defeat.

Whether Cornyn’s remark about “ending my career” targeted Trump or Cruz remains unresolved. The reported sequence leaves little doubt about the structure of the grievance: Trump delivered the endorsement, Cruz’s operation helped convert it into a primary victory, and Cornyn still controls one lever they need.

item.title: Nicolle Wallace marvels at 'queen of right-wing media' defection
item.description:
Megyn Kelly’s supposed “defection” from Donald Trump’s coalition amounted to something narrower: she called Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin an “idiot” and said she had no confidence in his handling of a reported wave of technology failures. Nicolle Wallace seized on the attack as evidence that the administration had lost one of the most influential voices in right-wing media. But criticism of an official during a crisis is not necessarily a break with the president who empowered him—and calling it one risks mistaking conservative discontent with incompetence for opposition to Trump’s politics.

A crisis without a credible messenger

AlterNet reports that widespread technology outages affected major systems, including what Wallace described as the country’s largest email provider and a nationwide aviation ground stop. According to Wallace, Mullin had served as the administration’s public face on the disruptions since the previous Friday.

The administration’s credibility problem was the focus of a discussion between Wallace and The Bulwark’s Sam Stein. Even if the failures had a benign explanation—rather than a malicious actor—Stein argued that the White House needed officials whom the public could trust to explain what was happening.

“The absence of trusted communicators feeds the anxiety,” Stein wrote. He said the administration should offer explanations through people the public could reasonably believe were “operating in good faith.”

That is not merely a communications defect. The administration controls the agencies responsible for responding to the crisis and the information available about that response. When its chosen representative inspires distrust, the institutional failure belongs to the president and the officials he placed in charge—not to an anxious public supposedly lacking reassurance.

Kelly attacks the official, not the power that installed him

Wallace then played Kelly’s denunciation of Mullin.

“No offense to Markwayne Mullen, but he seems like an idiot,” Kelly said, referring to him as the DHS director. “I have zero faith in this man. Zero. Less than zero.”

Kelly added that Homeland Security was “a very serious agency” and said she wanted some confidence in the person leading it. Wallace characterized the remarks as extraordinary because they came from “the queen of right-wing media ecosystem.”

The insult is politically revealing, but “defection” oversells it. Nothing in the reporting establishes that Kelly abandoned Trump, rejected his administration, or broke with the political project she had supported. Her criticism instead isolates Mullin as the problem. That framing can protect the president by turning an administration-wide test of competence into the personal failure of a subordinate.

Presidents do not merely suffer the quality of their appointees. They select, retain and authorize them. If Mullin was unfit to manage the response, the relevant question extends beyond whether Kelly considers him stupid: Why was he entrusted with a powerful department, and why did the White House continue using him as its public representative?

Privilege became part of the failure

Bill O’Reilly’s criticism was more concrete. He faulted Mullin for reportedly taking a private jet to a college football game while other travelers remained stranded.

“I can’t understand how anybody can get on a private jet and go to a football game when every other American can’t take off from an airport,” O’Reilly said. He called the spectacle “insulting” and rejected a mechanical-failure explanation as inadequate.

The political damage lies in the contrast O’Reilly identified: an official associated with the government’s response could apparently escape the disruption through private travel while ordinary passengers absorbed the consequences. Whether or not Mullin personally caused the outages, leaving for a football game conveyed insulation from the emergency he was supposed to address.

That is more than a bad “look.” Public officials routinely use the language of optics to reduce substantive failures to presentation. Here, the reported conduct exposed the hierarchy plainly: government power and private access for the official; delays, uncertainty and thin explanations for everyone else.

Kelly and O’Reilly’s attacks show that the administration’s response had become difficult even for sympathetic media figures to defend. They do not yet establish a political realignment. The sharper fact is that influential conservatives could condemn Mullin while leaving Trump—the person with the authority to appoint, direct or remove him—conveniently outside the frame.

item.title: MAGA election loser suffers another humiliation
item.description:
Bo French’s latest rejection came not from voters but from River Crest Country Club, the Fort Worth institution whose board terminated his membership effective immediately. In a Nov. 10 letter obtained by Politico, the club cited “reasons relating to the reputation and general welfare of the Club.” River Crest did not specify what conduct prompted the decision, leaving any connection to French’s racist campaign rhetoric unconfirmed.

The expulsion followed French’s failed Republican campaign for Texas railroad commissioner, during which he built his candidacy around hostility toward immigration and questioned the Americanness of nonwhite Texans. Losing access to an elite golf club is hardly a public sanction. But it is another measure of how thoroughly French converted racial provocation into political and social liability.

A private institution protects its reputation

River Crest’s board had the power to remove French, and it used it. The club, founded in 1911, markets itself as a Fort Worth “who’s who” and operates a 6,368-yard golf course known as a training ground for prominent golfers.

That institutional self-image matters because the board framed French’s removal around the club’s interests, not any public principle. River Crest’s general manager declined to discuss the former member or the board’s reasoning, citing a policy against commenting on past, current or prospective members and club operations.

The available reporting therefore does not establish why French was expelled. Politico identified his campaign controversy as a possible explanation, not a confirmed cause. The distinction is essential: the club condemned nothing publicly. It acted to protect its “reputation and general welfare” and then withheld the facts behind that judgment.

French targeted students he could not identify

The controversy began when French reacted to a photograph of cheering University of Texas football fans that included many students of South Asian descent. He treated their appearance as grounds to question their place in American life.

The photograph did not reveal anyone’s citizenship or nationality. As National Review noted while denouncing French’s remarks, state law requires 90 percent of the university’s students to be Texans. His attack relied on a racial inference: people who looked South Asian were recast as foreigners, regardless of who they actually were.

French’s online defenders tried to redirect the dispute toward the university—claiming that it served too many foreign students or discriminated against white Texans. Those arguments did not fit the relevant facts. National Review observed that the university had no preferential admissions standards for Indian Americans. It also noted that French had previously joined other Texas Republicans in supporting an admissions system designed to eliminate consideration of race.

That retreat exposed the misdirection. Faced with criticism for judging students by appearance, French and his defenders shifted attention to admissions policy. The weaker actors in the story—the photographed students—were made to answer for an imagined institutional offense, while the candidate who racialized them posed as the aggrieved party.

Condemnation without ambiguity

Some Texas Republicans criticized French, with varying degrees of force. Bishop Michael Olson of Fort Worth was more direct.

“This is racist and sinful rhetoric that seeks to harm and to divide,” Olson wrote. “It is disturbing that it comes from a candidate for public office. An apology is called for.”

That rebuke prompted anger from MAGA supporters, illustrating the political function of French’s rhetoric. The point was not a serious inquiry into enrollment rules or citizenship. It was to make racial appearance a test of belonging—and then punish anyone who named the tactic plainly.

French failed to win the state office he sought. River Crest has now decided it no longer wants him as a member. The country club’s silence prevents its action from becoming a clear institutional repudiation of his campaign, but its letter still records the practical verdict: French’s presence had become, in the board’s judgment, incompatible with the club’s reputation and welfare.

item.title: $1,700 stimulus checks could unintentionally help Trump’s war effort
item.description:
Rep. Ro Khanna’s proposed $1,700 checks would not end the financial damage attributed to the Trump administration’s war with Iran. They would reimburse families for part of it. That distinction is the core of Zeeshan Aleem’s criticism: relief aimed at higher gasoline, grocery and electricity bills could also make an open-ended war easier for the government to sustain by cushioning some domestic consequences without changing the policy producing them.

Khanna wants the incoming Congress to pass the payments immediately. The proposal’s fate remains unresolved, and the claim that it could provide political cover for the war is Aleem’s argument in an MS Now op-ed, not an established outcome. But it identifies a real problem in the proposal’s design. The government would continue financing military operations while taxpayers received a one-time payment drawn from the same public purse.

Compensation without constraint

Khanna’s proposal recognizes that the war’s costs do not stop at military appropriations. AlterNet reports that it is intended to offset rising household expenses, including fuel, food and electricity. Sending cash would offer tangible help to people struggling with those increases.

But the payment contains no mechanism, as described, for limiting the war responsible for the added expense. It would compensate households after the administration imposed the costs rather than constrain the administration’s ability to keep imposing them.

Aleem calls this “slopulism,” meaning a flashy, internet-friendly imitation of economic populism. The label is less important than the institutional mismatch it describes. Congress holds spending and legislative power. If lawmakers believe the war is producing unacceptable economic harm, their first responsibility is to confront the policy and its financing—not merely distribute partial rebates for the damage.

That does not make relief worthless. It makes relief inadequate when presented as the principal response to a continuing cause. A family can spend $1,700 once. A war can keep raising public expenditures and destabilizing energy costs long afterward.

The war bill does not disappear

Aleem argues that military deployments and munitions had already cost roughly $50 billion. Under Khanna’s plan, the checks would become another war-related public expense rather than a substitute for those costs.

He also warns that a large round of payments could contribute to inflation. The supplied reporting does not establish that economic outcome, and the proposal has not been enacted. But the broader fiscal contradiction is already visible in the plan itself: taxpayers would finance both the military campaign and an effort to soften the campaign’s domestic economic effects.

That arrangement shifts attention from the officials directing and funding the war toward the household task of surviving it. Higher bills become a consumer-affordability problem to be managed with a check, while the decision generating those bills escapes the same immediate scrutiny.

The misdirection is politically convenient even if it is not Khanna’s intention. A payment bearing Congress’s promise of relief can make government action look responsive while leaving the administration’s underlying policy intact. The public receives a temporary benefit; the executive branch retains the capacity to continue the war.

Relief cannot substitute for a war policy

Aleem’s strongest objection is chronological: Congress should address the ongoing conflict before advertising compensation for its consequences. As he puts it, Khanna is “putting the cart before the horse.”

That criticism need not require withholding aid from families until lawmakers resolve the war. Congress could pursue material relief while also confronting military spending and the conflict’s duration. The defect in the proposal, as reported, is that the check is concrete and immediate while any challenge to the war is absent.

The headline’s claim is therefore conditional, not proven: the checks could help Trump’s war effort by reducing political pressure from rising living costs. Whether they would do so depends on what Congress does alongside them. If lawmakers send money while allowing military expenditures and household costs to keep mounting, they will have converted opposition to the war’s consequences into a rebate program.

Khanna’s proposal promises families $1,700 against gasoline, groceries and electricity. It offers no reported answer to the more consequential question: how many additional bills Congress is prepared to let the war generate after that money is gone.

item.title: Experts sound dementia alarms over Trump’s wobbly walking
item.description:
President Donald Trump’s visibly unsteady gait during a November 18 walk with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos has renewed public questions about his health, but the available reporting does not establish that he has dementia. The footage shows a concerning physical irregularity. It does not identify its cause.

That distinction matters because the headline converts a medical hypothesis into an alarm. Psychologist and cognitive neuroscientist Frank George told David Pakman that Trump’s movements could fit behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia when considered alongside other behavior George has observed. Yet George also named stroke and vestibular problems as possible explanations for the same S-shaped walking pattern. His analysis is a differential judgment, not a reported diagnosis.

The White House supplied the footage

The video did not emerge from a covert recording or an adversary’s camera. The White House’s official “Rapid Response” account posted Trump walking across the grounds of Malacañang Palace in Manila with Marcos during Trump’s Asia trip. Viewers then focused on Trump veering from a straight path and appearing unstable on the red carpet.

The New Republic cited multiple videos from the Manila appearance and pointed to an October clip in which Trump seemed to swerve while approaching a newly installed White House helipad. George has also highlighted Trump dragging his right leg and tapping his thigh while walking. AlterNet reported that John Paul Garrison has separately suggested Trump displays signs consistent with dementia and a possible stroke.

Those observations justify scrutiny. The president exercises extraordinary authority, and evidence that may bear on his physical or cognitive capacity is not private trivia. The institutional question is whether the White House will provide a credible account of conspicuous symptoms visible in footage distributed by the White House itself.

Concern is warranted; certainty is not

George’s reasoning was more qualified than the headline built around it. He said Trump’s gait should be evaluated as part of an “overall constellation of symptoms.” He argued that the pattern did not show other features he would associate with Parkinson’s disease or tardive dyskinesia, while frontotemporal dementia remained consistent with what he observed.

“Consistent with” is doing essential work. George said he did not eliminate frontotemporal dementia; he did not report that it had been confirmed. His own list of possible causes makes a categorical conclusion impossible from the material described.

AlterNet’s plural “experts” framing also outruns the substance presented. The article explains George’s assessment in detail and notes Garrison’s similar suspicions, but it reports no medical finding establishing dementia, a stroke or any other condition. Trump’s walking may be abnormal without proving the particular disease that attracts the most political attention.

The real obligation belongs to the presidency

Online spectators do not control Trump’s medical disclosures. Trump and the White House do. That is where institutional power sits, and where responsibility for resolving legitimate questions belongs.

Speculation flourishes when visible evidence and official presentation diverge. A communications account meant to project presidential strength instead circulated footage that prompted questions about Trump’s stability. Treating every irregular movement as proof of dementia would be irresponsible. Treating repeated, publicly visible motor difficulties as beneath scrutiny would be institutional cowardice.

The defensible conclusion is narrower than the viral one: Trump was recorded walking unsteadily in Manila, similar movement reportedly appeared in an October video, and two specialists cited by the reporting believe the pattern may indicate serious neurological impairment. The footage raises a question the White House has the power to answer. It does not answer it for them.

item.title: Judge warns Trump prosecutors’ guillotine theory 'could go the other way'
item.description:
A D.C. judge refused to dismiss the weapons case against Philan Le, the California tattoo artist arrested after bringing a homemade guillotine to Capitol Hill. But Superior Court Judge Judith Bartnoff also identified the prosecution’s central problem: Jeanine Pirro’s office must prove Le intended to use the device against another person, and the guillotine’s presence in a parked pickup truck may not prove that at all.

That distinction is the case. Le’s machine was large, sharpened and, by his own reported description, “the real deal.” Those facts make it alarming. They do not automatically establish the criminal intent prosecutors have alleged.

Pirro’s office chose a charge that requires intent

Capitol Police arrested Le on Aug. 25 after officers found the 10-foot guillotine in his pickup bed near the Library of Congress and Supreme Court. The truck occupied a permit-only space on East Capitol Street. According to a police affidavit, Le said he was not there for any particular reason. An officer determined that the machine’s metal blade had been sharpened.

Police initially arrested Le for carrying a dangerous weapon. Prosecutors from Pirro’s office—the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia—instead charged him with misdemeanor attempted possession of a prohibited weapon. Their allegation is not merely that Le possessed a functioning guillotine, but that he intended to use it “unlawfully against another.”

Le pleaded not guilty. A magistrate judge rejected the prosecution’s effort to jail him before trial, finding that he had not threatened anyone.

The defense sought dismissal on the ground that guillotines do not appear on the District’s list of prohibited weapons. Bartnoff denied that motion Wednesday, allowing the prosecution to proceed. She did not, however, accept the government’s contention that unlawful intent can simply be inferred from possession.

“If the only issue is inference, and it’s in the back of a truck, conceivably, that inference could go the other way,” Bartnoff said. She left the ultimate question for trial.

A frightening object is not a substitute for proof

The prosecution’s theory invites a shortcut: begin with an object associated with execution, let its symbolism do the evidentiary work and treat possession as proof of a plan to harm someone. But the government chose a charge requiring it to establish that plan beyond a reasonable doubt. It cannot erase that burden by pointing repeatedly at the blade.

The available facts, as reported by The Washington Post and summarized by AlterNet, support more than one inference. Le’s father, Huy Le, told NBC San Diego that his son spent three months building the guillotine in the family’s Carlsbad backyard as a political statement and “really meant no harm to anyone.” Before traveling across the country, Le posted videos criticizing unelected officials and the United States’ “forever wars.” He also said he did not intend to hurt anyone.

Those statements do not settle the case in Le’s favor, just as the guillotine does not settle it for the government. They establish why Bartnoff’s warning matters: the same physical evidence prosecutors present as proof of intended violence may also be consistent with provocative political theater.

Legal experts told the Post in September that the charge would be difficult to prove because prosecutors must show Le planned to use the machine on another person. Bartnoff’s comments confirm that the evidentiary gap remains unresolved.

The state must prove the conduct it alleged

A sharpened guillotine outside institutions of government is designed to command attention and evoke political violence. Authorities had reason to investigate it. But investigation is not conviction, and disturbing symbolism does not relieve prosecutors of the obligation to prove each element of their chosen offense.

The institutional power here belongs to Pirro’s office. It selected the charge, sought Le’s pretrial detention and advanced the inference that possessing the device demonstrated unlawful intent. Le’s failure to make his stunt reassuring does not strengthen the government’s evidence.

Bartnoff has permitted the case to reach trial, not endorsed the prosecution’s theory. If Pirro’s office has evidence that Le meant to behead or injure someone, it will have the opportunity to present it. If it has only a frightening machine in the back of a truck, the image that made the case politically potent may be precisely what exposes its legal weakness.

item.title: Leaker claims Trump gutted America’s top cyber defense agency
item.description:
A wave of outages disrupted email and airline travel, and the Trump administration said it found no sign of a coordinated attack. But former Department of Homeland Security official Miles Taylor argued Wednesday that the more consequential problem is Washington’s diminished ability to recognize and answer such an attack quickly. His charge is specific: President Donald Trump’s administration has stripped the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency of staff and readiness just as artificial intelligence is expanding the scale of potential cyberattacks.

The outages were not established as terrorism, sabotage or even related events. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that officials saw no indication they were connected or caused by “malign actors.” Taylor did not claim otherwise. Instead, he challenged the administration’s implied assurance that the federal government would be equipped to handle a genuine AI-enabled cyberattack.

That distinction matters. The immediate outages may prove mundane. The institutional damage Taylor described would persist after the systems come back online.

Reassurance without readiness

Rubio said the government remains “hyper vigilant” about threats to the public, the economy and national security. Vigilance, however, is a posture, not a capability. It does not establish that the government retains enough specialists to investigate disruptions, distinguish technical failures from hostile operations and coordinate a response.

Speaking with CNN anchor Kasie Hunt, Taylor said an honest answer about preparedness would be grim: “We are as unprepared as we have been in years.” He attributed that condition largely to the administration’s reduction of domestic cyber defenses.

Taylor is not a detached observer. He served as a DHS official during Trump’s first term and later became a whistleblower and prominent critic of the president. His account rests partly on conversations he said he has continued to hold with current and former CISA employees. According to Taylor, they describe an agency with a “threadbare staff” confronting what he called a historic period of AI-enabled vulnerabilities.

The claim is therefore attributed, not an official finding about the outages or a demonstrated assessment of every federal cyber unit. But it raises a question Rubio’s comments did not answer: whether the government possesses the personnel and institutional capacity required to support its public confidence.

The punishment of Chris Krebs

Taylor traced the deterioration back to Trump’s treatment of Chris Krebs, the former CISA director. Congress created the agency to protect federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure, and Trump signed the establishing legislation. Taylor said he helped develop that legislation and stood behind Trump at the signing.

Krebs was fired by Trump in 2020 after refusing to endorse the false claim that the presidential election had been stolen. Taylor described that dismissal as the beginning of a broader assault that continued after Trump returned to office and, in Taylor’s account, left CISA badly weakened.

That history gives the staffing dispute its political meaning. Trump used presidential power against an official who would not validate his election narrative. The target was not merely Krebs’s job; the consequence, Taylor argues, was damage to an agency responsible for defending systems on which government, commerce and ordinary life depend.

An agency built to assess threats cannot function reliably if technical judgment carries a political loyalty test. Removing an official for contradicting the president also sends a clear message to everyone who remains: accuracy can cost you your position when it collides with presidential demands.

The outages are a warning, not proof

Taylor called the recent disruptions a preview of what AI-assisted attacks could produce. That is an analogy about vulnerability, not evidence that AI caused these outages. The administration’s statement that it had found no connection among the events does not resolve the separate question of whether CISA could manage a more sophisticated, coordinated crisis.

This is where official messaging can misdirect attention. Rubio addressed whether investigators currently saw hostile coordination. Taylor addressed whether the government could cope if they did. Those are not competing answers to the same question, and repeating that officials are watchful does not substitute for disclosing whether the country’s principal civilian cyber-defense agency has enough people to do its job.

The consequences would not remain confined to Washington. Email failures can paralyze workplaces; aviation disruptions can strand passengers and destabilize tightly connected transportation networks. A serious coordinated attack would require fast attribution, competent communication and sustained technical response. Those capacities cannot be improvised after an incident begins.

Taylor’s allegation is ultimately about a governing choice: an administration that punished unwelcome professional judgment and then, he says, hollowed out the institution responsible for detecting digital threats. The outages may not have been an attack. If Taylor’s account is accurate, the more alarming fact is that the next one could be—and the government’s assurances may arrive faster than its answers.

item.title: 'Name me one': Trump official stumped as incredulous lawmaker demands answer
item.description:
Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia could readily identify “antifa” when a House lawmaker asked him Wednesday to name organizations fitting the FBI’s definition of domestic terrorism. Asked for a single right-wing counterpart, he could not—or would not—provide one. The exchange before the House Committee on Homeland Security exposed more than an official struggling under questioning. It showed how the Trump administration’s political classification of enemies can override Raia’s own stated insistence that the bureau targets individuals, not organizations.

A standard that changed with the subject

Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Mississippi Democrat, initially asked Raia for three organizations that met the FBI’s domestic-terrorism criteria. Raia named antifa and 764, then stalled when Thompson asked whether any right-wing organization qualified.

“I don’t want to paint a broad brush here,” Raia said. He argued that constitutionally protected organizations on both the right and left could contain people whose conduct satisfied the three relevant qualifiers for opening a domestic-terrorism investigation.

That distinction is important: political association is not itself terrorism, and law enforcement should not treat protected beliefs as evidence of a crime. But Raia did not apply the distinction consistently. When Thompson repeatedly asked for one right-wing organization, Raia first said, “There isn’t,” then retreated to the claim that the FBI deals with people inside organizations rather than the organizations themselves.

Thompson identified the contradiction in four words: “But you said antifa.”

According to Raia, antifa counted because President Donald Trump had designated it that way. In other words, the official’s categorical answer did not emerge from the careful, conduct-based standard he invoked when the questioning reached the right. It came from a presidential declaration.

Presidential labeling in place of consistent analysis

Antifa is a political tendency rather than a single organization with a centralized membership and command structure. That makes Raia’s answer especially revealing. He was willing to place a diffuse label associated with the left into an organizational category, yet became solicitous about precision when Thompson asked him to identify a group on the right.

AlterNet cited the Proud Boys, Oath Keepers, Three Percenters and Ku Klux Klan as formally structured right-wing organizations widely regarded as domestic-terror groups. Raia named none of them. His refusal did not establish that every member of any such organization is a terrorist, nor would naming an organization erase constitutional protections. It demonstrated that the administration’s language is not being applied symmetrically even at the level of congressional testimony.

The institutional power here belongs to the president who supplies the designation and the senior FBI official who repeats it. Thompson could expose the inconsistency, but he could not compel Raia to use one standard across ideological lines. Raia instead cycled among incompatible positions: organizations can be named; organizations should not be named; antifa can be named because Trump named it.

That is not caution. It is selective caution—the kind that protects favored political territory while leaving the government’s designated enemies exposed to sweeping labels.

The threat record cuts against the administration’s story

The administration’s fixation on left-wing extremism is also at odds with the record described in the hearing’s broader context. AlterNet reported that FBI data attribute roughly 75% to 80% of domestic-terrorism deaths since 2001 to right-wing extremists, compared with less than 5% attributed to left-wing groups.

Those figures do not justify criminalizing right-wing belief or treating every conservative organization as violent. They do make the administration’s asymmetry consequential. A federal law-enforcement apparatus that foregrounds a politically useful left-wing enemy while its own data identify substantially greater lethal violence from the right is not merely choosing imprecise terminology. It is directing attention and institutional force away from the dominant reported source of deaths.

The Trump administration has repeatedly emphasized threats from the left, including by convening an international meeting focused on left-wing “extremism.” Raia’s testimony fit that project. The weaker actors in the exchange were not nameless officials trapped by ambiguous definitions; the FBI’s deputy director had every opportunity to explain a consistent rule. Instead, he preserved the administration’s framing until Thompson’s questioning made the contradiction impossible to miss.

Raia’s most defensible principle was that the FBI should investigate people based on conduct rather than police organizations based on ideology. But an agency cannot credibly shelter behind that principle only after the questioning turns toward the political right. If antifa is an organization when Trump wants an enemy named, but organizations dissolve into isolated individuals when right-wing violence is raised, the operative distinction is not legal rigor. It is political convenience.

item.title: Trumpworld in disarray as top advisers trade accusations of embezzlement
item.description:
The widening legal fight around MAGA strategist Alex Bruesewitz is exposing a political operation at war with itself over money, influence and access. X Strategies, the firm Bruesewitz built with former business partner Derek Utley, has accused Utley of embezzling millions to support gambling and an expensive lifestyle. Utley, in turn, has accused Bruesewitz of accepting Qatar-linked money without properly disclosing it. Both sets of claims are allegations in an unresolved dispute, but their emergence in court has forced a usually opaque influence business to describe how its insiders accuse one another of operating.

The latest filing escalates that fight. According to reporting by Sherwood news editor Jake Lahut, an attorney for Bruesewitz alleged that Utley fabricated a medical record and forged a doctor’s signature while seeking six months of paid medical leave. X Strategies said Radius TBI told the company that the document did not appear in its system and did not use its standard letterhead or format. The filing says the company attached an email from Radius TBI and received the same answer by phone.

Utley has not been found liable for embezzlement or fraud on the facts presented here, and the filing’s accusations remain contested claims by an adversary in litigation. Their political significance lies elsewhere: people who sold Trumpism as a campaign against corrupt elites are now asking judges to sort through their own allegations of stolen money, concealed foreign influence and forged records.

The business behind the movement

Bruesewitz was not a peripheral volunteer in Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign. He led its podcast strategy, helping reach politically disengaged young men through an ecosystem that presented Trump as the answer to their economic frustrations. That pitch helped convert grievance into votes while placing consultants such as Bruesewitz between the candidate and a valuable audience.

X Strategies’ prominent work reportedly included managing social-media accounts for Team Trump and Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast. Those clients illustrate the firm’s real commodity: proximity to a political movement whose media channels can turn attention into money and money back into influence.

That arrangement matters because the court dispute is not merely office gossip. A company involved in distributing MAGA’s message now alleges that one of its own principals diverted millions. Its former principal alleges that the company’s leader took undisclosed Qatar-linked funds. X Strategies has asked a federal judge to strike those retaliatory claims. The New York Times has also reported Utley’s lawsuit over the alleged Qatari money.

The available reporting does not establish who will prevail. It does establish that the movement’s messaging apparatus and its financial interests are inseparable enough that a business breakup can expose politically sensitive allegations about foreign-linked payments.

Rival camps compete for access

Lahut places the litigation inside a broader struggle among Trump-aligned factions. He describes one camp as generally aligned with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and supportive of Israel, and another as aligned with Vice President JD Vance and more isolationist on foreign policy. His shorthand is revealing: an “Open For Business” wing and a “Super Hardcore” wing.

Those labels describe differences in posture, but the conflict repeatedly returns to control over money, audiences and proximity to power. Technology figures reportedly appear in both camps, though Lahut said much of the tech right’s energy is concentrated around the Vance-aligned faction.

Bruesewitz’s separate clash with activist Laura Loomer followed the same trajectory. Lahut reported that a disagreement over midterm messaging became a fight about money. Bruesewitz said he had paid Loomer to publish social-media posts and compared her to left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. Loomer later announced an indefinite hiatus from her podcast.

The episode cuts through the fiction that this ecosystem consists simply of independent voices spontaneously expressing a shared ideology. At least some of its political content operates through paid relationships, consulting firms and strategic distribution. When those relationships collapse, the participants stop describing themselves as comrades and start producing invoices, accusations and exhibits.

Accountability begins as mutually assured disclosure

AlterNet frames the story as Trumpworld falling into disarray amid Trump’s unpopularity and self-absorption. The documented development is narrower and more instructive: competing MAGA operatives are using litigation and public feuds to disclose allegations that their own institutions did not resolve internally.

That is not yet accountability. It is mutually assured exposure. Each side has an incentive to reveal damaging information because each is trying to defeat a rival, recover money or protect access. The courts are becoming the venue where a political network built on loyalty and personal influence is forced to create a record.

The approaching possibility of congressional scrutiny raises the stakes, as Lahut noted. But lawmakers would be investigating more than personal misconduct if they examined these disputes. The central questions concern how political messaging was financed, whether foreign-linked interests entered that system, and what disclosure obligations applied. Those questions reach beyond the consultants trading allegations because the operation they helped run was designed to shape public power.

For now, the sharpest evidence of the system’s character comes from its own participants. A movement that markets suspicion of hidden elites has generated a court fight over alleged embezzlement, alleged undisclosed Qatar-linked money and an allegedly forged medical document. Its insiders are not exposing that machinery for the public’s benefit. They are exposing it because they no longer trust one another.

item.title: The Devil Made You Think: How Religious Clickbait Masquerades as Profound Wisdom
item.description:
When ordinary human psychology gets repackaged as supernatural warfare, critical thinking becomes the enemy, unquestioning obedience becomes a virtue, and the Devil becomes the world's most convenient scapegoat.

There is something almost impressive about the religious content industry's ability to take the most mundane observations about human existence, wrap them in biblical quotations, sprinkle a little Satan on top, and present the resulting intellectual casserole as profound spiritual revelation.

The latest specimen comes courtesy of an MSN slideshow titled “9 Lies the Devil Wants You to Believe.”

Nine lies. Apparently, the Prince of Darkness has been reduced from the cosmic adversary of an omnipotent deity to a motivational speaker specializing in negative self-talk.

And what are these diabolical deceptions? That your past mistakes define you. That you need to handle everything yourself. That forgiveness means excusing wrongdoing. That unanswered prayers might actually be unanswered.

In other words, ordinary human insecurities, moral dilemmas, and perfectly reasonable questions.

But according to this particular brand of religious publishing, these aren't simply thoughts worth examining. They're Satanic propaganda.

And therein lies the problem.

This isn't merely harmless religious encouragement. It is an example of an extraordinarily persistent intellectual fraud: presenting theological assumptions as established facts, dressing ordinary psychological advice in supernatural authority, and treating skepticism itself as evidence of evil.

The result is an exercise in circular reasoning so thoroughly insulated from scrutiny that it could survive a direct collision with reality without developing so much as a dent.

First, Invent the Disease. Then Sell the Cure.

Consider the first supposed lie:

“Your private sin isn't affecting anybody else, so it doesn't really matter.”

The article warns that hidden moral failings gradually corrupt a person's character, diminish spiritual awareness, and eventually contaminate their relationships.

Notice what it doesn't bother establishing.

What exactly qualifies as sin? Who gets to decide? And what evidence demonstrates that every private violation of religious doctrine causes harm?

There is a fundamental distinction between immorality and disobedience to religious rules.

A person who privately exploits another human being has committed a moral wrong, regardless of whether anyone discovers it.

A person who privately entertains doubts about God has not.

Neither has someone who masturbates, engages in consensual intimacy outside marriage, or violates any number of religious prohibitions that cannot be connected to demonstrable harm.

Yet the article neatly collapses the distinction.

Once something receives the label “sin,” its moral condemnation is treated as settled. No evidence of injury is required. No injured party needs to exist. The offense is against an invisible authority whose existence and jurisdiction are themselves articles of faith.

That's not moral reasoning. That's obedience masquerading as morality.

And when the author invokes Luke 8:17 to warn that nothing hidden will remain concealed, the argument becomes even more revealing.

Apparently, the ultimate problem with private conduct isn't necessarily that it hurts someone.

It's that someone might eventually find out.

What a wonderful foundation for an ethical system.

Ordinary Psychology, Now With Added Supernatural Packaging

Several entries contain advice so unremarkable that they could have been lifted from a bargain-bin self-help book.

Your past mistakes don't have to define your future.

You don't need to be perfect before seeking compassion.

Material comfort doesn't necessarily mean you're living correctly.

Excessive independence can become exhausting.

These are not profound discoveries.

Human beings have been exploring such ideas through philosophy, literature, psychology, and ordinary conversation for centuries.

But add a biblical quotation, and suddenly they become divine revelations.

Take the claim that people shouldn't believe their past mistakes permanently limit their worth.

Excellent advice.

People can change. People can learn. People can recover from failure.

But the article doesn't simply say that.

It warns against believing that previous mistakes limit one's “usefulness to God.”

Usefulness?

What an extraordinary choice of words.

Here we have a supposedly omnipotent being who created the universe, governs reality, and requires absolutely nothing to accomplish anything.

Yet human beings are apparently expected to evaluate themselves according to their usefulness to him.

The language of human dignity has been replaced with the language of divine employment.

You aren't valuable because you're a conscious human being capable of relationships, creativity, compassion, and growth.

You're valuable because you might still be useful to the celestial management department.

How inspiring.

And the supposed solution is always the same: you need God.

Not because the author has demonstrated that the psychological benefit cannot exist without religion, but because the entire argument begins with the assumption that religion is necessary.

It's the theological equivalent of claiming that drinking water only works because an angel blesses every glass.

The water still hydrates you.

The angel is an unnecessary addition.

Forgiveness: The Perfect Tool for Protecting the Wrong People

Then comes the claim:

“If you forgive them, you are just letting them off the hook and erasing what they did.”

Here the article argues that refusing forgiveness traps people in bitterness while their offenders continue living freely.

It's a familiar religious refrain, and one that deserves substantially more scrutiny than it usually receives.

Forgiveness can be psychologically beneficial.

So can accountability.

So can distance.

So can refusing to allow a dangerous person back into your life.

What is not psychologically necessary is the belief that everyone who has harmed you deserves forgiveness.

A person can overcome anger without forgiving an abuser.

A person can build a fulfilling life without absolving someone who betrayed them.

A victim can recognize that an offender remains responsible for their actions without spending every waking moment consumed by resentment.

The article reduces these complex experiences to a convenient false choice: forgive or remain imprisoned by bitterness.

And that's where this particular religious teaching can become genuinely harmful.

In abusive families, controlling relationships, and religious institutions protecting their own reputations, the demand for forgiveness can become a weapon.

The offender asks for mercy.

The community demands reconciliation.

The victim is told that continued anger demonstrates a spiritual failing.

Suddenly, the person who suffered the injury is made responsible for restoring everyone's comfort.

Forgiveness is a personal choice, not a moral debt owed to an offender.

And no amount of scriptural quotation changes that.

When Logic Becomes the Devil's Accomplice

Of all nine entries, the seventh is perhaps the most intellectually revealing.

“You can wage war in the spiritual realm with your mind, strength and logic.”

According to the article, relying on human wisdom and psychological explanations leaves people defenseless against the spiritual forces supposedly responsible for their struggles.

Let's examine the extraordinary claim being made here.

Someone experiences anxiety.

Someone struggles with depression.

Someone has intrusive thoughts, persistent fear, or emotional exhaustion.

These experiences may have biological, psychological, environmental, or social explanations.

We can investigate them. We can test hypotheses. We can develop treatments. We can measure outcomes.

But the article introduces another explanation: invisible spiritual forces.

And how do we determine that these forces exist?

Scripture.

How do we determine scripture accurately describes reality?

Faith.

And what happens when logic leads someone to question the explanation?

Apparently, logic is the wrong weapon.

How remarkably convenient.

The moment a belief system teaches people to distrust the intellectual tools that might expose its errors, it has stopped defending truth and started defending itself.

This is not a trivial concern.

Religious faith can provide genuine psychological comfort. Many believers combine prayer with professional treatment, and the article does not explicitly tell anyone to abandon medical care.

But portraying psychological explanations as inadequate because an invisible spiritual war is supposedly taking place risks encouraging vulnerable people to misidentify the nature of their distress.

A person experiencing mental illness does not need to be told that demons might be participating.

They need compassion, competent assessment, and appropriate support.

The supernatural explanation adds fear without adding evidence.

And dismissing logic as insufficient does not transform an unsupported claim into a fact.

It merely protects that claim from examination.

The Garden of Eden: Where Asking Questions Became a Crime

Another alleged Satanic deception is that God withholds good things because he wants to restrict human happiness.

The article invokes the Garden of Eden, naturally portraying the serpent as the original manipulator who convinced humanity that divine restrictions were oppressive.

But there's an inconvenient detail in the Genesis narrative.

God forbids Adam and Eve from eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil.

The serpent tells Eve that eating the fruit will open their eyes and make them like God, knowing good and evil.

They eat.

Their eyes are opened.

And in Genesis 3:22, God declares:

“The man has now become like one of us, knowing good and evil.”

Well, that's awkward.

The serpent's prediction about acquiring knowledge is substantially confirmed within the story itself.

The narrative also involves mortality, disobedience, and consequences, so it would be simplistic to claim that everything the serpent said was true.

But the irony is difficult to ignore.

Humanity's foundational transgression, in this telling, involves acquiring knowledge that a divine authority had forbidden.

And the lesson commonly emphasized is obedience.

Don't question the rule.

Don't challenge the authority.

Don't assume restrictions might be unjustified.

Just trust the one issuing them.

That is a remarkably useful lesson for any institution that depends on unquestioning compliance.

And we should be exceptionally suspicious when religious authorities attempt to extend that principle from an ancient myth into contemporary human relationships.

A parent, employer, government, or religious leader who says, “You don't need to understand my rules; you simply need to obey them,” is not offering a compelling moral argument.

They're demanding submission.

Authority does not become legitimate merely because it claims to be benevolent.

Its decisions still require justification.

And telling people that questioning restrictions is a temptation from Satan is an excellent way to avoid providing one.

The Unanswered Prayer: A System That Cannot Lose

Finally, consider the ninth alleged lie:

“Delay means denial, so God must have forgotten about your prayers.”

According to the article, unanswered prayers don't indicate divine absence. They simply mean God's timing differs from yours.

Now consider what that interpretation accomplishes.

Someone prays for employment.

Nothing happens.

God is teaching patience.

Someone prays for recovery.

The illness progresses.

God has another plan.

Someone prays for a suffering child.

The child dies.

God works in mysterious ways.

Whatever happens, the underlying belief survives.

A favorable outcome becomes evidence of divine intervention.

An unfavorable outcome becomes evidence of divine wisdom beyond human understanding.

An absence of observable results becomes evidence that the answer hasn't arrived yet.

The proposition is structured so that no possible outcome can count against it.

And a claim that accommodates every conceivable result without distinguishing among them offers no useful predictive explanation.

This does not mean every religious person believes prayer guarantees particular results. Many sophisticated theological traditions explicitly reject that understanding.

But the article's treatment offers little more than a comforting assertion presented as an explanation.

God didn't ignore you.

God isn't late.

God has a plan.

How do we know?

Because the religion says so.

Again.

The more troubling implication is the suggestion that people who become impatient and take action may be trying to force outcomes rather than trusting divine timing.

Sometimes waiting is prudent.

Sometimes waiting is disastrous.

A person experiencing medical symptoms should seek medical attention.

Someone facing abuse should seek safety.

Someone whose livelihood is collapsing should take practical steps to protect themselves.

Prayer may offer comfort to believers, but inaction does not become wisdom merely because it has been given a religious justification.

The Devil: Christianity's Universal Technical Support Excuse

Here is the underlying brilliance of this entire rhetorical system.

Every unwanted thought can be attributed to Satan.

Every comforting thought can be attributed to God.

Every fortunate outcome can demonstrate divine favor.

Every unfortunate outcome can demonstrate divine wisdom.

Every doubt can be interpreted as spiritual attack.

And every demand for evidence can be dismissed as reliance on inadequate human understanding.

It's an intellectual machine designed to produce the same conclusion regardless of its input.

Consider the exchange:

“I don't believe Satan exists.”

That's exactly what Satan wants you to believe.

“I don't believe the Bible is divinely inspired.”

Satan is deceiving you.

“I've examined the evidence and found the claims unconvincing.”

You're relying too much on human logic.

“What evidence would demonstrate that your explanation is wrong?”

You need faith.

The argument isn't merely circular.

It's self-sealing.

It converts every objection into additional confirmation.

And that's precisely what distinguishes an honest investigation from an ideological system designed to protect itself.

An honest investigation permits the possibility that its initial assumptions are mistaken.

This kind of religious argument makes that possibility practically unavailable.

The Real Problem Isn't Faith. It's Intellectual Dishonesty.

People are entitled to religious beliefs.

They're entitled to find meaning in scripture, comfort in prayer, and guidance in spiritual traditions.

They're even entitled to believe that Satan personally spends his afternoons planting insecurities in the human mind.

But belief is not evidence.

And faith-based interpretations should not be presented to a general audience as though they were established descriptions of reality.

There is an enormous difference between saying:

“My religious tradition teaches that these thoughts may represent spiritual temptation.”

And declaring:

“These are nine lies the Devil wants you to believe.”

The first is an honest statement about religious belief.

The second presents a supernatural claim as fact without demonstrating that it is true.

That distinction is not pedantic.

It's the difference between explaining a worldview and attempting to impose its assumptions on reality.

What makes this particular genre so irritating is how often it borrows credibility from genuine psychological insights.

Yes, excessive self-criticism can be destructive.

Yes, isolation can worsen anxiety.

Yes, forgiveness can sometimes contribute to healing.

Yes, past mistakes need not determine a person's future.

But none of those observations establishes that Satan exists.

None demonstrates that a supernatural intelligence implants thoughts.

And none proves that the Bible is an authoritative account of human psychology.

A correct observation does not validate every explanation attached to it.

If someone tells you that exercise improves health because invisible angels massage your cardiovascular system, the demonstrated benefits of exercise do not establish the existence of the angels.

Yet religious clickbait routinely performs exactly that maneuver.

Take a genuine human experience.

Attach an unverifiable supernatural explanation.

Quote scripture.

Declare victory.

Publish.

Repeat.

The Business of Manufacturing Profundity

There is also something particularly cynical about the presentation.

Nine lies.

Nine things Satan wants you to believe.

Nine hidden spiritual dangers threatening your happiness, relationships, and salvation.

The format is practically indistinguishable from the endless internet slideshows promising “Ten Secrets Doctors Don't Want You to Know” or “Seven Habits That Are Secretly Destroying Your Brain.”

Only here, instead of medical professionals supposedly concealing information, we have the Devil.

And instead of offering evidence, the article offers Bible verses.

It's religious engagement bait: familiar anxieties packaged as supernatural revelations, designed to sound urgent and profound.

The reader arrives with ordinary human uncertainties and leaves with a new interpretive framework in which those uncertainties may be evidence of cosmic malevolence.

What an extraordinary service.

Take someone's existing insecurity.

Tell them an invisible enemy is exploiting it.

Then direct them toward the belief system that claims exclusive knowledge of the enemy and the means to resist him.

This doesn't mean every author producing devotional content is consciously manipulating readers. Many undoubtedly believe what they're writing.

Sincerity, however, does not rescue an argument from intellectual bankruptcy.

And the fact that such content appears on mainstream news aggregators only adds another layer of absurdity.

Religious devotional writing is being distributed alongside news and general-interest articles, potentially reaching readers without much indication that its foundational claims are matters of faith rather than independently established facts.

The medium lends the material an appearance of informational legitimacy that the argument itself has not earned.

Stop Calling Unsupported Assertions “Deep Truths”

The most exhausting feature of this genre is its insistence on presenting ancient theological assumptions as if they were astonishing insights into human nature.

You're insecure?

Satan.

You're angry?

Satan.

You're questioning authority?

Satan.

You're trying to solve problems through reason?

Believe it or not, Satan.

Meanwhile, God is credited with comfort, forgiveness, patience, and every positive personal transformation the author can identify.

It's a cosmic accounting system where the books are guaranteed to balance because the rules determine the outcome in advance.

And beneath the theological decoration lies a deeply consequential message:

Your thoughts are not always trustworthy.

Your judgment may be compromised by invisible enemies.

Your understanding is inadequate.

Your doubts are suspicious.

Your safest option is to trust the religious framework explaining all of this.

That is not necessarily how every reader will interpret the article. But it is a disturbing pattern embedded in its reasoning.

Healthy skepticism doesn't require rejecting every piece of advice contained in religious literature.

It requires distinguishing the advice from the unsupported supernatural claims used to justify it.

You can recognize the value of forgiveness without believing in demons.

You can acknowledge that excessive independence causes stress without surrendering your autonomy to a deity.

You can learn from mistakes without considering yourself a sinner in need of supernatural redemption.

You can accept uncertainty without inventing a cosmic plan.

And you can confront emotional distress without imagining an invisible war being fought inside your skull.

Human beings are complicated.

We experience fear, guilt, hope, love, anger, doubt, and uncertainty because we are human.

We don't need to outsource the explanation of those experiences to competing supernatural entities.

Sometimes a troubling thought is simply a troubling thought.

Sometimes an unanswered prayer is simply an unanswered prayer.

Sometimes a restriction is genuinely unjustified.

And sometimes the person telling you not to trust your own reasoning is the person whose claims deserve the most scrutiny.

The Devil doesn't need to be deceiving you for religious propaganda to be misleading.

Human beings are perfectly capable of doing that all by themselves.

And unlike Satan, we can actually hold them accountable.

item.title: Top historian: Trump conceded on Election Night —but the danger isn’t over
item.description:
AlterNet reports that Donald Trump conceded after Democrats won commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterms, despite later posting that the elections were rigged. The immediate result is clear: Democrats are set to take control of the House and Senate. The political meaning is less comforting. Trump’s relatively restrained Election Night response did not erase his record of trying to overturn the 2020 presidential election, and his selection of Stephen Miller as chief of staff points toward confrontation, not accommodation, during his remaining two years in office.

Historian Federico Finchelstein’s warning is straightforward: accepting a defeat that cannot plausibly be reversed is not the same as accepting democratic limits. Trump may have yielded to the scale of the result while retaining the authoritarian politics that made another attempted power grab a reasonable concern in the first place.

A concession imposed by arithmetic

The precise character of Trump’s reported concession is not described in the supplied account. AlterNet says he conceded, while also noting that he subsequently alleged the midterms were rigged. That is materially different from a democratic leader acknowledging the legitimacy of an election and the authority voters transferred to the opposition.

Finchelstein, an historian of fascism and author of A Brief History of Fascist Lies and The Wannabe Fascists, told AlterNet that Trump appeared surprised by the result. He cited an unnamed person close to Trump who reportedly described the Democratic victory as “too big to rig.” Finchelstein presented that as a possible explanation for Trump’s delayed and initially less hostile response.

The phrase captures the limit Trump encountered: not principle, but scale. On Finchelstein’s reading, the vote produced a reality too overwhelming for Trump’s usual machinery of denial to contest effectively. That interpretation remains an interpretation, not a demonstrated account of Trump’s private reasoning. But it fits the public contradiction AlterNet describes—a reported concession followed by another unsupported claim that an election he lost was rigged.

Trump’s conduct after the 2020 election supplies the relevant context. He attempted to remain in power after losing, culminating in the effort to overturn the result associated with January 6. Against that record, a quieter response in 2026 cannot reasonably be treated as evidence that he has become committed to democratic succession.

Miller’s promotion answers the reconciliation question

The clearest reported indication of Trump’s intended course is personnel. After voters rejected his governing coalition and handed Congress to Democrats, Trump chose Stephen Miller as his chief of staff. Finchelstein characterized Miller as perhaps one of the most fascistic figures in the administration and described the appointment as an almost immediate turn toward radicalization.

That decision matters more than the fleeting presidential tone celebrated by pundits. A chief of staff controls access, coordinates policy and helps determine which impulses become government action. By elevating Miller, Trump did not signal that he intended to bargain with the incoming congressional majorities. He placed a central architect of his hard-line politics near the core of executive power.

Finchelstein expects the conflict to intensify as Trump confronts the gap between his self-image and his diminished position. Trump urged voters to treat the midterms as a referendum on him; they returned Democratic majorities in both houses. He is now a lame-duck president who built his politics around personal dominance and the leader cult Finchelstein identifies as central to Trumpism.

“The less power he has,” Finchelstein told AlterNet, “the more potential for violence, erratic behavior and illegality we might have.” That is a forecast, not a report of acts that have already occurred. But Congress changing hands does not itself remove the executive authority Trump retains until his term ends. It changes the institutional balance and creates stronger legislative opposition; it does not make presidential power disappear.

The myth behind the program

Finchelstein describes Trumpism as “wannabe fascism”: an aspiration marked by fascist tendencies that remains incomplete, erratic and perhaps incapable of full realization. The distinction is useful because it avoids treating fascism as a costume that either fits perfectly or not at all. The relevant question is what Trump’s movement attempts to do with the power it possesses.

One element is a politics of national rebirth built around a fabricated past. Trump presents himself as the agent who can restore an earlier American greatness while remaking the country through architectural projects and the removal of so-called DEI material from public monuments. Finchelstein argues that the glorious past invoked by this project never existed as advertised. Whatever prosperity or status it offered some Americans came with exclusion and suffering for others.

That mythology has an immediate political function. It defines the nation narrowly, casts selected groups as intruders or contaminants, and gives the leader permission to “restore” a social order that exists mainly as propaganda. Finchelstein calls Trump’s conception of the nation extremely chauvinistic and exclusionary. The invented history is not decorative rhetoric around the governing program; it supplies the program’s justification.

Congress won power, not automatic compliance

AlterNet asked whether Democratic control of Congress had permanently prevented Trump from attacking democratic institutions, including through emergency powers, martial law or an attempt to entrench one-party rule. Finchelstein did not claim those outcomes were imminent. He said they could not be ruled out, given Trump’s prior conduct and the history of authoritarian movements.

That is the properly bounded warning. The election created a substantial institutional obstacle to Trump, and voters denied him the mandate he sought. It did not retroactively change his behavior after the 2020 election, convert him into a conventional lame duck or guarantee that every part of the state apparatus will resist an unlawful demand.

The most revealing misdirection came in the first hours after the defeat, when, according to Finchelstein, media figures and pundits began imagining that Trump’s initial response marked his transformation into a responsible presidential leader. That familiar ritual grants the powerful rehabilitation for briefly refraining from their worst expected conduct. It treats compliance with an election result as statesmanship rather than the minimum obligation of anyone entrusted with public office.

Finchelstein argues that resistance now depends not only on voters reiterating what they already decided, but on Congress and other state officials enforcing that decision. Voters transferred legislative power. Whether that verdict constrains Trump will also depend on officials with actual institutional authority refusing to assist any renewed attempt to evade it.

The Democratic victory therefore settled who will control Congress. It did not settle how a president who still calls elections rigged, previously tried to overturn a defeat and has now elevated Stephen Miller will use the power he retains. Trump’s reported concession closed the count. It did not close the danger.
