item.title: Psychotherapist details what Trump’s angry outburst reveals about his brain
item.description:
A psychotherapist’s viral-style analysis of Donald Trump’s angry exchange with a reporter does not establish that Trump has Alzheimer’s disease, dementia or any other neurological disorder. It establishes that Elliott Connie watched Trump snap at a question, heard a disjointed answer and interpreted both as signs of cognitive decline. AlterNet nevertheless packaged that interpretation as a revelation about the president’s brain—a certainty the reported facts cannot support.

The episode raises a legitimate question about presidential capacity. But Connie’s attempt to answer it remotely, then speculate that undisclosed medical treatment kept Trump from public view during a nationwide aviation disruption, substitutes clinical-sounding conjecture for evidence. It also shifts attention away from what the exchange plainly showed: a president responding with hostility when asked how he was allocating his time during a crisis.

A question about priorities met with an outburst

Before leaving Monday for meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, Trump took questions from reporters. One asked whether he was spending too much time on renovation projects while more serious matters demanded attention, including the nationwide ground stop for aircraft the previous Friday.

Trump said the construction work consumed only “10 minutes per day.” According to Connie, Trump then defended the projects by pointing to the White House’s appearance, its stonework and a helipad. Connie described the answer as “extremely disjointed” and likened Trump’s enthusiasm to a child seeking approval for a new toy.

The political issue does not depend on that analogy. A reporter asked the president to account for his priorities during a major disruption. Trump’s answer, as described by AlterNet, turned toward the beauty and importance of his renovations. His anger and deflection are matters of observable conduct. Whether a neurological condition caused them is not.

That distinction matters because presidents exercise power through decisions, attention and delegation—not through a public performance that must first be medically decoded before it can be judged. If Trump neglected a crisis, the relevant questions concern what he did, what his administration did and who was responsible. A speculative diagnosis can blur that line of accountability by recasting chosen behavior as a symptom.

Clinical language outruns the evidence

Connie, identified as a practicing psychotherapist of 20 years, argued in a Tuesday video that Trump’s behavior was more than disrespectful or “non-presidential.” He called it evidence of cognitive decline or neurological disruption associated with advancing Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

His explanation centered on the prefrontal cortex, which he described as the brain’s “mental stop sign”—the mechanism that restrains a person from acting on every irritated impulse. Connie contended that Trump’s angry responses show this system deteriorating. AlterNet also said clinical and forensic psychologist John Paul Garrison had noticed something concerning in Trump’s eye contact, though the supplied report does not detail Garrison’s conclusion.

None of that turns an observed outburst into a diagnosis. Irritability, rambling and poor impulse control may prompt questions, but the article reports no examination by Connie and no medical finding from Trump’s treating clinicians. Connie’s professional credentials do not erase the evidentiary gap between watching a press exchange and determining what is happening inside a person’s brain.

The headline’s promised revelation therefore exceeds the story. What the outburst “reveals” about Trump’s brain is Connie’s interpretation, not an established medical fact.

Speculation becomes an alibi

Connie went further. He said he believed Trump was probably receiving medical treatment that affected his speech, gait and general functioning, requiring aides to keep him from cameras until he could appear publicly again. He offered that theory as “the most likely reason” Trump was absent while flights were grounded.

AlterNet’s account provides no factual basis for that conclusion beyond Connie’s reading of Trump’s public behavior. The claim must remain what it is: one psychotherapist’s speculation about treatment he was not reported to have witnessed and a presidential schedule he was not reported to control.

That speculation is not merely medically tenuous. It redirects responsibility from the institution with the power to answer. If the president was unavailable during a nationwide aviation emergency, the White House can account for his whereabouts and role. If officials concealed a health problem affecting his capacity, that would be an institutional act requiring evidence. If Trump simply devoted his attention elsewhere, that would be a political choice. Guessing at secret treatment resolves none of those possibilities.

Connie concluded that the country must be honest about the president’s health and capacity because, in his view, Trump is “unwell.” Scrutiny of presidential fitness is warranted precisely because the office carries extraordinary power. But serious scrutiny requires more discipline than converting belligerence into a brain scan and absence into proof of hidden care.

Trump’s reported conduct already supplies a concrete basis for judgment: confronted about his priorities during a national disruption, he lashed out and promoted his construction projects. Turning that documented exercise of power into an unsupported neurological story does not sharpen accountability. It gives the president’s behavior a speculative medical explanation when the available facts support a simpler political question: why did the man holding the office answer a crisis-management challenge by demanding admiration for his stones and helipad?

item.title: Ex-aide reveals 'crazy' backstory behind Hegseth's Pentagon makeup room
item.description:
Pete Hegseth wanted a makeup studio inside the Pentagon because, according to his former spokesman, a friend of Hegseth’s wife said the defense secretary expected one for media appearances. The request matters less as a story about cosmetics than as evidence of how Hegseth reportedly runs the country’s military headquarters: public image elevated into an operational priority, even as he sells himself as an enemy of institutional softness and enforces ideological discipline on others.

John Ullyot, Hegseth’s former spokesman, told The Daily Beast Podcast that the proposed studio became emblematic of disorder inside the Pentagon. Ullyot described a defense secretary intensely attentive to presentation, from his light-blue suits to his flag-themed pocket squares—an image strategy that Ullyot suggested had helped Hegseth advance at Fox News.

A Fox News imperative enters the Pentagon

The request reportedly came through a friend of Jennifer Hegseth, the secretary’s wife. Ullyot recalled her saying, “Pete expects to have a makeup studio if he’s going to be talking to the media.” He said he found the demand unprecedented and “crazy,” adding that he had never known another defense secretary to install such a facility.

Makeup itself is not the scandal. Television officials routinely prepare for cameras, and looking polished does not impede military administration. The revealing part is the expectation that the Pentagon should create a dedicated studio around one official’s media persona—and that a friend of his wife apparently had enough access to convey the demand to his spokesman.

That arrangement blurs the line between public administration and personal brand management. The Pentagon is not a cable-news greenroom, and the defense secretary’s communications apparatus exists to inform the public about military policy, not to reproduce the production conditions that sustained his television career.

“Lethality” for the institution, vanity for the boss

Ullyot identified the contradiction directly. Hegseth speaks in the language of “lethality” and attacks “wokeness,” yet reportedly wanted a private makeup studio in his Pentagon office. The inconsistency is not that a man might wear makeup on television. It is that Hegseth’s political posture treats presentation, identity and perceived softness as legitimate grounds for policing other people while exempting his own image-conscious demands from the ridicule he directs outward.

That asymmetry is the point of the performance. “Wokeness” functions as a flexible accusation against disfavored personnel and priorities; it does not impose a coherent standard on the secretary himself. Hegseth can cultivate pocket squares, camera lighting and a dedicated cosmetic space while presenting his opponents as distractions from combat readiness. The branding remains masculine because the person with authority gets to define masculinity.

A story focused only on the room’s absurdity risks letting the spectacle conceal the power behind it. The consequential issue is not that Hegseth reportedly wanted to look good on camera. It is that the official empowered to shape military leadership appears, in his former spokesman’s account, to have made personal presentation part of the Pentagon’s institutional business.

The image campaign has personnel consequences

AlterNet also reports that Hegseth has purged dozens of officers for purportedly ideological reasons, with women and people of color disproportionately represented among those fired or denied promotion. That is where the politics of image cease to be merely embarrassing. Hegseth’s preferred picture of the military is backed by appointment, promotion and removal power.

The administration’s pursuit of Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia further illustrates the imbalance between the official controlling the message and the officers subjected to that control. Citing earlier reporting by The Daily Beast and The Washington Post, AlterNet says the military was preparing criminal charges against Sylvia after Hegseth fired him the previous month. Sylvia, who led plans and policy and reported to Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, was accused of sharing information with journalists.

The reported case does not establish Sylvia’s guilt, and the supplied account does not specify the contemplated charges. But The Daily Beast characterized the effort as unusually aggressive punishment of a senior military leader over alleged contact with the press. Set beside Ullyot’s account, it exposes the governing hierarchy: Hegseth’s own media presentation reportedly warrants special accommodation, while unauthorized communication by subordinates can bring dismissal and potential prosecution.

The makeup room is therefore not the central abuse. It is the clarifying detail. Hegseth’s Pentagon, as described by his former spokesman and in the reporting on Sylvia, is preoccupied with controlling what the public sees, who gets to speak and which officers fit the leadership’s ideological image. The cosmetic studio was simply the most literal expression of that priority.

item.title: Psychologist spots telltale dementia sign Trump can’t hide on camera
item.description:
A psychologist who reviewed video of President Donald Trump’s remarks after a nationwide ground stop said the president’s swaying, repetitive answers, agitation and possible memory lapse could be consistent with neurological dysfunction. But Dr. John Paul Garrison explicitly said he was not conducting a psychological evaluation. The footage may raise legitimate questions about Trump’s capacity; it does not establish the dementia diagnosis implied by AlterNet’s headline.

That distinction matters because the conduct under scrutiny belongs to the sitting president, whose memory, judgment and command of policy carry consequences far beyond the usual spectacle of a disordered press appearance. The public interest lies in examining that capacity honestly—not converting a clinician’s qualified observations into a medical verdict the available evidence cannot support.

A denial with two troubling explanations

The most consequential exchange concerned national security. A reporter asked whether Trump believed U.S. intelligence connecting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Trump asked, “Who told me that?”

When the reporter named Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Trump replied: “I haven’t heard that. I haven’t heard that.” AlterNet cited New York Times reporting that Rubio had overseen a classified memo warning senior officials about Huang’s relationship with the woman.

Garrison identified two possible explanations. Trump might have been lying, he said, or he might genuinely have forgotten being told. Neither possibility is reassuring, but they are not interchangeable. One would concern presidential candor; the other would concern memory. The video alone cannot determine which explanation applies.

“He may actually not remember that he was told that,” Garrison said. “That’s entirely possible at this point.” He described the answer as evidence of potentially poor memory and judgment, adding: “I cannot overstate how concerning that answer was.”

The institutional question is sharper than the speculative diagnosis. Trump has access to classified intelligence and authority over the executive branch. If he received the warning, his administration knows whether and when that occurred. A press exchange cannot resolve the discrepancy, but Trump’s denial leaves the public with an unresolved question about what the president was told and whether he retained it.

The ballroom answer

Asked whether he had devoted too much attention to construction while the air traffic system was deteriorating, Trump did not offer a focused account of his administration’s handling of aviation infrastructure. He instead delivered an extended defense of White House renovations, discussing “18 broken windows,” the helipad and his ballroom.

Garrison characterized the response as possible perseveration: becoming stuck on a subject or repeatedly returning to it. Such behavior can appear in people experiencing neurological dysfunction, he said, though that observation was framed as a possibility rather than a finding about Trump.

Whatever its medical significance, the political function of the answer is visible without clinical speculation. A question about failing public infrastructure became an opportunity for Trump to discuss a favored construction project. That redirection displaced the government’s responsibility for the air traffic system with a monologue about the presidential estate. It was not an answer to the issue reporters raised.

Garrison also pointed to Trump’s increasing agitation as questioning continued, describing his reaction as “very childlike” and saying the president appeared to regress when upset. He questioned whether Trump understood the subjects being put to him, arguing that Trump did not seem able to discuss them “with any real depth.”

Those are Garrison’s judgments based on recorded behavior, not the results of an examination. His own disclaimer—“not a psychological evaluation of any kind”—sets the evidentiary boundary that the headline strains to cross.

Capacity cannot be settled by camera diagnosis

Garrison’s most concrete observation concerned Trump’s movement. He said the president had difficulty standing still and repeatedly shifted back and forth. The behavior had become more pronounced with age, Garrison argued, and can sometimes occur in dementia when a person has less ability to inhibit bodily motion.

“Can sometimes occur” is not the same as “reveals dementia.” Similar caution applies to repetition, anger and an apparent failure to remember a briefing. The footage supports scrutiny of the president’s performance. It does not allow viewers—or a publication—to turn several nonspecific behaviors into a definitive medical conclusion.

That does not make the underlying questions trivial. The presidency concentrates extraordinary power in one person, while the White House controls much of the information available about that person’s health and daily functioning. When Trump cannot or will not recall a reported intelligence warning, substitutes renovation talk for an infrastructure answer and struggles to address policy in depth, the relevant issue is not merely whether a remote observer can attach a diagnostic label. It is whether the president is demonstrating the memory, judgment and command his office requires.

AlterNet’s framing offers the seduction of certainty: a “telltale” sign caught on camera. Garrison’s actual comments were more conditional. The responsible conclusion is narrower and more serious. Trump’s performance produced observable reasons for concern, while leaving unresolved whether the cause was cognitive decline, habitual evasion, poor preparation or some combination of them. The administration holds information that could clarify at least part of that record. A YouTube analysis does not.

item.title: White House melts down after Haberman’s Susie Wiles bombshell
item.description:
The White House answered a report that Donald Trump began belittling chief of staff Susie Wiles after her breast cancer diagnosis by attacking the reporter who aired it. Maggie Haberman said people close to Trump traced a period of increasingly visible disorder inside the administration to Wiles’s illness and reduced physical presence. The official response did not address that account. It called Haberman obsessed, irrelevant and greedy.

The allegation is serious but precisely bounded: Haberman, speaking on Jessica Tarlov’s Raging Moderates podcast, attributed it to people who spoke privately. She did not claim direct knowledge of Wiles’s condition or Trump’s conduct. The White House nevertheless treated scrutiny of the president’s behavior toward a sick subordinate as a personal offense against the president.

Illness became a test of standing

Wiles had been fighting breast cancer since February and later said she was cancer-free, according to Haberman. She announced that status publicly in September. During her treatment, Haberman said, Wiles was less physically present but continued trying to work.

That absence reportedly changed how Trump treated her. “Trump does not like… illness,” Haberman told Tarlov. “He sees it as weakness. And so he started picking on her.”

Haberman connected that treatment to a shift inside the White House. People who spoke with her said the administration’s chaos became more visible around Wiles’s diagnosis—not necessarily because the disorder began then, but because the official charged with controlling it could no longer be everywhere at once.

If that account is accurate, the power relationship is unmistakable. Wiles’s illness did not merely limit her ability to manage the president. It reportedly made her a target of him. The president held the authority; the aide undergoing cancer treatment carried the professional risk.

Following the Republicans’ midterm wipeout, the 80-year-old Trump replaced Wiles with Stephen Miller. The supplied reporting does not establish that her cancer caused her removal. It does, however, place her illness, Trump’s alleged hostility and her eventual replacement in the same political chronology. That sequence warrants scrutiny without pretending it proves more than Haberman reported.

The White House attacked the messenger

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle used the administration’s Rapid Response account on X to call Haberman a journalist with a “creepy obsession” who “clings onto” Trump for money and relevance. None of that rebutted her account. It offered no alternative description of Trump’s relationship with Wiles, no denial that he mocked or mistreated her and no explanation of the reported deterioration inside the White House.

That is not a substantive defense. It is an institutional attempt to redirect attention from presidential conduct to a reporter’s character.

The tactic also mirrors Trump’s earlier response to unwelcome coverage from Haberman. After she helped report that he planned to miss New York’s 25th-anniversary commemoration of the September 11 attacks because he was not permitted to speak, Trump reportedly called her unattractive, a stalker and a scammer. The insults did not resolve the factual question then, either.

Haberman is hardly an incidental antagonist in Trump’s political world. She and New York Times colleague Jonathan Swan wrote Regime Change, a bestselling account of the first year of his second administration. The book examined his relationship with aide Natalie Harp, the administration’s response to the Epstein files and the first couple’s sleeping arrangements. The White House’s grievance with her therefore sits within a sustained contest over reporting that exposes Trump’s private behavior and internal operations.

A presidency organized around one man’s sensitivities

AlterNet framed the response as a White House “meltdown,” but the more consequential fact is simpler: public communications staff used government infrastructure to deliver personal abuse on the president’s behalf.

That choice reveals the administration’s priorities. A chief of staff reportedly underwent cancer treatment while trying to continue working. People close to the president alleged that he interpreted her reduced presence as weakness and began targeting her. When that allegation became public, the White House deployed its communications apparatus against the journalist rather than supplying facts that would challenge it.

The result is not exoneration but misdirection. Haberman’s anonymous sourcing leaves her account as an attributed report, not an established public record of every interaction between Trump and Wiles. Yet the administration’s response gave readers no factual reason to reject it. It merely demonstrated, in public, the same reflex the report described in private: identify a perceived vulnerability, personalize the conflict and attack.

item.title: The Right to Die, and the Heartbreak of Defending It
item.description:
Sometimes respecting another person's freedom means accepting a decision you desperately wish they wouldn't make.

There are news stories that make you angry. Others make you question humanity. And then there are those that simply leave you profoundly sad.

I recently read the story of Annaliese Holland, a 26-year-old Australian woman who has chosen to end her life through voluntary assisted dying.

My immediate reaction wasn't outrage. It wasn't condemnation. It wasn't even disagreement.

It was sadness.

Because I believe she has that right. I would defend her right to make that decision, even though I desperately wish she didn't have to.

And there's something profoundly uncomfortable about defending a choice that breaks your heart.

Twenty-Six Years Old. A Lifetime of Suffering.

Annaliese suffers from autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy, a rare disease that attacks the autonomic nervous system, which controls functions such as digestion, blood pressure, and heart rate.

Her childhood was marked by relentless nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and an illness doctors struggled to explain. She wasn't properly diagnosed until she turned 18.

Imagine spending your childhood sick, your adolescence searching for answers, and your early adulthood discovering that having a diagnosis doesn't necessarily mean having an effective treatment.

While other young adults were planning careers, relationships, families, and futures, Annaliese was trying to survive another day.

In an interview, she compared living with her illness to walking through a field of landmines. You never know when the next explosion of suffering will come.

But what affected me most wasn't the description of her pain.

It was her grief over the life she would never experience.

She spoke about never getting the chance to become a mother, to accumulate a lifetime of memories, to look back one day and say she'd lived a good life.

She isn't merely losing her future.

She's mourning a future that illness never gave her the opportunity to build.

And she's only 26.

“I'm Not Giving Up. I've Had Enough.”

Perhaps the most heartbreaking part of her story is a conversation with her father.

A man who had spent countless nights beside her hospital bed, helping with medications and comforting her through unimaginable suffering.

When Annaliese told him she had reached her limit, he asked whether she was giving up.

Her answer was devastating.

She wasn't giving up, she explained. She'd simply had enough.

“Please, let me go.”

There is an enormous difference between those two ideas.

We have an unfortunate cultural tendency to portray people suffering from terrible diseases as warriors engaged in some noble battle. They're expected to fight, remain positive, never surrender, and somehow triumph through sheer determination.

And when they die, we say they “lost their battle.”

As though disease were a sporting event, and death a failure of determination.

But illness doesn't negotiate. It doesn't respect courage. It doesn't surrender because someone has a positive attitude.

And enduring suffering indefinitely is not a moral obligation.

Annaliese has spent years fighting something most of us cannot begin to imagine.

At what point do we stop demanding that she keep fighting simply because we cannot bear the thought of her stopping?

The Right to Choose Isn't the Obligation to Agree

Here's where I stand.

I believe a competent adult should have the right to make deeply personal decisions about their own body and life, including, under carefully regulated circumstances, the decision to seek medical assistance in dying.

That doesn't mean I celebrate those decisions.

It doesn't mean I consider death a desirable solution to suffering.

And it certainly doesn't mean society should abandon people who are seriously ill, disabled, elderly, or otherwise vulnerable.

Quite the opposite.

I believe we have a moral obligation to provide the best medical care, pain management, psychological support, disability assistance, and palliative care we can possibly offer.

We should invest in treatments. We should remove financial barriers to care. We should ensure that nobody feels compelled to die because treatment is unaffordable, assistance is unavailable, or society has made them feel like a burden.

A choice made because society refuses to provide reasonable alternatives is not the kind of autonomy worth defending.

And that is why safeguards matter.

Voluntary assisted dying must involve rigorous medical assessment, informed consent, protection against coercion, and meaningful access to appropriate care. The person's wishes must be their own, not the result of pressure from relatives, insurers, institutions, or a government eager to reduce expenses.

These protections must be substantive, not merely bureaucratic boxes to check.

But once those conditions are satisfied, whose suffering are we talking about?

Mine?

Yours?

The politician who believes every life must be prolonged regardless of circumstances?

The religious leader who believes suffering serves some divine purpose?

Or the person who wakes up every morning inside the body that is causing that suffering?

We can offer care. We can offer alternatives. We can ask someone to reconsider. But compassion does not automatically grant us the authority to make the ultimate decision for them.

The Cruelty of Good Intentions

Much of the opposition to assisted dying comes from sincerely held beliefs.

Some people believe human life is sacred and must never be deliberately ended. Others worry, reasonably, that legalizing assisted dying could expose vulnerable people to pressure or gradually expand eligibility beyond its original purpose.

These concerns deserve serious consideration.

But there is another moral danger that deserves equal scrutiny.

What happens when our determination to preserve life overrides the expressed wishes of someone enduring severe, unrelenting suffering?

We may tell ourselves we're protecting that person.

But we must also ask whether we're protecting them for their benefit, or because accepting their decision is emotionally unbearable to us.

There is a difference between preserving life and prolonging suffering.

Not every painful life is without value. Not every serious diagnosis makes death inevitable or treatment futile. And no outsider should presume that disability, dependence, or illness makes someone's life less worth living.

Nevertheless, there are circumstances in which medicine cannot provide relief sufficient for a particular patient's suffering.

In those circumstances, refusing to consider the patient's wishes doesn't automatically become compassionate merely because the refusal is motivated by love.

Sometimes the hardest expression of respect is accepting that another person has reached a conclusion we wish they hadn't.

When Death Becomes a Relief

One detail from Annaliese's story has stayed with me.

When she learned that her application for voluntary assisted dying had been approved, she cried with happiness.

Happiness.

A 26-year-old woman received permission to end her life, and her response was relief.

I find that almost unbearably sad.

Not because she was wrong to feel relieved, but because of what her reaction tells us about the suffering she describes.

Most people at 26 are still imagining what the next fifty years might bring.

Annaliese was relieved that she would no longer have to face the next fifty years under the circumstances she knew.

And that's the tragedy.

Not merely that a young woman has chosen to die, but that her illness has made the prospect of continuing to live so dreadful to her.

Medical science has accomplished extraordinary things. We transplant organs, treat cancers once considered invariably fatal, and keep people alive through conditions that would have been death sentences a generation ago.

Yet there remain diseases for which we cannot offer an adequate answer.

And sometimes, despite extraordinary medical efforts, keeping someone alive and giving them a life they find bearable remain two very different things.

We should never stop trying to close that gap.

Her Father's Impossible Position

I keep returning to Annaliese's father.

Imagine raising a daughter, watching her grow, comforting her when she's frightened, holding her hand through years of hospital visits, and hoping that the next doctor, the next treatment, the next discovery might finally change everything.

And then, one day, that daughter looks at you and asks you to let her go.

How do you answer?

Every instinct tells you to protect your child. To fight for her. To find another doctor, another treatment, another possibility.

But what happens when the person you're trying to protect tells you that continuing the fight has become unbearable?

I don't believe there's a painless answer.

A father can love his daughter with every fiber of his being and still be unable to cure her.

He can respect her decision and still wish she'd made a different one.

He can understand her suffering and still be devastated by the prospect of losing her.

And none of those feelings contradict one another.

Love doesn't always give us the power to save someone.

Sometimes it leaves us with the terribly difficult task of respecting a decision we cannot bring ourselves to welcome.

I Will Defend Her Right. And I Will Mourn Her Choice.

There is a principle I have always considered essential to individual liberty:

A right means very little if we defend it only when people exercise it in ways we approve of.

It's easy to support freedom when we agree with the choices people make.

The real test comes when someone makes a decision that horrifies us, saddens us, or contradicts everything we personally would have chosen.

Do we still believe the decision belongs to them?

In Annaliese's case, I do.

I don't know what it's like to live inside her body. I haven't endured her years of suffering. I haven't faced her medical prognosis or the limits of the treatments available to her.

And I have no moral authority to pretend that my discomfort outweighs her experience.

That doesn't mean every request for assisted dying should be granted. It means each request deserves careful, compassionate consideration, with the person's autonomy and welfare at the center.

I wish Annaliese could recover.

I wish researchers could discover a treatment tomorrow that would give her the future she wanted.

I wish she could fall in love, become a mother if she chose, grow old, accumulate memories, and one day look back on a long and fulfilling life.

I wish she had been given the chance to experience everything her illness has taken from her.

But wishing those things doesn't make them possible.

And my sadness doesn't give me the right to substitute my wishes for hers.

There is no triumph in this story. No victory to celebrate. Just a young woman, a terrible disease, a family facing an unimaginable loss, and a decision nobody should have to make.

I will defend her right to make that decision.

I will also wish, with all my heart, that she never had to.

And I refuse to believe there is anything contradictory about that.

item.title: Anything But Metric: How America Spent Fifty Years Refusing to Count to Ten
item.description:
The United States can land astronauts on the Moon, build supercomputers, and measure the universe. But ask Americans to measure a road in kilometers, and suddenly civilization is under threat.

How Many Elephants Long Is That?

There's a peculiar American tradition that deserves scientific examination.

Whenever something needs to be measured, Americans appear willing to use absolutely anything except the metric system.

An area the size of 200 football fields.

An asteroid approximately three school buses long.

A building as tall as 40 giraffes.

A whale weighing as much as 15 elephants.

A sinkhole large enough to swallow six Olympic swimming pools.

At some point, you begin to wonder whether the American educational system includes a mandatory course in comparative zoological measurements.

And naturally, the football fields are American football fields, not the soccer pitches most of the planet would recognize.

Let's consider the asteroid example.

An asteroid is approaching Earth. Scientists calculate its diameter at 30 meters. Perfectly understandable to billions of people.

But apparently, telling an American audience that an asteroid is 30 meters across would cause mass confusion. So the news reports that it's approximately three school buses long.

Excellent.

Which school buses? The little ones? The conventional yellow ones? The articulated monsters?

And how closely should we park them together?

This isn't because Americans are incapable of understanding metric measurements. American scientists, engineers, medical professionals, and manufacturers use them routinely.

It's because the United States has somehow managed to normalize a system where a person's height is measured in feet and inches, their weight in pounds, their soda in fluid ounces, and their medication in milligrams.

Buy a two-liter bottle of soda, then drive two miles to purchase a gallon of milk.

It's an impressive achievement in measurement schizophrenia.

And what makes the situation particularly absurd is that America actually tried to convert to the metric system fifty years ago.

It just forgot the part where a conversion is supposed to result in something changing.

America Was Metric Before It Wasn't

Here's a fact that might surprise people: the metric system has been legal in the United States since 1866.

That's right. President Andrew Johnson signed legislation permitting its use in trade and commerce nearly 160 years ago.

In 1875, the United States became one of the original signatories to the Treaty of the Meter, helping establish the international institutions responsible for measurement standards.

The country wasn't ignorant of metrication. It was involved in building the international measurement framework.

And since 1893, the official definitions of American customary units have been based on metric standards.

Think about that.

The inch is defined as exactly 25.4 millimeters. The pound is defined as exactly 453.59237 grams.

American customary measurements are, at their foundations, dependent on the very system that Americans supposedly refuse to adopt.

It's metric wearing a cowboy hat.

By the 1960s, countries including Britain were moving toward metrication. International trade increasingly depended on common measurements. American industries operating globally had good reasons to follow.

In 1968, Congress commissioned a comprehensive study of metric conversion.

The National Bureau of Standards delivered its findings in 1971, concluding that coordinated conversion would serve the country's interests.

The recommendation was sensible: a planned transition over approximately ten years.

And then Washington got involved.

Gerald Ford and the Great Voluntary Conversion

On December 23, 1975, President Gerald Ford signed the Metric Conversion Act.

The legislation established a national policy encouraging metrication and created the United States Metric Board to coordinate the transition.

It sounds promising.

Until you read what Ford said when signing it:

“It is important to stress that the conversion contemplated in this legislation is to be a completely voluntary one.”

There it is.

The single word that helps explain an enormous part of the subsequent failure.

Voluntary.

To understand the political environment, remember who Ford was.

He became president in August 1974 without having been elected either president or vice president. Following Spiro Agnew's resignation, Richard Nixon appointed Ford vice president under the Twenty-Fifth Amendment. Nixon then resigned, elevating Ford to the presidency.

Ford initially enjoyed considerable public goodwill. Gallup measured his approval rating at 71%.

Then, on September 8, 1974, he pardoned Nixon.

By late September, his approval had fallen to 50%. By January 1975, it reached 37%.

Ford wasn't technically a lame duck in 1975, but he was an unelected incumbent facing substantial political difficulties, economic problems, and an increasingly difficult path toward winning a presidential election in his own right.

This was hardly an ideal environment for championing a potentially unpopular national transition.

That doesn't prove the pardon caused the voluntary provision. Congress, industry, and public resistance all mattered. But the political context helps explain why a compulsory national conversion was never an easy proposition.

Instead, the federal government effectively told American businesses:

“We've concluded that adopting this international measurement standard would benefit the economy. We encourage you to convert.”

And American businesses quite reasonably asked:

“Do we have to?”

“No.”

“Will our competitors have to?”

“No.”

“Will our suppliers have to?”

“No.”

“Then why should we spend the money?”

An excellent question.

And Washington didn't have a particularly convincing answer.

Why Voluntary Standardization Doesn't Work

Imagine you're running an American manufacturing company in 1976.

Your machinery operates in inches. Your engineering drawings use feet. Your suppliers manufacture components to customary specifications. Your workers have spent their careers using those measurements.

Converting means retraining employees, modifying documentation, potentially retooling equipment, and coordinating changes with suppliers.

These costs may be justified over time, especially if you export products.

But if your competitors aren't converting, why should you bear those costs first?

Worse, if your suppliers continue manufacturing in customary units, you've merely introduced another layer of conversions into your operation.

This is a classic coordination problem.

A common standard can benefit everyone, but individual participants have incentives to wait for everyone else.

And when everyone waits, nothing happens.

It's the sort of problem governments are uniquely positioned to address.

Not necessarily by requiring every citizen to throw away their tape measures, but by establishing predictable standards, deadlines, and incentives.

Instead, the United States created a Metric Board with coordination responsibilities but without the authority to compel nationwide conversion.

Then the Reagan administration eliminated the board's funding in 1982.

The country had successfully created a national conversion program that didn't require conversion, then dismantled the institution responsible for encouraging it.

An impressive bureaucratic accomplishment.

The Solution Was Sitting in Washington's Checkbook

Here's where this story becomes especially frustrating.

The government didn't need to prohibit inches, feet, or gallons.

It already possessed an enormously powerful instrument for changing industrial standards.

Federal purchasing power.

Imagine if the 1975 legislation had included one additional provision:

Effective January 1, 1980, all new federal procurement contracts shall require metric units for applicable technical specifications, engineering drawings, measurements, packaging, labeling, and deliverables.

That's it.

You can manufacture anything you like in whatever units you prefer.

But if you want to sell it to the federal government, the products and relevant documentation must comply with metric specifications.

And the same requirements flow down to subcontractors supplying components or services for those contracts.

Nobody is forced to do business with Washington.

But businesses that want federal contracts suddenly have a strong financial incentive to operate in metric.

Consider the consequences.

A defense contractor needs metric components.

Its suppliers adapt.

Their suppliers begin manufacturing metric-compatible products.

Manufacturers serving both federal and private customers begin asking whether maintaining separate measurement systems is worthwhile.

Eventually, for some industries, metric becomes the economically convenient default.

That's how you make a supposedly voluntary transition commercially consequential.

Not by appealing to everyone's better nature, but by changing the incentives.

And there's an extraordinary historical irony here.

Congress actually moved toward this idea in 1988.

The Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act declared metric the preferred system for American commerce and required federal agencies to move toward metric use in procurement, grants, and other business activities.

President George H. W. Bush reinforced the policy through Executive Order 12770 in 1991.

But the legislation permitted exceptions where metrication was impractical or could create significant inefficiencies or losses of markets for American businesses.

Some exceptions were genuinely necessary. Others left substantial room for retaining customary practices.

It was progress, but thirteen years later than it could have been, and without the comprehensive market transformation that a consistently enforced standard might have encouraged.

The opportunity was there.

The implementation lacked consistency.

The Other Half of the Solution Was Sitting Beside the Highway

Federal procurement could influence American industry.

But how do you make ordinary Americans comfortable with kilometers?

Simple.

Put kilometers where Americans encounter distances every single day.

On road signs.

And here's the clever part: you don't need to replace every sign in the country overnight.

You establish another straightforward rule:

Every newly installed or replaced road sign displaying a measurement must use metric units.

That's it.

A new highway? Metric signs.

A damaged distance marker? Replace it with a metric one.

A speed-limit sign needs replacement? Install a sign displaying km/h.

A road undergoes reconstruction? Metric signs go up wherever signs displaying measurements are replaced.

No nationwide demolition-and-replacement campaign.

No massive effort to rip functioning signs out of the ground.

Just an instruction that every time a sign is replaced, the new sign uses metric.

Naturally, for a while, America's highways would be a mixed bag.

One sign might say:

“New York — 120 mi”

Another, farther along the highway:

“New York — 177 km”

So what?

Both are perfectly understandable measurements, provided the units are clearly displayed.

And that brings us to a surprisingly important engineering principle.

A number without a unit isn't a complete measurement.

American speed-limit signs traditionally display a bare number under the words “SPEED LIMIT.”

That's an unnecessary ambiguity during a transition.

Instead, every new or replaced sign should explicitly display its units:

“SPEED LIMIT 65 mph”

Or:

“SPEED LIMIT 100 km/h”

Notice that the units are visibly different. American customary speed uses mph; the standard SI-compatible notation is km/h.

There is no reason to mix both systems on the same sign.

In fact, dual-unit signs would undermine the transition.

If every sign reads “100 km/h (62 mph),” drivers who know customary units can simply ignore the metric measurement indefinitely.

One sign. One measurement system. Explicit units.

For safety, speed-limit conversions should be coordinated along entire road corridors, not introduced randomly at successive intersections. Drivers should have clear advance notice, and temporary transition information can be provided separately.

Distance signs are considerably less troublesome.

Within a few years, drivers would encounter kilometers regularly.

They wouldn't need to perform elaborate conversions. They'd begin developing an intuitive understanding of the new measurements.

Just as they previously learned that 65 mph was highway speed, they'd learn that 100 km/h was highway speed.

And yes, the cars themselves would need attention.

But let's remember what automotive speedometers looked like in the late 1970s and 1980s.

They were largely analog instruments with printed numerical dials.

For a compatible, correctly calibrated instrument, converting the speed display could be as straightforward as installing a replacement dial face. Other instruments would need different modifications.

Many American vehicles already displayed both miles and kilometers per hour anyway.

And the funny part?

Nobody ever called the instrument a “speedomiler.”

“But the States Control Their Roads!”

Quite right.

The federal government doesn't own or manage every street, county road, and state highway in America.

Which is where the third provision comes in.

States seeking designated federal highway funding must enact equivalent metric-signage requirements for newly installed and replaced signs.

Before someone starts screaming about states' rights, there's an important precedent.

In 1984, Congress passed the National Minimum Drinking Age Act.

Rather than directly imposing a national drinking age of 21, Congress threatened to withhold a portion of federal highway funding from states that refused to establish that minimum.

South Dakota challenged the law.

In 1987, the Supreme Court upheld the arrangement in South Dakota v. Dole.

The principle was straightforward: Congress could attach certain conditions to federal funds, subject to constitutional limitations.

Those conditions must be clear, related to the federal interest, and not impermissibly coercive.

A metric-signage requirement tied to a reasonable, designated portion of highway funding would have a plausible constitutional foundation, although its legality would depend on the details.

Congress would also need to amend existing statutory restrictions on federal mandates for metric highway signage.

But the mechanism is hardly revolutionary.

It's a familiar feature of American federalism.

States remain responsible for their roads.

States establish their own implementing legislation.

And federal highway funding encourages them to adopt a common standard.

Put together, the plan is remarkably simple:

  1. Federal procurement: Metric measurements become the required standard for applicable new federal contracts and deliverables, including relevant subcontracted work.

  2. Road signage: Every newly installed or replaced sign displaying measurements uses metric units exclusively, with coordinated transitions for speed limits.

  3. Federal highway funding: States qualify for designated funding by adopting equivalent metric-signage requirements.

No nationwide confiscation of rulers.

No prohibition against measuring your height in feet.

No requirement to replace functioning equipment immediately.

Just a clear rule: everything new moves toward the new standard.

Everything old disappears through ordinary replacement, modernization, and market pressure.

And Here's the Part That Really Stings

The Federal Highway Administration actually considered metric highway signage.

In the 1970s, it received more than 5,000 public comments about the idea. According to the agency, approximately 98% opposed conversion.

Later, following the 1988 legislation, highway authorities again explored metric conversion.

The response was politically hostile.

In 1994, the FHWA backed away from mandatory metric signs.

In 1995, Congress went further and prohibited federal highway authorities from requiring states to spend money converting highway signs to metric measurements.

Then, in 1998, Congress made metric usage optional in the federal-aid highway construction program.

Consider the sequence.

The government first establishes a voluntary national conversion program.

Then it recognizes the limitations of voluntary conversion and attempts to strengthen metric requirements.

Then political resistance leads it to weaken those requirements again.

And finally, Congress legislates to prevent highway officials from imposing one of the most visible forms of metrication.

That isn't merely a lack of enthusiasm.

It's an institutional history of starting, stopping, reversing, and preserving the very practices that made conversion difficult.

Meanwhile, a 1996 study commissioned by the FHWA estimated that metric highway-sign conversion could cost approximately $15.6 million through routine replacement, compared with as much as $826 million for dual posting, under the scenarios studied.

Those are historical estimates, not present-day costs, and they aren't interchangeable nationwide conversion budgets.

But they illustrate something important.

Replacing signs as part of ordinary maintenance can be dramatically less expensive than installing duplicate signage across the network.

The incremental approach wasn't some fanciful invention.

It had an identifiable economic rationale.

Would This Actually Have Worked?

Here's where we should separate what is plausible from what can be demonstrated.

Would the three-part strategy have guaranteed complete nationwide metrication within two years?

No.

Even if several million road signs are replaced annually, some signs remain in service for a decade or longer. And only a subset of signs display speed, distance, weight, or clearance measurements.

Federal procurement would influence substantial parts of industry, but not every private-sector transaction.

Businesses selling exclusively to domestic consumers could continue using customary measurements. Retail packaging, building codes, food sales, and household habits might require additional policies to achieve complete standardization.

And introducing metric measurements on roads would create genuine transitional challenges.

Drivers would need clear, consistent signage. Older vehicles might require updated speed displays. Emergency services, transportation databases, mapping systems, and road-maintenance agencies would need coordinated changes.

All manageable.

None necessarily trivial.

But there is a fundamental difference between a transition that takes longer than expected and one that never establishes an effective mechanism for completion.

Under the proposed system, metrication would advance every year.

Every federal procurement cycle.

Every highway construction project.

Every qualifying sign replacement.

Every new generation of vehicles.

Schools would be teaching a measurement system that children actually encounter in the world outside the classroom.

Industry would be responding to predictable standards rather than guessing whether the country intended to convert.

And ordinary Americans would gradually stop thinking of kilometers as foreign measurements.

Would the entire country have become metric in two years? Almost certainly not.

Could the United States have become substantially more metric within a decade, with a disciplined program beginning in 1975?

That is a credible possibility.

And by 2026, more than fifty years after Ford signed the legislation, the distinction would probably be enormous.

The Real Problem Was Never Mathematics

Americans can learn the metric system.

They already use it when measuring medication, purchasing certain beverages, conducting scientific experiments, and working in many technical industries.

The United States has sent robotic explorers across the solar system, developed extraordinarily precise instruments, and helped establish international measurement standards.

This isn't a country incapable of understanding decimals.

It's a country that never completed a coordinated change in everyday measurement practices.

And to be fair, resistance wasn't necessarily irrational.

Converting industrial equipment and infrastructure costs money. Established habits have practical value. A poorly managed transition can create genuine risks.

But those are arguments for planning, financial assistance, clear deadlines, and careful implementation.

They aren't arguments for permanent paralysis.

The irony is that today's American customary units are already defined through metric standards.

The country never truly escaped metric measurements.

It simply maintained an additional layer of conventions between those standards and everyday life.

And then, whenever a journalist needs to explain the size of an asteroid, the country reaches for a school bus.

Or an elephant.

Or a football field.

Because apparently “30 meters” is hopelessly incomprehensible, but “three school buses parked bumper to bumper” is a triumph of clarity.

Fifty years ago, the United States had a chance to make metrication an orderly, incremental national transition.

It chose to make the transition voluntary, inconsistent, and politically expendable.

A few clear procurement rules, coordinated road-sign standards, and carefully structured federal funding conditions might not have solved every problem.

But they would have given the project something it consistently lacked:

A direction, a timetable, and a reason for anyone to actually participate.

Instead, America continues to measure the world in football fields, elephants, and school buses.

And somewhere, a scientist quietly writes down the answer in meters.

Sources and further reading

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology — U.S. Metrication FAQs

  • Gerald Ford's statement signing the Metric Conversion Act, December 23, 1975

  • Congressional Research Service — Metric Conversion and the Federal Role

  • Gallup — Gerald Ford Retrospective

  • Federal Highway Administration — Metrication in Highway Construction

  • Federal Highway Administration — Interstate FAQs, Metric Signs

  • U.S. Code, Title 15, §205b — Metric Policy

  • South Dakota v. Dole, 483 U.S. 203 (1987)

item.title: Rachel Maddow knows who to blame for Democrats’ bungled impeachment fail
item.description:
Rachel Maddow blamed House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries for a failed procedural effort to advance the impeachment of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, arguing that Jeffries neglected one of leadership’s most basic obligations: getting his members into the room. Eleven Democrats missed the vote, according to AlterNet, weakening the effort and allowing a consequential opportunity to collapse through an avoidable failure of caucus management.

That is more than embarrassing logistics. Party leaders control schedules, coordinate attendance and decide which votes receive the full pressure of the institution behind them. If Hegseth’s impeachment was important enough to pursue, Democrats had a responsibility to treat the vote accordingly. Maddow’s accusation is that Jeffries did not.

Eleven absences and one leadership failure

Appearing on The Best People With Nicolle Wallace, Maddow contrasted Jeffries with former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, whose reputation for counting votes rested on enforcing discipline before bringing major matters to the floor.

Maddow credited Pelosi with stepping aside and supporting a generational transition rather than clinging indefinitely to power. But she questioned whether Pelosi’s chosen successor had mastered the operational skill that made her formidable: “Did she teach him to count as well as she can count?”

The line was pointed, but the substance matters more. Eleven missing Democrats did not merely register individual indifference or scheduling trouble. Their absence exposed a collective failure that falls within the opposition leader’s remit. Rank-and-file lawmakers remain responsible for missing the vote, but leadership exists precisely to prevent scattered individual decisions from defeating the caucus on a priority it claims is urgent.

Blaming only the absent members would therefore misdirect attention downward. Jeffries holds the institutional authority to coordinate his caucus, impress upon members the stakes and determine whether Democrats are prepared before proceeding. Maddow’s criticism places responsibility where that authority sits.

A transition praised before it was tested

Pelosi has publicly described Jeffries as an effective messenger and a leader capable of maintaining Democratic unity. Maddow did not attack the decision to elevate him; she called Pelosi’s willingness to pass the torch “noble” and appropriate. Her argument was narrower and more damaging: succession rhetoric is not a substitute for competent execution.

“This was a bad first one,” Maddow said. “And so that tactical stuff, you can’t make those mistakes.”

That distinction strips away a familiar form of Washington misdirection. Political leadership is often assessed through speeches, television appearances and declarations of unity. Floor power is less glamorous and more concrete. It requires knowing who will be present, where the votes stand and whether a proposed action can survive contact with the chamber.

On that measure, Maddow said Jeffries failed. The consequence was not merely poor optics for Democrats. It was a lost chance to advance an impeachment effort against a powerful administration official.

Waiting for another opening

Maddow suggested Democrats could get “a second bite at the Pete Hegseth-shaped apple” after January 3, when new members are sworn in. AlterNet reported that she expects another opportunity if Democrats take control in 2027.

That possibility does not erase the failed attempt. It postpones accountability while placing the outcome behind another round of electoral and procedural contingencies. New members must take office, control must shift, and Democratic leaders must decide to act again. Each condition gives Hegseth more time and gives the caucus another opportunity to lower the priority.

The episode also reveals the limit of treating opposition as performance. Democrats can describe an official’s conduct as grave enough to warrant impeachment, but that claim loses force when party leadership cannot secure attendance for the vote needed to move it forward. Institutional power is exercised through preparation and discipline, not simply through the severity of the language surrounding a measure.

Maddow’s criticism arrived while she was promoting Department of Fate, her book about the Justice Department’s reach into political freedom, economic life and equal treatment under law. But her judgment here concerned a more elementary institutional function. Jeffries did not need a new theory of democratic accountability. He needed eleven Democrats to show up.

item.title: Haberman reveals shocking reason Trump started 'picking on' Susie Wiles
item.description:
AlterNet reports that Susie Wiles’s departure as President Donald Trump’s chief of staff followed months of mounting hostility from Trump as she underwent treatment for breast cancer. According to New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, Trump began “picking on” Wiles because he regards illness as weakness—a revealing exercise of presidential power against an aide whose diminished physical presence made her vulnerable inside an administration organized around one man’s appetites.

The break reportedly intensified after the 2026 midterm elections. Trump was “furious” with Wiles afterward, according to earlier reporting cited by AlterNet, and appeared to blame her for the outcome. She offered to resign after a deterioration that Haberman said had begun around her March cancer diagnosis. Wiles has since announced that she is cancer-free.

Illness became an opening for humiliation

Haberman told the Raging Moderates podcast that Wiles tried to continue working through her treatment but was less physically present. Colleagues noticed her absence, and the administration’s existing disorder became more visible.

That was when Trump’s treatment of her changed, Haberman said. “He sees it as weakness. And so, he started picking on her.”

The account does not describe a policy disagreement or an ordinary dispute over performance. It describes a president interpreting an aide’s cancer treatment as personal weakness and responding with harassment. Wiles held an extraordinarily powerful office, but her authority remained conditional: it depended on retaining the favor of a president who, in Haberman’s telling, treats vulnerability as an invitation to attack.

Haberman cautioned that the illness was not the only reason Wiles left. “There were a lot of reasons,” she said, describing every Trump associate as operating under an “hourglass timer” that eventually runs out. People may return to his orbit, but their standing is temporary and revocable.

The daughter allegation does not explain the rupture

Podcast host Jessica Tarlov asked whether the rift grew out of allegations that Wiles’s daughter had been “trading influence” through her position at a lobbying firm. Haberman rejected that as a complete explanation, saying the collapse had been building for months.

That distinction matters. The influence allegation may be politically consequential, but Haberman’s account places the decisive pressure elsewhere: Wiles became less available while receiving cancer treatment, Trump turned on her, and the post-midterm blame campaign accelerated her exit. Centering the daughter’s alleged conduct would divert attention from the person who actually controlled Wiles’s position and reportedly subjected her to escalating scrutiny.

Wiles was reportedly well-liked by other Trump aides. That offered little protection. A White House staff can privately respect a chief of staff, but only the president holds the institutional power to sustain or destroy that person’s authority. Once Trump made Wiles a target, internal goodwill could not compensate for presidential hostility.

Loyalty flowed toward Trump, never from him

Wiles had stood by Trump in 2021, when his political position was at its weakest. Trump had also supported her after her break with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, whom she had helped elect. Haberman described that earlier relationship as mutually useful, not durable.

The distinction is central to Wiles’s rise and fall. Haberman called her “a transactional political figure,” unlike ideological hard-liner Stephen Miller. Transactional loyalty can survive only while both parties continue to see value in the arrangement. Trump’s version appears narrower: loyalty to him is treated as a continuing obligation, while any loyalty he extends remains subject to immediate cancellation.

Wiles helped manage Trump’s return to power and then occupied one of the most influential positions in the federal government. Yet when cancer limited her presence and an election created a need for blame, that record reportedly counted for less than Trump’s aversion to perceived weakness. The shocking element is not that another Trump alliance ended badly. It is that, according to Haberman, the president used a senior aide’s illness as the occasion to begin tearing her down.

item.title: Fox News host fact checks Trump official to his face: You’re 'in charge!'
item.description:
Laura Ingraham’s question cut through Vice President JD Vance’s attempt to blame obsolete technology for the government’s infrastructure failures: Republicans had controlled the federal government for two years, she said, so why had they not fixed it? Vance’s answer effectively conceded the point. The administration had applied patches, he said, while a genuine rebuild still required Congress to provide the money.

That exchange, reported by AlterNet from a Mediaite account of Ingraham’s Monday interview, matters because it exposed the evasive structure of Vance’s argument. Aging equipment may explain why systems fail. It does not explain why officials with governing power have not replaced them.

An explanation that doubles as an indictment

Vance described a system operating with technology that is 50 years old. He praised Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and said officials sometimes must assemble a “patchwork of solutions” to keep it running.

That is a description of deferred maintenance, not an alibi for it. When Vance asked rhetorically why the country still had such an old system and declared that it needed rebuilding, Ingraham interrupted with the relevant fact: “Well, you guys have been in charge the last two years. Why hasn’t it gotten fixed?”

Vance replied that the administration had been fixing and patching what it could. Modernization, he said, would require Congress to “reinvest” and supply the necessary resources.

His answer relocated responsibility from the officials holding executive power to an institution Republicans had also controlled during the period Ingraham identified. Congress does control appropriations, and a replacement project cannot materialize by administrative command alone. But that makes spending priorities, legislative choices and governing competence central to the story. It does not make the failure ownerless.

An airline pilot appearing with Ingraham broadened the blame across decades, saying the problem had been developing for 30 years and was “on all of us.” The first part provides useful context: infrastructure neglect typically outlives one administration. The second obscures agency. Passengers and workers did not write federal budgets, decide which upgrades to defer or settle for temporary repairs. “All of us” is what institutional failure becomes when the people empowered to act prefer a constituency too diffuse to answer back.

The pilot’s sharper point was that superficial repairs were no longer adequate: “The spackle on the drywall is not enough anymore.” Vance’s account suggested the administration knew exactly that while continuing to emphasize its patching work.

Fox’s criticism follows Republican defeat

The confrontation did not amount to a political conversion by Ingraham. AlterNet placed it within a broader shift by outlets that had reliably supported President Donald Trump but became more critical after Republicans suffered what the article describes as historic setbacks in the 2026 midterm elections.

Ingraham’s own criticism has remained rooted in a dispute over how Trump wielded power, not whether he should have held it. After the election, she attributed the Republican losses to Trump and other party leaders abandoning what she regarded as MAGA’s central commitments.

She singled out Trump’s invasion of Iran, arguing that he had neither escalated toward decisive victory nor withdrawn after failure. Her preferred analogy was George W. Bush’s escalation in Iraq, while her alternative was the logic of a businessman ending an unsuccessful venture: “cut your losses.” She said that was what voters wanted and therefore “the whole point of politics.”

That framing is revealing. Ingraham was not challenging the administration from outside its political project; she was policing it after voters imposed a cost. Her interview with Vance performed the same function. The vice president offered deteriorating technology, decades of neglect and congressional funding needs as explanations. Ingraham forced the responsibility back toward the governing coalition whose record voters could actually judge.

Her question was potent because it applied the standard that partisan media routinely suspends for favored officials: authority brings accountability. Vance could identify the age of the technology, praise his transportation secretary and request more resources. He could not turn two years in power into somebody else’s tenure.

item.title: Trump Media plunges as nearly $1 billion cash demand looms
item.description:
Trump Media & Technology Group’s share price fell 12 percent to $4.10 in early trading, extending its one-month decline to 43 percent as the Truth Social operator confronted a potential cash demand of nearly $1 billion. The immediate problem is not merely sour investor sentiment: holders of the company’s convertible notes may soon be entitled to demand repayment of $976.8 million in cash, threatening resources Trump Media wants available for its proposed merger with fusion-energy developer TAE Technologies.

The selloff exposes the weakness behind Trump Media’s headline profit. The company reported $409.7 million in third-quarter earnings despite generating only about $3 million in revenue. That apparent windfall came entirely from $496.1 million in unrealized gains on cryptocurrency and stock investments—not from operating Truth Social or building a durable media business.

A profit produced by market swings

Strip away those paper gains and Trump Media remains an unprofitable operation. It lost about $12.3 million on an operating basis in the quarter, improved from a $29.1 million loss during the same period a year earlier. It also burned through $28.4 million in cash during the first nine months of the year.

That distinction matters because unrealized investment gains can reverse without warning, while debt holders asking for cash require actual money. Trump Media CEO Kevin McGurn said the company’s balance sheet provides “real flexibility.” The convertible notes will test whether that language describes usable financial capacity or simply an asset portfolio whose value depends heavily on volatile markets.

The company’s political branding cannot alter the arithmetic. Truth Social may function as the preferred platform of President Donald Trump and as a vehicle for his political influence, but Trump Media’s reported operating results show a business producing little revenue relative to the financial obligations now hanging over it.

Noteholders hold the near-term leverage

Trump Media’s management can promote its treasury and its expansion plans, but the noteholders possess the consequential power in the immediate dispute. If the terms of the convertible debt allow them to demand repayment, they can force the company to choose between preserving cash and financing its next speculative venture.

Every dollar returned to those investors would be unavailable for the proposed combination with TAE. The merger cleared a regulatory step on Nov. 5, when the Securities and Exchange Commission declared its registration statement effective, but shareholders still must approve the plan.

The transaction offers Trump Media investors a prospective stake in fusion energy, a technology with enormous promise that has not yet established itself as a commercial business. That makes the merger less a solution to Trump Media’s weak operating performance than another wager on a future breakthrough. TAE’s technology may reach the market, fail to do so, or never generate the returns implied by the pitch. The merger itself could also collapse.

The spectacle cannot carry the balance sheet

Some investors argue that Trump Media’s treasury gives the company room to maneuver and that TAE provides access to fusion’s potential upside. Others are focused on the cash burn, cryptocurrency volatility, possible debt repayment and the risk that the merger or TAE’s technology fails.

Those concerns are not equivalent to routine turbulence across social media companies. Meta, which owns Facebook, was down 2 percent, but it reported $64.6 billion in quarterly revenue, an increase of 26.1 percent. Trump Media produced roughly $3 million. Invoking both companies as participants in the same market obscures the decisive difference between a vast profitable enterprise and a politically branded platform whose reported quarterly profit rested on asset-price fluctuations.

The coming shareholder vote may settle one part of Trump Media’s proposed transformation. It cannot manufacture operating revenue, commercialize fusion technology or erase the rights of noteholders. For now, investors are pricing in that imbalance: a company advertising flexibility while nearly $1 billion in potential cash claims sits between its current business and its next promise.
