item.title: White House blocks all employees from complying with subpoenas
item.description:
The White House has ordered executive-branch personnel not to accept congressional testimony requests without prior approval from its legislative affairs and counsel offices, according to a memo reported by PBS News and described by AlterNet. That is not literally a ban on every federal employee complying with every subpoena, as the headline claims. It is a centralized permission regime—one that gives presidential aides control over whether agency personnel agree to appear before lawmakers and places those employees between conflicting institutional commands.

Bill Scharf, counsel to the president, told executive departments and agencies that personnel must secure approval from both the White House Office of Legislative Affairs and the Office of White House Counsel before agreeing to appear before any congressional committee. The memo applies broadly enough to obstruct routine oversight, but the supplied reporting does not establish that the White House has rejected every subpoena or forbidden all testimony outright.

That distinction narrows the headline. It does not make the directive benign.

The White House claims a gatekeeping power

Scharf presented the order as an “established White House consultation process,” insisting that agencies remain “disciplined” by obtaining notification and approval before personnel agree to testify. The bureaucratic language conceals the institutional shift: Congress seeks information from officials charged with carrying out federal policy, while the president’s lawyers assert authority to decide whether those officials may provide it.

Consultation between agencies and the White House is ordinary. Making presidential approval a precondition for any appearance is something more consequential. It allows the institution subject to oversight to control access to the people who possess the relevant information.

The memo also transfers much of the immediate risk away from the officials who issued it. Employees who follow White House instructions could face congressional contempt proceedings for failing to comply with a lawful subpoena. Employees who cooperate without permission could defy a direct executive-branch order. The White House gets centralized control; individual workers inherit the legal exposure.

Congress still has coercive authority

Congress is not limited to sending sternly worded letters. Either chamber can use inherent contempt proceedings, directing its sergeant-at-arms to detain a person found to have obstructed legislative work. That process does not depend on the Justice Department, although it requires the chamber itself to conduct proceedings and order detention.

Congress can also refer contempt findings to the Justice Department for possible criminal charges. AlterNet notes that the usual statute of limitations for contempt of Congress is five years, extending potential exposure beyond the remaining two years of Trump’s term as described in the report.

A president could attempt to pardon someone facing federal criminal contempt charges. But, according to the account, the Supreme Court has not definitively resolved that precise question, and a pardon would not necessarily extinguish Congress’s separate inherent authority to detain a recalcitrant witness. The directive therefore does not settle the conflict. It prepares the ground for a confrontation among Congress, the executive branch and, potentially, the courts.

That confrontation would also test congressional will. Formal authority matters only when lawmakers are prepared to use it. A White House can gamble that legislative leaders will hesitate before ordering arrests, sustaining prolonged litigation or imposing meaningful costs on officials who refuse to testify.

Former officials remain outside the chain of command

The administration’s control is weaker over people it has already discarded. AlterNet points to generals fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and former officials such as Kristi Noem and Pam Bondi as possible witnesses who could testify without seeking current White House approval.

That creates an obvious limit to the memo. The administration can instruct serving personnel, but it cannot reconstruct a chain of command over former officials. An effort to purge or force out officials may consolidate control inside the government while simultaneously creating a pool of witnesses with direct knowledge and fewer professional reasons to remain silent.

Whether any of those former officials will receive subpoenas or cooperate is not established in the supplied reporting. Their availability nevertheless matters because it prevents the White House from converting an internal directive into complete control over congressional access to information.

Oversight is being recast as criminal victimization

The memo followed a letter from Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, directing Sen. Elizabeth Warren to preserve documents and communications. Reitz accused Warren of attempting to “weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights.”

Warren and other Democrats have publicly warned that “accountability is coming.” Instead of answering that prospect on the merits, presidential allies have answered with allegations against the investigators themselves. Stephen Miller amplified the dispute by citing 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242, federal civil-rights provisions associated with the Ku Klux Klan Act.

The reporting does not establish that Warren committed a crime, that charges are pending, or that Miller’s citation constituted a literal prosecutorial pledge. What it does show is a coordinated political inversion: congressional scrutiny is framed not as a constitutional function but as potential criminal abuse by the lawmakers conducting it.

That framing serves the same purpose as the approval memo. One mechanism restricts who may provide information; the other raises the prospective cost of requesting it. Together, they put witnesses under executive discipline and investigators under accusatory pressure.

The immediate question is not whether the White House has successfully blocked every employee from testifying. AlterNet’s own details do not support that sweeping conclusion. The consequential fact is narrower and more precise: presidential lawyers have claimed the power to preclear agency testimony before Congress, while allies of the administration portray threatened oversight as grounds for criminal suspicion. The next decisive acts belong to Congress—whether it issues subpoenas, whether witnesses refuse them, and whether lawmakers enforce the authority the White House is testing.

item.title: GOP analyst predicts 'the end' for Trump as 2-party system fractures
item.description:
Donald Trump’s political era is not demonstrably “over.” That is the forecast Republican-politics scholar John Kenneth White drew from the 2026 midterms: Republican losses, a coming struggle between MAGA loyalists and traditional conservatives, and an electoral realignment that he believes could outlast Trump himself. The immediate result is less conclusive but still consequential. According to White, the House Republican conference has become more thoroughly Trump-aligned even as Republican senators acquire stronger incentives to protect their careers by breaking from the president.

That distinction matters. Trump may be losing the power to guarantee Republican victories without yet losing the power to command Republican loyalty. A diminished party can remain firmly under his control.

Four factions inside two ballot lines

Writing in The Hill, White argued that the United States is returning to the “four-party politics” described by political scientist James MacGregor Burns in the 1960s. The formal Democratic and Republican organizations remain, but each contains two increasingly distinct political blocs.

White divides Democrats between moderates, whom he calls the “majority-makers” of 2026, and socialists seeking a larger government. Republicans, in his account, are split between Trump loyalists bound to the president by “superglue” and Reagan Republicans seeking a return to older conservative principles.

The symmetry is organizational, not necessarily practical. White expects Democrats to suppress internal conflict because they see an urgent need to address damage caused by Trump. He predicts a more destabilizing Republican rupture because electoral defeat has sharpened the conflict between presidential loyalty and political survival.

That argument identifies the central pressure inside the GOP: officeholders do not need to experience a principled conversion to defy Trump. They need only conclude that obedience has become an electoral liability. Parties often describe that calculation as ideological renewal after voters have already imposed the cost.

A MAGA House and a more restive Senate

White sees the House and Senate moving differently. Republican losses have left the House GOP increasingly concentrated around Trump-aligned members, with newly selected leader Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio representing the MAGA faction. Defeat, under those conditions, did not purge Trumpism from the House conference. It reduced the ranks while leaving loyalists with greater internal control.

The Senate presents a different power structure. Senators elected in 2024 and 2026 can expect to remain in office after Trump leaves the presidency. White argues that the scale of the party’s 2026 losses, combined with senators’ instinct for self-preservation, will push some of them to resist Trump and seek another direction for the party.

This is not yet proof of a successful post-Trump coalition. It is a prediction about incentives. Senators with longer terms and independent electoral constituencies have more room to distance themselves than House members operating inside a MAGA-dominated conference. Whether they use that room depends on what they fear more: Trump’s remaining hold over Republican voters or another general-election defeat.

The Cleveland analogy has limits

White reaches back to Grover Cleveland, the only president besides Trump to serve nonconsecutive terms. Cleveland narrowly returned to office in 1892, then watched his Democratic Party suffer a landslide defeat in 1894. Republicans captured both chambers, gained 110 House seats and added four senators. William McKinley’s 1896 landslide then opened what White describes as 36 years of Republican presidential dominance.

The comparison supplies a precedent for a returning president whose party collapses in the following midterm. It does not make the sequel automatic. White is betting that the 2026 elections will similarly become the opening event in a durable partisan realignment favoring Democrats, with Republican infighting deepening the damage.

That is a much larger claim than the reported midterm result alone can establish. Electoral defeats can reorder parties, but they can also intensify control by the faction most resistant to admitting why the defeat occurred. White’s own description of the House illustrates that possibility: Republicans lost strength while the remaining conference became more MAGA, not less.

“The end” is a forecast, not an event

White’s declaration that “the Trump era is over” resolves the headline’s teaser but outruns the political condition he describes. His evidence points to a party facing serious losses and an emerging Senate rebellion, while its House leadership remains in the hands of a prominent Trump ally and its core loyalists remain attached to the president.

The more defensible conclusion is narrower. The 2026 midterms may have ended the assumption that Trump’s control of the Republican Party reliably produces power for Republicans. They did not, on White’s account, end his control over the faction now dominating the House GOP.

That creates an ugly institutional bargain. Republican senators may distance themselves to preserve their careers, while House loyalists retain influence precisely because less devoted members disappeared. Trump’s electoral weakness and his internal party power can therefore grow at the same time. If White is right that a long Republican exile has begun, the first response from one of the party’s most powerful remaining blocs has not been to abandon Trump. It has been to consolidate around him.

item.title: Blow to Trump DOJ as judge rules government must answer questions
item.description:
A federal judge rejected the Justice Department’s attempt to keep career prosecutors beyond the court’s reach, ruling that the government could not broadly invoke privilege to prevent questions about alleged misstatements in a pending case. The decision matters because the department was not merely disputing which questions were relevant; it was asserting the power to decide which of its officials a judge could hear from while warning that it could appeal if she refused to accept those terms.

U.S. District Judge April Perry addressed the dispute after the Justice Department made a last-minute request that she refrain from directly questioning the frontline career prosecutors who handled the case, according to Jose Pagliery of The Washington Sun. The department wanted Perry to rely instead on Andrew Boutros, the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney and political head of the office.

Perry refused to treat much of the information as privileged and therefore unavailable to the court, The Washington Sun reported, citing two people in the courtroom. The government must now answer questions it had tried to restrict.

The department tried to choose the court’s witness

The Justice Department’s proposed arrangement would have placed Boutros between the judge and the career employees with firsthand involvement. Henrique Carneiro, counsel to the associate attorney general, argued that “there is plainly no need for anyone but the U.S. Attorney to provide information,” according to Pagliery.

That was not a neutral dispute over courtroom efficiency. The department sought to substitute a political appointee for the prosecutors who worked directly on the case, limiting Perry’s ability to question the people closest to the conduct under examination. It also signaled that it would challenge her on appeal if she rejected that restriction.

The department had previewed its position in an earlier filing seeking a protective order ahead of a hearing scheduled for December 2, 2026. It asked Perry to narrow the testimony to preserve “all applicable governmental privileges” and confine questioning to the “purported misstatements” she had identified.

Courts routinely adjudicate privilege claims and limits on testimony. What made this confrontation significant was the department’s broader institutional demand: it wanted the executive branch to control how the judicial branch investigated representations made in a case before it. Perry’s ruling rejected that attempted insulation.

Transparency is not the same as speculation

Former Democratic congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, who was among those charged in the case, told The Washington Sun that transparency “should be in the government’s interest” if it had done nothing wrong. She then asked what could be “so horrible” in the communications that the department would work so hard to conceal them.

The first point follows from the government’s conduct; the second remains speculation. The reporting does not establish what the communications contain or why the department resisted their disclosure beyond its stated privilege arguments. Perry’s ruling is not proof of hidden misconduct, and Abughazaleh’s suspicion should not be converted into a finding.

But the department’s procedural maneuver is consequential on its own. Government lawyers answer to courts when their conduct or representations become material to judicial proceedings. By trying to channel all questioning through a Trump-appointed officeholder, the department sought control over both the witness and the account the court would receive.

Perry’s decision does not resolve the underlying case or establish what the prosecutors will say. It does establish that the Justice Department cannot simply announce that its preferred official is sufficient and expect the court to abandon its inquiry. The immediate setback for the Trump administration is therefore concrete: the judge, not the department, retains authority over the questions needed to examine what happened in her courtroom.

item.title: Here’s who approved the fancy private jet purchase for Noem’s donor
item.description:
The order to keep and complete Kristi Noem’s private-jet deal reportedly came from Stephen Miller, according to unnamed White House and Department of Homeland Security sources cited by the PunchUp newsletter. The administration publicly disputes that account: DHS says Noem acted without White House input, while the White House says officials decided only after her departure that paying for the aircraft was preferable to swallowing an enormous cancellation fee. What is uncontested in the competing accounts is the institutional failure: senior officials committed hundreds of millions of public dollars to aircraft linked to a Noem donor, accepted prices reportedly above market value, and left taxpayers trapped in a contract designed to make cancellation ruinously expensive.

A donor’s company and a captive government

Noem initially sought two Gulfstream G700s to replace an aging Coast Guard executive aircraft. The publicly documented contract was worth $172 million, with training and modifications reportedly pushing the total toward $200 million. Before leaving DHS, however, she ultimately purchased 10 aircraft from Daedalus Aviation Corporation.

Daedalus is chaired by a donor to Noem’s political operation. The Week reported that the company obtained roughly $464 million to more than $500 million in combined business after a $10,000 contribution to American Resolve, Noem’s political action committee. The contribution does not by itself establish that the contracts were bought. It does establish a relationship that demanded severe scrutiny before the government signed unusually expensive agreements favorable to the contractor.

The prices deepen that concern. The New York Times reported that Daedalus paid about $83 million for two smaller Gulfstreams and sold them to the government for $103 million. Aviation experts told the Times that two 17-year-old Boeing 737s were also purchased for several million dollars above market value.

Those are not marginal discrepancies buried in an ordinary procurement. They describe a government paying a politically connected company premiums for luxury aircraft, then discovering that the contract made retreat almost as costly as surrender.

The rescue-mission story did not survive scrutiny

When Congress questioned Noem about the first two planes, she said the government’s existing G5 aircraft had exceeded their usable hours. She then invoked Coast Guard search-and-rescue work, saying the replacements would help the service “continue to serve our country.”

That explanation was implausible on its face: luxury executive jets do not retrieve people from the water. Noem subsequently offered other missions, including “high-profile deportations” and “long-range command and control.” The shifting rationale matters because the aircraft’s practical beneficiaries reportedly included Noem and adviser Corey Lewandowski, not merely Coast Guard crews carrying out urgent operations.

One plane described by PunchUp as the $108 million “Mile High Boudoir Jet” came with bedrooms, a bar, a kitchen, showers and flat-screen televisions. According to AlterNet, Noem and Lewandowski — whom she had been accused of having an extramarital affair with — were among the aircraft’s most frequent users. That allegation does not resolve the procurement question, but the amenities and reported travel pattern make the public-service justification look less like an operational case than an effort to retrofit one around an indulgent purchase.

Noem had already testified that President Donald Trump approved a separate $220 million advertising campaign featuring her in staged appearances promoting immigrant deportations. That campaign and the aircraft purchases shared a governing instinct: public money could be deployed not simply to administer policy, but to furnish senior officials with spectacle, branding and comfort.

The disputed order from Miller

The final jet deal was completed immediately before Markwayne Mullin replaced Noem as DHS secretary. PunchUp reporters Tom Latchem and Will Neal cited several White House and DHS sources who said Miller — then deputy chief of staff with substantial authority over DHS and later chief of staff — was behind an urgent demand to spend $303 million on five aircraft on the evening Noem officially left office.

A senior DHS source with direct knowledge told PunchUp that approval “would have come down to Miller” and said Miller would not deny his role on the record. The source suggested officials pushed the transaction through before the incoming DHS leadership arrived so it could be identified as the work of the departing team and spare Trump political damage.

That account remains contested. DHS Deputy Secretary Troy Edgar said the planes “were purchased under Secretary Noem without input from White House officials.” A White House spokesperson likewise assigned the purchase to Noem, saying Mullin raised the matter after taking office and the White House then concluded that retaining the planes was the fiscally responsible option because termination would be so expensive.

The official version narrows White House responsibility to managing a disaster Noem had already created. PunchUp’s sources describe a different chain of command: Noem signed the damaging arrangement, but Miller exercised enough control over DHS that ignorance would itself be difficult to explain. As one source put it, Miller “ruled his agencies with an iron fist.” That is evidence of the source’s assessment of his power, not independent proof that he gave the final order. But it makes the administration’s attempt to isolate responsibility at Noem’s desk politically convenient as well as disputed.

A penalty that converted failure into policy

According to PunchUp, Noem signed a lease-to-buy agreement carrying a cancellation fee of about $200 million. One senior DHS official described the provision as a “win-win for the other side”: the government could terminate the deal and pay heavily for nothing, or purchase the aircraft and then struggle to justify and use them.

The White House chose the second option. Its claim of fiscal responsibility begins only after officials allowed the government to be cornered. Keeping overpriced planes may have cost less than paying an extraordinary termination penalty, but that does not make the underlying decision prudent. It means the contract successfully converted a questionable procurement into a fait accompli.

The planes are now reportedly sitting unused on the tarmac. Noem is gone, officials are contesting who authorized the last push, and the contractor has the benefit of terms that made the government pay whether it wanted the aircraft or not. The administration’s defense amounts to an argument over which powerful official should own the liability. Taxpayers already do.

item.title: The verdict is in —and it’s time for MAGA to beg for forgiveness
item.description:
AlterNet columnist D. Earl Stephens says MAGA must beg forgiveness before any political reconciliation can begin. But the “verdict” promised by his headline never arrives. His column supplies no completed election result and identifies no actual judgment rendered against Trump’s movement. Instead, it converts an election still being finished — with an Alaska Senate contest described only as hanging in the balance — into a sweeping moral mandate, then substitutes collective abuse for an account of who exercised power, through which institutions, and with what consequences.

That is not accountability. It is catharsis dressed as a news judgment.

An unfinished election becomes a blank check

Stephens writes as Alaska appears to lean toward electing a Native American woman to the U.S. Senate and as the country completes what he calls extraordinarily consequential midterm elections. The column does not name the candidate, provide results or establish that the outcome produced the repudiation he claims. Nevertheless, he declares that “the vast majority of the American people have spoken” and are ready to leave Trump behind.

The supplied reporting does not support that conclusion. An election can weaken a political movement, deny it offices or expose the limits of its appeal. It cannot establish that every voter shares one motive, much less authorize a columnist to speak for “tens of millions” without evidence presented here.

Stephens is right to reject the familiar ritual in which powerful officials invoke reconciliation before investigating misconduct or repairing harm. Calls to “move on” have often protected officeholders, donors and institutions from consequences. But his column does not distinguish reconciliation from impunity. It demands abasement from a mass of voters while leaving the machinery of power largely offstage.

Collective contempt obscures institutional responsibility

The column’s bill of particulars includes support for Trump, participation by some supporters in the Capitol attack, resistance to masks during the pandemic, tolerance of corruption, hostility to science and book bans. It also accuses MAGA supporters of celebrating lethal government violence and accepting the return of measles. These are serious claims, but Stephens assigns them indiscriminately to “you” — a political population treated as a single culpable body.

That framing misdirects scrutiny. Voters can enable political harm, and those who joined an attack bear responsibility for their own conduct. But voters did not all possess the same authority as the president, lawmakers, party officials, agency heads, wealthy donors or corporate interests that Stephens mentions only near the end. The people with institutional power made decisions, financed campaigns, controlled government machinery and shaped the information environment. Collapsing them into one despised crowd blurs crucial differences between architects, beneficiaries, operatives and followers.

Stephens ultimately gestures toward “billionaires” and “crooked corporations” that he says have polluted Congress and taken government from the public. Yet his fury remains concentrated on ordinary MAGA adherents, especially white men. The result is politically convenient for the powerful: structural decisions disappear into a morality play about the personal depravity of millions of people.

Accountability cannot mean “extermination”

Stephens repeatedly says he wants justice rather than accommodation. He calls for defending science, books, equal rights and truth, and for confronting corruption instead of ignoring it. Those are recognizable political objectives. But he sabotages them with language that treats opponents not as people subject to law, organizing and democratic defeat, but as contamination to be removed.

He writes that Trump’s movement must be “dead and gone,” threatens to cut its members into “tiny bite-sized pieces” with words, warns Democrats against appeasing rather than “exterminating” evil, compares supporters to Confederates and Nazis, and tells them it is “time to meet your maker.” In context, some of this is plainly figurative invective. It is still reckless. A demand for accountability should specify investigations, prosecutions where evidence warrants them, electoral defeat, removal from office, institutional reform or restitution. Stephens instead offers humiliation and vaguely described “punishment.”

That choice matters because dehumanization is not redeemed by the speaker’s preferred policy agenda. Calling people “worthless,” describing them as diseased and imagining them scrubbed clean with a steel brush does nothing to establish legal culpability. It replaces standards with tribal permission: the righteous may speak without restraint because the condemned deserve whatever follows.

The most striking contradiction is Stephens’s insistence that truth must displace lies while his own argument outruns the facts he presents. He calls Trump a rapist, felon and thief without providing the legal or factual context necessary to distinguish adjudication, conviction and accusation. He describes the Capitol attack as the worst assault on that building since the War of 1812, but uses the conduct of participants to condemn an entire voting bloc. He demands precision from his enemies and exempts himself from it.

Reconciliation is not the immediate question

Stephens frames the choice as appeasement or vengeance. That is a false constraint. A government can investigate crimes without assigning hereditary guilt to a political identity. It can protect public health without declaring dissenters subhuman. It can defeat an authoritarian movement without adopting that movement’s habit of dividing the population into the pure and the disposable.

Nor does forgiveness belong chiefly to a columnist. People directly harmed by violence, discrimination, official neglect or corruption decide for themselves whether forgiveness is possible. Public institutions have a different obligation: establish facts, apply law consistently, constrain abusive power and prevent recurrence. An apology from a MAGA voter cannot substitute for any of those tasks, just as refusing an apology cannot accomplish them.

Stephens’s anger points toward real political conflicts over democratic government, public health, racial equality, corruption and truth. His column then evacuates those conflicts of institutional substance. Who authorized abuses? Who funded the officials involved? Which laws failed, which agencies complied and which officeholders escaped consequences? Those questions would locate power. Demanding that millions crawl forward and beg instead locates a target.

The supposed verdict, then, is not an election result established by the material AlterNet published. It is Stephens’s own sentence: collective guilt, compulsory contrition and indefinite contempt. That may satisfy a desire to reverse the humiliation Trumpism imposed on its targets. It does not explain how the people who wielded power will be made to surrender it.

item.title: What a night in Chicago exposes about the end of the Trump era
item.description:
The Chicago night did not, by itself, reveal the end of Donald Trump’s political era. A woman relieving herself on a downtown sidewalk near Trump Tower was not evidence of a regime’s collapse; she was a stranger in public distress, drafted into Chauncey DeVega’s argument as a symbol of national degradation. The actual evidence AlterNet presents is institutional: voters rejected Trump’s appeal in the 2026 midterms, Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and an administration facing defeat continued to wield federal power against migrants while the incoming majority remained unable to intervene until January.

That distinction matters. Visible disorder is easy to photograph and easier to blame on people with little power. The consequential disorder described in DeVega’s essay came from officials, agencies and contractors authorized to detain, deport, spend and conceal.

A mandate delayed by the calendar

According to AlterNet, Democrats won a “blue tsunami” in the midterm elections, capturing the House and Senate with unexpected victories in Texas, Georgia and Mississippi. Trump had urged Americans to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. By DeVega’s account, they did—and delivered control of Congress to his opponents.

Yet electoral rejection is not the same as immediate removal from power. The new Congress will not take office until January. Trump’s administration retains the machinery of the executive branch during that interval, including the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The political era may be ending in the electoral sense described by AlterNet, but the state’s coercive authority has not entered an intermission.

DeVega’s image of a nearly empty final Trump campaign rally on November 2—dozens of people gathered before a fouled Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool—captures diminished spectacle. It does not establish diminished capacity. Crowd size cannot measure the reach of detention systems, federal contracting or military spending. An unpopular administration can still impose lasting harm, particularly on people who have no meaningful leverage over it.

Deportation presented as achievement

The clearest account of power in the essay is not the Chicago anecdote or Trump’s shrinking audience. It is a Department of Homeland Security press release celebrating the removal of 483,200 people described by the agency as “illegal aliens” during the last fiscal year.

That figure was offered as proof of “success.” DeVega instead describes what the bureaucratic category contained: an 8-year-old Haitian child detained for deportation after arriving at a hearing in dress clothes; unaccompanied migrant children offered $3,000 to “self-deport”; and a nurse who reportedly became untraceable inside a detention network where ICE contractors received scripts that helped prevent thousands of detainees from being located. He also reports that at least 59 people died in ICE custody, while cautioning that the real number may be higher.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin answered concerns about conditions with contempt: “We’re not providing Holiday Inns.” The remark performs a familiar piece of political misdirection. Nobody described in the essay was demanding resort accommodations. The concern was whether people held by the government could be found, kept alive and treated lawfully. Mullin substituted ridicule for an answer because detainees have little institutional power and the department controls both their confinement and much of the public account of it.

The administration did not merely oversee these outcomes, according to the reporting. DHS advertised the deportation total as an accomplishment. That turns suffering into a performance metric and invites the public to evaluate state violence by volume.

Trumpism after Trump’s crowds disappear

Former Republican strategist Steve Schmidt told viewers that a political movement nearing its end can become more concentrated rather than less dangerous in its conduct—“hotter,” “brighter,” “denser” and “crazier.” He predicted that MAGA’s final form would gather at Mar-a-Lago as its “purest and vilest and meanest distillation.”

The stellar metaphor is vivid, but the institutional point is more useful: electoral contraction can reward the most committed faction. Politicians who lose persuadable voters may become more dependent on loyalists who treat escalation as proof of authenticity. The result is not necessarily an organized ideology called Trumpism. It can be a governing method built from loyalty tests, cruelty toward politically isolated groups and the conversion of public office into personal protection and profit.

DeVega argues that Trump did not create the conditions that made this possible. He identifies a broader leadership class that enabled him. That is the harder claim for Washington to confront because it implicates more than one man’s character. Trump’s rise required party officials, donors, corporate interests and officeholders willing to accommodate conduct they could have opposed. His electoral decline does not automatically dismantle those incentives or remove the people who benefited from them.

Congress will decide whether defeat has consequences

AlterNet’s essay calls on the incoming Democratic majority to investigate alleged corruption, self-dealing, influence-peddling, profiteering and abuses of law and democratic norms. DeVega argues for public hearings, impeachment proceedings against officials who violated their duties, and a third impeachment of Trump. He also wants Congress to dismantle the measure promoted as the “Big Beautiful Bill,” defund what he calls Trump’s illegal war in Iran and use its spending authority to address rising costs for food, housing, gasoline and health care.

Those are demands, not reported decisions by the incoming majority. The crucial unresolved question is whether Democrats will convert their electoral victory into oversight and legislation or retreat into gestures of bipartisanship. Ray Richmond, writing at Raw Story, warned against extending Republicans an olive branch they could turn into a spear. The metaphor points to a record of asymmetric politics: one side uses institutional restraint as a norm, while the other treats that restraint as an exploitable weakness.

Accountability also requires distinctions DeVega’s rhetoric sometimes compresses. Investigations must establish facts. Impeachment must identify particular misconduct. Spending restrictions must be written and passed. Justice is not made more legitimate by calling it dirty; it is made legitimate through evidence, public process and consequences proportionate to established acts.

That work would reach beyond Trump’s television presence or the attendance at his rallies. The administration described by AlterNet exercised power through appropriations, agency directives, detention contracts and official euphemism. If the incoming Congress leaves those mechanisms intact, Trump’s era will not have ended so much as lost its principal salesman. The decisive image is therefore not the stranger on the Chicago sidewalk. It is DHS placing a number—483,200—under the heading of success, confident that the people counted beneath it could be reduced to evidence of political performance.

item.title: NYT's Maggie Haberman: Trump’s China trip has intelligence officials worried
item.description:
AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump was unlikely to confront Chinese President Xi Jinping over an alleged espionage operation involving Nvidia, even after receiving two intelligence briefings about it. According to New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, Trump had shown little interest in discussing the allegation and was expected to use his Asia trip chiefly for photographs with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The sharper national-security question was not Trump’s indifference to a personal scandal. It was whether restricted American artificial-intelligence chips were reaching China—and whether his administration was enforcing the export controls meant to stop them.

Intelligence Trump reportedly did not want to address

Haberman said Trump had been briefed twice that Alice Huang, described in the report as Jensen Huang’s mistress, was a Chinese spy. One briefing reportedly occurred aboard Air Force One while Trump was traveling to China after picking up Jensen Huang, who had not been invited on the trip because of the alleged espionage concern.

The reported operation extended beyond a private relationship. Haberman described an effort to infiltrate Huang’s life and company and manipulate sales of advanced AI chips allegedly being smuggled into China in violation of export restrictions. She said there was “no credible debate” within the relevant intelligence assessment that Alice Huang was a spy, while people working for Nvidia disputed that characterization.

Those are grave allegations, and AlterNet’s account attributes them largely to Haberman. The political significance lies in the reported presidential response: Trump had access to the intelligence and, according to Haberman, did not want to engage with it.

Asked whether the disclosures would affect Trump’s meeting with Xi, Haberman said she did not expect Trump to raise the matter proactively. She instead wondered whether Xi might introduce it. That inversion is revealing. The American president reportedly entered the encounter holding intelligence about a suspected Chinese operation, yet the initiative appeared more likely to belong to the foreign leader whose government stood accused.

A summit built for deference

Haberman expected the trip to function primarily as a photo opportunity, giving Trump a stage alongside Xi and Putin—leaders toward whom, she noted, he has displayed “deference and affinity.”

That assessment matters because presidential meetings are exercises of power, not celebrity tableaux. If Trump declined to press Xi about suspected espionage or the movement of controlled technology, the absence would itself carry diplomatic meaning. China would not need Trump to endorse its conduct. It would need only for him to leave the available leverage unused.

Haberman connected that risk to Trump’s first term, when he publicly favored Putin’s denial of Russian election interference over the conclusions of US intelligence agencies. Her comparison did not establish what Trump would do in the forthcoming meetings. It identified a documented governing pattern: intelligence can reach the president without governing his conduct when it conflicts with a relationship or performance he values more.

The affair is the distraction; the chips are the power

The salacious framing around Jensen Huang’s alleged affairs threatens to shrink an export-control and counterintelligence story into gossip. Haberman explicitly identified the larger issue: a Justice Department investigation, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s reported refusal to implement export bans, and the possibility that advanced chips barred from China were nevertheless reaching the country.

Restricted Blackwell chips could help develop sophisticated Chinese AI models, Haberman said, and technology experts believed such chips were already contributing to Chinese development efforts. Alice Huang was reportedly one element of that inquiry, not its full extent.

That shifts scrutiny toward the officials with actual authority. A suspected spy can seek access. A company can contest the government’s characterization. But the Justice and Commerce departments possess investigative and regulatory power, and the president directs the executive branch. If export controls were violated or left unenforced, responsibility does not end with the alleged intermediary. It runs through the companies handling the technology and the officials charged with protecting it.

Haberman also supplied an important operational distinction: US intelligence agencies reportedly avoided alerting China to what they knew while investigations continued. That could explain silence during an active inquiry. It does not explain a broader refusal to address the intelligence internally or enforce applicable export restrictions. Protecting an investigation and disregarding its implications are not the same act.

Joe Scarborough framed the obvious question on Morning Joe: Why would Trump fail either to stop restricted chips from reaching China or to warn an associate about an alleged intelligence operative? AlterNet’s account offers no definitive answer. It does, however, report where Trump’s attention was expected to go: toward appearing beside two authoritarian leaders he admires, while the agencies beneath him confronted an espionage and technology-transfer problem he reportedly preferred not to discuss.

item.title: Nobel economist turns Trump’s disaster excuse against him
item.description:
Donald Trump blamed Joe Biden for the nationwide air-travel breakdown that grounded departures for nearly five hours on Nov. 13. Economist Paul Krugman turned that excuse back on the administration now controlling the Federal Aviation Administration: Trump paused infrastructure spending that included billions for the agency, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy accelerated an air-traffic-control overhaul despite warnings that the effort lacked basic planning.

The precise cause of the outage remains under investigation. But the institutional failures surrounding it belong to the officials currently exercising power, not to the former president Trump invoked after thousands of flights were canceled.

A national breakdown, followed by a political diversion

The FAA temporarily halted departures nationwide in what CNBC described as the largest grounding of US flights since Sept. 11, 2001. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the disruption affected 12,000 flights. FlightAware recorded more than 6,400 cancellations on Saturday, followed by roughly 1,500 more on Sunday as the system recovered. Krugman, stranded in Chicago, arrived home a day late.

Trump responded Sunday on Truth Social by declaring that the Biden administration “was an FAA disaster” and asking Congress for additional air-traffic-control funding. The post assigned blame backward while directing the remedy toward lawmakers, neatly avoiding the decisions made by Trump and his own appointees.

Krugman rejected that account in a Substack post, writing: “It wasn’t weather, it wasn’t a terrorist attack, it was simple incompetence.” His argument was not that investigators had already identified which official caused the equipment failure. It was that the administration had made a fragile system more vulnerable while treating speed as a substitute for competent management.

Trump froze money; Duffy accelerated the overhaul

Biden signed the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021, including $25 billion for the FAA. Shortly after returning to office, Trump signed an executive order pausing spending under that law. His demand for more money after the outage therefore omitted a pertinent fact: his administration had already interrupted congressionally approved infrastructure funding.

Duffy, meanwhile, has pushed an expedited transformation of the air-traffic-control system. According to Krugman, the transportation secretary proceeded without adequately consulting air-traffic workers or respecting warnings about the risks.

The Government Accountability Office supplied one such warning about two months before the outage. Reviewing the FAA modernization initiative launched in May 2025, the nonpartisan watchdog said the agency “could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions.” It found that the program lacked both a lifecycle cost estimate and a master schedule.

Those are not ornamental planning documents. A lifecycle estimate establishes what a project is likely to cost beyond its opening phase; a master schedule maps the dependencies and timing needed to replace critical infrastructure without disabling it. Racing ahead without either is an administrative choice, not an inheritance.

Krugman also noted that Duffy voted against FAA funding legislation in 2019 while serving as a Wisconsin congressman. After the outage, Duffy reportedly used his press conference to blame Democrats and praise Trump. That record makes the administration’s presentation especially evasive: officials who opposed or interrupted funding now depict themselves as rescuers from a failure assigned to people no longer running the government.

The failed equipment does not erase the policy failure

Federal officials traced the incident to a router installed by contractor L3Harris at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and another device in Amarillo, Texas. The router’s manufacturer said that, based on the information available to it, the equipment operated as intended. Investigators had not established the precise cause when AlterNet published its account.

Krugman said he had no particular reason to reject the official explanation. Nor does a hardware-level account resolve the larger question. Critical systems are supposed to withstand isolated equipment trouble through redundancy, maintenance, controlled transitions and experienced personnel. Finding the component associated with an outage does not explain why its failure—or the failure of the system around it—could paralyze departures across the country.

The FAA’s dependence on technology so old that it does not expect to eliminate floppy disks until 2028 illustrates the accumulated vulnerability. Krugman traces that deterioration to a Republican governing tradition, beginning with Ronald Reagan, that disparages public administration and then starves the services Americans still depend upon.

Trump added a more aggressive version through the Department of Government Efficiency. According to Krugman, DOGE eliminated or pushed out about 13 percent of the federal workforce within months, without consulting relevant experts. The supplied reporting does not establish that those personnel losses caused this particular outage. It does establish the governing posture surrounding it: dismantle capacity quickly, disregard institutional knowledge and blame the predecessor when a public system breaks.

The router investigation may eventually identify a narrower technical cause. It cannot make Biden responsible for Trump’s spending pause, Duffy’s accelerated modernization effort or the administration’s response after the grounding. The immediate malfunction remains under review; the attempt to redirect accountability is already in plain view.

item.title: Democrats fear impeachment is exactly what Trump wants
item.description:
House Democrats are not rejecting a third impeachment of President Donald Trump. They are arguing over whether pursuing one would impose accountability or hand Trump the political spectacle he wants. With Democrats reportedly preparing to control the House after the midterms, the question is no longer whether members can introduce articles of impeachment. It is whether they can build a coherent case, conduct a credible investigation and justify acting when Senate conviction appears unlikely.

That distinction matters. Trump’s preference for portraying every investigation as persecution does not erase Congress’s constitutional responsibility to investigate misconduct. But impeachment without an agreed charge or a disciplined factual record could turn that responsibility into campaign theater—terrain Trump knows how to exploit.

Trump welcomes the fight

According to Politico, House Democrats involved in Trump’s first two impeachments are urging colleagues not to rush into a third. Their concern is not that Trump has become restrained. Democrats have accused him during his second term of self-enrichment, accepting foreign gifts, trading pardons for favors, directing government power against perceived enemies and launching an illegal war in Iran. The immediate problem is that the caucus has not agreed on which allegations could support articles of impeachment or what investigation should come first.

Trump has encouraged the confrontation. Speaking to reporters earlier this month, he claimed impeachment would “destroy the Democrat Party” because it would be “for no reason.”

That is political misdirection, not a legal argument. The question is not whether Trump declares the country successful. It is whether evidence establishes conduct that meets the constitutional standard for impeachment. By substituting a slogan about national success for an answer to specific allegations, Trump seeks to make scrutiny itself appear illegitimate.

Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who led Trump’s second impeachment and is poised to take over the House Judiciary Committee in January, told Politico that Trump may see another impeachment drive as his best chance to revive an eroding coalition.

“I think Donald Trump would love us to organize a campaign of impeachment against him right now because he thinks that’s his last hope for rallying the dwindling MAGA base at this point,” Raskin said.

That warning identifies the trap without resolving the underlying duty. A president’s ability to profit politically from oversight cannot give him immunity from it. But Congress also has no obligation to supply him with a poorly constructed proceeding that begins with a desired punishment and searches afterward for a case.

No agreement on the purpose

Politico interviewed 14 House Democrats and found no caucus-wide consensus. Their disagreement is partly strategic, but it also reflects competing ideas about what impeachment is for.

Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the Homeland Security Committee, said impeachment was not his priority, though he would vote for a resolution if another member brought one to the floor. Rep. Zoe Lofgren emphasized the near-certain obstacle in the Senate, asking whether conviction was possible and calling for a national conversation.

Rep. Gregory Meeks was more categorical: “You don’t indict somebody if you don’t think you can convict.”

That prosecutor’s analogy compresses two different institutional functions. Impeachment is not a criminal indictment, and the House’s obligation to determine whether a president committed impeachable offenses is not identical to the Senate’s willingness to convict. If senators refuse to remove a president despite persuasive evidence, that is a judgment for which those senators bear responsibility. Their anticipated refusal does not automatically settle what the House should document or charge.

Still, an impeachment undertaken with no plausible path beyond a symbolic House vote carries costs. It can consume investigative capacity, crowd out other oversight and allow Trump to collapse distinct allegations into a single narrative of partisan retaliation. Democrats would then have exercised their power without demonstrating that they knew what they wanted that power to accomplish.

Accountability is not vengeance

Other Democrats reject making political convenience the controlling test. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam told Politico that conduct warranting impeachment should produce impeachment “even if it’s bad politics.” Rep. Becca Balint likewise argued that some Democratic voters are concerned less with revenge than with whether the constitutional system can survive repeated violations without a formal response.

Balint’s distinction is essential because “revenge” is an easy label for Trump and his allies to attach to any attempt at accountability. It converts allegations about presidential conduct into a story about the emotions of his opponents. Democrats would assist that maneuver if they treated impeachment principally as catharsis for their base.

The House’s actual power lies in investigation: obtaining records, compelling testimony, establishing a chronology and deciding whether particular conduct warrants a constitutional charge. That process does not require Democrats to announce impeachment before they know what the articles would say. Nor does caution require them to abandon scrutiny because Trump is term-limited or because Senate Republicans may protect him.

A methodical investigation could end without impeachment. It could also produce a narrower and stronger case than the sprawling inventory of accusations now circulating. What it cannot honestly do is begin from the premise that Trump’s preferred political reaction determines whether Congress enforces its own constitutional authority.

Trump may want another impeachment fight. That is not a reason to manufacture one, and it is not a reason to grant him impunity. The decisive issue is whether House Democrats can distinguish an evidence-driven proceeding from a performative vote—and whether they are prepared to make Senate obstruction visible instead of using it as an excuse to avoid their own decision.

item.title: 'More to it': Expert flags signs of deception in Trump officials' presser
item.description:
A body-language analyst says Trump administration officials appeared stressed and evasive while explaining Friday’s nationwide ground stop, but the supplied reporting does not establish that either official lied—or identify what supposedly remains concealed. Dr. John Paul Garrison’s case rests on lowered eyes, heavy breathing, blinking, facial movements and an awkward exchange between Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Those observations may show discomfort. Calling them signs of deception is an inference, not a finding.

That distinction matters because the ground stop involved federal authority over air travel, and the public explanation reportedly centered on a software problem. The officials responsible for explaining such a sweeping disruption owe the public a coherent account. Yet speculation about their involuntary gestures cannot substitute for testing that account against the system failure, the government’s decisions and the resulting operational consequences.

A press conference read as a confession

AlterNet reports that Garrison, a clinical and forensic psychologist who produces YouTube body-language videos, examined Mullin and Duffy’s appearance at a press conference following the ground stop.

Garrison interpreted Mullin’s conduct as evidence of anxiety. Mullin gripped the microphone stand as though bracing himself, breathed heavily and repeatedly looked away from reporters while trying to dismiss rumors about the software issue. Garrison argued that Mullin’s glance toward reporters after speaking could have been an unconscious attempt to determine whether they believed him.

He also focused on Mullin’s unusually flat delivery. According to Garrison, Mullin ordinarily gestures and uses expressive facial movements for emphasis, making the subdued presentation seem “peculiar.” Both men blinked frequently, which Garrison read as stress.

Duffy appeared more comfortable while discussing technical matters, Garrison said, but his behavior changed when a reporter raised the possibility that routers had been overloaded with data. Garrison interpreted movements Duffy made with his tongue as an effort to “hold something back.”

None of those reactions identifies a false statement. Anxiety can accompany deception, as Garrison suggested, but he also acknowledged that the officials could have been uncomfortable for other reasons. That concession is not incidental. It is the boundary between observing conduct and claiming knowledge of what caused it.

The exchange that deserves scrutiny

The more consequential moment involved what the officials actually said. Mullin began discussing “new patches into the system” and “new equipment,” while Duffy reportedly lowered his head and shook it. Garrison inferred that Duffy wanted Mullin to stop because Mullin was effectively assigning blame to him.

Duffy then turned to funding, arguing that he could not act without money. Garrison characterized that pivot as a distraction from questions about the administration’s explanation and its insistence that the situation was under control.

That exchange raises legitimate questions without requiring anyone to diagnose a blink. Did the failure involve obsolete equipment, inadequate upgrades, overloaded routers or some combination of problems? Were patches or replacement hardware already required? What did Duffy lack the money to do, and who controlled that funding? The officials’ words point toward institutional responsibility; their facial movements do not resolve it.

Duffy’s funding argument also relocates agency. Saying an official cannot act without money may describe a real constraint, but it does not explain who set the budget, which repairs or upgrades went unfunded, or why the system reached the point of a nationwide stoppage. “Money” is not an autonomous force. Elected officials and administration leaders decide what to request, prioritize and defend.

Speculation can protect the powerful

The story’s framing risks misdirecting scrutiny away from the government’s decisions and toward a psychologist’s interpretation of physical behavior. That is convenient for officials even when the resulting coverage sounds accusatory. Readers are invited to wonder what secret lurks behind a lowered gaze instead of examining the administration’s account line by line.

Garrison concluded that there was “very likely” more to the incident than the Trump administration had disclosed. The reporting supplies evidence of tension and apparent disagreement, but it does not establish what that “more” might be. It does not identify a concealed cause, a knowingly false assertion or a specific deceptive act.

The administration still bears responsibility for explaining a nationwide ground stop clearly and consistently. If Mullin and Duffy offered conflicting accounts, shifted responsibility or used budget complaints to evade the immediate question, those are concrete subjects for reporting. Treating stress as proof of dishonesty weakens that scrutiny by replacing accountable statements with an interpretive performance.

The revealing detail is not that two officials blinked under questioning. It is that discussion of a national aviation disruption moved from software rumors to routers, patches, equipment and money without producing a clear account of responsibility. That unresolved chain—not speculative body-language analysis—is where the pressure belongs.

item.title: Historian Jon Meacham warns Trump’s ‘incompetence’ is spooking Americans
item.description:
Jon Meacham’s answer was blunt: Americans are unnerved because the Trump administration has put its lack of competence on public display when basic government functions are under strain. Speaking Monday on MS Now’s “Morning Joe,” the historian said people facing crises want experienced officials who know more than they do—not reality television personalities treating public administration as another spectacle.

The anxiety Meacham described is not abstract. The discussion centered on failures involving the Federal Aviation Administration, grounded planes and a president whose attention, as co-host Joe Scarborough framed it, remained fixed on a grand ballroom while families struggled to afford groceries. Scarborough also pointed to Trump calling affordability a “hoax.” Whatever entertainment value the president extracts from controversy, an aircraft safety system cannot run on provocation.

Government becomes visible when it fails

Meacham argued that the episode exposed the hollowness of decades of rhetoric about government itself being the problem. Americans may disagree over the size and reach of the public sector, but they still expect it to keep planes separated in the sky, food safe and essential infrastructure operating.

The FAA belongs in the same category as traffic signals and utilities, he said: systems whose value rests on their reliability. Passengers do not care about polling when they board an airplane. They need “a basic level of competence.”

That distinction matters because political theater can misdirect responsibility. A failure of government is not evidence that government is inherently incapable. It can also be the foreseeable result of placing incapable people in charge of institutions that require expertise, continuity and disciplined attention. The officials who control appointments, staffing and administrative priorities hold the power; travelers stranded or frightened by the consequences do not.

Meacham did not claim that Democrats would “magically” manage the FAA better. But his insistence that this was not partisan risked sanding down the central fact under discussion: Trump is president, and his administration is responsible for governing. Hypothetical Democratic failure does not distribute accountability for decisions made by the people currently holding federal power.

A presidency organized as spectacle

Scarborough asked whether Americans might again value experience and rationality more than entertainment. He contrasted the recent political era with President Harry Truman’s willingness to retain George Marshall even after Marshall reportedly told Truman that he had not voted for him. The point was not nostalgia for some flawless age. It was that competent government requires leaders capable of valuing expertise above personal loyalty.

Trump has advertised a different model. Meacham recalled Trump saying in 2017 that he wanted a presidency resembling a reality show in which he would “vanquish my opponents.” That conception turns public office into an endless contest of dominance, grievance and audience retention. Agencies then become props, personnel become loyalists or enemies, and administrative failures become opportunities to blame predecessors.

Pointing backward at a former president, Meacham said, does nothing to make government work. It does, however, serve Trump’s preference for keeping public attention fixed on conflict. The controversy is not incidental to the performance; it sustains it. The material consequences—grounded aircraft, disrupted travel and diminished confidence—land elsewhere.

The memory of crisis

Meacham said Friday’s events returned him to the early days of COVID, when Americans looked toward those in authority and wanted reassurance that the people managing the emergency were knowledgeable and capable. As the afternoon unfolded, he said, he was not “filled with confidence, to say the least.”

That comparison identifies the political danger in a government built around personality. Crisis strips away branding. A president can label affordability a hoax, redirect attention toward a ballroom or keep the conversation entertaining, but none of those maneuvers can perform the technical work of aviation safety or restore public confidence in a failing system.

Meacham said the demand for competence had “sure as hell manifested itself in the midterm.” His larger observation was simpler: people expect the public sector to perform certain essential tasks well. Trump may still imagine the presidency as a show about defeating his adversaries. As Meacham put it, “he thinks it’s a reality show, but it’s our reality.” The administration controls the set; the public absorbs the failure.

item.title: ‘Who’s getting fired?’ Trump official cornered on travel chaos live on Fox
item.description:
A nationwide aviation shutdown stranded travelers and disrupted thousands of flights on Friday, but the Trump administration’s response was immediate: nobody would lose a job. Appearing on Fox News on Sunday, the official AlterNet identified as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed the rare ground stop on an approximately 50-year-old system struggling to operate alongside modern technology.

That answer established the administration’s position before the investigation described in the interview was entirely conclusive. The failure belonged to antiquated equipment; accountability would extend to no one currently in charge.

A system can fail without absolving its stewards

Fox anchor Peter Doocy opened with the blunt question: “Who’s getting fired over this?”

“Oh, I don’t think anybody’s going to get fired over this,” Mullin replied. “This was an issue with the equipment.”

He characterized the infrastructure as “basically an old dial-up system” whose interaction with newer technology had caused problems. That may explain the technical mechanism behind the disruption. It does not answer the institutional question Doocy raised.

Obsolete federal infrastructure does not maintain itself, decide its own budget or set modernization priorities. Officials and lawmakers do. A system can be old enough to have passed through many administrations without making the current administration responsible for five decades of neglect. But the age of the machinery is not a substitute for examining who knew its vulnerabilities, what safeguards existed and why one failure could halt flights nationwide.

Mullin’s refusal to anticipate firings may ultimately prove justified; a technical malfunction does not necessarily establish individual misconduct. But announcing that conclusion while describing the cause with less than complete certainty reverses the usual order of accountability. The personnel verdict arrived before the technical one was final.

Fox offered a foreign villain; Mullin mostly declined

Doocy then steered the interview toward a more politically convenient possibility: a cyberattack. He asked whether a government or hacker might have flooded routers in Arkansas with data and forced the shutdown.

Mullin left a sliver of uncertainty but said the available assessment pointed elsewhere. “I would love to point it at a bad actor because then we know who to go back and punch,” he said. “But the fact is, it isn’t.” He put the likelihood that the aging system caused the failure at 98 percent.

The remark was unusually revealing. A hostile actor would provide a clean antagonist and an uncomplicated show of retaliation. Infrastructure decay offers neither. It instead raises tedious but consequential questions about appropriations, procurement, maintenance and the officials responsible for keeping critical systems functional.

Mullin did not claim certainty beyond what he said investigators had established, and he rejected an unsupported connection between the Federal Aviation Administration failure and a Microsoft outage on consecutive days. When Doocy suggested that viewers understandably suspected “something big,” Mullin acknowledged the conspiracy theories but said there was no basis to connect the incidents.

That was the most responsible part of the exchange. Speculation about hackers may be more dramatic than a legacy-system failure, but drama is not evidence.

The breakdown had consequences; responsibility remains abstract

Thousands of flights were delayed or canceled after the nationwide ground stop, according to AlterNet. Travelers experienced the government’s infrastructure problem as missed connections, abandoned plans and airport uncertainty. Yet the official account distributed responsibility in precisely the opposite direction: the public absorbed concrete consequences while the government blamed an impersonal machine.

No evidence in the reported interview establishes that a particular employee deserved dismissal. It does establish that the administration was prepared to rule out that consequence while the cause still carried a stated 2 percent margin of uncertainty. It also shows how easily scrutiny of institutional competence can be diverted into speculation about sabotage.

If the eventual finding remains what Mullin described—a decades-old system failing under the demands of contemporary aviation—the central problem will not be that the machinery was old. It will be that the federal government entrusted nationwide air travel to infrastructure officials knew was old, and its first clear accountability decision after the resulting chaos was that no one would be fired.

item.title: 'Spitting fire': Rick Wilson warns Trump could pay the price for messy fight
item.description:
Donald Trump could pay a political price for the Democratic Senate’s leadership revolt, but only if the party converts its anger into legislative power. Rick Wilson’s warning rests on a specific chain of events that has not yet occurred: Democrats would have to reject Chuck Schumer’s accommodationist instincts, organize a more combative majority and recruit enough Republicans to strip Trump of tariff authority over his veto.

That is not a forecast so much as a test. Democrats’ historic midterm gains gave them power; the fight now is over whether their leaders will use it.

Schumer’s record is now the issue

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2015, had been widely expected to become majority leader in January. Instead, he faces resistance from voters and incoming senators who regard him as unable or unwilling to mount an effective challenge to Trump.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen has entered the leadership contest after winning support from parts of the Democratic base for opposing Trump’s deportation agenda. Schumer still appears favored, according to AlterNet, but the result was unresolved when Wilson spoke Sunday on Molly Jong-Fast’s “Fast Politics” podcast.

The contest is not merely generational or stylistic. It concerns what Democrats believe their new majority is for. Schumer has already promised to pursue compromise and bipartisanship next year. The voters and senators driving the revolt appear to see that approach as a refusal to recognize the mandate that produced the majority.

Wilson said younger House and Senate members are “spitting fire” because they understand that voters did not send them to Washington for ceremonial collegiality. His language about lawmakers being sent to “burn down this corrupt system” was hyperbolic, but the institutional conflict he described is concrete: new members want investigations, confrontation and rapid policy reversals, while established leaders remain attached to a governing culture built around negotiated routine.

A majority can investigate—or manage decline

Wilson warned Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries against offering limited investigations before returning to minor bipartisan legislation. The crude joke he used to make that point—contrasting timid oversight with a bill on “toilet seat standards”—captured the insurgents’ accusation: Democratic leaders too often treat confrontation with presidential power as an interruption before normal business resumes.

But control of Congress is not symbolic opposition. A majority determines committee leadership, investigative priorities and which bills receive votes. If Democrats confine those powers to gestures, Trump will not “pay the price” for the leadership dispute. He will benefit from it.

That is why the focus on Democratic infighting can itself misdirect. The weaker actors here are not the voters demanding resistance or the incoming senators carrying that demand. The consequential decisions will be made by caucus members choosing their leader—and by whichever leader then controls the Senate’s agenda. A mandate can be diluted without anyone openly repudiating it. Institutional caution, procedural delay and appeals to bipartisanship can accomplish the same result.

Wilson’s tariff scenario remains a wager

Wilson identified tariff authority as the clearest opportunity for a Democratic majority to impose a material defeat on Trump. Congress controls tariffs and taxes, he argued, and could pass legislation revoking the president’s tariff power. He further predicted that enough Republicans would support the measure to override a Trump veto.

That veto-proof coalition is Wilson’s assertion, not a reported fact. So is his claim that ending Trump’s trade policies would cause the economy to rebound and lead voters to credit Democrats. Economic outcomes do not arrive on a commentator’s timetable, and congressional Republicans would have to choose an institutional limit on a Republican president over party discipline.

Still, the proposal exposes the stakes more clearly than the leadership personalities do. Trump’s tariff power depends on authority Congress can contest. If lawmakers believe his trade policy is damaging the economy, they possess tools beyond denunciation. The relevant question is whether they will use those tools when doing so requires a direct fight with the White House and a veto override.

Wilson’s case against Schumer is therefore less about temperament than sequence: win power, act early, produce a visible result. Democrats have completed only the first step. The Senate leadership vote will help determine whether the rest becomes policy or remains podcast bravado.
