item.title: MLK Jr.’s only grandchild just made family history at the polls
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Yolanda Renee King, the 18-year-old granddaughter of Martin Luther King Jr., cast her first ballot, becoming the first of his grandchildren—and his only grandchild—to vote. King told CNN the experience was deeply meaningful after years of accompanying her parents, Martin Luther King III and Arndrea Waters King, to polling places.

King said her parents taught her from childhood that voting was a way to make her voice heard. The article does not identify the election, polling location, ballot she cast, or calendar date behind its use of “today,” leaving the event’s immediate political context unspecified.

Symbolism without a power struggle

King’s vote carries historical resonance, but she holds no institutional authority in this story. She is a young voter and activist exercising an existing right. The officials who determine registration rules, polling access, district boundaries, and election administration hold the relevant power, yet none appears in AlterNet’s account.

That absence turns politics into inheritance and inspiration. The article offers a family milestone while largely avoiding the institutions that decide whether voting is accessible, burdensome, or effectively obstructed.

The missing decision-makers

No government action caused the reported event beyond the ordinary age requirement that previously made King ineligible to vote. No official is accused of blocking her ballot, and the reporting establishes no new voting policy or dispute.

That matters because a sentimental narrative cannot support claims the evidence does not. The weakness is more basic: the piece invokes “voting rights” and “systemic inequality” without naming any law, administrator, or political decision. It gestures toward systems while declining to examine one.

A legacy made safe

Martin Luther King Jr.’s legacy is presented primarily as civic encouragement: participate, speak, imagine progress. That is the least disruptive version of a tradition rooted in organized pressure against institutions that denied Black Americans political power.

Yolanda Renee King’s own advocacy—on gun violence, inequality, homelessness, climate change, and voting rights—suggests a broader politics than the article develops. AlterNet reduces that record to evidence of continuity rather than asking what she advocates, which authorities she is challenging, or what resistance those demands encounter.

What the framing conceals

The headline promises family history, and the reporting delivers it. But the framing substitutes proximity to a famous name for political analysis. King becomes a symbol of democratic continuity; the machinery governing democratic participation disappears.

There is no demonstrated scapegoating of a weaker actor here. The misdirection is softer: attention moves from institutional power to individual virtue. Voting is treated as a personal rite rather than an act conducted inside rules written and enforced by identifiable authorities.

The systemic pattern

American political coverage often honors civil-rights history most comfortably when it can convert conflict into ceremony. A first ballot is meaningful. It is not, by itself, evidence that the struggle over political equality has been resolved—or even a description of where that struggle currently stands.

The larger pattern is journalism celebrating participation while leaving power unnamed. A democracy cannot be understood through voters’ sincerity alone. The consequential questions remain who writes the rules, who administers them, who benefits from them, and whose political agency those institutions expand or constrain.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Right-wing Newsmax is already licking their wounds
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reported that Newsmax guests reacted angrily as early Tuesday vote counts showed Democrats gaining ground and threatening Republican control of the House and Senate. Former White House political director Matt Schlapp claimed Democrats had “bamboozled” voters into blaming President Donald Trump’s policies for unresolved economic problems.

Former senator Rick Santorum predicted Democrats would use congressional power to investigate or impeach Trump rather than address inflation, grocery costs or gasoline prices. The article also cited election forecaster Charlie Cook predicting a severe Republican defeat, but it did not provide final results establishing which chambers or seats had changed hands.

Power was on the ballot

The central fact was not that television personalities felt wounded. Trump held the presidency, and Republicans entered the election with congressional power that Democrats were attempting to reduce or take away. Voters—not Newsmax, Biden or some unnamed socialist force—were deciding whether that arrangement would continue.

Schlapp conceded the durability of presidential power even while lamenting possible Republican losses: Trump would remain president for two more years. His reference to Senate voting rules also exposed the real concern beneath the complaints. Losing seats could constrain the administration’s legislative leverage, oversight protection and control over federal priorities.

Losing became deception

Schlapp’s explanation stripped voters of agency. If they supported Republicans, their judgment counted; if they rejected Republicans, they had been “bamboozled.” That is not analysis of an electorate. It is a permission structure for dismissing an unfavorable result without examining why people voted that way.

The maneuver also redirected responsibility toward Biden, who was not described as holding office in the article, while Trump was the sitting president whose party controlled Congress. Whatever responsibility Biden’s prior policies may bear for economic conditions, the reporting supplied no evidence establishing Schlapp’s claim that he “caused” the problem under debate. Institutional power belongs to current officeholders, and accountability follows power.

Santorum invented the alibi early

Santorum moved immediately from prospective defeat to prospective Democratic misconduct. Before the article established final control of Congress, he predicted investigations, impeachment and neglect of household costs. He also alleged that Biden-era policy deliberately increased prices, but AlterNet provided no evidence supporting that accusation.

This is preemptive blame allocation. If Democrats won, their victory supposedly reflected Trump’s usefulness as a political target rather than voter judgment about Republican governance. If economic problems persisted, Democrats would own those too—even though Trump would still control the executive branch. The argument assigns Democrats responsibility in advance while preserving Republican power from responsibility after the fact.

AlterNet blurred forecast and fact

AlterNet correctly exposed the grievance logic in the Newsmax remarks, but its own framing outran the evidence it presented. “Devastation” and a predicted “hell of a beating” are not final election results. Early tallies and an experienced forecaster’s judgment can indicate direction; they do not establish completed outcomes.

The article also declared that analysts showed Santorum was right that Democrats could thank Trump for victories and turnout. Yet the supplied text named only Cook’s prediction and did not present turnout data or analysis proving that causal claim. Mockery is not a substitute for precision, especially when the underlying story is about powerful actors trying to replace electoral accountability with narrative warfare.

The system protects power with stories

The larger pattern is familiar: officeholders exercise power, voters register consequences, and partisan media recast those consequences as fraud, manipulation or irrationality. The defeated side then treats public judgment as illegitimate while preparing to blame its opponents for governing constraints it still retains the power to impose.

That narrative does political work. It shields leaders from internal accountability, teaches audiences that adverse elections require no self-examination and turns ordinary democratic opposition into a plot against the country. The wound Newsmax displayed was not merely disappointment. It was the discovery that holding power does not guarantee protection from its consequences.

item.title: South Carolina Senate seat flips to Democrat who defeated Darline Graham
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Democrat Annie Andrews won South Carolina’s 2026 U.S. Senate race against Republican Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Peter Hamby called the race, Decision Desk confirmed that projection, and WIS10 reported that with 80 percent of votes counted, Graham had no remaining path to victory.

Andrews, a pediatrician who had initially entered the race against Lindsey Graham before his death, prevailed despite South Carolina’s Republican lean and an apparently stronger GOP showing in the governor’s race. The split result indicates that some voters supported Republicans elsewhere on the ballot but rejected Graham.

Graham emerged from a bruising late primary against Rep. Ralph Norman with Donald Trump’s support. Her campaign then faced sustained questions about her qualifications after she acknowledged little national-security expertise, redirected a discussion of Taiwan toward transgender athletes, and incorrectly said South Carolina had 50 million residents. Republicans ultimately spent $5 million defending a seat they had not expected to be competitive.

The power behind the candidacy

Darline Graham did not reach the general election through demonstrated command of the office she sought. According to AlterNet’s account, she reached it with a famous family name and Trump’s endorsement, which consolidated MAGA support after an ugly primary.

That is the central power structure: party elites and a national political leader helped convert proximity to a deceased senator into a credible claim on his seat. Voters retained the final authority, but Republican institutions determined which candidate would carry their banner—and then committed millions to rescuing that choice.

The Senate Leadership Fund’s $5 million “insurance policy” is especially revealing. The party recognized the danger clearly enough to spend heavily, yet its response was not to reconsider how Graham had been elevated. It was to purchase protection from the consequences.

Incompetence was not the whole story

Graham’s errors mattered because senators exercise power over war, trade, diplomacy, and federal spending. Saying national security was not her area of expertise while seeking a Senate seat was not merely an awkward debate moment. It exposed a gap between the authority she wanted and the preparation she brought.

Her pivot from the South China Sea to “boys in girls’ sports” showed the function of culture-war politics when substantive knowledge fails: change the subject to a familiar grievance. The reporting establishes the pivot, not its motive. But its political effect was plain. A question about geopolitical judgment became an opportunity to invoke a Republican social wedge.

Calling the campaign a collection of “gaffes” would therefore understate the problem. The issue was not verbal polish. It was whether partisan identity, inherited recognition, and presidential patronage could substitute for competence.

The voters rejected the substitution

The apparent ticket-splitting strips away the easiest partisan explanation. If the Republican candidate for governor performed better while Andrews won the Senate contest, at least some voters distinguished between party preference and the specific candidate placed before them.

Even Norman’s son announced that he was likely to vote Democratic for the first time rather than support Graham. That does not establish why the broader electorate voted as it did, but it demonstrates that opposition crossed an unusually intimate Republican boundary.

Andrews and Norman both attacked Graham as unqualified. That convergence mattered because it denied Graham the usual shelter of polarization. The criticism could not be dismissed simply as a Democratic line when her Republican primary opponent had made the same case.

A machine defeated by its own selection

The weak framing would be to present this result as an inexplicable Democratic upset or a personal collapse caused by debate-stage embarrassment. The stronger explanation in AlterNet’s reporting is institutional: Republican power brokers enabled a vulnerable nominee, Trump helped rally the base behind her, and national Republican money tried to contain the resulting damage.

South Carolina voters then imposed a consequence the party apparatus had attempted to prevent. The broader pattern is not that political machines always fail. It is that they routinely confuse their power to manufacture a nomination with the public’s obligation to ratify it.

Dynastic access opened the door. Patronage carried Graham through the primary. Money arrived when scrutiny exposed the candidate’s limitations. None of it guaranteed consent. That is the systemic error: institutions built to select capable public officials instead protecting their own choices—until voters make the cost impossible to hide.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: 'A drunk man waving a steak knife': Leaker unfurls new Trump prediction
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Miles Taylor, a former Department of Homeland Security chief of staff and first-term Trump administration critic, predicts President Donald Trump will react more aggressively to Republican midterm losses in 2026 than he did after Democrats gained 40 House seats in 2018. The article does not establish that a “blue wave” has occurred; it presents an Election Day forecast based on unspecified predictive metrics and Taylor’s expectations.

Taylor says Trump responded to the 2018 defeat by privately raging about prospective investigations, publicly threatening a “war-like posture,” forcing out Attorney General Jeff Sessions, and overseeing the revocation of CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass. His “drunk man waving around his steak knife” remark described that 2018 press conference, not a new incident. Taylor now predicts Trump could contest close counts, pressure state officials, direct the Justice Department toward districts he calls stolen, and resist congressional investigations. Those are predictions, not reported events.

The power is presidential

The central political fact is not Trump’s temperament. It is his control of the executive branch. A president can remove senior officials, influence federal law-enforcement priorities, command public attention, and place subordinates throughout the government. Describing such a figure chiefly as “angry” or “unhinged” risks reducing institutional power to a personality disorder.

Taylor’s account of 2018 supplies the more useful evidence: Trump answered an electoral setback with an attorney general’s removal, threats toward an incoming congressional majority, and retaliation against a confrontational reporter’s access. Whatever one thinks of Taylor’s interpretation, those were exercises of presidential authority or actions taken by the White House—not merely embarrassing behavior at a press conference.

Loyalty changes the machinery

Taylor argues that two restraints from 2018 are now absent: advisers willing to refuse Trump and the incentive imposed by another presidential campaign. His first point matters most. Personnel determine whether extraordinary demands die in conversation or become government action.

If senior officials were selected primarily for loyalty, the danger Taylor describes would not come from one man becoming more furious. It would come from officials deciding that serving him requires using public institutions against electoral and congressional opponents. Taylor predicts pressure on state certification officials and Justice Department intervention in disputed districts. AlterNet provides no evidence that those steps have occurred, but the forecast identifies the relevant chain of agency: presidential demand, subordinate compliance, institutional consequence.

Prediction is not reporting

AlterNet weakens its own case by presenting a projected Democratic “blowout” with sweeping confidence while offering no named forecast, polling average, race analysis, or probability. “Most predictive metrics” is not a substitute for evidence. Neither is “blue wave” when votes and control of Congress have not been established in the supplied reporting.

That framing turns a serious account of possible executive abuse into political suspense. The article has firsthand testimony about Trump’s conduct after the 2018 election and a former official’s explicit forecast about 2026. It should distinguish those categories cleanly. Instead, it packages prediction as momentum and speculation as near-certainty.

The scapegoat script

Taylor’s predicted sequence is familiar in structure: reject an adverse result, portray ordinary counting or certification as theft, pressure weaker state actors, and enlist federal power in the accusation. The officials administering elections would then become targets for a conflict created from the top.

That is political misdirection with practical consequences. Attention shifts from the president’s refusal to accept institutional limits toward local officials forced to defend routine procedures. The supposed scandal becomes the count itself, while the actual power play—the attempt to make government validate an unsupported claim—recedes into the background.

A system built on voluntary restraint

The larger pattern is institutional dependence on officials choosing not to abuse the authority they possess. Taylor’s account suggests that advisers constrained Trump in 2018, at least intermittently. That is not a durable safeguard. It is an admission that formal power was being checked by personnel willing to risk saying no.

The decisive question is therefore not whether Trump will leave quietly, become angrier, or produce another grotesque spectacle. It is whether officeholders with concrete authority will obey improper demands, whether Congress can investigate without executive obstruction, and whether election officials can perform their legal duties without coercion. Political systems fail through decisions made by identifiable people. Temperament may generate the demand; compliant institutions deliver the consequence.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Under-the-radar Supreme Court petition could make Trump’s DOJ untouchable
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that disbarred lawyer John Eastman asked the Supreme Court to restore his California law license after disciplinary authorities found that he misled two courts while helping Donald Trump challenge the 2020 election. The court had not decided whether to hear his petition when the article was published.

Eastman argues that officials punished protected political advocacy and compares his case with retaliation against civil-rights and human-rights lawyers. UCLA legal ethics professor Scott Cummings rejects those comparisons, arguing that Eastman was enabling government power and that his petition minimizes conduct the California bar treated as professional misconduct.

Cummings warns that a ruling for Eastman could also strengthen the Trump Justice Department’s campaign against independent attorney discipline. AlterNet cites a proposed DOJ rule allowing the attorney general to seek pauses in ethics investigations and a DOJ lawsuit intended to stop the D.C. Bar from disciplining former Justice Department official Jeffrey Clark.

The power is institutional

Eastman is the petitioner, but the Supreme Court holds the immediate power. It can decline the case, leaving California’s disciplinary judgment intact, or use it to redefine how far bar authorities may go when lawyers characterize professional conduct as political advocacy.

The larger power belongs to the Justice Department. State bars can investigate individual lawyers; the attorney general directs a federal institution with prosecutors, litigation authority and rulemaking capacity. Treating these forces as evenly matched would invert the hierarchy.

Politics is not professional immunity

Eastman’s argument, as described, attempts to move the dispute away from what disciplinary authorities found he did and toward the political identity of the person punished. That shift matters. If professional scrutiny becomes presumptively partisan whenever misconduct occurs during political advocacy, lawyers serving powerful officials acquire an escape hatch unavailable in ordinary practice.

The First Amendment concern raised by scholars supporting Eastman is legitimate but narrower than the immunity his argument could produce. Retaliatory discipline by partisan state bars would be dangerous. That does not establish that bar authorities must ignore findings that a lawyer misled courts. Political context cannot erase professional obligations without turning legal ethics into a privilege granted by proximity to power.

The civil-rights comparison reverses reality

Eastman’s comparisons to persecuted human-rights lawyers and NAACP attorneys do more than exaggerate his predicament. They recast a lawyer working to preserve presidential power after an election as the equivalent of lawyers confronting abusive state power.

That is the story’s central misdirection. The relevant distinction is not conservative versus liberal advocacy. It is whether disciplinary institutions punished political belief or responded to professional conduct within their jurisdiction. According to AlterNet, the California review department found the latter: Eastman misled two courts. His petition may contest that judgment, but historical analogy cannot substitute for rebutting it.

Accountability is being recoded as weaponization

The DOJ actions described by AlterNet reveal a broader strategy: label outside scrutiny “weaponization,” then use government power to disable the scrutinizing institution. The proposed rule would permit the attorney general to seek suspension of ethics investigations into department lawyers. The lawsuit against the D.C. Bar similarly places federal power behind an attempt to block discipline of Jeffrey Clark over his reported role in advancing Trump’s false election-fraud claims.

The article identifies the alignment but could state the power relationship more bluntly. Bar complaints may indeed be abused. Yet an administration does not cure that risk by giving its own leadership leverage to interrupt investigations of its lawyers. That arrangement makes the institution under scrutiny a participant in deciding whether scrutiny may proceed.

The system behind the petition

This case is not merely about whether Eastman practices law again. It tests whether lawyers acting for political leaders remain answerable to professional bodies outside the executive branch—and whether courts will preserve that external constraint.

The recurring pattern is institutional self-protection through rhetorical inversion. Powerful officials and their lawyers portray accountability mechanisms as partisan aggression, then invoke that alleged aggression to justify weakening the mechanisms. If that logic prevails, the consequence is larger than any single disciplinary case: legal ethics remain formally universal while becoming practically negotiable for lawyers backed by federal power.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Trump's admin fires a desperate Election Day salvage shot
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that the Trump Justice Department was preparing to send roughly 20 target letters in a criminal investigation involving the campaign of Alaska Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan. Citing NBC News and unnamed sources, it says the department had already issued 120 subpoenas. A target letter identifies someone as a focus of an investigation; it does not mean that person will be charged.

The action followed a separate Justice Department lawsuit arguing that Sullivan’s presence on the ballot could confuse voters because Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan was also running. A court dismissed the administration’s attempt to block certification for lack of standing. The Alaska Supreme Court had already addressed the naming issue and prescribed how the candidates would be distinguished on the ballot.

AlterNet does not establish exactly when the target letters were sent, who received them, what suspected crimes underlie the investigation, or whether charges followed. It reports that the civil litigation continued separately and that the Justice Department filed a notice indicating an appeal, though legal commentator Chris Geidner questioned whether that notice was properly drafted.

The power sits with Justice

Dan J. Sullivan did not control federal prosecutors, subpoena authority, or the machinery that can place a criminal investigation over an election. The Justice Department did. According to the reporting, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Alaska and officials from the Civil Rights Division participated in the investigation.

That imbalance is the political core of the story. A candidate can defend himself in court and answer subpoenas. The executive branch can compel records, designate investigative targets, litigate over certification, and force everyone else to spend time and money responding. Even without charges, that power can reshape an election’s closing atmosphere.

Confusion was not the unresolved problem

The administration’s stated concern was ballot confusion between two men with similar names. But Alaska’s courts had already considered that problem and imposed rules for distinguishing them. The federal government nevertheless tried to turn the issue into grounds for blocking certification if the Republican lost.

That is not merely concern about clear ballot design. It is an attempt, as described by AlterNet, to make certification conditional on a preferred electoral outcome. The weaker actor—the candidate whose lawful ballot presence allegedly created confusion—became the focus, while the institution escalating a settled naming dispute wielded the real coercive power.

The article outruns some of its evidence

AlterNet calls the Justice Department “politicized” and presents the investigation as an Election Day salvage attempt. The sequence it reports supports serious scrutiny: extensive subpoenas, prospective target letters, certification litigation, and an election-related dispute already adjudicated by Alaska’s highest court.

But the article does not establish the letters’ precise timing or reveal the criminal evidence. Nor does it prove that every investigative step was ordered to rescue the Republican candidate. That motive is the article’s inference, not a demonstrated fact. The strongest indictment rests on documented institutional conduct: federal officials escalated an already-litigated ballot issue and sought leverage over certification.

Process can become punishment

The absence of charges does not make 120 subpoenas and approximately 20 target letters politically weightless. Investigations impose legal costs, generate damaging headlines, and allow insinuation to travel faster than adjudicated facts. When deployed around an election, prosecutorial process can create consequences before any court determines that a crime occurred.

The reported departure from the Justice Department’s traditional caution near elections matters for precisely that reason. Those norms exist because prosecutors possess powers that candidates cannot match and because an investigation’s public shadow can affect voters even when it produces no conviction—or no charge at all.

The systemic error

The larger pattern is executive power converting an electoral loss contingency into a legal controversy: if the favored candidate loses, challenge certification; if courts reject the theory, appeal; alongside that litigation, continue a broad criminal investigation carrying its own pressure and stigma.

Institutional abuse does not require polished lawyering or a successful courtroom result. It can operate through repeated escalation, forcing weaker actors to answer the government while officials present their own intervention as a response to disorder. Here, the reported disorder was two similar names. The consequential decision was the Justice Department’s choice to turn that manageable ballot issue into federal litigation and prosecutorial pressure.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Trump just woke up a force far bigger than himself
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that historian Heather Cox Richardson sees the midterm backlash surrounding Donald Trump as part of a larger revolt against concentrated wealth and government structured for a powerful minority. She argues that Trump did not create this political force but helped activate it by making exploitation under his second administration unusually visible.

Richardson pointed to Trump’s unfocused appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, private Republican fears of heavy losses, Elon Musk’s reported spending of at least $446 million on the midterms, and voters traveling long distances to cast ballots. She also noted that the Supreme Court rejected the administration’s emergency request to set aside roughly 20,000 California ballots.

But the outcome was not settled when Richardson wrote. Early voting and polling suggested a Democratic wave; only the completed count could establish whether one occurred.

Power is the point

Richardson’s argument is not fundamentally about Trump’s personality. It is about who controls government and who collects the rewards.

Presidents, congressional majorities, wealthy political patrons and the Supreme Court possess institutional power. Ordinary voters can remove elected officials, but only after navigating rules, money and administrative barriers largely shaped by people already holding power. A billionaire spending at least $446 million and citizens undertaking long journeys to vote are not equivalent forms of participation. One is concentrated influence; the other is the labor required to resist it.

Trump remains central because presidential power is real. His trade policies, the war with Iran, attacks on immigrants and governing priorities are not atmospheric disturbances. AlterNet says Richardson identified them, alongside corruption and ties to Vladimir Putin, as sources of his unpopularity. Republicans enabled that agenda through their control of governing institutions and their continued political dependence on him.

The convenient scapegoat

The unnamed Republican strategist’s reported remark—“We all know who the problem is”—captures the party’s preferred escape route. If electoral losses can be assigned to Trump alone, Republican officials can treat themselves as spectators to decisions they supported, excused or declined to stop.

That framing hides agency. Trump may dominate the party, but he does not enact an entire governing program by himself. Legislators vote. Donors finance. Operatives organize. Officials implement. Party leaders decide which conduct will carry consequences and which will be absorbed as the price of power.

Private blame after public obedience is not accountability. It is reputation management by people hoping voters will punish the figurehead while preserving the machinery around him.

Spectacle covers extraction

Trump’s reported speech offered a revealing contrast. Richardson described him spending roughly the first 16 minutes discussing the Reflecting Pool, blaming vandalism rather than poor workmanship, before turning to exaggerated claims and favored construction projects, including a golf course and a triumphal arch.

The spectacle matters because it consumes attention that might otherwise settle on material power. Arguments about a pool, monuments and presidential aesthetics are easier to stage than an accounting of whose wealth increased, whose rights narrowed and whose government was used for private advantage.

Richardson places that performance within a longer economic story beginning well before Trump. She cites tax cuts and deregulation since the Reagan era and an estimate that $50 trillion in income shifted toward the richest Americans over several decades beginning in 1975. Trump’s role, in her telling, is less architect than brazen exhibitor of an established arrangement.

History is not a guarantee

Richardson compares the present with earlier coalitions against enslaver power, robber barons and the concentration of wealth preceding the New Deal. The comparison identifies a recurring political conflict: elites accumulate economic and institutional control until a sufficiently broad coalition recognizes a common adversary.

But history does not operate like a pendulum with a preset return. Earlier reforms required organization, electoral victories and sustained use of government power. Public disgust alone produces nothing. Polls and early turnout can indicate movement without proving its scale, durability or cause.

AlterNet’s framing becomes weakest when possibility begins to sound like inevitability. Trump may have provoked opposition larger than himself, but the reporting had not yet established that this coalition would win, remain united or build the broadly responsive government Richardson anticipates.

The system survives its frontman

The larger pattern is not that one uniquely destructive politician periodically awakens the country. It is that concentrated wealth repeatedly finds political institutions willing to convert private advantage into public policy, while the officials involved insist the resulting hardship is accidental, technical or somebody else’s fault.

Trump’s conspicuous self-interest may make that structure easier to see. Removing him from the foreground would not remove the donors, lawmakers, courts, policies or incentives that sustained it.

The consequential question is therefore not whether voters reject one man. It is whether they identify the network of power behind him—and deny that network the opportunity to rebrand itself after using him.

item.title: Donald Trump is a radical hate preacher —and MAGA is his sick church
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet argues that President Donald Trump used racist and anti-Muslim attacks to mobilize supporters ahead of the midterm elections, casting him as a “hate preacher” and MAGA as a political congregation organized around personal loyalty. The essay points to his attacks on Somali Americans, Rep. Ilhan Omar, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and former President Barack Obama.

According to the essay, Trump called Omar “garbage,” questioned her rights and citizenship, labeled El-Sayed a “jihadist,” and invoked a “special metal detector” at an Iowa rally. It also says Trump answered Obama’s criticism of his White House renovations with insults and a stereotype about Black people and cleanliness.

AlterNet predicts major Republican losses and cites polls suggesting weakened support for Trump, including among white evangelical Christians. Those forecasts are not outcomes: the supplied text does not provide election results, a publication year, or enough methodological detail to evaluate every polling claim.

Power is not a pulpit metaphor

The church analogy describes Trump’s political culture, but it can obscure the more important fact: he is not merely preaching. In the account presented here, he holds the presidency, commands the executive branch, influences federal law enforcement and dominates his party.

That distinction matters. A demagogue with an audience can spread prejudice. A president who suggests sending federal forces to support a racialized “fight back” message can place state power behind that prejudice. The institutional danger lies in the combination of stigmatizing rhetoric, executive authority and Republican officials unwilling to impose limits.

The targets did not create the conflict

Somali Americans, Omar and El-Sayed do not control the presidency or the Republican Party. Yet Trump’s rhetoric makes them the objects around which political conflict is organized: immigrants become thieves, Muslim politicians become suspected extremists, and Black critics become people whose belonging or cleanliness can be questioned.

That is scapegoating, not policy analysis. It redirects attention from the officials exercising power toward minorities portrayed as alien, criminal or dangerous. The immediate political benefit is obvious even without claiming knowledge of Trump’s private motives: supporters are invited to treat vulnerable communities as the source of national disorder while the administration escapes scrutiny for its own decisions.

Republican agency cannot be baptized away

AlterNet’s fixation on Trump as preacher and MAGA voters as parishioners risks shrinking a governing coalition into a personality cult. Trump’s power depends on officials who can refuse him but instead validate, amplify or accommodate him. The essay names Vice President JD Vance and refers to congressional Republicans and governors as enablers, but gives Trump most of the analytical attention.

That imbalance matters. Party leaders possess votes, offices, budgets and procedural authority. When they repeat dehumanizing claims or decline to constrain the president, they are making political choices. “MAGA” is not a supernatural force that seized otherwise helpless institutions. Officeholders opened the doors.

Moral clarity needs evidentiary discipline

The essay is strongest when it identifies specific words, targets and offices. It is weaker when metaphor outruns proof. Calling Trump “fascist,” describing MAGA as a “sick church,” or predicting an electoral apocalypse may express the author’s judgment, but those labels do not substitute for demonstrating which powers were used, who enabled their use and what consequences followed.

The unsupported certainty is especially conspicuous in the election predictions. Polls measure opinion within defined samples and periods; they do not establish future results. A serious indictment of political conduct does not need prophecy. The documented rhetoric and the institutional authority behind it are damning enough to examine on their own terms.

The system behind the sermon

The larger pattern is rule through hierarchy: a powerful officeholder defines favored citizens as the nation and marks disfavored groups as suspect, while allied officials convert personal grievance into party messaging. The consequence is not confined to uglier campaigns. It makes citizenship conditional in political language and teaches supporters to see equal rights as privileges that leaders may revoke from designated enemies.

Trump is the central actor in AlterNet’s account, but the system is larger than one man’s appetite for adulation. It includes politicians who amplify him, institutions that accommodate him and coverage that can mistake spectacle for the machinery producing it. The sermon matters. The state power, party discipline and calculated scapegoating carrying it into public life matter more.

item.title: Election law expert makes bold prediction about the future of Trump’s big lie
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that election-law expert Rick Hasen expects Republicans around President Donald Trump to keep “dancing around” his false claim that he won the 2020 election because they do not want to offend him. Despite the headline, the article supplies no clear prediction about when or whether Trump’s “big lie” will disappear.

Republican candidates and strategists reportedly see election denial as a liability in general elections, where voters are more focused on the economy. California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton has rejected Trump’s voter-fraud claims, while Senator Lisa Murkowski criticized a Justice Department lawsuit concerning an Alaska ballot issue involving two candidates named Dan Sullivan.

The retreat is selective. According to the reporting, some Republicans are distancing themselves publicly, some are staying quiet, and advisers are urging Trump to discuss more current issues. The party has not reached a principled reckoning; it is making an electoral calculation.

Power sets the boundary

Trump holds the institutional power identified in this story: the presidency, control over the MAGA base, and enough influence within the Republican Party that candidates and consultants fear contradicting him directly. Hasen’s description of advisers avoiding offense exposes the hierarchy. Trump establishes the permissible fiction; everyone else decides how delicately to evade it.

The officials and operatives around him still have agency. They can reject election denial plainly, as Hilton reportedly has, or challenge related government action, as Murkowski has. Those who remain silent are not trapped by confusion. They are choosing political safety within a system that rewards submission to the party’s dominant figure.

A tactical retreat is not accountability

The Republicans quoted here object mainly because the message is losing usefulness. Consultant Samuel Chen argues that economic conditions will drive more voters than “election integrity.” Consultant Christopher Nicholas says 2020 is old and that newer subjects are available.

That is not a repudiation of election denial on factual or democratic grounds. It is campaign triage. The concern is that the claim distracts from issues more likely to win votes—not that rejecting legitimate outcomes corrodes public trust and licenses future attacks on election administration.

The framing softens the conduct

AlterNet describes Trump as “flirting” with election denialism and Republicans as walking a “fine line.” Those phrases turn sustained false claims and calculated avoidance into awkward social behavior. The relevant actors are not struggling to understand what happened in 2020. According to the article, they are deciding how much truth they can state without angering Trump.

The headline also oversells Hasen’s remark as a bold prediction. What the reporting actually establishes is narrower: Republicans are trying to move away from an electorally damaging message while avoiding a direct confrontation with the man who continues promoting it.

The lie remains available

A message abandoned because it polls badly has not been discredited inside the institution that amplified it. It has merely been shelved. If Republican leaders refuse to say clearly that Trump lost in 2020, they preserve the underlying permission structure: election results may be treated as legitimate when convenient and suspect when defeat requires an explanation.

That is the larger pattern. Party elites tolerate propaganda while it mobilizes supporters, then quietly change subjects when it becomes costly. Their restraint is not powerlessness. It is an exercise of agency designed to preserve access to power without accepting responsibility for how that power was built.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Frank Luntz: Trump’s GOP made 'cardinal mistake of politics'
item.description:
What happened

Frank Luntz said Republicans made the “cardinal mistake of politics” by promising voters results and failing to deliver. AlterNet reported that, during a CNN appearance on Election Day, the Republican pollster described a panel of 2024 Trump voters who planned to support Democrats in the midterms, chiefly because of broken promises and the affordability crisis.

Most panelists were voting against Republicans rather than expressing firm support for Democrats. One said the country had declined sharply over two years and that Democrats deserved another chance. Luntz also warned that political leaders might answer Republican losses with revenge instead of solutions, though the report offered no evidence that Trump or anyone else had decided to do so.

At the time of the report, polling suggested Republicans could lose the House, possibly the Senate, and key governorships. The article did not provide election results. Luntz urged Democrats, if they won, to address affordability and quality of life rather than begin with impeachment.

Power produced the backlash

These voters did not abandon the party because it lacked influence. They turned against it after Republicans held enough institutional power to be judged on results. Trump and the Republican Party made the commitments; people living with high costs assessed the delivery.

That distinction matters. “Distrust” did not simply descend upon American politics. Luntz’s panel described a recognizable chain of responsibility: officials sought power with promises, exercised power, and failed to produce the outcomes some of their own voters expected. The electorate’s response was not mysterious alienation. It was judgment.

Accountability becomes “partisanship”

Luntz’s advice to Democrats collapses two separate obligations into one convenient warning. Improving daily life and investigating official misconduct are not mutually exclusive. Calling impeachment inherently “political” evades the relevant question: whether conduct warrants constitutional scrutiny.

This framing protects powerful actors by making accountability sound like emotional retaliation. Republicans may be punished at the ballot box for governing failures, yet Democrats are instructed to treat any further examination of those failures as proof that they are equally partisan. That is not neutrality. It is an asymmetrical demand for restraint from the party that may inherit power.

The weaker actors are not the cause

The story gestures toward a public that believes neither the media, Congress, nor the Supreme Court. But generalized distrust can blur responsibility. Institutions do not lose legitimacy through some spontaneous defect in the population; their conduct, leadership, and incentives shape whether people consider them credible.

The panelists were not fickle consumers disappointed by branding. They were voters responding to material conditions and perceived broken commitments. Describing the result mainly as a crisis of belief risks shifting attention from officeholders who controlled policy to citizens who stopped trusting them.

A warning without evidence

Luntz said he feared Washington figures might use electoral losses as an excuse to “get even” or “seek revenge.” AlterNet sharpened that concern into a warning that Trump may seek revenge, but the reporting supplied no stated plan, decision, or action establishing that outcome.

The concern may be politically significant, but it remains Luntz’s forecast. A responsible analysis should not convert apprehension into fact—especially when the article’s stronger evidence concerns something more concrete: former Trump voters blamed Republicans for unmet promises and worsening affordability.

The governing bargain is breaking

The larger pattern is a political class eager to convert material failure into a story about tone. Voters name costs, quality of life, and promises that went unfulfilled; elite commentary answers with abstractions about trust, revenge, and excessive partisanship.

That maneuver narrows the consequences of governing failure. Republicans are permitted to seek and wield power, but their opponents are warned that accountability could look uncivil. Democrats, meanwhile, are offered a false choice between improving lives and examining abuses. The system’s recurring error is not simply overpromising. It is treating the exercise of power as legitimate while portraying serious consequences for those who exercised it as dangerously political.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Fox News 'caught off-guard' by Trump’s 'shocking' last-minute Hail Mary
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump used an Election Day call to Fox & Friends to announce that the United States would end $4 billion in aid to Israel after the end of the year. Trump said he had reached the agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “months ago.” Fox News hosts Bret Baier and Stuart Varney said the unsolicited announcement shocked them and questioned whether it was intended to influence midterm voters.

The report supplies no confirmation from Netanyahu, the administration, or any documentary record that such an agreement existed. It says the arrangement had not previously been discussed publicly. Baier connected the timing to campaigns where Israel funding had become an issue, including Michigan, but neither host established Trump’s reason.

AlterNet also reports severe political headwinds for Republicans: a poll put Trump’s approval at 32 percent, gave Democrats an eight-point generic-ballot lead, and found that 50 percent of independents viewed their congressional vote as a vote against Trump. Baier said inflation, negative economic sentiment, and the Iran war would weigh heavily on voters, while warning that Republicans could lose their Senate majority.

The power was in the announcement

Trump was not a bystander floating an opinion. According to the report, he was the president announcing a major reversal of American policy and attributing it to a private agreement with a foreign leader. That institutional position gave an unsupported claim immediate political force.

Fox’s hosts possessed media power, but not executive power. Their surprise is therefore secondary. The consequential act was Trump’s decision to announce the purported deal without prior public explanation, supporting evidence, or an identified policy process.

Surprise is not scrutiny

The article’s “caught off-guard” framing turns attention toward the hosts’ reaction when the more important question is whether the president’s claim was true and operationally meaningful. AlterNet does not establish either point.

Baier and Varney wondered aloud about Trump’s motive and the electoral timing. That is reasonable speculation, clearly presented as such. But surprise is not accountability. A network that provides the president a live platform cannot substitute its presenters’ astonishment for verification of a claim involving billions of dollars and a major ally.

The Hail Mary remains an inference

The electoral context makes tactical intent plausible: Trump made the announcement on Election Day, Israel funding was reportedly salient in some races, and his approval numbers were dismal. Varney explicitly asked whether Trump was trying to affect the vote.

But the reporting does not prove that motive. Calling the statement a desperate electoral maneuver goes beyond the established facts. What can be said is narrower and more damaging: Trump injected an unverified foreign-policy announcement into the final hours of voting, and Fox broadcast it before its own prominent hosts could explain why it had happened.

A referendum he claimed

Baier said Trump had encouraged voters to act as though his name were on the ballot. That matters because it assigns agency where it belongs. If Republican candidates suffered from public anger over prices, war, or the administration’s performance, weaker actors did not manufacture that liability. Trump deliberately attached himself to the election.

The polling cited by AlterNet does not predict the result or prove why any voter chose a candidate. It does show the scale of the exposure: independents were far more likely to describe their vote as opposition to Trump than support for him, while voters preferred Democrats on the cost of living by 43 percent to 32 percent.

Government by last-minute spectacle

The larger pattern is executive politics conducted as media interruption. A president announces an enormous policy change on friendly television; the network treats its own confusion as the story; motive speculation outruns verification; and voters are left to sort policy from campaign theater in real time.

That structure rewards the official who can create the disruption. The claim dominates attention whether it is implemented, abandoned, clarified, or denied later. Institutional power produces the spectacle, media power amplifies it, and the absence of evidence becomes another segment of television suspense.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Another 'Mitch McConnell situation' underway as GOP rep goes MIA
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reported that 84-year-old Republican Rep. John Carter of Texas had largely disappeared from the campaign trail, appearing for some votes in mid-September but seldom in public for months. Carter attributed his absence only to “issues at home” and said he remained capable of serving.

Former Georgetown Mayor Dale Ross told reporter Jake Lahut that he had heard Carter was experiencing serious memory loss and other possible illnesses. Those claims were not confirmed by Carter or established through medical evidence. Lahut said he decided to publish after Austin NPR affiliate KUT aired a brief interview in which Carter’s speech appeared difficult to understand.

Carter did not attend an event outside his campaign office where Democratic opponent Justin Early and supporters asked where he was. The reporting did not establish Carter’s medical condition or precisely why he had remained out of public view.

The office is not personal property

Carter holds the institutional power. He occupies a congressional seat, casts federal votes and benefits from the authority, staff and political infrastructure attached to incumbency. His opponent and constituents can ask questions, stage events and vote. They cannot compel a candid account of whether Carter remains able to perform the job.

Ross’s explanation cuts to the entitlement underneath the mystery: Carter “just likes being a congressman.” That is an observation from a former Republican official, not proof of Carter’s motives. But the surrounding structure is plain. Long tenure can turn public office into something an incumbent and his circle treat as theirs to retain until defeat, resignation or death forces the issue.

The gatekeepers made the absence possible

Carter alone did not create the information vacuum. Staff and party allies possess the access needed to clarify his schedule, explain his prolonged absence or provide credible evidence that he is actively performing his duties. According to the reporting presented here, the public received only a vague reference to problems at home and an assertion that he was well enough to serve.

That response protects the officeholder while transferring uncertainty to everyone else. Constituents are left to interpret scattered votes, an unclear phone interview and secondhand claims about his health. The people controlling access keep control; the public gets speculation.

Age is the hook, accountability is the issue

The comparison to Mitch McConnell encourages a familiar discussion about elderly politicians. Age matters when health may affect official capacity, but age alone proves nothing. The relevant question is whether an officeholder can perform public duties and whether those shielding him will provide enough evidence for voters to judge.

Reducing the story to another gerontocracy spectacle lets the party machinery escape scrutiny. The scandal is not that an 84-year-old might become ill. It is that an incumbent can become largely unavailable while the institution around him supplies no adequate public accounting.

Uncertainty serves the powerful

The weakest framing would make this a quirky disappearance story: supporters chant, an opponent brings coffee and doughnuts, and reporters hunt for an elusive congressman. That theater risks misdirecting attention toward campaign antagonists or rumor rather than toward the people with the power to answer basic questions.

Lahut was right to acknowledge suspicion about late campaign tips. Ross’s account remains hearsay, and an unclear interview is not a diagnosis. But uncertainty does not require journalistic paralysis. It requires precise reporting about what can be established: Carter was reportedly absent, his explanation was limited, and neither he nor his operation supplied a clear account resolving legitimate questions about his capacity and activity.

Incumbency thrives behind closed doors

This episode exposes a broader failure of American political institutions: they rely heavily on officeholders and their loyalists to disclose incapacity that may threaten their own control. The incentive is obvious. A candid admission can weaken an incumbent, end a career or cost a party a seat. Silence preserves every option for those already holding power.

The consequence is government by gatekeepers. Staff, allies and party officials can maintain the appearance of continuity while voters are denied the information needed to evaluate who is actually exercising authority. The systemic error is not human aging. It is a political order that treats transparency about an officeholder’s capacity as optional whenever disclosure might inconvenience the people protecting the seat.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Trump has reached his expiration date — and favorite excuse no longer works
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that Donald Trump’s familiar defense—claiming credit for favorable developments while blaming Joe Biden for economic pain—had lost much of its political force before the November 3, 2026 midterms. Although Biden had left office 21 months earlier, a Reuters review found that Trump mentioned him nearly 900 times over nine months, frequently while discussing prices and affordability.

The article says voters increasingly held the sitting president responsible. Polls cited by AlterNet placed Trump’s economic approval mostly in the low 30s, while a late-September Reuters/Ipsos poll put it at 17 percent. The same reporting linked his political decline to public dissatisfaction with tariffs, immigration policy and the conflict with Iran, though the precise economic effect of the fluctuating tariff regime remained uncertain.

Republican candidates in vulnerable states were therefore confronting an election shaped by Trump’s record, not Biden’s. The article was written before the reported election result was available, so it establishes the political conditions surrounding the vote, not its outcome.

The power belongs to the incumbent

Trump was not a commentator diagnosing somebody else’s economy. He controlled the executive branch. His administration chose to expand tariffs, intensify immigration restrictions and enter a conflict with Iran after he had campaigned on stopping wars.

That institutional power makes the Biden refrain less an explanation than an attempt to detach authority from accountability. A president can reasonably argue that inherited conditions constrain policy. But after 21 months, repeatedly invoking a predecessor cannot erase who now signs executive orders, directs foreign policy and sets the administration’s economic agenda.

The decisions have names

The tariff expansion did not arrive as an atmospheric disturbance. Trump announced a new regime through an April 2025 executive order and branded the occasion “Liberation Day.” AlterNet appropriately notes that the shifting rates, reversals and suspensions make the policy’s exact effects difficult to isolate. What is not difficult to identify is who imposed the policy and who possessed the power to alter it.

The same distinction applies to Iran. Trump had explicitly promised that he would stop wars rather than start one. Seven months of conflict did not prove every voter’s theory about fuel prices, but it exposed a direct contradiction between campaign positioning and presidential conduct. Pew’s finding that 73 percent of Americans were highly concerned about higher fuel costs shows the consequence Republicans faced: foreign policy was being judged through household budgets.

Blame is not an economic program

The article’s strongest evidence is not that every price increase can be traced neatly to one Trump policy. It cannot. Its stronger point is political: voters no longer accepted Biden as the default answer to every unfavorable condition.

That shift matters because Trump’s 2024 campaign depended on making the incumbent own economic dissatisfaction. Once restored to office, he tried to preserve the same allocation of blame while reversing its direction of accountability. The argument was structurally absurd: presidential power was supposedly decisive when conditions improved, yet irrelevant when voters disliked the results.

Republicans cannot separate themselves

Trump reportedly urged voters at battleground-state rallies to imagine that he was on the ballot. For vulnerable Republican candidates, that invitation converted congressional races into judgments on an unpopular president whose economic record they had little appetite to defend. Their reluctance to discuss tariffs was itself revealing. A governing party confident in its signature policy does not treat that policy as hazardous material.

The cited generic-ballot advantage for Democrats and the large share of voters describing their vote as opposition to Trump did not guarantee an electoral result. Polls measure opinion at a particular moment; they do not count future ballots. But they showed the governing coalition losing control of the argument on the issue that had helped return it to power.

Accountability eventually changes address

This story reveals a recurring political pattern: leaders exploit public anger at incumbents, then resist the same standard once they inherit the office. Trump’s problem was not simply that an excuse had grown old. It was that his presidency had accumulated decisions, consequences and contradictions that a predecessor’s name could no longer obscure.

Political messaging can delay responsibility, but it cannot permanently relocate power. The person occupying the presidency commands the government and receives the judgment attached to it. Trump asked voters to treat the midterms as a referendum on him. According to the evidence AlterNet assembled before the vote, many were prepared to do exactly that.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Trump chief squirms as affordability brag unravels on camera
item.description:
What happened

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed in an ABC13 interview that food costs had “dropped substantially,” then immediately corrected himself: the rate at which food costs are increasing had dropped. As AlterNet notes, ABC13 clarified the essential point—food prices were still rising, just more slowly.

Bessent acknowledged that conditions remained short of the Trump administration’s goals. He attributed some hardship to the war with Iran and the resulting energy-price spike, while pointing to lower egg prices and unemployment, claimed real-wage growth of 1 percent since Trump took office, and declining core inflation in three of the previous four months. ABC13 also reported that gasoline cost roughly a dollar more than a year earlier and interest rates were higher.

The interview aired as voters prepared for Tuesday’s midterm elections, though the report does not provide a calendar date. With affordability shaping votes in Texas and some polls giving Democrats a narrow advantage on the economy, Bessent offered the prospect of relief after hostilities ended rather than evidence that household costs had already fallen.

The correction contains the story

Prices and inflation are not interchangeable. Slower inflation means prices continue rising at a reduced pace; it does not restore what households have lost to previous increases. Bessent’s first formulation converted a deceleration into a decline, producing a more favorable claim than the facts described by ABC13 supported.

That distinction is not academic at the grocery register. Administration officials can celebrate an improving rate while families still pay more in absolute dollars. The correction exposed the distance between the metric being advertised and the condition voters actually experience.

Power owns the result

Bessent is not a detached commentator. As Treasury secretary, he speaks for an administration that holds executive power and asks voters to credit it for favorable indicators. That same administration must therefore answer for the conditions under which its economic claims are made.

The reporting does not establish that every price increase resulted from a White House decision. It does establish a political asymmetry: officials claim agency when wages, employment, or core inflation improve, then shift attention to war and energy markets when living costs remain painful. External forces may be real, but they cannot serve as an all-purpose exemption from accountability.

A promise substituted for relief

Bessent’s case depended partly on anticipated improvement: oil markets would be better supplied after hostilities, and a prospective deal with Iran had helped oil prices fall 7 percent that day. Those developments may support optimism. They do not prove durable relief for households, and the report does not say that the prospective agreement was completed.

This is the administration’s weaker political offer: endure current costs and trust that postwar conditions will eventually repair them. The official with institutional authority presented a forecast; voters were left with the bill.

The framing softens responsibility

AlterNet’s language about Bessent being “forced” into an “embarrassing correction” personalizes the episode as an on-camera stumble. The more consequential issue is not discomfort. It is the use of statistical language to make continuing price increases sound like falling costs.

Calling the moment a squirm risks turning economic messaging into theater. The institutional act was simpler and more serious: a senior official made an inaccurate boast, corrected it only within the same sentence, and continued selling partial indicators as evidence of recovery. ABC13’s clarification supplied the accountability the claim itself lacked.

The systemic error

Modern economic messaging routinely asks the public to judge power through rates of change while living with accumulated prices, debt costs, rent, health expenses, and wages. That gap is politically useful because officials can identify a favorable trend without demonstrating that ordinary people are materially better off.

The larger pattern is selective ownership. Governments present improvement as the product of leadership and hardship as the product of circumstance. Bessent’s correction briefly stripped away that arrangement: food costs had not substantially dropped. The administration had a better statistic, a future promise, and an election arriving before either became cheaper groceries.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Psychologist exposes Trump falling asleep standing up in disaster speech
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump appeared to drift off while standing during Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s remarks at a Monday event near the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Psychologist John Paul Garrison reviewed footage and said he believed Trump briefly fell asleep, appeared “barely conscious” while attempting to applaud, and displayed spasms.

The event was presented as Trump’s closing midterm message, but AlterNet says he spent at least ten minutes discussing the pool’s troubled renovation and did not mention the midterms during the first 20 minutes. The outlet also reports that viewers described him as exhausted after a month of campaign travel.

Garrison suggested the behavior could indicate disrupted wakefulness and broader decline, possibly accelerated by a stroke. Those are his interpretations of public footage, not a reported medical diagnosis. The article supplies no examination, medical records, or confirmation that Trump suffered a stroke—or even definitive proof that he was asleep.

Power does not require alertness

The institutional fact is more consequential than the body-language speculation: the person delivering this disjointed address was the president. Trump held executive authority; Burgum served in his administration; the event’s staging placed presidential power behind every wandering minute.

If a president cannot deliver a coherent closing argument without becoming consumed by a renovation project, that is politically relevant. But the relevance comes from the authority attached to the speaker, not from the spectacle of drooping eyelids. A visibly tired private citizen controls little. A president controls an administration whether or not a public appearance inspires confidence.

Diagnosis by video is not accountability

AlterNet’s headline framing promises an “exposure.” The reporting establishes something narrower: one psychologist watched footage and offered an interpretation. Garrison may have relevant expertise, but the article does not establish that he examined Trump or had access to clinical evidence.

That distinction matters because “he appeared to drift off” is an observation; claims about impaired neurological pathways, severe decline, or a possible stroke are medical inferences. Packaging inference as revelation gives sensational certainty to evidence that remains ambiguous.

The strongest criticism requires no remote diagnosis. Trump gave an address meant to close a midterm campaign and, according to AlterNet, failed to mention the election for 20 minutes. That is documented political conduct. Speculating about his nervous system can distract from what he chose—or failed—to communicate while exercising presidential power.

The spectacle displaces the decision-makers

The article turns Trump’s apparent fatigue into the central scandal, leaving the surrounding power structure largely untouched. Someone scheduled the event. Officials stood beside him. Political staff presented the appearance as a closing message. Burgum continued speaking while the president reportedly drifted in and out of attention.

Those actors had agency even if Trump was exhausted or impaired. Yet the coverage treats them as scenery. Institutions often protect themselves this way: attention settles on one leader’s physical condition while the aides and officials who normalize, stage, and sustain the performance escape scrutiny.

A presidency reduced to symptom watching

The fixation on whether Trump was technically asleep offers audiences a simple mystery with an irresistible clip. It is also a political dead end. If he was asleep, the episode raises questions the article does not answer about his capacity and the judgment of those presenting him. If he was merely exhausted, the speech was still unfocused and poorly aligned with its stated purpose.

This is the larger pattern: personality-driven coverage converts failures of governing institutions into medical theater. The president becomes a collection of symptoms; his administration becomes background furniture; responsibility dissolves into frame-by-frame conjecture. The sharper indictment is not that one psychologist saw possible decline. It is that presidential authority remained intact while everyone around it carried on as though coherence were optional.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.itunes:author: Paulo Santos

item.title: Your car is being tracked 24/7 — and not for the reasons you think
item.description:
What happened

AlterNet reports that automatic license plate readers are not merely traffic or crime-fighting tools: they feed searchable networks that can reveal where vehicles have traveled. The article does not establish that every car is continuously tracked “24/7,” but it describes systems capable of recording and sharing location data at enormous scale, sometimes beyond the awareness of the municipalities that installed them.

In the reporting period, voters in Wellfleet, Massachusetts, unanimously banned the technology, and the Selectboard enacted the policy as local law, also prohibiting tracking of boats in town waters. Local police joined activists in concluding that the readers were unnecessary for the town. Similar resistance was reported in Minneapolis, San Diego, and 14 Texas jurisdictions amid concern that federal immigration authorities had obtained plate data while pursuing the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

Flock Safety said cities control data-sharing permissions, its federal pilot program had ended, and ICE could not directly access its databases. But AlterNet cites reporting that federal agencies conducted tens of thousands of lookups or obtained information through other agencies, sometimes without local departments being actively notified about particular searches. The article says the constitutional limits remain unsettled and notes that separate bills backed by Democratic-aligned and Republican lawmakers sought to restrict the systems through federal funding penalties.

The power sits in the network

A camera bolted beside a road is not the central political fact. The database behind it is.

Municipal officials may purchase readers for stolen-car investigations or traffic enforcement, but vendors such as Flock, Axon, and Motorola operate networks that can make local observations available far beyond the locality that collected them. That architecture shifts practical control from the residents being watched—and potentially from their elected officials—to corporations and agencies equipped to search across jurisdictions.

The decisive power is therefore distributed but identifiable. Vendors build and administer the infrastructure. Local governments authorize its installation and set sharing rules. Police departments generate and query records. Federal agencies possess the reach and institutional leverage to seek access. Drivers supply only the data; they make no meaningful choice about its collection.

Consent at the bottom, access at the top

The article’s most important claim is not that officials secretly installed every camera. It is that many local officials reportedly approved systems without understanding the reach of the resulting network.

That is not informed public consent. It is procurement politics: sell a narrow function to a town, then connect the resulting data to a much broader surveillance apparatus. Flock’s position that municipalities control sharing does not resolve reports that federal authorities obtained information without local police being kept apprised of specific searches. A permission screen is a weak safeguard when access can travel through other departments, federal logs, or legal demands whose limits the article says remain unclear.

Wellfleet’s ban shows where agency still exists. The town meeting acted, the Selectboard converted that decision into law, and local police supported the restriction. Institutional helplessness was not the obstacle. Other governments made different choices—or failed to examine what they had purchased.

Public safety is the sales pitch

License plate readers can serve legitimate, concrete purposes. AlterNet notes that one helped locate the suspect in the Brown University shooting far from Providence, and that New York uses plate-reading infrastructure to administer congestion pricing. Those examples establish utility, not a blank check.

The misdirection begins when a successful search in one case is treated as justification for retaining everybody’s movements in a network available for other purposes. The relevant question is not whether a database can help solve a serious crime. Almost any sufficiently intrusive database can. The question is who may search it, under what legal standard, for how long, with whose knowledge, and with what remedy when the system is abused.

“Public safety” collapses those questions into a slogan. It asks residents to judge the most sympathetic use while officials and vendors preserve the capacity for far broader ones.

Surveillance follows political priorities

The reported backlash intensified because immigration enforcement exposed how quickly infrastructure bought for one rationale can serve another. Border and immigration authorities hold federal enforcement power; migrants and people traveling through camera networks do not. Blaming individuals for being “found” by neutral technology would invert responsibility. Governments installed the systems, companies networked the records, and agencies sought the data.

AlterNet also cites reports involving reproductive-health travel and warrantless stalking. Those accounts are not proof that every reader is used that way. They demonstrate the predictable danger of a system designed to reconstruct movement: its uses will follow the priorities—and abuses—of whoever gains access.

The article’s headline overstates its own evidence by implying universal, uninterrupted tracking and by teasing a single hidden reason. The reporting supports a more precise and more consequential conclusion: plate readers create persistent records that can be searched for purposes substantially broader than the local justification offered when the cameras were approved.

The systemic error

This is the familiar conversion of administrative convenience into political power. A town buys a tool. A vendor builds a network. Agencies discover that the network can answer questions residents never authorized them to ask. Each institution points to another part of the chain, and accountability dissolves while the data remain usable.

The bipartisan congressional proposals described by AlterNet differ in sponsorship and scope, but both recognize the same structural problem: local surveillance systems become national systems when databases cross jurisdictional lines. Without firm limits, the actor with the broadest mandate and greatest coercive power gains the advantage.

Wellfleet interrupted that process at its point of entry. Its decision matters not because one small town can dismantle a national surveillance market, but because it rejected the fiction that expansive monitoring is merely a technical upgrade. The cameras record plates. The system records power—and power rarely confines itself to the purpose printed on the purchase order.
